title: A tick is a promise
summary: Follow one reserve through a tick, then separate the world's state from the way it is drawn.
text: Fern is standing still, but her reserve has fallen from 60 to 57. Has something gone wrong, or has the world done useful work that the picture doesn't show? You'll inspect the current maintenance-only Moss build and run a standalone Rust lab. Ordinary functions and structs are enough to begin; we'll introduce Bevy later. The live movement exercise remains in NOW.md . Tell a changing world from a changing view Start by pairing Fern's reserve with the completed-tick counter, then follow the same distinction in a small Rust program. Comparing three advances with different numbers of reads will show which operation changes the state. Finally, check the installed maintenance rule separately, so you can explain both the expected 57 units and what each kind of evidence establishes. Read the reserve together with the tick In the current fixture, Fern and Flint each start with 60 reserve units and pay one unit of maintenance per executed simulation tick. After three ticks, each should have 57. Their positions can stay exactly where they were: the application has a maintenance rule, while movement is still unfinished and unscheduled. A changing reserve is already a consequence we can investigate. To see that consequence clearly, we need to control how much work the world performs. Run the following command from the repository root, then open the local Moss preview . This starts the simulation application alongside the course you're reading. scripts/with-toolchain.sh trunk serve --locked --release Pause the simulation, reset the run, and make sure it is paused before stepping. Select Fern and read both her reserve and the completed-tick counter. Press Step three times. At this checkpoint, the expected pair is tick 3 and reserve 57. Now pan or zoom while paused and read the same pair again. You have changed the view, so there may be many new pictures, but you haven't requested any more simulation work. The two numbers help diagnose a surprising result. If Fern already has less than 60 when you first inspect her, a nonzero tick counter may explain it: the run advanced before you paused. If three presses leave the counter at zero, follow the Step control before changing the maintenance arithmetic. Without the tick, “reserve 57” leaves us guessing when the measurement was taken. Keeping observation separate from advancement also protects the simulation from its viewer. If drawing a creature charged its upkeep, a faster monitor could make it run out of reserve sooner. An offscreen creature might avoid the charge altogether. Moss gives advancement its own operation so that watching more often doesn't change the outcome. Follow one request through the world Open crates/moss-sim/src/simulation.rs and look for the installed schedule. It runs maintenance before complete_tick increments the counter. That order gives SimClock.tick a specific meaning: it counts work that has completed. The public tick(&mut World) function requests this schedule once, producing the transition shown below. One requested tick, followed by any number of observations A request reaches maintenance, which deducts one unit. The completion counter then advances. The renderer reads that completed state repeatedly without changing it. Request one tick state: 0, 60 Maintenance reserve: 59 Complete tick state: 1, 59 Read for display still: 1, 59 The ordered pair is (completed ticks, reserve units). Maintenance changes reserve before the counter reports completion. Reading the completed state does not execute another tick. Notice where the first tick becomes visible. Maintenance has already reduced reserve to 59 by the time the counter says 1. A reader of that completed state can therefore interpret the two numbers together. Reading it again follows only the last box; it doesn't send another request through maintenance. The host still has to decide when to request ticks. It can use elapsed time for pacing, and the browser may draw at a variable rate or become hidden. Those are reasons to make advancement explicit, rather than to ignore time altogether. For the same executed ticks and accepted inputs, a change in presentation should leave the simulation result unchanged. Moss also avoids catching up automatically after a hidden tab. There is a useful limit to what the counter tells us. Tick 3 means the work installed in the schedule has completed three times. It can't establish that an unscheduled function ran. This explains the opening scene: maintenance can reduce Fern's reserve while the unfinished movement helper has no effect on her position. Give two viewers the same three ticks Let's make the distinction small enough to test without a browser. Imagine two sessions beginning at reserve 60. Session A advances three times and reads the state twice after each advance. Session B also advances three times, but reads it two hundred times after each one. Before looking at the Rust, predict their final reserves and identify which operation would have to be wrong for the results to differ. We'll use an ordinary State struct containing the completed tick and the reserve. The function advance receives &mut State , allowing it to change the caller's state. The inspector receives &State , allowing it to read these fields. The signatures give us a place to look before tracing every call: the assignment to reserve belongs in the function with mutable access. Hint 1: find the write Look for the assignment to reserve_units inside advance . Calling the inspector doesn't reach that assignment, regardless of how often the caller asks for a reading. Hint 2: trace completed states Begin with (0, 60), then follow (1, 59), (2, 58), and (3, 57). Observations between two advances read the same pair. They don't add another pair to the trace. Answer: both finish at 57 Each session makes three calls that change the state. The extra observations in session B leave it at the same completed tick and reserve as session A. A comparison of these runs can test that promise in the small program; we'll return to the real schedule after running it. Run the small example The complete file below contains both sessions, a program that prints one result, and three tests. Start with advance and inspect , then follow the loop in run . This deliberately small world has no movement, feeding, or death, so every change to its two fields is visible here. #[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)] struct State { completed_ticks: u64, reserve_units: u32, } fn initial_state() -> State { State { completed_ticks: 0, reserve_units: 60 } } fn advance(state: &mut State) { state.reserve_units = state.reserve_units.saturating_sub(1); state.completed_ticks = state.completed_ticks .checked_add(1).expect("tick counter overflow"); } fn inspect(state: &State) -> (u64, u32) { (state.completed_ticks, state.reserve_units) } fn run(reads_per_tick: usize) -> State { let mut state = initial_state(); for _ in 0..3 { advance(&mut state); for _ in 0..reads_per_tick { assert_eq!(inspect(&state).0, state.completed_ticks); } } state } fn main() { let state = run(200); println!("ticks={} reserve={}", state.completed_ticks, state.reserve_units); } #[cfg(test)] mod tests { use super::*; #[test] fn observations_do_not_advance_time() { let state = initial_state(); for _ in 0..120 { assert_eq!(inspect(&state), (0, 60)); } assert_eq!(state, initial_state()); } #[test] fn observation_frequency_does_not_change_outcome() { assert_eq!(run(2), run(200)); assert_eq!(inspect(&run(2)), (3, 57)); } #[test] fn empty_reserve_still_completes_a_tick() { let mut state = State { completed_ticks: 8, reserve_units: 0 }; advance(&mut state); assert_eq!(inspect(&state), (9, 0)); } } From the repository root, the course runner extracts and checks this exact reference file: python3 learning/scripts/labs.py check observe If you'd like to work directly with Rust, save the block as observe.rs in a scratch directory. Run the following commands from that directory. They select this edition's pinned compiler, build the program, and then build and run its tests: rustc +1.93.1 --edition=2024 observe.rs -o observe ./observe rustc +1.93.1 --edition=2024 --test observe.rs -o observe-tests ./observe-tests The expected output is ticks=3 reserve=57 , with three passing tests. The comparison test checks the two observation frequencies from our prediction. The repeated-read test starts before any advance and checks that inspection alone leaves the initial state intact. Together, they give us more confidence than a printed result from just one session. The last test starts with an empty reserve. Advancing still completes a tick, while reserve remains zero. That follows from two separate choices in advance : saturating_sub floors reserve at zero, and checked_add advances the counter or fails if its next value cannot be represented. A floor makes sense for this reserve model; silently freezing or wrapping the completed-tick counter would hide how much work occurred. An empty reserve also doesn't remove a creature in this example. The current Moss maintenance rule has the same floor, with death still outside that live checkpoint. Arithmetic can tell us that an account is empty; deciding what happens to its owner requires a lifecycle rule. We'll keep those questions separate as the terrarium grows. Check the rule where it is installed The two read frequencies tested the separation between observation and advancement in our small program. They don't tell us whether Moss actually installs and runs its maintenance rule. To follow the same claim into the real world, run the existing focused maintenance test from the repository root: scripts/with-toolchain.sh cargo test -p moss-sim --locked --test maintenance maintenance_spends_energy_and_stops_at_zero -- --exact Look for one passed test with that exact name. A report of zero tests means the filter selected nothing, while a compilation error means execution never reached the assertion. If you run a broader suite and encounter the unfinished movement exercise, treat that failure as its own result; it doesn't replace this maintenance check. We now have three ways to investigate Fern's reserve. Each follows a different part of the path from a requested tick to a displayed number: Evidence for each part of the path Question Useful check Can the small example be observed without advancing it? Its standalone tests compare state after different read counts. Does the installed Moss schedule charge both animals per tick? The named native integration test creates a world, executes ticks, and asserts reserves. Do the browser controls and inspector show that result? Pause, reset, and Step three times, observing tick and reserve together. A native assertion can catch incorrect reserve arithmetic even if the picture looks plausible. Checking the browser can reveal a stale label even when that arithmetic is correct. When the two disagree, you've learned where to look next instead of having to question the entire program at once. You can also inspect the installed Rust schedule inside this course through the Rust terrarium . It runs a locally compiled WebAssembly build of moss-sim . The small State example above remains useful because you can trace its access rules on one page; the terrarium lets you follow the corresponding behavior in the actual simulation crate. A tick explains the change; a reading records it Fern's stationary square now has an explanation: three maintenance ticks changed her reserve, and observing her added no further charge. The small program made that separation easy to trace. The installed test checks Moss's scheduled work, while the browser observation checks what its controls and inspector show. In each case, reading tick and reserve together lets you connect a measurement to completed work instead of guessing from the picture. There is another kind of observation we haven't built yet. Suppose the inspector saves a reading at tick 0 and keeps it while Fern advances to tick 3. Should the saved reserve become 57 too, or should it remember 60? The answer depends on what we kept: access to the original value, or an independent value of our own. Recall the access distinction A shared borrow lets a function read the original state under Rust's borrowing rules. A copied measurement can remain unchanged after the original changes. Both are useful, but a saved historical reading needs to retain what was true when it was captured. In ownership at the inspector boundary , we'll build that saved reading and use it to work out when to borrow, copy, and take ownership. The Rust Book's references and borrowing chapter develops the access rules used here. The schedule and test names match this edition's repository source. The browser results above describe what to check in your running build.

title: Who owns the next change?
summary: Predict which value changes when you move, copy, or borrow it. Make the compiler part of the experiment.
text: Suppose you pause beside Fern and write down her reserve: 60 units. You let the world run for three more ticks, then check again. Fern now has 57, while your note still says 60. Both readings are useful, provided you know which moment each describes. This is an isolated Rust exercise in ownership.rs , using the distinction between ticks and observations from the previous lesson . You'll implement capture in a scratch project; the live movement assignment in NOW.md stays where it is. Save a reading the world can leave behind You'll build an observation that keeps Fern's earlier reserve and name while the caller continues using its live values. First we'll decide what the function needs to borrow and what its result needs to own; then you'll complete the capture and examine a borrow the compiler rejects. The finished example should explain why a saved 60 and a current 57 can coexist without either being wrong. Read Fern's reserve without taking it away The inspector needs to see the reserve that belongs to the simulation. Afterward, the simulation still needs that value so it can pay Fern's upkeep on the next tick. That gives us a useful starting point for the function's signature: capture should borrow the reserve while it reads it. In Rust, the parameter reserve: &Reserve asks for that access. The & means the function receives a reference to the caller's value, so it can inspect the reserve without becoming its owner. Borrowing is enough to read the value now, but our note needs to survive what happens next. If we want it to remember 60 after Fern's reserve becomes 57, the returned observation must store a number of its own. We'll therefore borrow the live reserve at the entrance to capture , then put a copy into the observation we return. These two choices fit together: borrowing describes how we access the input, while copying describes what we keep. Our Reserve is a small struct containing one u32 . It derives Copy , which allows Rust to duplicate that value when an expression needs to provide an owned Reserve . The copy is independent of the original. Once we have saved it, a later assignment to Fern's live reserve affects only the live value, just as changing a measurement doesn't rewrite an earlier note. You can read a function's parameter types as a description of this relationship with its caller. Keep the following table nearby while working through the example; the important distinction is what the function receives and what the caller can still use afterward. How each parameter relates to the caller's value Parameter Meaning in this lab reserve: Reserve The function receives an owned value. Because Reserve implements Copy , passing it also leaves the caller's value available. reserve: &Reserve The function borrows the caller's value for reading. reserve: &mut Reserve The function borrows exclusive mutable access, allowing it to change the caller's value. name: String The function receives ownership of the string. Passing an existing variable moves that string unless the caller explicitly provides a clone. The String row shows why we need to look at the type, rather than guess from the size of a variable or whether it sits on the stack. A String owns a growable text buffer and doesn't implement Copy . Duplicating its text requires an explicit operation. We'll use that distinction to give the saved reserve a name. Keep the name with the measurement A reserve of 60 isn't much of a historical record unless we also know whose reserve it was. Our Observation will contain both the copied Reserve and an owned String . Keeping its own name means that the observation can still say “Fern” even if someone later changes the live nickname to “Fern the hare.” The whole reading should describe the moment we captured it. To read the name, capture takes a &str : a borrowed view of UTF-8 text, also called a string slice. This gives callers some flexibility. They can pass the literal "Fern" , or borrow an existing String with &nickname ; Rust can convert that reference to the string slice the function expects. In either case, the function can read the text while its existing owner keeps it. Inside the function, we'll turn that borrowed text into an owned string with name.to_owned() . This allocation is doing useful work: it gives the observation text that can outlive changes to the nickname. The reserve field takes a different route. Writing *reserve reads through the reference, and using that expression to initialize the field copies our Copy value. The asterisk is a dereference operator; it isn't a request to clone an arbitrary object. If Reserve instead owned a non-copyable buffer, Rust would reject an attempt to move it out through this shared reference. Our Observation contains that owned String and does not implement Copy , so transferring the whole observation will move it. Before filling in the function, follow one observation through its caller. We capture Fern at 60, change the live reserve to 57, and then write let saved = reading; . Predict the live reserve, the saved reserve, and the saved name at the end. In particular, consider whether giving the observation a new owner changes the values stored inside it. Hint 1: what access do the inputs allow? Both inputs are shared references. They let capture read the caller's data, but they don't let it take an owned string away from the caller or assign a new value to the caller's reserve. The returned observation therefore needs its own values. Hint 2: build the two fields Construct an Observation with name.to_owned() in its name field and *reserve in its reserve field. The first expression creates owned text; the second provides a copy of this small struct. Prediction answer The live reserve ends at 57, while the saved observation contains 60 and “Fern.” The assignment to saved moves ownership of the existing observation, including its string. It doesn't make another observation or alter the one we already captured. After that move, use saved to access it; reading is no longer available as an observation. Build the saved observation From the repository root, run the commands below to prepare and check your practice file. The destination must be a new directory, so choose another name if you've used this one before. The first check should compile successfully and then fail when capture reaches its unfinished todo! . That failure gives you the starting point for the edit. python3 learning/scripts/labs.py prepare ownership --dest work/ownership-practice python3 learning/scripts/labs.py check ownership --file work/ownership-practice/ownership.rs Replace the body of capture and run the second command again. The three tests follow the promises we've made: capturing must leave the source usable, the stored reserve must survive a later reserve change, and the saved name must survive a later nickname change. If the compiler rejects your edit before those tests run, use its diagnostic to resolve the type or syntax problem first. Complete starter file: ownership.rs #[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)] struct Reserve { units: u32 } #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq)] struct Observation { name: String, reserve: Reserve, } fn capture(name: &str, reserve: &Reserve) -> Observation { let _ = (name, reserve); todo!("save owned text and a copied reserve") } fn main() { let nickname = String::from("Fern"); let mut reserve = Reserve { units: 60 }; let reading = capture(&nickname, &reserve); reserve.units = 57; let saved = reading; println!("{}: live={} saved={}", nickname, reserve.units, saved.reserve.units); } #[cfg(test)] mod tests { use super::*; #[test] fn capture_preserves_the_source() { let name = String::from("Fern"); let reserve = Reserve { units: 60 }; let reading = capture(&name, &reserve); assert_eq!(name, "Fern"); assert_eq!(reserve.units, 60); assert_eq!(reading.name, "Fern"); assert_eq!(reading.reserve.units, 60); } #[test] fn captured_reserve_is_independent() { let mut reserve = Reserve { units: 60 }; let reading = capture("Fern", &reserve); reserve.units = 57; assert_eq!(reserve.units, 57); assert_eq!(reading.reserve.units, 60); } #[test] fn captured_text_is_independent() { let mut name = String::from("Fern"); let reading = capture(&name, &Reserve { units: 60 }); name.push_str(" the hare"); assert_eq!(name, "Fern the hare"); assert_eq!(reading.name, "Fern"); } } Complete worked answer: ownership.rs #[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)] struct Reserve { units: u32 } #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq)] struct Observation { name: String, reserve: Reserve, } fn capture(name: &str, reserve: &Reserve) -> Observation { Observation { name: name.to_owned(), reserve: *reserve } } fn main() { let nickname = String::from("Fern"); let mut reserve = Reserve { units: 60 }; let reading = capture(&nickname, &reserve); reserve.units = 57; let saved = reading; println!("{}: live={} saved={}", nickname, reserve.units, saved.reserve.units); } #[cfg(test)] mod tests { use super::*; #[test] fn capture_preserves_the_source() { let name = String::from("Fern"); let reserve = Reserve { units: 60 }; let reading = capture(&name, &reserve); assert_eq!(name, "Fern"); assert_eq!(reserve.units, 60); assert_eq!(reading.name, "Fern"); assert_eq!(reading.reserve.units, 60); } #[test] fn captured_reserve_is_independent() { let mut reserve = Reserve { units: 60 }; let reading = capture("Fern", &reserve); reserve.units = 57; assert_eq!(reserve.units, 57); assert_eq!(reading.reserve.units, 60); } #[test] fn captured_text_is_independent() { let mut name = String::from("Fern"); let reading = capture(&name, &Reserve { units: 60 }); name.push_str(" the hare"); assert_eq!(name, "Fern the hare"); assert_eq!(reading.name, "Fern"); } } In the answer, the only persistent data created by capture is the observation it returns. Its inputs are borrowed for the duration of the call, so the caller can carry on using the nickname and reserve afterward. Running the program prints Fern: live=57 saved=60 , making the difference between the live value and the saved measurement visible. Check the printed reference or use rustc directly The command python3 learning/scripts/labs.py check ownership checks the course's printed answer. Keep using --file to check your own edit. If you'd like to run the file without the course runner, use the commands below from the directory containing ownership.rs . They run the example and its three tests with the pinned compiler. rustc +1.93.1 --edition=2024 ownership.rs -o ownership ./ownership rustc +1.93.1 --edition=2024 --test ownership.rs -o ownership-tests ./ownership-tests Why can the caller change Fern afterward? The saved reading works, but we should also be able to explain why Rust permits the caller's next change. We have borrowed Fern's reserve and then changed it in the same caller. That may seem at odds with the idea of a shared reference: if somebody is reading the reserve, shouldn't Rust prevent us from changing it? The missing detail is when that access is still needed. Our capture function returns owned data, so nothing in its result continues to borrow the input. Once the call finishes, that shared borrow has done its job, and the caller can mutate the live reserve. Now keep a reference to the live value instead of making a saved observation. The following fragment intentionally fails to compile; consider it separately from your working file. Pay attention to the order of the assignment and the final print. let mut reserve = Reserve { units: 60 }; let borrowed = &reserve; reserve.units = 57; println!("{}", borrowed.units); The print still needs borrowed , so the shared borrow remains in use across the attempted assignment. Rust rejects that mutation because we would be changing the value while the shared reference is still needed. Moving the print before the assignment gives the borrow an earlier last use and allows the later change. Keeping an independent copy would solve a different problem: it would let us print the earlier value after changing the live one, which is exactly what our observation does. The word mut has a specific part in this story. Declaring let mut reserve allows us to assign to that local value; lending &mut reserve would let a function change it through an exclusive reference. Our inspector asks only for &Reserve , because reading is all it needs. What if the variable holding the reference is mutable? A mutable binding that holds a shared reference lets you assign a different reference to that binding. It still holds a shared reference, so it doesn't gain permission to mutate the referred-to reserve. This gives us a more useful response to an ownership error than cloning everything until the compiler accepts it. Decide what needs to remain usable and what needs to be remembered. Here, a short borrow provides access, a copy preserves the measurement, and an owned string preserves its name. Each operation has a reason in the design. An old reading can be the right reading We can now explain the two numbers that opened the lesson. Fern has 57 because the world has continued to change; the saved observation has 60 because it owns the measurement taken earlier. The remaining responsibility belongs to the interface: it must tell the reader that 60 is historical. If it labels that value “current reserve,” correct ownership won't rescue the misleading display. A fuller journal would attach a tick and run identity to each observation, then decide how many old observations to keep. Before leaving the example, trace the data once more and identify where duplication actually occurs: when we pass &reserve , when we store *reserve , or when we move reading into saved . Being able to distinguish these operations will help when an ECS query lends you access to a much larger world. Recall answer Passing &reserve gives borrowed access. Storing *reserve copies our Copy struct, producing an independent measurement. Moving the observation into saved transfers ownership of the existing data, without allocating another string. The text was duplicated earlier, when to_owned() created the observation's name. The exercise checks those ownership decisions in a small function. In the next lesson , we'll use the same reasoning to describe an ECS system's access: which entities it can read, and which components it is allowed to change. For another explanation of moves and borrows, follow the Rust Book's ownership chapter into its borrowing chapter . The Copy documentation and String reference are useful when you want to check a particular type's behavior. Keep our inspector's question in mind as you read: what must the caller still be able to use after this function returns?

title: Ask the world a typed question
summary: Use a query signature to say which entities matter and which data the system may change.
text: Suppose you add an animal to the world, run maintenance, and find that nothing happened to it. The subtraction may be perfectly correct: the animal might never have entered the loop. Before changing the calculation, we need to find out whether the system could reach that animal at all. This isolated lab uses Bevy ECS 0.18.1, matching the repository. It builds on borrowed and copied values from the ownership lesson . We'll inspect Moss's existing maintenance system afterward; the live movement assignment stays in NOW.md . Explain which entities a system can change A query states which entities a system can visit and what access it receives to their components. We'll read those two promises in a maintenance signature, predict the results for four deliberately different entities, and check the prediction in a small Bevy world. Comparing its writer with a more inclusive audit will let you distinguish a missing component from a zero value before you investigate the installed Moss system. Decide which entities maintenance can use A list of identical animal structs would give every animal the same fields. An ECS world lets different entities carry different combinations of data. An entity supplies an identity; its components might hold a species, reserve, or name. Systems request access to the components they need and operate on the entities that satisfy that request. That flexibility makes “the animal exists” insufficient for our maintenance rule. To choose a cost, we need its species. To charge the cost, we need mutable access to its reserve. We also want a creature marker, because some other entity could have species and reserve data for a display experiment without belonging to the simulated population. The query can express all three requirements. Here are the parameters from the lab's maintenance function. Read the query as a description of both membership and access: rates: Res<Rates>, mut creatures: Query<(&Species, &mut Reserve), With<Creature>>, The tuple asks for Species and Reserve together on each matching entity. The species reference is shared because the rule only reads it; the reserve reference is mutable because the rule changes it. With<Creature> adds a membership requirement without returning the marker's value. An entity must have all three components to appear in the loop. The other parameter, Res<Rates> , borrows a resource from the world. Resources hold shared world-level data, while components belong to entities. Our Rates resource contains one table of species costs. The system reads the table on each execution, so changing it affects later charges without rewriting every stored reserve when the new rates are inserted. Try the query against an awkward fixture We'll start Fern and Flint at 60 units and give them all the required components. To check the boundaries, we'll also create “Incomplete,” a creature with no reserve, and “Display sample,” an entity with species and reserve but no creature marker. These last two make mistakes visible that a world full of ordinary creatures would conceal. Before running the program, use the query signature to decide which rows reach its body. Then apply a Hare rate of one unit and a Fox rate of two units over three executions. The table gives the expected result for comparison: Membership and reserve after three maintenance executions Entity and components Expected result Fern: Creature, Hare, Reserve(60), Name Included; reserve becomes 57. Flint: Creature, Fox, Reserve(60), Name Included; reserve becomes 54. Incomplete: Creature, Hare, Name Excluded; no Reserve exists to change. Display sample: Hare, Reserve(60), Name Excluded; its reserve remains 60. “Incomplete” is different from a creature with Reserve(0) . Zero is a value that the system can read and leave at the floor. A missing component means there is no reserve for this required query to return. We need that distinction to explain an unchanged entity without inventing a number for it. Hint 1: check every required component Start with entities carrying Species , keep those that also carry Reserve , then apply the Creature filter. A familiar name doesn't compensate for a missing component. Hint 2: apply the rate after membership The shared rates resource supplies the numbers used inside the loop. It doesn't select entities. Only after an entity matches does its species determine which configured cost the body reads. Answer: Fern and Flint pay Fern pays three units and Flint pays six. “Incomplete” never enters the mutation loop, while “Display sample” is excluded by the marker filter. Both exclusions matter: a test with only Fern and Flint could pass even if that filter were missing. Follow the access into the loop The body of maintenance uses two mutable bindings that are worth distinguishing before reading the full file. mut creatures lets the loop request mutable access through the query. Each returned reserve is a Bevy mutable component wrapper; mut reserve lets the assignment operate through that wrapper. The value being changed still belongs to the entity in the world. The species borrow stays shared throughout. A match chooses the Hare or Fox rate and the reserve assignment applies it. The name plays no part in that decision, so renaming Fern wouldn't change her cost. You can see most of this separation in the signature before reading the arithmetic: the system asks to change reserve, read species, and restrict its work to creatures. We'll run that system with the single-threaded executor to keep the execution setup simple. There is only one system here, so we haven't yet had to decide which of two rules goes first. Adding more systems will require explicit dependencies when their order matters; one thread alone doesn't state that policy. Moss's maintenance-then-completion chain is an example of an order chosen by the application. The 0.18.1 executor documentation describes the execution modes separately from those scheduling choices. Run the world you just traced The following is a complete isolated src/main.rs . Its declarations use #[derive(Component)] and #[derive(Resource)] to supply the traits Bevy needs for entity data and world resources. Start with maintenance , then find the four entities in fixture . In main , three calls to schedule.run execute maintenance three times. This lab has no simulation clock; the installed Moss schedule additionally records tick completion. For now, use audit as supplied reporting code. It will help us see “Incomplete” even though maintenance can't act on it. After the run, we'll look at the small change in its query that makes this possible. The later collections lesson will return to the iterator and sorting operations used to assemble its output. use bevy_ecs::{prelude::*, schedule::ExecutorKind}; #[derive(Component)] struct Creature; #[derive(Component)] struct Name(&'static str); #[derive(Component, Clone, Copy)] enum Species { Hare, Fox } #[derive(Component, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)] struct Reserve(u32); #[derive(Resource)] struct Rates { hare: u32, fox: u32 } fn maintenance( rates: Res<Rates>, mut creatures: Query<(&Species, &mut Reserve), With<Creature>>, ) { for (species, mut reserve) in &mut creatures { let cost = match *species { Species::Hare => rates.hare, Species::Fox => rates.fox, }; reserve.0 = reserve.0.saturating_sub(cost); } } fn fixture() -> (World, Schedule, Entity) { let mut world = World::new(); world.insert_resource(Rates { hare: 1, fox: 2 }); world.spawn((Creature, Name("Fern"), Species::Hare, Reserve(60))); world.spawn((Creature, Name("Flint"), Species::Fox, Reserve(60))); world.spawn((Creature, Name("Incomplete"), Species::Hare)); let display = world.spawn((Name("Display sample"), Species::Hare, Reserve(60))).id(); let mut schedule = Schedule::default(); schedule.set_executor_kind(ExecutorKind::SingleThreaded); schedule.add_systems(maintenance); (world, schedule, display) } fn audit(world: &mut World) -> Vec<(&'static str, Option<u32>)> { let mut query = world.query_filtered::<(&Name, Option<&Reserve>), With<Creature>>(); let mut rows: Vec<_> = query.iter(world) .map(|(name, reserve)| (name.0, reserve.map(|value| value.0))) .collect(); rows.sort_by_key(|row| row.0); rows } fn main() { let (mut world, mut schedule, _) = fixture(); for _ in 0..3 { schedule.run(&mut world); } for (name, reserve) in audit(&mut world) { println!("{name}: {reserve:?}"); } } #[cfg(test)] mod tests { use super::*; #[test] fn required_components_and_marker_define_membership() { let (mut world, mut schedule, display) = fixture(); for _ in 0..3 { schedule.run(&mut world); } assert_eq!(audit(&mut world), vec![ ("Fern", Some(57)), ("Flint", Some(54)), ("Incomplete", None), ]); assert_eq!(world.get::<Reserve>(display), Some(&Reserve(60))); } #[test] fn optional_read_exposes_missing_data() { let (mut world, _, _) = fixture(); let required_count = world.query_filtered::<&Reserve, With<Creature>>() .iter(&world).count(); assert_eq!(required_count, 2); let rows = audit(&mut world); assert_eq!(rows.len(), 3); assert_eq!(rows.iter().filter(|(_, reserve)| reserve.is_none()).count(), 1); } #[test] fn next_execution_reads_the_current_resource() { let (mut world, mut schedule, _) = fixture(); world.resource_mut::<Rates>().hare = 4; schedule.run(&mut world); assert_eq!(audit(&mut world), vec![ ("Fern", Some(56)), ("Flint", Some(58)), ("Incomplete", None), ]); } } To check this exact reference from the repository root, run python3 learning/scripts/labs.py check queries . For a manual Cargo run, create a scratch directory with the file above at src/main.rs and this Cargo.toml . The empty workspace section keeps a copy nested inside the Moss checkout independent of the parent workspace. [package] name = "moss-query-lab" version = "0.1.0" edition = "2024" publish = false [workspace] [dependencies] bevy_ecs = { version = "=0.18.1", default-features = false, features = ["std"] } Run the following commands from that scratch directory. Generating the lockfile resolves dependencies for your manual copy; keep it for later runs so they use the same resolved versions. This example's build output stays in its own target directory. cargo +1.93.1 generate-lockfile CARGO_TARGET_DIR=target cargo +1.93.1 test --locked CARGO_TARGET_DIR=target cargo +1.93.1 run --locked Expect three passing tests and the following three output lines. The audit sorts its rows explicitly, so their printed order doesn't depend on how the ECS visits entities. Fern: Some(57) Flint: Some(54) Incomplete: None If compilation says a type isn't a component or resource, compare its declaration with its use in the query. The Component and Resource derives provide the required trait implementations; naming a struct Creature or Rates doesn't do that by itself. If dependencies fail to resolve, the program hasn't reached the query yet. Resolve that build problem before interpreting any missing output as a membership result. Explain the extra row in the audit The maintenance results tell us what happened to the included creatures. To explain a creature the writer left out, we need a report that can include one without a reserve. That's why the audit also contains “Incomplete,” and why its signature differs from the writer's. The audit asks for (&Name, Option<&Reserve>) with With<Creature> . Name and the creature marker are still required. Reserve is now optional: a matching entity gives us Some(reference) when it has that component and None when it doesn't. This is why the third row can be reported without assigning it a reserve of zero. Option describes two alternatives, carrying a value only in Some . The audit's map copies the numeric field when a reference is present and preserves None otherwise. Its returned vector owns the numbers and holds references to static name literals; it doesn't keep borrows of the world's components. We can continue working with the world after collecting the reading. The two queries serve different purposes. Maintenance needs a reserve to perform its operation, while the audit needs to describe creatures whose reserves may be missing. Making maintenance's reserve optional would force its body to decide what to do without one. That may suit some systems, but it isn't necessary to make this report useful. There is still a boundary to the audit: a creature without Name wouldn't appear either. It reports this missing-reserve case, rather than validating every possible malformed entity. When consulting Bevy's versioned Query reference , keep asking which terms change membership and which change the data returned. That question connects its type signatures to the rows you actually see. Use the same questions in the installed system Open crates/moss-sim/src/lessons.rs for a read-only comparison. The existing spend_energy signature asks for shared species rules, shared species, mutable energy, and creatures only. Inside its body, the resource method returns an optional applicable rate. There are therefore two decisions to follow: whether the entity matches the query, and whether the configured species rule applies to it. The installed-world test below gives Hare and Fox different costs, just as our lab did. Run it from the repository root to check the real schedule: scripts/with-toolchain.sh cargo test -p moss-sim --locked --test maintenance maintenance_uses_species_rates_and_stops_at_zero -- --exact Expect one passing test. Unequal rates make a universal one-unit subtraction fail, whereas equal rates could hide that mistake. As in the opening lesson, the native result checks state in the simulation; observing the browser inspector is the next step if you want to establish how that state is displayed. Return once more to the display sample. If you remove only With<Creature> from the maintenance query in your scratch copy, predict its new reserve and decide whether “Incomplete” will start paying too. Prediction answer The display sample now has both required data components, so it pays the Hare rate. “Incomplete” still lacks Reserve and remains excluded. The display assertion should fail after this change, demonstrating that the test checks a category boundary as well as arithmetic. Explain the row before changing the arithmetic The unchanged animal from our opening now gives you several specific places to investigate. Check whether it matches, whether its rule applies, and whether the schedule runs the system. Once you've established those, the subtraction inside the loop becomes a much smaller question. The writer's required reserve and the audit's optional reserve also explain why a creature can be visible in a report without being eligible for maintenance. Next we'll examine that smaller arithmetic question closely. In a forecast with explicit units and bounds , a six-unit request can produce only a four-unit payment. Keeping both amounts will let the report explain a shortage without inventing expenditure.

title: Give the number a unit
summary: Separate a requested cost, an actual payment, and the reserve left. Let types and boundary tests keep the distinction visible.
text: Fern has four reserve units left. A forecast says that the next three ticks will cost six. If reserve stops at zero, how much will she actually pay? A useful report needs to keep all three facts together: six requested, four paid, and zero remaining. This is an isolated forecast built from copied inputs. You'll implement one function in units.rs ; it won't change a live reserve or add a rule to Moss. The illustrative rate belongs to this calculation, and the active movement exercise remains in NOW.md . Make a forecast that accounts for every unit You'll turn a starting reserve, a duration, and a rate into a report of requested cost, actual payment, and remaining reserve. We'll give the inputs distinct types, choose a separate response for each arithmetic limit, and test the boundaries of the completed function. The four-unit example should return six requested, four paid, and zero remaining; a request too large to represent should produce no forecast at all. Account for the missing two units In the query lesson , different species rates gave us different reserves after three executions. Here we'll examine the arithmetic for a rate of two units per tick. Three ticks multiplied by two units per tick requests six reserve units. If we start with 60, there is enough to pay all six and finish at 54. Starting with four changes the payment, but it doesn't change the requested cost. Under a rule that floors reserve at zero, only four units can be removed. Calling that a six-unit payment would invent expenditure; reporting only “zero remaining” would lose the explanation of the shortage. Our forecast therefore needs separate fields for the requested charge, actual payment, and remaining reserve. Before choosing Rust operations, put a few cases beside one another. The zero-duration case helps check that we're measuring simulated time rather than the number of times someone asks for a forecast: Three forecasts under the same maintenance rule Inputs Requested, actually paid, remaining 60 units; 3 ticks; 2 units per tick 6 units requested; 6 paid; 54 remaining. 4 units; 3 ticks; 2 units per tick 6 units requested; 4 paid; 0 remaining. 4 units; 0 ticks; 2 units per tick 0 units requested; 0 paid; 4 remaining. All three rows assume a constant rate, no replenishment, and a nonnegative reserve. Those assumptions are part of the forecast. If Fern eats during the interval or her upkeep changes, this calculation no longer predicts the whole outcome. A reader needs to know what a report includes before deciding whether its answer explains the world. Help the caller keep quantities apart The inputs contain three numbers with different jobs: a reserve, a duration, and a rate. If all three parameters were plain u32 , Rust would accept them in the wrong positions. Good names help when reading the function, but distinct types can also catch the mistake where the function is called. We'll use three tuple structs: Units(u32) , Ticks(u32) , and UnitsPerTick(u32) . Each stores one integer, yet each is a different type. Their unnamed field is accessed as .0 . Inside forecast , we'll read those fields to do the arithmetic, then wrap each result in the type that describes its unit. This is enough structure for the calculation we need. We aren't defining multiplication for every possible unit combination. Instead, one function states the dimensional relationship: ticks multiplied by units per tick produces units. Keeping that decision in one place makes it easier to inspect than several call sites each assembling the same formula. All three wrappers derive Copy because they contain small integer values that we want to duplicate freely. Passing them by value leaves the caller's inputs available. This also makes the forecast's relationship to the world clear: it receives copies and returns an owned report. It has no mutable reference through which it could deduct anything from Fern's live reserve. Once you've read the complete signature below, compare its correct call with forecast(Units(60), UnitsPerTick(3), Ticks(2)) . The two final arguments have the wrong types, even though both contain integers. That intentional compiler experiment should be corrected by putting a Ticks value in the duration position and a UnitsPerTick value in the rate position. The Rust Book's tuple-struct section explains why these wrappers remain distinct. Decide what each arithmetic limit means The input types help us keep quantities apart; we still have to decide what happens when arithmetic reaches a limit. We'll compare two limits because they need different outcomes. For a reserve smaller than the requested charge, the remainder should stop at zero. Rust's saturating_sub expresses that rule. After calculating the bounded remainder, we can recover the payment as starting reserve minus remaining reserve. That subtraction is safe because the remainder cannot exceed the starting amount. There is another limit that needs a different response. Our requested total is stored in a u32 , whose largest value is 4,294,967,295. If ticks multiplied by rate exceeds that value, no exact total fits in the report. Saturating the product would print a plausible number that is smaller than the real request. Wrapping would make the discrepancy even harder to recognize. We'll therefore use checked_mul for the requested total. It returns Some(total) when the product fits and None when it doesn't. Our function will return None in the latter case too, telling the caller that it couldn't produce the promised exact forecast. The explicit match in the answer keeps both paths visible. These methods aren't interchangeable choices about how cautious to be. The zero floor is an intentional rule for reserve; an unrepresentable product prevents us from completing the calculation accurately. The references for checked multiplication and saturating subtraction define the operations. Our reporting contract explains why we use each one here. A successful report may legitimately contain zeros. With zero ticks, for example, requested and paid are both zero while reserve stays unchanged. Returning an all-zero report on overflow would confuse that successful calculation with a failure to calculate. The next lesson will develop this distinction between a value being zero and a value being unavailable. Build the forecast Before editing, follow the four-unit example through the two operations: first calculate the requested amount, then calculate what can actually be paid. Compare it with a request for u32::MAX ticks at two units per tick. The extreme input is useful because it forces the overflow policy to become observable. Hint 1: preserve the exact request Multiply ticks by the rate with checked_mul . A successful product becomes the requested field. An unsuccessful product should return None before constructing a report. Hint 2: derive payment from the remainder Subtract the request from the starting reserve with saturation. The actual payment is the start minus that bounded remainder, so it can never exceed the amount available. Prediction answer Four starting units, three ticks, and a rate of two produce requested 6, paid 4, remaining 0. The maximum tick count multiplied by two can't fit in the requested field, so that forecast returns None . Run these commands from the repository root to prepare a new practice directory and check its starter. Choose another destination if this directory already contains earlier work. python3 learning/scripts/labs.py prepare units --dest work/units-practice python3 learning/scripts/labs.py check units --file work/units-practice/units.rs The first check should compile and then reach the intentional todo! inside forecast . Replace that function body and run the check again. The declarations and tests are already supplied, leaving you to translate the reporting contract into arithmetic. Complete starter file: units.rs #[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)] struct Units(u32); #[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)] struct Ticks(u32); #[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)] struct UnitsPerTick(u32); #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq)] struct Forecast { requested: Units, paid: Units, remaining: Units, } fn forecast(start: Units, ticks: Ticks, rate: UnitsPerTick) -> Option<Forecast> { let _ = (start, ticks, rate); todo!("report the bounded forecast, rejecting an overflowing request") } fn main() { let report = forecast(Units(4), Ticks(3), UnitsPerTick(2)) .expect("the example's product fits in u32"); println!("requested={} paid={} remaining={}", report.requested.0, report.paid.0, report.remaining.0); } #[cfg(test)] mod tests { use super::*; #[test] fn duration_and_rate_both_affect_the_request() { assert_eq!(forecast(Units(60), Ticks(3), UnitsPerTick(2)), Some(Forecast { requested: Units(6), paid: Units(6), remaining: Units(54), })); } #[test] fn actual_payment_cannot_exceed_available_units() { assert_eq!(forecast(Units(4), Ticks(3), UnitsPerTick(2)), Some(Forecast { requested: Units(6), paid: Units(4), remaining: Units(0), })); } #[test] fn zero_duration_and_zero_rate_keep_the_starting_amount() { for (ticks, rate) in [(Ticks(0), UnitsPerTick(u32::MAX)), (Ticks(u32::MAX), UnitsPerTick(0))] { assert_eq!(forecast(Units(4), ticks, rate), Some(Forecast { requested: Units(0), paid: Units(0), remaining: Units(4), })); } } #[test] fn unrepresentable_request_is_rejected() { assert_eq!(forecast(Units(4), Ticks(u32::MAX), UnitsPerTick(2)), None); } #[test] fn exact_numeric_limit_is_still_a_valid_request() { assert_eq!(forecast(Units(u32::MAX), Ticks(u32::MAX), UnitsPerTick(1)), Some(Forecast { requested: Units(u32::MAX), paid: Units(u32::MAX), remaining: Units(0), })); } } Complete worked answer: units.rs #[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)] struct Units(u32); #[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)] struct Ticks(u32); #[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)] struct UnitsPerTick(u32); #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq)] struct Forecast { requested: Units, paid: Units, remaining: Units, } fn forecast(start: Units, ticks: Ticks, rate: UnitsPerTick) -> Option<Forecast> { let requested = match ticks.0.checked_mul(rate.0) { Some(units) => units, None => return None, }; let remaining = start.0.saturating_sub(requested); Some(Forecast { requested: Units(requested), paid: Units(start.0 - remaining), remaining: Units(remaining), }) } fn main() { let report = forecast(Units(4), Ticks(3), UnitsPerTick(2)) .expect("the example's product fits in u32"); println!("requested={} paid={} remaining={}", report.requested.0, report.paid.0, report.remaining.0); } #[cfg(test)] mod tests { use super::*; #[test] fn duration_and_rate_both_affect_the_request() { assert_eq!(forecast(Units(60), Ticks(3), UnitsPerTick(2)), Some(Forecast { requested: Units(6), paid: Units(6), remaining: Units(54), })); } #[test] fn actual_payment_cannot_exceed_available_units() { assert_eq!(forecast(Units(4), Ticks(3), UnitsPerTick(2)), Some(Forecast { requested: Units(6), paid: Units(4), remaining: Units(0), })); } #[test] fn zero_duration_and_zero_rate_keep_the_starting_amount() { for (ticks, rate) in [(Ticks(0), UnitsPerTick(u32::MAX)), (Ticks(u32::MAX), UnitsPerTick(0))] { assert_eq!(forecast(Units(4), ticks, rate), Some(Forecast { requested: Units(0), paid: Units(0), remaining: Units(4), })); } } #[test] fn unrepresentable_request_is_rejected() { assert_eq!(forecast(Units(4), Ticks(u32::MAX), UnitsPerTick(2)), None); } #[test] fn exact_numeric_limit_is_still_a_valid_request() { assert_eq!(forecast(Units(u32::MAX), Ticks(u32::MAX), UnitsPerTick(1)), Some(Forecast { requested: Units(u32::MAX), paid: Units(u32::MAX), remaining: Units(0), })); } } After the edit, expect five named tests to pass. If compilation stops before they run, compare the argument wrappers and return type with the signature first. You can check the printed reference separately with python3 learning/scripts/labs.py check units , or use Rust 1.93.1 directly from the directory containing your saved file: rustc +1.93.1 --edition=2024 --test units.rs -o units-tests ./units-tests rustc +1.93.1 --edition=2024 units.rs -o units ./units The expected program output is requested=6 paid=4 remaining=0 . The expect in main asserts that this fixed demonstration has a representable product. The helper itself still returns None for an arbitrary input whose product doesn't fit; a caller accepting such input needs to handle that case. Use the failures to locate a mistaken assumption Each test challenges a different part of our account. If the ordinary three-tick case fails, look for a rate used as though it were already a total. If the shortage case reports six paid, check whether the payment was copied directly from the request. The zero-duration and zero-rate assertions catch an accidental minimum charge that the model never specified. The two numerical-limit tests are especially useful together. One rejects a product beyond the range; the other accepts the exact maximum. A guard that simply rejects “very large” values could satisfy the first while breaking the second. Testing both sides gives the boundary a precise meaning that we can reuse when validating dimensions and other bounded inputs. Passing these tests establishes the forecast under its stated assumptions. Moss's installed maintenance system doesn't call this helper, so the tests don't establish a new connection to the live schedule. If we later put the report in a chart, we would also need to check which ticks the chart requests and whether its labels describe projected or observed expenditure. Keep the requested and paid amounts distinct Return to Fern's four units. The report can now explain the two-unit shortfall without creating negative reserve or recording a payment she couldn't make. Yet calling the function has left her live reserve alone: the inputs were copies, and the returned account describes what would happen under our assumptions. Recall: why isn't an unavailable forecast an empty forecast? An empty forecast would still claim that the calculation succeeded and produced its fields. None says the exact requested amount couldn't be represented. Substituting zeros would erase that distinction and give the inspector a result it had no basis to display. That care with missing evidence will matter beyond arithmetic. In the next lesson , we'll ask whether an absent target identity, an empty patch, and a patch missing from a reading should produce the same inspector message.

title: Missing is a different state
summary: Describe an absent choice, an unresolved identity, and a present zero without turning them into the same result.
text: The inspector says “no food,” but Fern's situation is still unclear. Perhaps she hasn't selected a patch. Perhaps her selected patch is empty. Or perhaps its reading is missing. Those situations need different explanations before anyone decides what Fern should do next. You'll implement an isolated observer in options.rs , resolving a selected ID against supplied readings. The current Moss fixture authors its movement target; this exercise doesn't add target selection or feeding, and the live assignment remains in NOW.md . Give each missing fact its own meaning The observer we'll build must preserve three different answers: no target was selected, the selected patch has a reading, or that reading could not be found. We'll model those answers as enum variants, resolve an optional identity against borrowed readings, and return an owned description. By testing an empty patch alongside a missing one, you'll be able to explain why zero is sometimes the right result and sometimes an invented answer. Ask what is absent We've already encountered None in two places. In the forecast , it meant that the function couldn't represent the exact requested amount. In the audit query , it meant that a matched entity had no reserve component. The same Rust spelling answered different questions. To interpret an optional value, we need to know what was being requested. For Fern's target, the first question is whether an identity has been selected at all. We'll express that with Option<SimId> . A value of Some(SimId(3)) carries the selected identity, while None says no identity was supplied. Having a selected ID still doesn't tell us what a patch contains, or even whether the supplied readings include that patch. Resolving the identity therefore takes a second step: search the snapshot for a patch reading whose ID matches. If we find it, we can report its biomass, including a legitimate zero. If we don't, we can report that the selected ID is missing from this snapshot. Keeping the two steps separate lets an empty patch remain distinguishable from a missing reading. We should be careful about what that failed search proves. A snapshot could be partial, stale, or from a different run; the lab doesn't supply enough information to distinguish those explanations. “Missing from this reading” is supported by the lookup. “Destroyed” would require evidence that we haven't collected. Keep each answer with the data it needs Our returned TargetView will have three alternatives. Unchosen needs no further data. Present needs both the selected ID and observed biomass. Missing needs the unresolved ID so the inspector can say which reference it couldn't find. A Rust enum lets each alternative carry exactly those fields. Compare that with a struct containing separate has_target and found flags, plus an ID and biomass. Such a struct could say “no target” and “found” at the same time, leaving every consumer to work out which fields to trust. With the enum, a value is one variant at a time. Unchosen doesn't need a dummy ID, and Present can't omit its biomass field. The following cases will become the core of our tests. Notice that the first two can both look like “no food” in a vague display, even though they describe different evidence: Three facts the inspector should preserve Input evidence Inspector result No selected ID, even if patches are available Unchosen : there is no selected identity to resolve. Selected ID 3; its reading has biomass zero Present { id: SimId(3), biomass_units: 0 } : the reading exists and reports an empty amount. Selected ID 99; no matching reading Missing { id: SimId(99) } : the selected identity remains unresolved. The type removes contradictory combinations of these fields, but it can't establish the quality of the input snapshot by itself. Duplicate IDs, for example, would still make a lookup ambiguous. For this lab, we assume unique IDs in one coherent snapshot. Later history work will make run identity and coverage explicit. The Rust Book's enum chapter develops data-bearing variants and introduces Option . Our design gives you a concrete reason to use them: facts that belong together in one situation can stay together without forcing unrelated situations to carry unused fields. Resolve one alternative at a time We'll implement view_target with two matches, following the two questions above. The first examines the optional selected ID. In the Some(id) branch, the pattern binds the contained identity to id . In the None branch, there is no identity to look up, so the helper can return TargetView::Unchosen immediately. After that early return, the function has a definite ID and can search for its reading. Matching this search result gives a borrowed patch in Some(patch) , or no matching row in None . The successful branch copies the ID and biomass into Present . The unsuccessful branch keeps the selected ID in Missing . Neither match needs a default biomass. That's how the implementation preserves the difference we wanted at the beginning. Searching for a matching ID with positive biomass would lose it: an empty patch would disappear from the result even though its reading was present. The lookup asks about identity; a future feeding rule will ask whether the patch can supply a meal. Exhaustiveness makes match useful as this design grows. If we later add an alternative for an unavailable snapshot, a consumer that explicitly covers every existing variant must account for the new one. A catch-all can be appropriate when remaining cases truly share behavior, but using it merely to silence the compiler could hide a decision the new state needs. The official match chapter explains these rules. You may also recognize if let , which is convenient when only one alternative matters, such as displaying a badge for Present . Here the helper owes a status for every case. Keeping both matches visible makes it easier to check that each path preserves the evidence it received. Build the observer Before editing, try two calls on paper. First, supply no selected ID and a snapshot containing a patch with 80 units. Then select a patch whose recorded biomass is zero. The observer should describe each input as it stands. Choosing a rich patch in the first case or hiding the empty patch in the second would introduce behavior that the caller didn't request. Hint 1: begin with the selected identity For None , return TargetView::Unchosen . For Some(id) , keep that exact identity for the lookup instead of selecting the first available row. Hint 2: search by ID alone Compare each reading's ID with the selected ID. Zero biomass doesn't disqualify a reading from describing the selected patch. Prediction answer The rich patch doesn't change an unchosen target, so the first call returns Unchosen . The second returns Present with biomass zero. We have described the evidence without selecting food or claiming that a meal can succeed. From the repository root, prepare a new practice directory and run the starter's check. Use another destination if you already have work at this path. python3 learning/scripts/labs.py prepare options --dest work/options-practice python3 learning/scripts/labs.py check options --file work/options-practice/options.rs The starter compiles but reaches an intentional todo! in view_target . Replace that body, then repeat the check. Its inputs and return type already describe the contract, so the edit is about following the alternatives without losing their meaning. Complete starter file: options.rs #[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)] struct SimId(u64); #[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)] struct PatchReading { id: SimId, biomass_units: u32, } #[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)] enum TargetView { Unchosen, Present { id: SimId, biomass_units: u32 }, Missing { id: SimId }, } fn view_target(target: Option<SimId>, patches: &[PatchReading]) -> TargetView { let _ = (target, patches); todo!("distinguish unchosen, present, and missing targets") } fn main() { let patches = [ PatchReading { id: SimId(1), biomass_units: 80 }, PatchReading { id: SimId(3), biomass_units: 0 }, ]; println!("{:?}", view_target(Some(SimId(3)), &patches)); println!("{:?}", view_target(Some(SimId(99)), &patches)); } #[cfg(test)] mod tests { use super::*; #[test] fn no_selected_id_does_not_choose_an_available_patch() { let patches = [PatchReading { id: SimId(3), biomass_units: 80 }]; assert_eq!(view_target(None, &patches), TargetView::Unchosen); } #[test] fn selected_id_is_matched_instead_of_taking_the_first_row() { let patches = [ PatchReading { id: SimId(1), biomass_units: 80 }, PatchReading { id: SimId(3), biomass_units: 7 }, ]; assert_eq!(view_target(Some(SimId(3)), &patches), TargetView::Present { id: SimId(3), biomass_units: 7 }); } #[test] fn present_zero_is_not_missing() { let patches = [PatchReading { id: SimId(3), biomass_units: 0 }]; assert_eq!(view_target(Some(SimId(3)), &patches), TargetView::Present { id: SimId(3), biomass_units: 0 }); } #[test] fn missing_target_retains_the_selected_identity() { let patches = [PatchReading { id: SimId(3), biomass_units: 80 }]; assert_eq!(view_target(Some(SimId(99)), &patches), TargetView::Missing { id: SimId(99) }); assert_eq!(view_target(Some(SimId(99)), &[]), TargetView::Missing { id: SimId(99) }); } } Complete worked answer: options.rs #[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)] struct SimId(u64); #[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)] struct PatchReading { id: SimId, biomass_units: u32, } #[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)] enum TargetView { Unchosen, Present { id: SimId, biomass_units: u32 }, Missing { id: SimId }, } fn view_target(target: Option<SimId>, patches: &[PatchReading]) -> TargetView { let id = match target { Some(id) => id, None => return TargetView::Unchosen, }; match patches.iter().find(|patch| patch.id == id) { Some(patch) => TargetView::Present { id, biomass_units: patch.biomass_units, }, None => TargetView::Missing { id }, } } fn main() { let patches = [ PatchReading { id: SimId(1), biomass_units: 80 }, PatchReading { id: SimId(3), biomass_units: 0 }, ]; println!("{:?}", view_target(Some(SimId(3)), &patches)); println!("{:?}", view_target(Some(SimId(99)), &patches)); } #[cfg(test)] mod tests { use super::*; #[test] fn no_selected_id_does_not_choose_an_available_patch() { let patches = [PatchReading { id: SimId(3), biomass_units: 80 }]; assert_eq!(view_target(None, &patches), TargetView::Unchosen); } #[test] fn selected_id_is_matched_instead_of_taking_the_first_row() { let patches = [ PatchReading { id: SimId(1), biomass_units: 80 }, PatchReading { id: SimId(3), biomass_units: 7 }, ]; assert_eq!(view_target(Some(SimId(3)), &patches), TargetView::Present { id: SimId(3), biomass_units: 7 }); } #[test] fn present_zero_is_not_missing() { let patches = [PatchReading { id: SimId(3), biomass_units: 0 }]; assert_eq!(view_target(Some(SimId(3)), &patches), TargetView::Present { id: SimId(3), biomass_units: 0 }); } #[test] fn missing_target_retains_the_selected_identity() { let patches = [PatchReading { id: SimId(3), biomass_units: 80 }]; assert_eq!(view_target(Some(SimId(99)), &patches), TargetView::Missing { id: SimId(99) }); assert_eq!(view_target(Some(SimId(99)), &[]), TargetView::Missing { id: SimId(99) }); } } Expect four named tests to pass after the edit. The unchosen case catches a helper that silently selects an available patch, while the empty-patch case catches a lookup that mistakes zero for absence. You can check the printed answer with python3 learning/scripts/labs.py check options , or run these commands from the directory containing your saved file: rustc +1.93.1 --edition=2024 --test options.rs -o options-tests ./options-tests rustc +1.93.1 --edition=2024 options.rs -o options ./options The expected test result is four passed tests, and the program should print these two lines: Present { id: SimId(3), biomass_units: 0 } Missing { id: SimId(99) } The first line describes an existing reading with an empty amount. The second carries the ID the search couldn't resolve. If your output collapses those cases, follow the function back to the point where information was replaced with a default. Keep the result after the search finishes Our status preserves the distinction between a missing reading and an observed empty patch. To keep that status after the input snapshot changes, we also need to follow what it owns. The helper borrows its readings through &[PatchReading] , a slice. A caller can lend a sequence without handing over its array or vector. Calling iter() visits shared references, and find stops at the first one whose ID satisfies the comparison in the closure. Finding a borrowed reading doesn't require us to return that borrow. The status needs only its ID and numeric biomass, both of which we copy. After view_target returns, the caller can replace or discard the input snapshot while keeping the status. This is the same ownership pattern as our saved reserve: borrow while observing, then own the values needed for the record. The first-match behavior explains our uniqueness assumption. With two readings for the same ID, whichever appeared first would determine the result. One test puts a nonmatching row first to catch a helper that skips the ID comparison, but none of these tests validates all IDs for uniqueness. Construction of a real snapshot needs to preserve that separate invariant. Let the inspector say what it knows A shortcut such as unwrap_or(0) is useful when zero is the specified fallback. It would be misleading here because an observed zero and a failed lookup mean different things to the reader. The Option reference offers many ways to transform or default an optional value; the operation we choose should follow the question we're answering. Compare this helper's Option<SimId> with the audit query's Option<&Reserve> . One carries a selected identity; the other carries borrowed access to a component on a matched entity. Seeing Some in either case tells us what is present at that boundary. It doesn't establish that some other entity is still eligible for an action. Recall the two lookups The optional component answers whether reserve exists on a matched entity. The optional ID answers whether a target identity was supplied. Resolving that identity requires another lookup, which this lab performs only within its supplied snapshot. Live action-time validity, complete history, and successful feeding require further evidence. Our inspector can now replace “no food” with an explanation: no target was selected, the selected patch was observed empty, or its reading couldn't be found. In recoverable errors and validated configuration , we'll give an unsuccessful operation a reason too, so its caller can decide how to respond.

title: A rejected request has a reason
summary: Carry a form input through parsing and domain validation. Return a useful error instead of a misleading default.
text: Suppose an inspector form asks for a report beginning at tick 12 and covering three ticks. We can turn that into a window containing 12, 13, and 14. Now change the count to zero. The text still parses as a number, but the request no longer satisfies the report's rules. You'll implement a constructor in the isolated results.rs lab, then compare it with Moss's existing configuration code. The 4,096-tick limit is an illustrative reporting policy. This exercise doesn't add a live form or change the movement task in NOW.md . Turn a request into a value callers can trust You'll build a constructor that either produces a valid reading window or explains why it cannot. We'll separate parsing from the report's policy, follow errors through the supplied parsing function, and test both accepted and rejected endpoints. That gives a request for ticks 12 through 14 a dependable representation, while keeping a zero count or an overflowing endpoint from becoming a misleading report. Follow a request from text to meaning A form begins with strings, so our first question is whether each input can be read as the integer type we've chosen. “Three” can't be parsed as a u64 ; “3” can. But parsing only gives us a representable number. It doesn't know what our report considers a useful count, which is why “0” gets through this first step. We'll give the report an explicit policy: a requested window must contain at least one tick and at most 4,096. Its stored endpoints will be an inclusive start and an exclusive end. Starting at 12 with a count of 3 therefore produces an end of 15, describing ticks 12, 13, and 14. This convention makes the count equal to end minus start and lets adjacent windows meet without sharing a tick. The field name end_tick_exclusive keeps that convention visible in code. It also belongs in the explanation a reader sees. Two unlabeled endpoints would leave us wondering whether 15 was included, and a correct calculation wouldn't prevent the resulting off-by-one misunderstanding. There's one more numerical constraint: the exclusive end must fit in u64 . Even a valid count of one can overflow if the start is already the maximum. We'll check the count first and the addition second, giving each failure its own explanation. A value that passes these checks means “this is a well-formed requested window.” It doesn't establish that its ticks have happened or that observations were retained for all of them. When we build history, we'll compare the request with available coverage. Keeping those questions separate continues the previous lesson's distinction between a valid identity and an available reading. Give the caller enough information to respond The target lesson used Option when asking whether a selected ID was present. For a rejected form request, the caller also needs a reason. Result<ReadingWindow, WindowError> describes the two outcomes: Ok(window) carries the accepted value, and Err(reason) carries an explanation of failure. We'll make WindowError an enum, using the same data-bearing alternatives we used for target status. An invalid-integer error identifies the field. A count-range error keeps the rejected count. An end-overflow error keeps the start and count that couldn't be combined. The caller can match the variant and decide what to show beside the input. How four requests move through validation Request Outcome Start “12”, count “3” An accepted window containing 12, 13, and 14. Start “12”, count “three” The tick-count field can't be parsed as the required integer. Start “12”, count “0” Parsing succeeds, then the count-range check rejects zero. Start at the maximum u64 , count 1 The count is valid, but its exclusive endpoint can't be represented. The integer error deliberately groups malformed text, negative values, and text larger than the unsigned type can hold. That is enough detail for this lab to identify the field that needs attention. It doesn't retain the original text or the parser's full diagnostic. A form could keep the entered text separately; an import tool might preserve the underlying error as well. Result can carry whichever error type the caller needs. The Rust Book's recoverable-error chapter explains how these unsuccessful outcomes travel as values. That fits a form naturally: invalid input is something to report so the user can revise it, rather than a reason to pretend a report was successfully created. Make accepted windows dependable We want the same rules to apply whether numbers come from a form, a file, or a test. We'll put them in ReadingWindow::new , a constructor that accepts numeric inputs. It validates the count, checks the endpoint addition, and constructs the window only when both succeed. A failed check returns an error without supplying a partially validated value. This gives the later getters a useful fact to rely on. In a window produced by the constructor, the end is greater than the start and their difference is between 1 and 4,096. The tick_count getter can therefore subtract them directly. It doesn't need to repeat the count and overflow checks whenever someone asks how many ticks were requested. The fields are private, but Rust's privacy boundary needs a precise reading here. Code outside the owning module and its descendants can't directly access private fields. In this single-file lab, code in the defining module or a descendant module still could construct them itself. Using the constructor is therefore a local convention here; the next lesson will use modules to make the intended path enforceable for callers across that boundary. Keeping fields unchanged through the getter interface preserves the relationship established at construction. Direct construction inside the allowed module still carries responsibility for that relationship. “Private” doesn't mean that one particular method is the only code capable of touching a field. We also need to decide what rejection means. Clamping a request for 4,097 ticks to 4,096 would silently change what the caller asked for. This constructor rejects the unsupported count instead. An interface could offer a suggested correction afterward, but the accepted value should describe a request the caller actually agreed to make. Read the validation pipeline The constructor gives us one place to enforce the policy for numeric inputs; the form still begins with text. The supplied parse_window function connects those text inputs to the constructor. It parses the start, then the count, and finally calls ReadingWindow::new . Keeping that final call matters: successfully parsing two integers mustn't bypass the report's range policy. After each parse, map_err converts the parser's error into our field-specific WindowError . The following question mark either yields the successful integer for continued work or returns the error from parse_window . It saves us an explicit match for propagation. It doesn't log a message, retry, or decide which correction the user should make. Inside the constructor, checked_add presents a slightly different shape: it returns an Option , because its failed result carries no reason of its own. We know what failure means at this point, so ok_or turns None into EndOverflow with the relevant inputs. A question mark then propagates that error in the same way as the parsing failures.
