The Option conversion reference and Result error-mapping reference describe these transformations. In this example, they let several operations speak the same error language. The final constructor call already returns the right Result , so parse_window returns it directly. Write the constructor's checks Try the accepted and rejected edges before implementing them. Starting at 12, counts of 1 and 4,096 should succeed, while 4,097 should fail. For the endpoint, compare a count of one starting at u64::MAX - 1 with the same count starting at u64::MAX . Only the first can represent its exclusive end. Hint 1: include both supported count endpoints Check the inclusive range from 1 through MAX_WINDOW_TICKS . Outside it, return CountOutOfRange carrying the rejected count. Hint 2: construct only after successful addition Use checked_add for the endpoint. Convert its missing result into EndOverflow and return that error before constructing the window. Prediction answer Counts 1 and 4,096 are accepted, while 4,097 is rejected. Maximum minus one plus one reaches the exact representable endpoint and succeeds. Maximum plus one doesn't fit. Accepting the exact boundary matters just as much as rejecting the value beyond it. From the repository root, prepare a new practice directory and run the first check. Choose a different destination if this path already holds your work. python3 learning/scripts/labs.py prepare results --dest work/results-practice python3 learning/scripts/labs.py check results --file work/results-practice/results.rs The initial failure comes from the constructor's intentional todo! . Replace only the body of ReadingWindow::new and repeat the check. Parsing and tests are supplied so you can concentrate on when construction is allowed. Complete starter file: results.rs const MAX_WINDOW_TICKS: u64 = 4096; #[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)] struct ReadingWindow { start_tick: u64, end_tick_exclusive: u64, } #[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)] enum WindowError { InvalidInteger { field: &'static str }, CountOutOfRange { tick_count: u64 }, EndOverflow { start_tick: u64, tick_count: u64 }, } impl ReadingWindow { fn new(start_tick: u64, tick_count: u64) -> Result<Self, WindowError> { let _ = (start_tick, tick_count); todo!("validate the count, check the end, then construct the window") } fn start_tick(self) -> u64 { self.start_tick } fn end_tick_exclusive(self) -> u64 { self.end_tick_exclusive } fn tick_count(self) -> u64 { self.end_tick_exclusive - self.start_tick } } fn parse_window(start: &str, count: &str) -> Result<ReadingWindow, WindowError> { let start_tick = start.parse::<u64>() .map_err(|_| WindowError::InvalidInteger { field: "start tick" })?; let tick_count = count.parse::<u64>() .map_err(|_| WindowError::InvalidInteger { field: "tick count" })?; ReadingWindow::new(start_tick, tick_count) } fn main() { let window = parse_window("12", "3").expect("the example window is valid"); println!("ticks {}..{} ({} ticks)", window.start_tick(), window.end_tick_exclusive(), window.tick_count()); match parse_window("12", "0") { Ok(_) => println!("accepted"), Err(error) => println!("rejected: {error:?}"), } } #[cfg(test)] mod tests { use super::*; #[test] fn both_supported_count_boundaries_are_accepted() { for count in [1, MAX_WINDOW_TICKS] { let window = ReadingWindow::new(12, count).unwrap(); assert_eq!(window.start_tick(), 12); assert_eq!(window.end_tick_exclusive(), 12 + count); assert_eq!(window.tick_count(), count); } } #[test] fn zero_and_oversized_counts_are_rejected_not_clamped() { for count in [0, MAX_WINDOW_TICKS + 1] { assert_eq!(ReadingWindow::new(12, count), Err(WindowError::CountOutOfRange { tick_count: count })); } } #[test] fn exact_end_limit_is_valid_but_overflow_is_not() { let window = ReadingWindow::new(u64::MAX - 1, 1).unwrap(); assert_eq!(window.end_tick_exclusive(), u64::MAX); assert_eq!(ReadingWindow::new(u64::MAX, 1), Err(WindowError::EndOverflow { start_tick: u64::MAX, tick_count: 1 })); } #[test] fn parse_errors_identify_the_field_that_failed() { assert_eq!(parse_window("fern", "3"), Err(WindowError::InvalidInteger { field: "start tick" })); for text in ["three", "-1", "18446744073709551616"] { assert_eq!(parse_window("12", text), Err(WindowError::InvalidInteger { field: "tick count" })); } } #[test] fn parsed_integers_still_pass_through_domain_validation() { assert_eq!(parse_window("12", "0"), Err(WindowError::CountOutOfRange { tick_count: 0 })); assert_eq!(parse_window("12", "4097"), Err(WindowError::CountOutOfRange { tick_count: 4097 })); assert_eq!(parse_window("12", "3").unwrap().end_tick_exclusive(), 15); } } Complete worked answer: results.rs const MAX_WINDOW_TICKS: u64 = 4096; #[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)] struct ReadingWindow { start_tick: u64, end_tick_exclusive: u64, } #[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)] enum WindowError { InvalidInteger { field: &'static str }, CountOutOfRange { tick_count: u64 }, EndOverflow { start_tick: u64, tick_count: u64 }, } impl ReadingWindow { fn new(start_tick: u64, tick_count: u64) -> Result<Self, WindowError> { if !(1..=MAX_WINDOW_TICKS).contains(&tick_count) { return Err(WindowError::CountOutOfRange { tick_count }); } let end_tick_exclusive = start_tick.checked_add(tick_count) .ok_or(WindowError::EndOverflow { start_tick, tick_count })?; Ok(Self { start_tick, end_tick_exclusive }) } fn start_tick(self) -> u64 { self.start_tick } fn end_tick_exclusive(self) -> u64 { self.end_tick_exclusive } fn tick_count(self) -> u64 { self.end_tick_exclusive - self.start_tick } } fn parse_window(start: &str, count: &str) -> Result<ReadingWindow, WindowError> { let start_tick = start.parse::<u64>() .map_err(|_| WindowError::InvalidInteger { field: "start tick" })?; let tick_count = count.parse::<u64>() .map_err(|_| WindowError::InvalidInteger { field: "tick count" })?; ReadingWindow::new(start_tick, tick_count) } fn main() { let window = parse_window("12", "3").expect("the example window is valid"); println!("ticks {}..{} ({} ticks)", window.start_tick(), window.end_tick_exclusive(), window.tick_count()); match parse_window("12", "0") { Ok(_) => println!("accepted"), Err(error) => println!("rejected: {error:?}"), } } #[cfg(test)] mod tests { use super::*; #[test] fn both_supported_count_boundaries_are_accepted() { for count in [1, MAX_WINDOW_TICKS] { let window = ReadingWindow::new(12, count).unwrap(); assert_eq!(window.start_tick(), 12); assert_eq!(window.end_tick_exclusive(), 12 + count); assert_eq!(window.tick_count(), count); } } #[test] fn zero_and_oversized_counts_are_rejected_not_clamped() { for count in [0, MAX_WINDOW_TICKS + 1] { assert_eq!(ReadingWindow::new(12, count), Err(WindowError::CountOutOfRange { tick_count: count })); } } #[test] fn exact_end_limit_is_valid_but_overflow_is_not() { let window = ReadingWindow::new(u64::MAX - 1, 1).unwrap(); assert_eq!(window.end_tick_exclusive(), u64::MAX); assert_eq!(ReadingWindow::new(u64::MAX, 1), Err(WindowError::EndOverflow { start_tick: u64::MAX, tick_count: 1 })); } #[test] fn parse_errors_identify_the_field_that_failed() { assert_eq!(parse_window("fern", "3"), Err(WindowError::InvalidInteger { field: "start tick" })); for text in ["three", "-1", "18446744073709551616"] { assert_eq!(parse_window("12", text), Err(WindowError::InvalidInteger { field: "tick count" })); } } #[test] fn parsed_integers_still_pass_through_domain_validation() { assert_eq!(parse_window("12", "0"), Err(WindowError::CountOutOfRange { tick_count: 0 })); assert_eq!(parse_window("12", "4097"), Err(WindowError::CountOutOfRange { tick_count: 4097 })); assert_eq!(parse_window("12", "3").unwrap().end_tick_exclusive(), 15); } } Expect five passing tests. A failure at 4,096 often points to an exclusive upper bound; a failure at the maximum start points to unchecked addition. The parsing tests also make sure representable but unsupported counts still go through the constructor. You can check the printed reference separately with python3 learning/scripts/labs.py check results , or use these commands from your saved file's directory: rustc +1.93.1 --edition=2024 --test results.rs -o results-tests ./results-tests rustc +1.93.1 --edition=2024 results.rs -o results ./results The expected result is five passed tests and this program output: ticks 12..15 (3 ticks) rejected: CountOutOfRange { tick_count: 0 } The rejected line prints the error's debug representation so you can see its variant and payload. A form would translate that value into wording appropriate for its reader. The fixed valid example uses expect to assert our authored input; the other path demonstrates matching the result and reporting a rejected request. Find the same boundary in Moss For a read-only comparison, open crates/moss-sim/src/config.rs . Its WorldConfig::new accepts world dimensions from 8 through 256 cells and returns a configuration error with the rejected dimensions otherwise. Getters expose the accepted values. The domain is different, but the reasoning is familiar: validate once at construction, then let code using the value rely on that boundary. Run the following focused native test from the repository root to check the existing constructor. Expect one passed library test. scripts/with-toolchain.sh cargo test -p moss-sim --locked --lib config::tests::configuration_rejects_dimensions_outside_the_supported_range -- --exact This command doesn't resize a running world or exercise a browser form. It checks the actual dimension constructor, just as our isolated tests check the window calculation. Following an entered value through a real form would add another question: did the interface send the intended input and display the resulting acceptance or error? Carry the accepted value forward The request for zero ticks now has a useful outcome. Parsing recognizes the number, the constructor rejects its meaning for this report, and the caller receives the count-range reason. For a valid request, the caller instead receives a window whose getters can rely on the checks already performed. Recall why the getter can subtract directly The constructor establishes an end greater than the start, with a supported difference. Keeping those fields unchanged preserves the relationship. Parsing alone wouldn't establish it, and code that directly constructs fields inside the owning module must still uphold it. We have one remaining design task: make this construction path the one other parts of the program actually use. Put the boundary in the code follows the same contract into modules and visibility, where the layout of the program can help preserve the promises we've just tested.

title: Put the boundary in the code
summary: Give callers an honest public interface while keeping construction rules close to the values they protect.
text: The inspector prints “Fern: 60 units.” You want to move the reserve implementation into another file without changing that report or every caller that asks for it. Rust's modules let you separate the implementation from the names a caller uses, but the file move is only part of the work: we also need to decide which details the inspector may depend on. Isolated Rust lab and read-only source navigation. This lesson continues validated construction with Result . You'll complete a reporting function in a separate practice file containing two inline modules, then trace an existing public type through Moss. The live modules, biological rules, dependencies, and assignment remain unchanged. Protect the measurement while exposing the report We'll trace a public name through Moss, then recreate that boundary with a measurement module and an inspector in one practice file. Your reporting function will borrow through the public interface and return text it owns. A deliberate privacy error will help locate the boundary: the finished report should distinguish a measured zero from an unknown reserve without gaining access that could bypass construction rules. Follow the public name into the project Start with a caller's view of the real project. Open crates/moss-sim/src/lib.rs and find pub use energy::{Energy, MovementRules, SpeciesEnergyRules}; , then find mod energy; . The second declaration makes the implementation module part of the crate. The first offers selected names from that module at the crate root, so a caller can write moss_sim::Energy without including the implementation module's name in its path. That gives us a public route we can keep stable when the implementation moves. Follow the declaration into crates/moss-sim/src/energy.rs to see who implements the type. Then open crates/moss-web/src/browser/snapshot.rs and find the browser consumer's import. You don't need to understand the whole energy module yet. Trace the name from public entry point to implementation and back to a caller; that route shows where an internal change could stop without spreading into presentation code. Before moving any files, it helps to distinguish the three levels you've just crossed. A package is described by a Cargo.toml and can contain compilation units called crates, such as a library and a binary. Modules organize items inside a crate. Moss's workspace contains simulation and browser packages, while this lab needs only one binary crate with two inline modules. Splitting that binary's code into modules doesn't require another manifest or another application process. The separation between Moss's packages serves a larger purpose than navigation. The simulation owns authoritative state and uses ECS without requiring a renderer; the browser depends on that simulation and presents what it reports. A native test can therefore exercise the simulation library without opening a window. Moving a file inside one crate leaves that dependency direction alone, which is why source organization and application architecture are different decisions. Give two responsibilities one public reading We'll make the same boundary small enough to inspect in one file. A measurement module owns a validated Energy value, and an inspector module turns an optional borrowed measurement into owned text. The caller sees the re-exported Energy and report names. To produce Fern's line, the inspector only needs the public units() accessor; it doesn't need access to the representation that construction protects. For this lab, an energy value may contain zero through 100 units. That gives the constructor a boundary we can test: Energy::new(101) returns an error, while zero and 100 are valid. You already established that distinction in the preceding lesson. Putting the type in a module should protect the same distinction, so a caller can't bypass validation by writing an arbitrary number into a field. The inspector also has to describe a measurement that wasn't collected. Its input is Option<&Energy> , so it can receive either a shared reference to a valid measurement or no measurement at all. A reference to a zero reserve should produce “0 units”; the absent case should produce “unknown reserve.” The inspector can make that presentation choice without knowing why collection failed. Follow the ownership through the call: the caller first constructs a valid reserve, then lets the inspector borrow it through the public interface. The inspector returns a string that owns the finished description. Once the call ends, the caller can change or discard the nickname without affecting the already prepared text. The module boundary changes how the function finds the type, but it doesn't change those borrowing and ownership relationships. Complete the reporting function Now use that interface from inspector::report . Prepare the starter in a new directory and replace only that function's body; the preparation command refuses to overwrite an earlier attempt. Its initial todo! deliberately fails at runtime, so the first check should reach the unfinished function. If it fails on syntax or dependencies instead, resolve that setup problem before using the output to reason about reporting. python3 learning/scripts/labs.py prepare modules --dest work/modules-practice python3 learning/scripts/labs.py check modules --file work/modules-practice/modules.rs Before you edit, predict the two lines in main : one call receives a valid reserve and the other receives none. Then look at the return type and explain why changing the caller's nickname afterwards cannot alter the result. The function now lives across a module boundary, but the ownership question is the same one you've already practiced. Hint 1: use the same two cases as the input type Match the optional reference. The Some branch has an &Energy ; call its public units() method. The None branch has no reserve number to print, so preserve that absence in the wording. Hint 2: return text with its own storage format! constructs a String . Use the supplied name in both branches and place the available units only in the measured branch. You do not need to clone the reserve, expose its field, or take ownership of the caller's nickname. Complete starter file: modules.rs mod measurement { #[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)] pub struct Energy { units: u32 } #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq)] pub struct InvalidReserve; fn check_limit(units: u32) -> Result<(), InvalidReserve> { if units <= 100 { Ok(()) } else { Err(InvalidReserve) } } impl Energy { pub fn new(units: u32) -> Result<Self, InvalidReserve> { check_limit(units)?; Ok(Self { units }) } pub fn units(&self) -> u32 { self.units } } } pub use measurement::{Energy, InvalidReserve}; mod inspector { use crate::Energy; pub fn report(name: &str, reserve: Option<&Energy>) -> String { let _ = (name, reserve); todo!("format the public reading without reaching into private fields") } } pub use inspector::report; fn main() { let reserve = Energy::new(60).expect("the authored fixture is valid"); println!("{}", report("Fern", Some(&reserve))); println!("{}", report("Unmeasured", None)); } #[cfg(test)] mod tests { use super::{Energy, InvalidReserve, report}; #[test] fn callers_keep_the_same_public_names() { let reserve = Energy::new(60).unwrap(); assert_eq!(report("Fern", Some(&reserve)), "Fern: 60 units"); assert_eq!(reserve.units(), 60); } #[test] fn missing_measurement_is_not_a_zero_measurement() { let zero = Energy::new(0).unwrap(); assert_eq!(report("Fern", Some(&zero)), "Fern: 0 units"); assert_eq!(report("Fern", None), "Fern: unknown reserve"); } #[test] fn the_constructor_retains_its_boundary() { assert_eq!(Energy::new(100).unwrap().units(), 100); assert_eq!(Energy::new(101), Err(InvalidReserve)); } #[test] fn returned_text_does_not_borrow_the_nickname() { let mut nickname = String::from("Fern"); let text = report(&nickname, None); nickname.clear(); assert_eq!(text, "Fern: unknown reserve"); assert!(nickname.is_empty()); } } Complete worked answer: modules.rs mod measurement { #[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)] pub struct Energy { units: u32 } #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq)] pub struct InvalidReserve; fn check_limit(units: u32) -> Result<(), InvalidReserve> { if units <= 100 { Ok(()) } else { Err(InvalidReserve) } } impl Energy { pub fn new(units: u32) -> Result<Self, InvalidReserve> { check_limit(units)?; Ok(Self { units }) } pub fn units(&self) -> u32 { self.units } } } pub use measurement::{Energy, InvalidReserve}; mod inspector { use crate::Energy; pub fn report(name: &str, reserve: Option<&Energy>) -> String { match reserve { Some(value) => format!("{name}: {} units", value.units()), None => format!("{name}: unknown reserve"), } } } pub use inspector::report; fn main() { let reserve = Energy::new(60).expect("the authored fixture is valid"); println!("{}", report("Fern", Some(&reserve))); println!("{}", report("Unmeasured", None)); } #[cfg(test)] mod tests { use super::{Energy, InvalidReserve, report}; #[test] fn callers_keep_the_same_public_names() { let reserve = Energy::new(60).unwrap(); assert_eq!(report("Fern", Some(&reserve)), "Fern: 60 units"); assert_eq!(reserve.units(), 60); } #[test] fn missing_measurement_is_not_a_zero_measurement() { let zero = Energy::new(0).unwrap(); assert_eq!(report("Fern", Some(&zero)), "Fern: 0 units"); assert_eq!(report("Fern", None), "Fern: unknown reserve"); } #[test] fn the_constructor_retains_its_boundary() { assert_eq!(Energy::new(100).unwrap().units(), 100); assert_eq!(Energy::new(101), Err(InvalidReserve)); } #[test] fn returned_text_does_not_borrow_the_nickname() { let mut nickname = String::from("Fern"); let text = report(&nickname, None); nickname.clear(); assert_eq!(text, "Fern: unknown reserve"); assert!(nickname.is_empty()); } } The reference should print Fern: 60 units and Unmeasured: unknown reserve , with four passing tests. Run python3 learning/scripts/labs.py check modules to check that printed reference. The command with --file checks your saved implementation instead. Neither command edits the real moss-sim library. Use a privacy error to locate a responsibility A working report shows that the public interface gives the inspector enough access. Now we'll check which implementation details that interface keeps private. The inspector can name Energy because the type is public, yet it still can't reach the private units field directly. Rust lets a module expose a type while controlling how callers construct and inspect its values. That is useful here: making the field public to silence an access error would also let callers create the out-of-range value the constructor was meant to reject. Try the following intentional compile-error line inside the isolated program's main , then remove it. The expected diagnostic is E0603: the helper function is private. You are deliberately attempting to call an implementation detail from its parent module, not discovering a runtime failure in reserve validation. let _ = measurement::check_limit(60); Call Energy::new(60) instead. It validates the input and constructs the value in one operation, so a successful call gives you an energy value that meets the module's rule. Calling the hidden helper on its own would only validate a number; the caller could ignore that result and would still need another way to construct the value. Keeping those steps together gives the public method a clear responsibility. Private items are usable within their defining module and its descendants. Broader visibility can be deliberately limited with pub(super) for the parent scope or pub(crate) for the crate. Those tools serve real internal consumers; they are not a ladder every function must climb. Start with the caller that needs access, then choose the narrowest suitable scope. The Rust Reference's privacy rules supply the precise cases. Imports name existing items Inside the inspector, use crate::Energy; makes the root's re-exported name available without repeating its full path. It names the type that already exists; no energy value is copied and no second library is loaded at runtime. Here crate starts at the current crate root, while super would start at the parent module. These paths locate a definition. A borrow such as &Energy separately describes access to one of its values. Suppose you later rename measurement . If the crate root still re-exports Energy and preserves its behavior, the inspector and caller tests can keep using the same public path. This is the useful promise behind the re-export: callers depend on selected entry points, giving you room to reorganize implementation files without asking every consumer to follow along. The lab's tests live in the same crate, so they check its chosen names and behavior rather than the exact external API of the real Moss library. Moss also has separate integration tests that import its library as consumers. For this standalone exercise, the intentional privacy error is the additional compiler check that the helper stays hidden. Change file placement without inventing another architecture So far the module bodies have stayed inline to make the practice file complete when copied. When navigation would benefit from separate files, replace the inline mod measurement { ... } body with mod measurement; and put that body in src/measurement.rs in a normal Cargo binary. You can do the same for the inspector. Each module is still declared once, so remove the inline definition when you move its contents. This file move leaves the module paths and public calls intact. A use declaration cannot replace mod , because an import names an item that must already be part of the module tree. The Book's file-separation example is a useful reference when the compiler cannot find a newly moved module. For one final check, imagine moving report into another private implementation module while keeping its root re-export. The reporting, absence, construction, and ownership assertions should all remain the same: their inputs and results don't depend on an implementation folder. If a caller changes purely because you renamed that folder, trace whether it was reaching through the public boundary into an internal path. Recall answer: a path and a borrow answer different questions crate::Energy identifies the type through the crate's public route. &Energy describes shared access to an instance. Re-exporting the type does not change the borrow, and owning the returned string does not make the private reserve field accessible. Keep the public promise when the implementation moves Fern's report still says 60 units after the function crosses a module boundary, and its returned text still owns what it needs. Once your reporting check passes, return to the real Energy type and trace the same route from crate root to implementation to browser consumer. In the collection lesson , we'll turn this one owned description into a population report that stays understandable even when its inputs arrive in a different order. Optional reference: the Rust Book's module guide distinguishes crate roots and module trees; its imports and re-exports chapter explains the naming boundary. This original lab targets Rust 1.93.1, edition 2024; it has no external dependencies.

title: Collect a report, release the world
summary: Turn borrowed observations into owned report rows, with explicit ordering and honest missing data.
text: Flint appears first in one report and Fern appears first in the next, even though neither animal changed. If you're comparing the two reports, that rearrangement makes you do extra work to discover that the world is the same. Choosing a deliberate row order will make the actual changes easier to see. Isolated collection lab. This continues the inspector boundary and owned readings . The inputs are plain structs, not a second ECS or a new population system. Complete one function in a separate file. The live movement assignment remains unchanged. Collect a report that survives its inputs You'll build a collector that selects creatures, gives each row its own data, and orders the rows by numeric identity. We'll trace those decisions through an iterator, then use reversed inputs, missing measurements, and duplicate IDs to challenge the result. The completed report should stay usable after its sources change or disappear, with IDs 3, 5, and 9 in the same order and an unknown reserve still distinct from zero. Choose membership, ownership, then order Our input arrives as Flint, Fern, Meadow, and Unmeasured. It contains three creatures and one display source: Meadow isn't a creature, so it shouldn't become a report row. Among the creatures, Fern has 57 reserve units, Flint has a measured zero, and Unmeasured has no collected reserve. The finished report should keep all three creatures and order them by numeric ID: 3, 5, then 9. To produce that result, we need to make three decisions. We first select which sources belong in the report, then construct an owned Row for each selected source, and finally put those rows in display order. Keeping the stages visible gives us a useful way to diagnose a wrong result. Meadow appearing in the report points to membership; a historical name changing later points to ownership; shuffled rows point to ordering. The collector only needs to inspect the caller's existing sequence, so its input is a borrowed slice, &[Source] . A vector, an array, or a smaller contiguous view can supply that slice without handing over ownership or letting the collector grow the source sequence. The output has a different job: an owned Vec<Row> gathers the selected rows into a growable sequence that the caller can keep after collection ends. Owning the vector alone wouldn't make the report independent. A Vec<&Source> owns the sequence of references, but every reference still borrows a source value. We need each row to own its String and contain copied numeric data instead. Then dropping the source vector removes the original observations without removing the information saved in the report. Read an iterator as a sequence of decisions We can express those first two decisions as an iterator chain. Start with sources.iter() , which yields shared references to the source values. filter keeps the sources marked as creatures, and map describes how each one becomes a row. Those adapters describe work; collect is what asks the chain for results and builds the output vector. As it consumes the iterator, each source is examined and each selected source becomes an owned row. Without a consuming operation, constructing the chain wouldn't produce a completed report. The small expression |source| source.creature tells filter how to make its decision. It is a closure: a function expression whose argument is supplied by the iterator and whose result is the creature flag. The compiler can infer the argument type from that surrounding use. At the other end of the chain, the Vec<Row> annotation tells collect which kind of collection should receive the results. Inside map , cloning source.name gives the row its own text storage. The ID and Option<u32> can be copied directly. Notice what copying the option preserves: None is still absence, and Some(0) is still an available measurement whose value is zero. We don't have to invent a number for Unmeasured to keep that creature in the report. You might reach for filter_map when an input contains an option. That adapter transforms each item and discards results that are None , which would suit a request for only available measurements. Our question is different: which creatures were present, and what did we know about their reserves? Filtering on the reserve option would remove Unmeasured entirely. Select on the creature flag and carry the option into the row so its absence remains visible. Make order part of the output contract After collection, sort the rows by numeric ID. Fern then occupies the same place in the report even if the source sequence was reversed. This order is a presentation choice: it doesn't claim that a lower ID is older, closer, or entitled to food first. A later rule that resolves competition would need its own reason for choosing an order. There is a subtle limit to what sorting can guarantee. sort_by_key is stable, meaning equal keys retain their previous relative order. If two different rows share the same ID, reversing the input could therefore reverse those two rows in the output as well. More fundamentally, the report couldn't say which row that ID identifies. Rather than treating a stable sort as a solution to ambiguous identity, this lab rejects duplicate selected IDs. Sorting makes that validation easier: every repeated ID must sit beside another equal ID. windows(2) lends each adjacent pair so the function can compare their IDs and return ReportError::DuplicateId(id) on a collision. If no pair collides, return Ok(rows) . An empty input naturally produces an empty vector with no adjacent pairs to inspect. Before opening the worked answer, predict where the two optional-reserve cases will appear. Fern comes first with Some(57) , Unmeasured comes second with None , and Flint comes third with Some(0) ; Meadow contributes no row. Reverse the fixture mentally and check that every one of those statements remains true. That's the output contract your function needs to preserve. Build the owned report The starter leaves collect_report unfinished while supplying the fixture and lookup function. Your function will select the creature rows, give them owned fields, order them, and reject duplicate IDs. Prepare it in a new practice directory and run the first check; reaching its intentional todo! shows that the runner got as far as your unfinished collector. python3 learning/scripts/labs.py prepare collections --dest work/collections-practice python3 learning/scripts/labs.py check collections --file work/collections-practice/collections.rs Hint 1: make a complete row for each selected source Begin with sources.iter() . Filter using the creature flag, then map to Row . Clone the name, copy the ID, and copy the optional reserve. Collect into an explicitly typed mutable vector so you can sort afterward. Hint 2: validation follows ordering Sort by row.id , inspect adjacent pairs, and return the duplicate-ID error if either pair shares an ID. Otherwise return the whole vector inside Ok . Do not discard a row merely because its reserve is absent. Complete starter file: collections.rs #[derive(Debug)] struct Source { id: u64, name: String, reserve: Option<u32>, creature: bool, } #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq)] struct Row { id: u64, name: String, reserve: Option<u32> } #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq)] enum ReportError { DuplicateId(u64) } fn collect_report(sources: &[Source]) -> Result<Vec<Row>, ReportError> { let _ = sources; todo!("own the selected readings, sort by ID, and reject duplicate IDs") } fn find_row(rows: &[Row], id: u64) -> Option<&Row> { rows.iter().find(|row| row.id == id) } fn fixture() -> Vec<Source> { vec![ Source { id: 9, name: "Flint".into(), reserve: Some(0), creature: true }, Source { id: 3, name: "Fern".into(), reserve: Some(57), creature: true }, Source { id: 7, name: "Meadow".into(), reserve: None, creature: false }, Source { id: 5, name: "Unmeasured".into(), reserve: None, creature: true }, ] } fn main() { let rows = collect_report(&fixture()).expect("fixture IDs are unique"); for row in &rows { println!("#{} {}: {:?}", row.id, row.name, row.reserve); } assert!(find_row(&rows, 404).is_none()); } #[cfg(test)] mod tests { use super::*; #[test] fn empty_input_is_a_valid_empty_report() { assert_eq!(collect_report(&[]), Ok(vec![])); } #[test] fn reordered_input_has_one_canonical_report() { let mut sources = fixture(); let first = collect_report(&sources).unwrap(); sources.reverse(); assert_eq!(collect_report(&sources).unwrap(), first); assert_eq!(first.iter().map(|row| row.id).collect::<Vec<_>>(), vec![3, 5, 9]); } #[test] fn unknown_zero_and_unselected_are_different() { let rows = collect_report(&fixture()).unwrap(); assert_eq!(find_row(&rows, 5).unwrap().reserve, None); assert_eq!(find_row(&rows, 9).unwrap().reserve, Some(0)); assert!(find_row(&rows, 7).is_none()); assert!(find_row(&rows, 404).is_none()); } #[test] fn saved_rows_own_their_text_and_measurements() { let mut sources = fixture(); let rows = collect_report(&sources).unwrap(); sources[0].name.clear(); sources[0].reserve = Some(80); drop(sources); let saved = find_row(&rows, 9).unwrap(); assert_eq!(saved.name, "Flint"); assert_eq!(saved.reserve, Some(0)); } #[test] fn duplicate_identity_is_rejected_instead_of_overwritten() { let mut sources = fixture(); sources[0].id = 3; assert_eq!(collect_report(&sources), Err(ReportError::DuplicateId(3))); } #[test] fn lookup_borrows_a_row_already_in_the_report() { let rows = collect_report(&fixture()).unwrap(); assert!(std::ptr::eq(find_row(&rows, 3).unwrap(), &rows[0])); } } Complete worked answer: collections.rs #[derive(Debug)] struct Source { id: u64, name: String, reserve: Option<u32>, creature: bool, } #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq)] struct Row { id: u64, name: String, reserve: Option<u32> } #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq)] enum ReportError { DuplicateId(u64) } fn collect_report(sources: &[Source]) -> Result<Vec<Row>, ReportError> { let mut rows: Vec<Row> = sources.iter() .filter(|source| source.creature) .map(|source| Row { id: source.id, name: source.name.clone(), reserve: source.reserve, }) .collect(); rows.sort_by_key(|row| row.id); for pair in rows.windows(2) { if pair[0].id == pair[1].id { return Err(ReportError::DuplicateId(pair[0].id)); } } Ok(rows) } fn find_row(rows: &[Row], id: u64) -> Option<&Row> { rows.iter().find(|row| row.id == id) } fn fixture() -> Vec<Source> { vec![ Source { id: 9, name: "Flint".into(), reserve: Some(0), creature: true }, Source { id: 3, name: "Fern".into(), reserve: Some(57), creature: true }, Source { id: 7, name: "Meadow".into(), reserve: None, creature: false }, Source { id: 5, name: "Unmeasured".into(), reserve: None, creature: true }, ] } fn main() { let rows = collect_report(&fixture()).expect("fixture IDs are unique"); for row in &rows { println!("#{} {}: {:?}", row.id, row.name, row.reserve); } assert!(find_row(&rows, 404).is_none()); } #[cfg(test)] mod tests { use super::*; #[test] fn empty_input_is_a_valid_empty_report() { assert_eq!(collect_report(&[]), Ok(vec![])); } #[test] fn reordered_input_has_one_canonical_report() { let mut sources = fixture(); let first = collect_report(&sources).unwrap(); sources.reverse(); assert_eq!(collect_report(&sources).unwrap(), first); assert_eq!(first.iter().map(|row| row.id).collect::<Vec<_>>(), vec![3, 5, 9]); } #[test] fn unknown_zero_and_unselected_are_different() { let rows = collect_report(&fixture()).unwrap(); assert_eq!(find_row(&rows, 5).unwrap().reserve, None); assert_eq!(find_row(&rows, 9).unwrap().reserve, Some(0)); assert!(find_row(&rows, 7).is_none()); assert!(find_row(&rows, 404).is_none()); } #[test] fn saved_rows_own_their_text_and_measurements() { let mut sources = fixture(); let rows = collect_report(&sources).unwrap(); sources[0].name.clear(); sources[0].reserve = Some(80); drop(sources); let saved = find_row(&rows, 9).unwrap(); assert_eq!(saved.name, "Flint"); assert_eq!(saved.reserve, Some(0)); } #[test] fn duplicate_identity_is_rejected_instead_of_overwritten() { let mut sources = fixture(); sources[0].id = 3; assert_eq!(collect_report(&sources), Err(ReportError::DuplicateId(3))); } #[test] fn lookup_borrows_a_row_already_in_the_report() { let rows = collect_report(&fixture()).unwrap(); assert!(std::ptr::eq(find_row(&rows, 3).unwrap(), &rows[0])); } } Check the printed reference with python3 learning/scripts/labs.py check collections . Its expected result is six passing tests and the three lines below. Use the earlier --file command for your own copy. These checks concern a native reporting function; they do not establish browser rendering or an installed ECS system. #3 Fern: Some(57) #5 Unmeasured: None #9 Flint: Some(0) A loop can express the same ownership decision The iterator chain is useful when you can read it as those collection decisions. If it still feels dense, try the following alternative fragment inside the completed function , keeping sorting and validation afterwards. The loop performs the same temporary borrow of each source and the same construction of an owned row. Comparing the two forms can make it easier to see where selection ends and ownership of the output begins. let mut rows = Vec::new(); for source in sources { if source.creature { rows.push(Row { id: source.id, name: source.name.clone(), reserve: source.reserve, }); } } Use the same six assertions after substituting the loop. They should pass because the report's contract hasn't changed. Reordering the input checks that sorting still happens, while absence versus zero checks that selection hasn't erased missing measurements. The ownership test goes further: it edits the source nickname and reserve, then drops the whole source vector. The saved row can remain usable because it contains its own fields rather than borrowed links into that vector. Lookup is a different question from display order The ordered report is ready to keep or display. A caller asking about one creature has a narrower need, so we'll separate finding a stored row from collecting the report again. find_row returns Option<&Row> , where the outer option answers whether that ID appears in the report. The row's reserve is a separate option. ID 404 has no row at all; ID 5 has a row that records an unavailable reserve. Those are different answers, even though both involve absence. A successful lookup lends a row already stored in the report. It doesn't clone the name or collect another snapshot, and the pointer-identity assertion checks that it returns the existing row. While the caller continues using that reference, it can't make a conflicting change to the vector that owns it. If the caller only needs the small reserve value, copying that value lets the borrow end sooner. A linear search is enough for this small report. If a consumer repeatedly looks up many IDs, a map can provide an index after the collector has validated uniqueness. The following separate exploration fragment builds a borrowed index: the map owns its keys and references, while the vector continues owning the rows they point to. use std::collections::HashMap; let by_id: HashMap<_, _> = rows.iter().map(|row| (row.id, row)).collect(); assert_eq!(by_id.get(&9).unwrap().reserve, Some(0)); The index answers where to find an ID, but it doesn't inherit the vector's display order. Iterating that HashMap need not reproduce the sorted report. Keep using the vector for presentation and the map for lookup, or choose a collection with the ordering contract you need. Since a borrowed index also has a lifetime and a cost to rebuild, add one when an actual consumer benefits from those repeated lookups. Retain a reading without freezing the world We started with a display that changed when its input order changed. The completed collector makes the output order deliberate and owns enough information for the report to survive its sources. A later lookup can borrow from that report for as long as the caller needs a row. These two ownership choices let the world continue changing while a user reads or sorts a saved panel. Recall answer: why not replace every None with zero? A zero reserve is an observed number. An absent reserve is a gap in the observation. Replacing absence with zero would turn the unmeasured creature into evidence of depletion, even though the collector never recorded such a measurement. The row's identity survives both cases; the measurement's meaning does not. Reverse the inputs once more, then change their names and drop them: the saved report should keep the same ordered rows and the same distinction between zero and absence. The next lesson takes a closer look at the ID those rows rely on. We'll give identity its own type and decide what equality, copying, and ordering should mean for it. Optional references: Iterator documents the adapters; slice sorting specifies stability; HashMap explains lookup and iteration contracts. This original example targets Rust 1.93.1 with edition 2024 and uses only the standard library.

title: A trait is a promise you can use
summary: Give identities meaningful comparison and reporting capabilities, then let a generic function state the capability it needs.
text: Two readings both say “Fern,” but one has ID 2 and the other has ID 10. Another pair both refer to ID 10, yet their reserves differ because they were collected at different moments. Before asking Rust whether those values are equal, we have to decide what we're comparing. Isolated identity and reporting lab. This continues canonical reports and reuses a private representation with a public constructor . Complete one small generic helper. The ID type is a teaching type, not a replacement for Moss's existing IDs or a new live identity allocator. Order identities without taking their readings Our practical destination is a helper that turns IDs 10, 2, 10 into 2, 10 while leaving the caller's readings available. To choose its trait bounds sensibly, we'll first distinguish equality of identities from equality of whole observations, then connect copying and ordering to the operations the helper performs. Compiler experiments with the owned nickname will show why a capability suitable for the ID need not suit the reading around it. Make the identity contract smaller than the reading The report in the preceding lesson used integers as IDs. An integer can also describe an energy amount or a tick count, so a function accepting a plain number doesn't tell us which meaning belongs there. Wrapping one u64 in StableId gives identity a distinct type. Its module keeps the field private and provides a constructor that rejects zero, making that rule part of how callers obtain a valid ID. Zero is rejected because this lab explicitly chose that rule, not because an identity type or a derive automatically requires it. The constructor returns a Result , and the private field directs ordinary external callers through that constructor. The live simulation has its own ID rules; this small type lets us study the relationship between validation and traits without replacing that allocator. A Reading holds more than an identity: it contains the ID, an owned nickname, and an optional reserve. Derived equality compares all of those fields. If a later observation records a different reserve, it should differ from the earlier reading even when both describe the same individual. Comparing only their ID fields asks the narrower question of whether they name that same individual. That distinction resolves the opening pairs. Two Fern nicknames don't turn IDs 2 and 10 into the same ID, while equal IDs don't make two different observations equal. We can retain an application's stable identity long after collecting a reading. Discovering whether that identity still resolves to a living entity requires another operation against the current world. Read each derive as a capability To make those comparisons available, a type needs the appropriate trait implementations. PartialEq supplies == and != ; Eq adds the full equality contract, including the promise that a value equals itself. An integer-backed ID can meet that promise. A floating-point value illustrates why Rust distinguishes the traits: NaN does not equal itself, so a familiar-looking numeric value doesn't necessarily support the same equality contract. Our report also needs a predictable order. PartialOrd permits comparisons that may find no ordering for a pair, while Ord promises a total order. Deriving these traits compares a struct's fields in declaration order. StableId has one integer field, so its derived order puts 2 before 10, as the report expects. Sorting formatted strings would put “10” before “2” instead; that would order their written representation rather than their numeric identities. When one of those assertions fails, we want the diagnostic to show the values involved. Debug makes programmer-facing formatting such as {:?} available, and deriving it saves us from writing that inspection code by hand. Its output is helpful in a test failure, but an exported file would need its own defined schema rather than depending on derived debug text staying unchanged. The ID list also needs values it can keep after the input borrow ends. Clone provides an explicit duplication operation, while Copy allows implicit copying where an assignment would otherwise move ownership. A Copy type must also implement Clone . Our one-integer identity can derive both, letting a caller copy the ID without transferring ownership of the reading that contains it. These traits describe ownership behavior; they don't promise that every operation involving the type is free. The Ord reference , PartialEq reference , and Debug reference are useful when checking one of these contracts. Read the required relationship first, then the derive behavior. The macro saves repetitive implementations; it does not remove their meaning. Borrow the readings and copy the identities Now put those capabilities to work. A report helper can borrow a slice of readings and extract their small IDs into a new vector, leaving all the owned nicknames in place. Each output element is a copied StableId , so the list can outlive the borrowed slice. We get an independent list of identities without cloning all the text or moving the readings away from their owner. Suppose the extracted list is 10, 2, 10 and the caller wants each ID once, in numeric order. Sorting and removing repeated values don't require any knowledge of creatures, so we'll write ordered_unique<T: Ord + Copy> . The caller chooses a concrete T ; the bounds promise that its values can be copied and totally ordered. That is enough for the same helper to process stable IDs or a short list of signed integers. The bounds are also the agreement under which Rust checks the generic function body. It can use copying and ordering because every accepted caller must provide those capabilities. If a call fails with an unsatisfied-bound diagnostic, consider the operation you intended before adding more derives. A function that only needs a list of IDs may be asking too much if you hand it complete readings instead. To preserve the caller's original order, start by copying the borrowed slice into a vector with to_vec() . Sort that owned vector, then call dedup() to remove consecutive equal values. The order of those operations matters: on 10, 2, 10, deduplication alone doesn't bring the two tens together. Sorting first turns the sequence into 2, 10, 10, from which deduplication can produce 2, 10. Complete one helper and keep the inputs usable Try that implementation in a fresh practice file. Only ordered_unique is unfinished, so the initial check should compile and then reach its todo! . The result must leave the caller's source slice unchanged. It should also handle an empty slice naturally by returning an empty vector, without inventing a special identity to fill the space. python3 learning/scripts/labs.py prepare traits --dest work/traits-practice python3 learning/scripts/labs.py check traits --file work/traits-practice/traits.rs Hint 1: own a result before changing its order The input is borrowed. Build a vector using values.to_vec() and bind it mutably. Sorting that owned vector changes the result you will return, while leaving the caller's sequence untouched. Hint 2: equal values need to meet before deduplication Call sort() before dedup() . Return the vector. The trait bounds let the compiler verify those operations for every type accepted by this helper. Complete starter file: traits.rs mod identity { #[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq, PartialOrd, Ord)] pub struct StableId(u64); #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq)] pub struct InvalidId; impl StableId { pub fn new(value: u64) -> Result<Self, InvalidId> { if value == 0 { Err(InvalidId) } else { Ok(Self(value)) } } pub fn value(self) -> u64 { self.0 } } } pub use identity::{InvalidId, StableId}; #[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)] struct Reading { id: StableId, name: String, reserve: Option<u32> } fn ordered_unique<T: Ord + Copy>(values: &[T]) -> Vec<T> { let _ = values; todo!("return owned values in ascending order, with each distinct value once") } fn ids_of(readings: &[Reading]) -> Vec<StableId> { let ids: Vec<_> = readings.iter().map(|reading| reading.id).collect(); ordered_unique(&ids) } fn main() { let fern = Reading { id: StableId::new(10).unwrap(), name: "Fern".into(), reserve: Some(57), }; let mut renamed = fern.clone(); renamed.name.push_str(" the hare"); println!("same ID: {}", fern.id == renamed.id); println!("same reading: {}", fern == renamed); let ids = ordered_unique(&[fern.id, StableId::new(2).unwrap(), fern.id]); println!("IDs: {:?}", ids.iter().map(|id| id.value()).collect::<Vec<_>>()); assert_eq!(ids_of(&[fern, renamed]).len(), 1); } #[cfg(test)] mod tests { use super::*; #[test] fn identity_order_is_numeric_and_duplicates_collapse() { let two = StableId::new(2).unwrap(); let ten = StableId::new(10).unwrap(); assert_eq!(ordered_unique(&[ten, two, ten]), vec![two, ten]); assert_ne!(two, ten); } #[test] fn empty_input_stays_empty() { assert_eq!(ordered_unique::<StableId>(&[]), vec![]); } #[test] fn collecting_ids_does_not_take_the_readings() { let readings = vec![Reading { id: StableId::new(4).unwrap(), name: "Fern".into(), reserve: None, }]; let ids = ids_of(&readings); assert_eq!(readings[0].name, "Fern"); drop(readings); assert_eq!(ids[0].value(), 4); } #[test] fn equal_identity_does_not_mean_equal_observation() { let first = Reading { id: StableId::new(4).unwrap(), name: "Fern".into(), reserve: None, }; let mut later = first.clone(); later.reserve = Some(0); assert_eq!(first.id, later.id); assert_ne!(first, later); } #[test] fn cloning_owned_text_produces_independent_text() { let first = Reading { id: StableId::new(4).unwrap(), name: "Fern".into(), reserve: Some(57), }; let mut second = first.clone(); second.name.push_str(" the hare"); assert_eq!(first.name, "Fern"); assert_eq!(second.name, "Fern the hare"); } #[test] fn derives_do_not_replace_constructor_validation() { assert_eq!(StableId::new(0), Err(InvalidId)); let id = StableId::new(1).unwrap(); let copied = id; assert_eq!(id, copied); } #[test] fn the_same_bound_supports_another_ordered_copy_type() { assert_eq!(ordered_unique(&[7_i32, -1, 7, 0]), vec![-1, 0, 7]); } } Complete worked answer: traits.rs mod identity { #[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq, PartialOrd, Ord)] pub struct StableId(u64); #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq)] pub struct InvalidId; impl StableId { pub fn new(value: u64) -> Result<Self, InvalidId> { if value == 0 { Err(InvalidId) } else { Ok(Self(value)) } } pub fn value(self) -> u64 { self.0 } } } pub use identity::{InvalidId, StableId}; #[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)] struct Reading { id: StableId, name: String, reserve: Option<u32> } fn ordered_unique<T: Ord + Copy>(values: &[T]) -> Vec<T> { let mut result = values.to_vec(); result.sort(); result.dedup(); result } fn ids_of(readings: &[Reading]) -> Vec<StableId> { let ids: Vec<_> = readings.iter().map(|reading| reading.id).collect(); ordered_unique(&ids) } fn main() { let fern = Reading { id: StableId::new(10).unwrap(), name: "Fern".into(), reserve: Some(57), }; let mut renamed = fern.clone(); renamed.name.push_str(" the hare"); println!("same ID: {}", fern.id == renamed.id); println!("same reading: {}", fern == renamed); let ids = ordered_unique(&[fern.id, StableId::new(2).unwrap(), fern.id]); println!("IDs: {:?}", ids.iter().map(|id| id.value()).collect::<Vec<_>>()); assert_eq!(ids_of(&[fern, renamed]).len(), 1); } #[cfg(test)] mod tests { use super::*; #[test] fn identity_order_is_numeric_and_duplicates_collapse() { let two = StableId::new(2).unwrap(); let ten = StableId::new(10).unwrap(); assert_eq!(ordered_unique(&[ten, two, ten]), vec![two, ten]); assert_ne!(two, ten); } #[test] fn empty_input_stays_empty() { assert_eq!(ordered_unique::<StableId>(&[]), vec![]); } #[test] fn collecting_ids_does_not_take_the_readings() { let readings = vec![Reading { id: StableId::new(4).unwrap(), name: "Fern".into(), reserve: None, }]; let ids = ids_of(&readings); assert_eq!(readings[0].name, "Fern"); drop(readings); assert_eq!(ids[0].value(), 4); } #[test] fn equal_identity_does_not_mean_equal_observation() { let first = Reading { id: StableId::new(4).unwrap(), name: "Fern".into(), reserve: None, }; let mut later = first.clone(); later.reserve = Some(0); assert_eq!(first.id, later.id); assert_ne!(first, later); } #[test] fn cloning_owned_text_produces_independent_text() { let first = Reading { id: StableId::new(4).unwrap(), name: "Fern".into(), reserve: Some(57), }; let mut second = first.clone(); second.name.push_str(" the hare"); assert_eq!(first.name, "Fern"); assert_eq!(second.name, "Fern the hare"); } #[test] fn derives_do_not_replace_constructor_validation() { assert_eq!(StableId::new(0), Err(InvalidId)); let id = StableId::new(1).unwrap(); let copied = id; assert_eq!(id, copied); } #[test] fn the_same_bound_supports_another_ordered_copy_type() { assert_eq!(ordered_unique(&[7_i32, -1, 7, 0]), vec![-1, 0, 7]); } } The printed reference should pass seven tests and display the three lines below. Run python3 learning/scripts/labs.py check traits to check that reference independently. Use the command with --file for your saved solution; opening the answer never certifies your practice file. same ID: true same reading: false IDs: [2, 10] Owned text changes the copying decision The complete Reading makes a different ownership choice from its ID. It derives Clone but omits Copy because its String owns text storage. Cloning the reading clones that string too. The test then appends to one clone and checks that the original still says “Fern,” demonstrating the independence this particular reporting type needs. That independence comes from the fields' clone implementations, so don't generalize it into a promise that every clone duplicates all underlying data. Later, a shared-ownership type can clone a handle while keeping the data shared. Here, deriving clone field by field for a struct containing String gives the new reading its own text, which is the behavior the test observes. You can see the difference by adding Copy to the derive on Reading as an intentional compiler experiment . The expected E0204 error identifies a field that can't meet the copying contract. Remove the derive afterwards and connect the error back to the owned string: implicitly copying its owner would not be the operation that String provides. The repair is to keep the intended ownership behavior, not to hide the field behind an arbitrary pointer. For a second diagnostic, pass a slice of Reading to ordered_unique . The helper asks for copying and ordering that a reading doesn't offer. Adding every suggested derive would choose a new meaning for whole observations, including an order based on field sequence. If your question is which individuals appear in the report, extracting and ordering IDs expresses it more accurately. The Copy and Clone references explain these distinctions. A diagnostic's suggested operation is useful evidence, but the correct repair depends on whether the caller needs ownership, a borrow, a copyable identity, or an independent snapshot. A derive supplies integration, not a world rule Traits connect ordinary Rust types to Bevy too. The earlier ECS lesson used #[derive(Component)] and #[derive(Resource)] to supply implementations Bevy requires for those roles. Naming a struct Energy doesn't register it as a component; deriving Component supplies that capability. Neither the name nor the derive, however, schedules an upkeep system. For upkeep to affect an entity, the relevant components still have to be installed and the system still has to run. Validation must separately protect the energy range and identity rules, and lifecycle code must separately define what the outcomes mean. A Component implementation lets these pieces integrate with Bevy without deciding their behavior for them. The same distinction applies to our derived ID order. It makes the report reproducible, but it doesn't establish that the lowest ID should win a competition for food. If a later ecological rule uses that order, we'll need to choose and explain it as a rule of the model. A capability that's convenient for display shouldn't silently decide who eats. Recall answer: which equality belongs in each assertion? Compare IDs to ask whether two readings refer to the same named individual. Compare complete readings to ask whether their recorded fields match. Compare owned text after editing one clone to test independence. None of these assertions proves that the corresponding creature currently exists in the live world. Choose capabilities for the question you are asking Check the opening puzzle again: two equal IDs can belong to unequal readings, and two equal nicknames can belong to different IDs. Your helper should now put ID 2 before ID 10, collapse repeated IDs, handle empty input, and leave the borrowed readings available to their owner. In conflicting component access in Bevy , we'll carry that distinction between retained identity values and borrowed data into an actual system. This original lab targets Rust 1.93.1, edition 2024, with only the standard library. For the ECS connection, consult the exact-version Bevy 0.18.1 Component and Resource documentation. The standard-library links follow current documentation; the course runner uses its pinned compiler for actual checks.

title: Prove that the borrows cannot meet
summary: Make read and write sets explicit, then use a dual-role entity to test the boundary.
text: A source sample contains 60 and its preview contains zero. Copying 60 into the preview should be a small job, yet Bevy can reject the system before its loop runs. Both entities use the same component type, and the system's two query signatures may claim incompatible access to it. Isolated Bevy ECS 0.18.1 lab. These samples are presentation data in a separate test world. They are not creature reserves, movement, or live biological state. You will complete one preview-refresh body after understanding its access contract. The single live assignment remains in NOW.md . Refresh the preview while protecting the source You'll read the two query signatures as sets of permissions, decide what a row with both roles should mean, and then complete the lookup and assignment. An awkward fixture makes the policy observable: the ordinary preview should become 60 while the dual-role source remains 900. We'll also consider when overlapping access is intentional, so the repair follows the data relationship instead of merely silencing the diagnostic. Read access before the body In the preceding traits lesson , a Component derive supplied the capability Bevy needs to store a value. It didn't decide which systems could access that value together. For this refresh, we need to read some Sample components and write others, so Bevy has to understand the access declared by the whole system parameter list. With ordinary Rust values, a mutable borrow gives exclusive access while it is in use: a competing borrow can't read or write that same value at the same time. The compiler can often see those paths directly in local code. An ECS query instead describes a set of components selected from a world at runtime. Bevy therefore checks the query's declared access when it initializes a system, before the body starts iterating. The lab represents the relationship with two roles. A source entity carries Source , a RowId , and a Sample . A preview carries its own Sample and a PreviewFor that names the source row it wants. Reading the source while writing a distinct preview is valid. The difficulty is showing that the two queries really reach distinct components, rather than relying on what we meant those role names to imply. Consider this intentionally conflicting parameter excerpt . It is not part of the successful reference program. If registered as an ordinary system, it can compile as Rust and then fail Bevy's access validation with B0001 when initialized: sources: Query<(&RowId, &Sample), With<Source>>, previews: Query<(&PreviewFor, &mut Sample)>, Read the two signatures as permissions: the first may read Sample on a source entity, and the second may write Sample on an entity with preview data. An entity could carry both Source and PreviewFor , so it could match both queries. Its one sample would then be accessible through a shared path and a mutable path at once. The fixture might not contain such an entity today, but the parameter list hasn't ruled it out. Make the sets genuinely disjoint Before changing a filter, decide what should happen to that dual-role entity. In this lab, source samples are authoritative inputs to presentation. A source must therefore remain protected even if it also carries preview data. Adding Without<Source> to the mutable query expresses that policy directly: anything read by the source query has the marker, and anything written by the preview query lacks it. No entity can meet both conditions. The resulting asymmetry is intentional. The source query can still read a row with both roles, while the preview query can't write it. Excluding that row from both queries would make its source value disappear from lookup as well, which would be a different policy. This is why it's worth stating who owns the authoritative value before trying filters: a filter that makes the error disappear might also change the work you wanted. Membership under the selected policy Entity data Access granted to this system Source, RowId, Sample Read as a source; never write as a preview. PreviewFor, Sample, no Source Write as a preview; not read as a source. Source, RowId, PreviewFor, Sample Read as a source; excluded from preview mutation. Sample alone Neither query includes it. Bevy 0.18.1's disjoint-query documentation explains the access rule. The official B0001 explanation is a useful diagnostic reference. Here the meaningful question is “which entity could both queries reach?”, followed by “should that entity belong to both roles?” Use a fixture that could reveal a mistake We can test that policy by putting a dual-role row into the fixture rather than hoping none appears. Give it sample 900 and a request to preview row 1. The ordinary preview should copy row 1's sample of 60, while the dual-role row must stay at 900. A test with only separate source and preview entities would exercise copying, but wouldn't reveal whether we protected this boundary. The fixture also creates source row 2, with sample 20, before row 1. That order challenges a different mistake: copying the first source visited would update the ordinary preview to 20 instead of 60. Match the requested RowId explicitly. The relationship comes from those IDs, not from the order in which a query happens to visit entities. For a missing-source case, another preview asks for row 99 and begins with sample 777. This small helper leaves that value alone when lookup fails. That is retention behavior, not proof that 777 remains fresh. A production inspector would need to represent freshness or a missing-source status separately, as in the Option lesson; the lab isolates which assignments this updater is permitted to make. Before you write the loop, predict the ordinary preview, the dual-role row, and a sample with neither role after one refresh. The lookup body decides which value to copy into an eligible preview. Query membership decides which entities the body can touch at all. Keeping those two reasons separate will make a failed assertion easier to diagnose. Hint 1: decide eligibility before lookup The mutable query already excludes every source. The loop cannot write the protected dual-role row through that query, regardless of its requested ID. Hint 2: copy only a matching borrowed value For each eligible preview, search source rows by RowId . If a match exists, assign its sample number into the preview. If none exists, perform no assignment. Prediction answer The ordinary preview becomes 60, the dual-role row remains 900, and the unrelated sample remains 333. The source lookup explains the copied 60. The disjoint filter and required preview data explain the protected and unrelated values. Complete the refresh in isolation Create the starter from the repository root and complete only update_previews . It supplies the disjoint signature we've just reasoned through, leaving lookup and assignment as your focused edit. You can return to the conflicting signature above as a separate diagnostic once the successful refresh makes the intended behavior clear. python3 learning/scripts/labs.py prepare borrows --dest work/borrows-practice python3 learning/scripts/labs.py check borrows --file work/borrows-practice/borrows.rs The first check should compile and reach the starter's intentional todo! . After your edit, four named tests should pass. If you see B0001 instead, inspect the system signature: Bevy rejected its access before it could reach the assertions about copied or protected values. Complete starter: borrows.rs use bevy_ecs::{prelude::*, schedule::ExecutorKind}; #[derive(Component)] struct Source; #[derive(Component)] struct RowId(u32); #[derive(Component)] struct PreviewFor(u32); #[derive(Component, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)] struct Sample(i32); fn update_previews( sources: Query<(&RowId, &Sample), With<Source>>, mut previews: Query<(&PreviewFor, &mut Sample), Without<Source>>, ) { let _ = (sources, &mut previews); todo!("refresh only permitted previews from their matching source") } fn preview_schedule() -> Schedule { let mut schedule = Schedule::default(); schedule.set_executor_kind(ExecutorKind::SingleThreaded); schedule.add_systems(update_previews); schedule } struct Fixture { world: World, source: Entity, preview: Entity, protected: Entity, missing: Entity, unmarked: Entity, } fn fixture() -> Fixture { let mut world = World::new(); world.spawn((Source, RowId(2), Sample(20))); let source = world.spawn((Source, RowId(1), Sample(60))).id(); let preview = world.spawn((PreviewFor(1), Sample(0))).id(); let protected = world.spawn((Source, RowId(9), PreviewFor(1), Sample(900))).id(); let missing = world.spawn((PreviewFor(99), Sample(777))).id(); let unmarked = world.spawn(Sample(333)).id(); Fixture { world, source, preview, protected, missing, unmarked } } fn sample(world: &World, entity: Entity) -> i32 { world.get::<Sample>(entity).expect("fixture entity has a sample").0 } fn main() { let mut f = fixture(); preview_schedule().run(&mut f.world); println!("source={} preview={} protected={} missing={} unmarked={}", sample(&f.world, f.source), sample(&f.world, f.preview), sample(&f.world, f.protected), sample(&f.world, f.missing), sample(&f.world, f.unmarked)); } #[cfg(test)] mod tests { use super::*; #[test] fn matching_source_is_copied_without_mutation() { let mut f = fixture(); preview_schedule().run(&mut f.world); assert_eq!(sample(&f.world, f.preview), 60); assert_eq!(sample(&f.world, f.source), 60); } #[test] fn source_marker_protects_an_entity_that_also_has_preview_data() { let mut f = fixture(); preview_schedule().run(&mut f.world); assert_eq!(sample(&f.world, f.protected), 900); } #[test] fn missing_source_and_unmarked_rows_keep_their_previous_values() { let mut f = fixture(); preview_schedule().run(&mut f.world); assert_eq!(sample(&f.world, f.missing), 777); assert_eq!(sample(&f.world, f.unmarked), 333); } #[test] fn later_run_reads_the_changed_source() { let mut f = fixture(); let mut schedule = preview_schedule(); schedule.run(&mut f.world); f.world.get_mut::<Sample>(f.source).unwrap().0 = 41; schedule.run(&mut f.world); assert_eq!(sample(&f.world, f.preview), 41); assert_eq!(sample(&f.world, f.source), 41); assert_eq!(sample(&f.world, f.protected), 900); } } Complete worked answer: borrows.rs use bevy_ecs::{prelude::*, schedule::ExecutorKind}; #[derive(Component)] struct Source; #[derive(Component)] struct RowId(u32); #[derive(Component)] struct PreviewFor(u32); #[derive(Component, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)] struct Sample(i32); fn update_previews( sources: Query<(&RowId, &Sample), With<Source>>, mut previews: Query<(&PreviewFor, &mut Sample), Without<Source>>, ) { for (wanted, mut preview) in &mut previews { if let Some((_, source)) = sources.iter().find(|(id, _)| id.0 == wanted.0) { preview.0 = source.0; } } } fn preview_schedule() -> Schedule { let mut schedule = Schedule::default(); schedule.set_executor_kind(ExecutorKind::SingleThreaded); schedule.add_systems(update_previews); schedule } struct Fixture { world: World, source: Entity, preview: Entity, protected: Entity, missing: Entity, unmarked: Entity, } fn fixture() -> Fixture { let mut world = World::new(); world.spawn((Source, RowId(2), Sample(20))); let source = world.spawn((Source, RowId(1), Sample(60))).id(); let preview = world.spawn((PreviewFor(1), Sample(0))).id(); let protected = world.spawn((Source, RowId(9), PreviewFor(1), Sample(900))).id(); let missing = world.spawn((PreviewFor(99), Sample(777))).id(); let unmarked = world.spawn(Sample(333)).id(); Fixture { world, source, preview, protected, missing, unmarked } } fn sample(world: &World, entity: Entity) -> i32 { world.get::<Sample>(entity).expect("fixture entity has a sample").0 } fn main() { let mut f = fixture(); preview_schedule().run(&mut f.world); println!("source={} preview={} protected={} missing={} unmarked={}", sample(&f.world, f.source), sample(&f.world, f.preview), sample(&f.world, f.protected), sample(&f.world, f.missing), sample(&f.world, f.unmarked)); } #[cfg(test)] mod tests { use super::*; #[test] fn matching_source_is_copied_without_mutation() { let mut f = fixture(); preview_schedule().run(&mut f.world); assert_eq!(sample(&f.world, f.preview), 60); assert_eq!(sample(&f.world, f.source), 60); } #[test] fn source_marker_protects_an_entity_that_also_has_preview_data() { let mut f = fixture(); preview_schedule().run(&mut f.world); assert_eq!(sample(&f.world, f.protected), 900); } #[test] fn missing_source_and_unmarked_rows_keep_their_previous_values() { let mut f = fixture(); preview_schedule().run(&mut f.world); assert_eq!(sample(&f.world, f.missing), 777); assert_eq!(sample(&f.world, f.unmarked), 333); } #[test] fn later_run_reads_the_changed_source() { let mut f = fixture(); let mut schedule = preview_schedule(); schedule.run(&mut f.world); f.world.get_mut::<Sample>(f.source).unwrap().0 = 41; schedule.run(&mut f.world); assert_eq!(sample(&f.world, f.preview), 41); assert_eq!(sample(&f.world, f.source), 41); assert_eq!(sample(&f.world, f.protected), 900); } } Run python3 learning/scripts/labs.py check borrows to check the printed reference. The learner-file command above checks your implementation against the course's reference tests. For a manual native Cargo run, put the chosen full block in a new scratch package at src/main.rs and use this complete manifest: [package] name = "moss-borrow-lab" version = "0.1.0" edition = "2024" publish = false [workspace] [dependencies] bevy_ecs = { version = "=0.18.1", default-features = false, features = ["std"] } Run these commands inside that scratch package. Retain its generated lockfile. The explicit target directory belongs to this lab. cargo +1.93.1 generate-lockfile CARGO_TARGET_DIR=target cargo +1.93.1 test --locked CARGO_TARGET_DIR=target cargo +1.93.1 run --locked The expected test result is four passed tests. The literal expected program output is source=60 preview=60 protected=900 missing=777 unmarked=333 . A later-run test changes the source to 41 and checks that the existing schedule reads the changed value rather than preserving an old copy. When the same entities really must be visited twice The filter works because authoritative sources and writable previews are meant to be separate roles. Other systems may legitimately need to visit the same entities twice, first gathering measurements and then updating them from a summary. Excluding the overlap with Without would remove part of that requested work. Such a system needs to separate access in time instead. Bevy's ParamSet allows potentially conflicting parameters to be accessed in separate stages through methods such as p0() and p1() . You can use the first accessor to collect an owned summary, let that borrow end, and then obtain the second accessor for the update. The ownership of the summary matters: retaining a borrowed component from the first stage while asking for conflicting access in the second would keep the very overlap you're trying to remove, so the borrow rules reject it. Our preview updater doesn't need ParamSet , because its read and write roles really are disjoint. Another design could represent source samples and rendered values with distinct component types. That may be useful if they are different concepts in the application, but it should also make the ownership model easier to explain. Choose between these approaches by the data relationship you need, rather than treating them as interchangeable ways to suppress a diagnostic. Explain the permission that made the refresh safe Return to the rejected system and imagine commenting out the assignment inside its loop. It still declares a mutable query, so why would Bevy now assume that query won't reach a conflicting entity? The permissions arrive in the parameter list before any particular branch of the body runs. When writing is unnecessary, change the requested access itself. Recall answer An ordinary Query<&mut Sample> declares possible mutable access. Validation cannot assume that a branch will avoid the conflicting entity. Change the signature to shared access when writing is unnecessary, establish genuine disjointness when roles differ, or sequence overlapping access deliberately. The query validation and ParamSet contracts used here were checked against the cached bevy_ecs-0.18.1 source. The failing parameter excerpt remains a diagnostic exercise outside the successful reference. Passing the four tests establishes this small projection policy; when reviewing a different system, you'll still need to reason about that system's complete set of accesses. The source can now lend its sample while the preview updates, and the dual-role row stays protected because the signature states the policy. There is another way for a correct refresh to show the wrong value, though: it may run before the source has finished changing. Continue to ordering a schedule deliberately to see how two safe observations can disagree when they occur on different sides of a mutation.

title: Give the observations an order
summary: Bracket one real mutation with two observations. Explain how identical final values can hide different execution histories.
text: You add a “before” reading and an “after” reading to a counter update, expecting to see seven followed by eight. The counter does finish at eight in each of three schedules, but one trace says eight twice and another says seven twice. The arithmetic can be correct while both readings miss the moment they were meant to capture. Isolated Bevy ECS 0.18.1 schedule lab. You will wire three prepared systems around one ordinary counter. This is not an energy formula, simulation tick implementation, or new biological rule. The lab changes no live Moss schedule, and NOW.md remains the active assignment. Make before and after describe real moments You'll wire three supplied systems into a schedule that records the old counter, increments it, and records the new value. We'll derive the two required ordering relationships, predict a second execution, and compare deliberately wrong schedules with the correct one. The useful result is both seven before and eight after; a final counter of eight alone cannot show that the observations happened where they belonged. Safe access does not choose the right order The previous lesson made reading a source and writing a preview safe by proving that their queries reached different entity sets. That gives each system valid access to its data. It leaves another question open: does an observer read that data before the change it is supposed to report, or afterwards? To make our two labels meaningful, we need to express those relationships between systems. Keep the arithmetic small so we can follow that relationship directly. record_before reads the counter and appends a labeled observation; increment adds one to the counter; record_after reads the counter and appends its own observation. Both observers use the value they find in the world. If either one runs at the wrong time, it will faithfully record the wrong stage of the update rather than reconstructing the number we expected. Bevy already knows that these systems cannot all access the counter at once. The observers request shared access to Counter , while increment requests mutable access.
