The observers also both write the trace. Those declarations let the executor prevent incompatible work from overlapping, but either observation can safely happen before or after the mutation. Safety therefore leaves several possible sequences, only one of which meets our reporting requirement. Using a single-threaded executor makes the trace easier to follow because only one system runs at a time. It still leaves those possible sequences open. A system's name and its position in a registration tuple do not supply a guaranteed domain order without explicit dependencies, so changing the executor alone would leave our reporting requirement unstated. Draw the two required edges Start with what each observer needs to see. The “before” observer needs the old counter, so it must finish before increment runs. The “after” observer needs the new counter, so it must run after that mutation. These are the two edges shown below. If a test checks only the final eight, it cannot tell whether either edge was respected. All three traces begin with Counter(7) Explicit execution order Trace and final counter Before → Increment → After Before 7; After 8; final 8. Increment → Before → After Before 8; After 8; final 8. Before → After → Increment Before 7; After 7; final 8. The labels are ordinary values appended by the observer functions. Calling a function record_before does not make Bevy move it earlier: if it executes after the increment, it records “Before 8.” The number accurately describes the state it read. It is our choice of schedule that failed to make the label true. For this three-system sequence, .chain() adds the ordering constraints between successive systems in the tuple. The ordinary default prelude imports the configuration trait that supplies the method. Bevy 0.18.1's versioned schedule-configuration source describes the chain and the related before / after operations, which can express individual edges when a complete sequence is unnecessary. A chain is a good fit here because every pair of neighboring steps has a reason to be ordered. A larger schedule may contain independent work as well. Named system sets and selected edges let you preserve that independence while stating the relationships the model relies on. Drawing the needed dependencies first makes it easier to distinguish a real requirement from an order added merely because the functions appeared next to each other. Predict the next execution Now run the correctly ordered schedule twice, beginning at seven and keeping the trace between runs. The first increment changes the resource in the world; building the schedule did not capture a private copy of its initial value. Use that fact to predict all four observations, especially the second “Before” reading. Hint 1: the schedule owns instructions, not a copied initial counter Each system reads the resources of the world passed to that execution. The first run leaves the counter at eight, so the next run begins from eight. Hint 2: trace append order is part of the evidence The helper does not clear the trace. Preserve both pairs in their actual sequence rather than sorting observations afterward. Prediction answer The trace is Before 7, After 8, Before 8, After 9. The final counter is nine. Sorting the trace would destroy some of the timing evidence; its vector order records the sequence of append operations. Your edit is the body of observation_schedule , so you can focus on expressing those two edges. The three system bodies and world setup are already supplied. Create a single-threaded schedule, add the systems in their required chain, and return it. Reimplementing the counter calculation inside the factory would bypass the integration question the trace is meant to answer. Build and check the schedule Prepare a fresh practice copy from the repository root. The starter should compile and then reach the intentional todo! in the schedule factory. That first failure tells you the runner reached the function you are about to complete. python3 learning/scripts/labs.py prepare schedules --dest work/schedules-practice python3 learning/scripts/labs.py check schedules --file work/schedules-practice/schedules.rs After your edit, expect four named tests to pass. Use any failure to narrow the question: a changed counter with the wrong trace points to timing, while an empty trace suggests the observers may never have been added. Check the registration and dependency configuration before changing arithmetic that already produced the expected final value. Complete starter: schedules.rs use bevy_ecs::{prelude::*, schedule::ExecutorKind}; #[derive(Resource)] struct Counter(u32); #[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)] enum Phase { Before, After } #[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)] struct Observation { phase: Phase, count: u32, } #[derive(Resource, Default)] struct Trace(Vec<Observation>); fn record_before(counter: Res<Counter>, mut trace: ResMut<Trace>) { trace.0.push(Observation { phase: Phase::Before, count: counter.0 }); } fn increment(mut counter: ResMut<Counter>) { counter.0 = counter.0.checked_add(1).expect("counter overflow"); } fn record_after(counter: Res<Counter>, mut trace: ResMut<Trace>) { trace.0.push(Observation { phase: Phase::After, count: counter.0 }); } fn observation_schedule() -> Schedule { todo!("build a single-threaded schedule: before, increment, after") } fn world_at(count: u32) -> World { let mut world = World::new(); Its target directory is separate from the live simulation build. cargo +1.93.1 generate-lockfile CARGO_TARGET_DIR=target cargo +1.93.1 test --locked CARGO_TARGET_DIR=target cargo +1.93.1 run --locked The expected result is four passed tests and exactly this program output: Before 7 After 8 Before 8 After 9 final=9 Test meaning rather than scheduler luck The expected trace gives us a claim to test: each observer saw the intended stage of the update. To see whether the checks can establish it, follow what they read and which wrong schedules they distinguish. The first test reads both observation values and their sequence after one execution. That gives each edge a visible consequence. The second test changes the starting value and executes the schedule twice, so a hard-coded pair of readings cannot satisfy it. In both cases, the assertions examine resources changed by the installed systems; they do not substitute a second helper calculation for the work we wanted to run. To see why those observations matter, the final two tests construct deliberately wrong schedules with explicit ordering. One increments before both observations; the other increments after both. Each still reaches the correct final counter, but each produces a different trace. These counterexamples demonstrate a concrete mistake the trace catches and a counter-only assertion misses. Removing .chain() is a less reliable way to demonstrate the mistake. An unconstrained scheduler might happen to choose the desired order in your current build, so the trace could still pass on that run. The explicitly wrong schedules make the counterexample reproducible. When reviewing the real configuration, also look for the declared dependencies: an observed success alone cannot establish an ordering promise the program never made. The same reasoning explains why switching executors would not repair the missing relationship. The 0.18.1 executor reference describes the available execution modes, but the application still has to say which valid system must precede another. This lab uses one thread to simplify observation and explicit edges to establish meaning. Registration and order are separate responsibilities There are two places to check when expected work is absent. First, the function must actually be added to the schedule you run; defining it in a Rust module does not arrange an execution. Then its dependencies must be configured within that schedule. An ordering expression in another schedule cannot organize this run just because it names the same function. When using before or after , find both ends of the relationship and confirm that the referenced systems or sets are present in the relevant schedule. Mentioning a function as the other end of an edge does not replace registering its work. Our add_systems call and chain put registration and order together, making both responsibilities visible in one place. You can trace the same relationship in Moss's current crates/moss-sim/src/simulation.rs : its installed chain runs maintenance before complete_tick . The completed-tick count consequently describes scheduled work that has already finished. The prepared movement adapter is still absent at this checkpoint. It joins that sequence only after review of the active exercise and the explicit transition described in its guide; an isolated helper passing does not install its system. The vector is enough for this short experiment because we execute the schedule only once or twice. Keeping observations indefinitely in a browser would introduce further requirements: identities to say what was observed, a retention limit, and coverage labels to explain what remains. Correct timing gives a record its meaning, but it does not by itself make an unlimited journal a suitable design. Give each observation its place in the schedule Return to the original counter that reached eight under every schedule. Explain why its final value was insufficient, using the access declarations, the two ordering edges, and the collected trace. Each supplies a different part of the explanation. Recall answer Access declarations constrain which work can safely overlap. The chain supplies required relative execution order. The trace records the values actually observed during this specific run. A final counter alone could agree while either observation phase was misplaced. The schedule methods, chain semantics, and executor choice were checked against cached Bevy ECS 0.18.1 source and its versioned references. The lesson's native checks exercise a miniature installed schedule; they do not execute the real Moss schedule or verify browser presentation. No claim about deferred commands is implied by ordinary resource mutation here. The readings can now say seven and eight for a reason we have expressed and checked: one observer runs before the mutation and the other after it. The next module keeps that observation question but changes how the mutation happens. A structural change queued through commands is applied later, so even a correctly ordered observer needs to run on the right side of that application point.

title: Change structure at a known boundary
summary: Follow a queued row across an explicit application point, then retain an observation after its entity is gone.
text: The enqueue system has just saved a handle for a new row, but the next observer cannot find the row's components. Later in the same schedule, another observer finds application ID 7. Both readings can be correct if requesting the change and applying it happen at different moments. Isolated Bevy ECS 0.18.1 lab. The entities are report rows in a separate world. No creature is born or removed, and no biological behavior is installed. You will wire one schedule around deferred commands; the live assignment remains in NOW.md . Locate the moment a queued row becomes visible You'll wire enqueueing, a pending observer, an explicit application step, and a visible observer into one schedule. We first need to understand the manual settings that make those stages observable, then distinguish an ECS handle from the application identity copied into the trace. The finished run should explain why the first observer sees no row, the second sees ID 7, and the saved ID remains after removal. A request is not yet a component The previous lesson placed observers around an ordinary resource mutation. Once the increment system returned, that changed resource was available to the next reader. Structural work can take a different route: Commands records operations such as spawning, inserting components, and despawning for later application with exclusive world access. Ordering a reader after the system that requested a change is therefore only part of the visibility question. A queued spawn can reserve an entity handle before its components are query-visible. That allows further commands to refer to the intended entity while the structural work is pending. The versioned Commands reference describes this queue and its application; when following our example, keep the handle reservation separate from the later insertion of the row's components. Our enqueue system makes the distinction observable by doing some ordinary resource work alongside the queued spawn. It advances the application-ID counter and saves the reserved entity handle immediately. A later system can read those resources even while the row's component insertion remains pending. Seeing one effect of the enqueue system therefore does not tell us that every effect has reached the world yet. This explains the apparently contradictory log: “I have an entity handle, but the query finds nothing.” The saved handle shows that the request was made. The query answers whether matching components are available at the time it runs. Before changing its filter, follow the schedule far enough to find where the queued insertion is applied. Make the application point explicit There is a detail of Bevy 0.18.1 we need to control before making that experiment. Bevy can automatically insert deferred-application systems along ordering dependencies, so an ordinary chain following a command-producing system may already make the change visible. If we left that behavior implicit, our intended “pending” observer might run after an application we had not shown in the lesson. The supplied manual_schedule disables auto_insert_apply_deferred so the intermediate application point is ours to place. It also selects a single-threaded executor and explicitly enables final deferred application when the schedule ends. Inside that controlled sequence, your schedule will put ApplyDeferred between the pending observer and the visible observer. With those settings, we can distinguish three moments: before the chosen application point, immediately after it, and after the whole run returns. That is why this experiment changes the defaults. A different schedule configuration could have different visibility, so carrying the expected readings to another application requires checking its settings as well; there is no general need to disable automatic application throughout Moss. First execution in an initially empty lab world Phase What the observer can establish Enqueue the row An entity handle is saved and AppId(7) is queued for insertion. Observe pending work The AppId query still yields no rows under the explicit manual settings. Run ApplyDeferred The queued structural work is applied to the world. Observe visible rows The AppId query yields AppId(7). Notice that ApplyDeferred occupies its own place in the schedule. Bevy's executor recognizes that system and applies buffered work from systems that have already run. Merely putting the two observers in order would not perform that application under our manual settings. The schedule needs both the relationship between the readers and the operation that changes what the second reader can see. Separate application identity from an ECS handle The saved handle and the reported ID also serve different purposes. Entity is the handle this world uses to locate its current ECS entity. AppId(7) is application data we allocate and copy into an observation. After removal, that copied ID can still say which report row was observed, even though the handle no longer resolves to a living entity. That historical meaning depends on how we allocate IDs. The lab's NextId resource advances monotonically with checked arithmetic, preserving uniqueness during the run. If we reset the allocator but keep old records, another row could receive 7. We would then need a run identifier or another uniqueness policy to distinguish them. Moss includes a run context in retained identities for this reason. The trace can retain ID 7 because its vectors own copied values rather than references to components. Despawning the row removes those components from the world; it does not reach into a separate vector and erase an earlier observation. This is the ownership boundary we have used for reports, now applied to something whose current existence can end. Owning the records solves their lifetime problem, but it also makes us responsible for how long to keep them. This test runs only once or twice, so its small trace has no retention limit. A browser history needs a limit and visible coverage so the reader can tell which part of the past remains available. Predict two visibility boundaries Try removing the explicit ApplyDeferred step in your prediction, while leaving final application enabled. Follow the schedule to the visible observer first: has anything applied the queued insertion by then? Next follow it to the return from schedule.run . Separating those two moments should let you explain how an empty recorded observation and a current row can both be correct. Hint 1: keep the build settings in view Automatic intermediate application is disabled. Without the explicit step, neither scheduled observer runs after an application point. Hint 2: a saved observation is not updated afterward The final application can insert the row before the schedule call returns. It cannot change the earlier vector of IDs already copied into the trace. Prediction answer Both observers record empty vectors, but the row exists after the run returns because final application is enabled. The word “Visible” is only the observer's label; it does not create visibility. Its placement determines what it sees. Wire one schedule Now express the sequence in command_schedule , the only unfinished function. Use the supplied manual settings, then chain enqueue, pending observation, explicit application, and visible observation in that order. Prepare a separate practice file from the repository root so you can change this schedule without touching the live world. python3 learning/scripts/labs.py prepare commands --dest work/commands-practice python3 learning/scripts/labs.py check commands --file work/commands-practice/commands.rs The starter initially reaches its deliberate todo! . Once you complete the schedule, expect four named tests to pass. If the pending observer already sees ID 7, look for an automatic application point. If the visible observer sees nothing even though the row exists after the run, look for the missing intermediate application. Those two failures tell you about different parts of the configuration. Complete starter: commands.rs use bevy_ecs::{prelude::*, schedule::{ExecutorKind, ScheduleBuildSettings}}; #[derive(Component, Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq, PartialOrd, Ord)] struct AppId(u64); #[derive(Resource)] struct NextId(u64); #[derive(Resource, Default)] struct Handles(Vec<Entity>); #[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)] struct Seen { phase: &'static str, ids: Vec<AppId> } #[derive(Resource, Default)] struct Trace(Vec<Seen>); fn enqueue_row(mut commands: Commands, mut next: ResMut<NextId>, mut handles: ResMut<Handles>) { let id = AppId(next.0); next.0 = next.0.checked_add(1).expect("application ID overflow"); handles.0.push(commands.spawn(id).id()); } fn observe_pending(rows: Query<&AppId>, mut trace: ResMut<Trace>) { let mut ids: Vec<_> = rows.iter().copied().collect(); ids.sort(); trace.0.push(Seen { phase: "Pending", ids }); } fn observe_visible(rows: Query<&AppId>, mut trace: ResMut<Trace>) { let mut ids: Vec<_> = rows.iter().copied().collect(); ids.sort(); trace.0.push(Seen { phase: "Visible", ids }); } fn manual_schedule() -> Schedule { let mut schedule = Schedule::default(); schedule.set_executor_kind(ExecutorKind::SingleThreaded); schedule.set_build_settings(ScheduleBuildSettings { auto_insert_apply_deferred: false, ..Default::default() }); schedule.set_apply_final_deferred(true); schedule } fn command_schedule() -> Schedule { todo!("queue, observe pending, explicitly apply, then observe visible") } fn empty_world() -> World { let mut world = World::new(); world.insert_resource(NextId(7)); world.init_resource::<Handles>(); world.init_resource::<Trace>(); world } fn main() { let mut world = empty_world(); command_schedule().run(&mut world); for seen in &world.resource::<Trace>().0 { println!("{}: {:?}", seen.phase, seen.ids); } let handle = world.resource::<Handles>().0[0]; assert!(world.despawn(handle)); let count = world.query::<&AppId>().iter(&world).count(); println!("after removal: entities={} retained={:?}", count, world.resource::<Trace>().0[1].ids); } #[cfg(test)] mod tests { use super::*; #[test] fn queued_row_becomes_queryable_at_explicit_application() { let mut world = empty_world(); command_schedule().run(&mut world); assert_eq!(world.resource::<Trace>().0, vec![ Seen { phase: "Pending", ids: vec![] }, Seen { phase: "Visible", ids: vec![AppId(7)] }, ]); let handle = world.resource::<Handles>().0[0]; assert_eq!(world.get::<AppId>(handle), Some(&AppId(7))); } #[test] fn final_application_does_not_rewrite_an_earlier_observation() { let mut world = empty_world(); let mut schedule = manual_schedule(); schedule.add_systems((enqueue_row, observe_pending, observe_visible).chain()); schedule.run(&mut world); assert_eq!(world.resource::<Trace>().0, vec![ Seen { phase: "Pending", ids: vec![] }, Seen { phase: "Visible", ids: vec![] }, ]); let handle = world.resource::<Handles>().0[0]; assert_eq!(world.get::<AppId>(handle), Some(&AppId(7))); } #[test] fn retained_application_id_survives_entity_removal() { let mut world = empty_world(); command_schedule().run(&mut world); let handle = world.resource::<Handles>().0[0]; assert!(world.despawn(handle)); assert!(world.get_entity(handle).is_err()); assert_eq!(world.query::<&AppId>().iter(&world).count(), 0); assert_eq!(world.resource::<Trace>().0[1].ids, vec![AppId(7)]); } #[test] fn another_execution_preserves_old_rows_and_allocates_a_new_id() { let mut world = empty_world(); let mut schedule = command_schedule(); schedule.run(&mut world); schedule.run(&mut world); assert_eq!(world.resource::<Trace>().0[2..], [ Seen { phase: "Pending", ids: vec![AppId(7)] }, Seen { phase: "Visible", ids: vec![AppId(7), AppId(8)] }, ]); assert_eq!(world.resource::<NextId>().0, 9); } } Complete worked answer: commands.rs use bevy_ecs::{prelude::*, schedule::{ExecutorKind, ScheduleBuildSettings}}; #[derive(Component, Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq, PartialOrd, Ord)] struct AppId(u64); #[derive(Resource)] struct NextId(u64); #[derive(Resource, Default)] struct Handles(Vec<Entity>); #[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)] struct Seen { phase: &'static str, ids: Vec<AppId> } #[derive(Resource, Default)] struct Trace(Vec<Seen>); fn enqueue_row(mut commands: Commands, mut next: ResMut<NextId>, mut handles: ResMut<Handles>) { let id = AppId(next.0); next.0 = next.0.checked_add(1).expect("application ID overflow"); handles.0.push(commands.spawn(id).id()); } fn observe_pending(rows: Query<&AppId>, mut trace: ResMut<Trace>) { let mut ids: Vec<_> = rows.iter().copied().collect(); ids.sort(); trace.0.push(Seen { phase: "Pending", ids }); } fn observe_visible(rows: Query<&AppId>, mut trace: ResMut<Trace>) { let mut ids: Vec<_> = rows.iter().copied().collect(); ids.sort(); trace.0.push(Seen { phase: "Visible", ids }); } fn manual_schedule() -> Schedule { let mut schedule = Schedule::default(); schedule.set_executor_kind(ExecutorKind::SingleThreaded); schedule.set_build_settings(ScheduleBuildSettings { auto_insert_apply_deferred: false, ..Default::default() }); schedule.set_apply_final_deferred(true); schedule } fn command_schedule() -> Schedule { let mut schedule = manual_schedule(); schedule.add_systems((enqueue_row, observe_pending, ApplyDeferred, observe_visible).chain()); schedule } fn empty_world() -> World { let mut world = World::new(); world.insert_resource(NextId(7)); world.init_resource::<Handles>(); world.init_resource::<Trace>(); world } fn main() { let mut world = empty_world(); command_schedule().run(&mut world); for seen in &world.resource::<Trace>().0 { println!("{}: {:?}", seen.phase, seen.ids); } let handle = world.resource::<Handles>().0[0]; assert!(world.despawn(handle)); let count = world.query::<&AppId>().iter(&world).count(); println!("after removal: entities={} retained={:?}", count, world.resource::<Trace>().0[1].ids); } #[cfg(test)] mod tests { use super::*; #[test] fn queued_row_becomes_queryable_at_explicit_application() { let mut world = empty_world(); command_schedule().run(&mut world); assert_eq!(world.resource::<Trace>().0, vec![ Seen { phase: "Pending", ids: vec![] }, Seen { phase: "Visible", ids: vec![AppId(7)] }, ]); let handle = world.resource::<Handles>().0[0]; assert_eq!(world.get::<AppId>(handle), Some(&AppId(7))); } #[test] fn final_application_does_not_rewrite_an_earlier_observation() { let mut world = empty_world(); let mut schedule = manual_schedule(); schedule.add_systems((enqueue_row, observe_pending, observe_visible).chain()); schedule.run(&mut world); assert_eq!(world.resource::<Trace>().0, vec![ Seen { phase: "Pending", ids: vec![] }, Seen { phase: "Visible", ids: vec![] }, ]); let handle = world.resource::<Handles>().0[0]; assert_eq!(world.get::<AppId>(handle), Some(&AppId(7))); } #[test] fn retained_application_id_survives_entity_removal() { let mut world = empty_world(); command_schedule().run(&mut world); let handle = world.resource::<Handles>().0[0]; assert!(world.despawn(handle)); assert!(world.get_entity(handle).is_err()); assert_eq!(world.query::<&AppId>().iter(&world).count(), 0); assert_eq!(world.resource::<NextId>().0, 9); } } Use python3 learning/scripts/labs.py check commands for the printed reference. For a manual Cargo check, save a full block as src/main.rs in a fresh scratch package and use this manifest: [package] name = "moss-command-lab" version = "0.1.0" edition = "2024" publish = false [workspace] [dependencies] bevy_ecs = { version = "=0.18.1", default-features = false, features = ["std"] } Run these commands from that package, retaining its generated lockfile: cargo +1.93.1 generate-lockfile CARGO_TARGET_DIR=target cargo +1.93.1 test --locked CARGO_TARGET_DIR=target cargo +1.93.1 run --locked The expected test result is four passed tests. The literal expected program output is: Pending: [] Visible: [AppId(7)] after removal: entities=0 retained=[AppId(7)] Read the retained record carefully Visibility explains how the row enters the report. We can now test the other half of the record's purpose: retaining what was observed after the row is gone. After the schedule finishes, the program calls World::despawn directly. This immediate operation lets the removal test ask two questions independently: does the old handle still resolve, and does the trace still contain ID 7? It should find no current row and still find the recorded ID. Because this removal is direct, the test is about retained observation rather than the timing of a queued despawn. The last test keeps the first row and executes the same schedule again. This time the pending observer already sees ID 7, while the visible observer sees IDs 7 and 8. “Pending” describes the new insertion waiting to be applied; it does not imply an otherwise empty world. Starting the second run with existing state makes that distinction visible. Within each observation, we sort the copied IDs so membership can be compared without relying on query iteration order. Across observations, we preserve the outer vector's execution order. Sorting that outer sequence would erase the timing we are investigating, even though sorting the members of each individual snapshot makes the result easier to read. Do not treat queued removal as a lock Keep this visibility boundary in mind when we later resolve competing consumers. Suppose the first consumer queues removal of a food entity, then a second queries that food before the queue is applied. The components may still be available, so the pending despawn alone has not prevented a second reward. Our missing-row puzzle has become a question about who is still allowed to act. A resolver needs an authoritative availability change at the point where it accepts the outcome, followed by tests in which consumers compete for the same resource. Cleanup can then follow under the chosen command-application policy. We have not implemented that biological rule here, but we have established why acceptance and pending cleanup cannot be treated as the same event. Keep the request, the world, and the record distinct Use the opening row to explain both boundaries back to yourself. Why can the application retain ID 7 after its entity is removed? And why can the row exist after the schedule returns even though an earlier observer recorded an empty result? In each answer, identify the state being read and the moment it was read. Recall answer The retained ID is owned application data whose identity policy survives removal of this ECS entity. A snapshot copies what was visible at its observation time. Later structural application or removal changes the current world, not the contents of an earlier snapshot. The manual build settings, final-application control, and ApplyDeferred behavior were checked against cached Bevy ECS 0.18.1 source. Our tests establish the readings for this particular configuration. We can now explain the opening result by following the queued request to its application, rather than assuming a query lost a row. Continue to choosing evidence that can disagree with your implementation to turn that kind of explanation into checks that expose incorrect helpers, wiring, and presentation.

title: Make a test disagree with a plausible mistake
summary: Separate a correct helper from correct selection, schedule wiring, and the value an observer actually saw.
text: The percentage helper passes its tests, but the inspector still says 99. You fix the update and now its current value is 37, yet a downstream observer still records 99. Before changing the arithmetic again, we need evidence about the rest of that path: which sample was selected, whether the projection ran, and when the observer read its result. Isolated evidence lab. These are presentation samples in a miniature Bevy ECS 0.18.1 world. You will complete a projection system and investigate deliberately incomplete or misordered schedules. Nothing is installed into Moss, and the live movement exercise remains unchanged. Choose a check that can expose the mistake First you'll complete a projection and compare the value it leaves with the value its observer actually saw. Then you'll write your own tests and try them against six supplied defects, using their failures or survival to improve the evidence. The optional compiled-Rust panel extends that investigation into the browser. Throughout, the goal is to connect each claim to a check that reaches the part of the program capable of making it false. Name the claim before choosing a check Start by making the claim small enough to check. “The percentage is correct” might mean the helper floors a fraction correctly, the system chooses the intended entity, an observer sees the updated result, or the browser displays it. A test must reach the part of the program that could make its particular claim false. Otherwise the test can remain green while the defect survives somewhere it never looked. Give those possibilities different visible results. The selected sample contains three used units out of eight, which our floor-based reporting rule turns into 37. An unselected sample contains one out of two and would produce 50. The display begins at a stale 99. Choosing these distinct values is part of designing the fixture: 50 suggests the wrong input, while 99 suggests that an old value reached the observation. The projection writes a DisplayValue resource, and the observer copies that resource into a trace. Checking the resource tells us where the projection eventually left the world; checking the trace tells us what its consumer actually read. This is a native consumer in our miniature schedule. It lets us test the timing relationship before adding the separate question of browser presentation. Evidence for each claim in the lab Claim Discriminating check The helper's numeric contract holds. Test fractional rounding, a value beyond capacity, zero capacity, and large representable inputs. The system reads the selected row. Include an unselected row with a different result and assert the selected result in the display. The observer sees the current projection. Start with a distinct stale value and assert the actual trace after running the configured schedule. A browser presents the current value. Exercise the built browser control and inspect its real displayed value, separately from these native tests. A helper is a local contract The supplied percentage helper has a deliberately local job. Given used units and capacity, it returns absence for zero capacity, caps an amount above capacity, and floors the percentage otherwise. It widens the intermediate arithmetic to u64 before multiplying by 100, so a valid large u32 input does not overflow during that calculation. Neither integer tells the helper which entity was selected or when a system should execute. That makes its arithmetic easy to test in isolation: if an input produces the wrong percentage, there are few possible causes to inspect. It also explains why those tests cannot establish selection or scheduling behavior. Those relationships need fixtures that actually contain them. Your edit belongs in project_selected , where the query requests samples carrying Selected . When exactly one sample matches, the system projects it through the supplied helper. When no sample or several samples match, it must clear the display to None . Leaving 99 untouched would make an unsuccessful selection look like a successful reading retained from the previous run. For this exercise, both zero capacity and nonunique selection lead to an unavailable display. A fuller interface could keep their reasons distinct, as the Result lesson did. Our immediate requirement is narrower: the display must contain a newly justified value or explicitly say none is available. That gives the projection a useful contract without adding error wording to the task. Let the world supply the result To check that contract in use, install the projection and observer as real Bevy systems and chain them in that order. The integration fixture creates their entities and resources, executes the schedule, and reads the changed display and collected trace. It asks the world for evidence of what ran. Calculating the percentage a second time in a test would only repeat the arithmetic and leave the schedule unexamined. Inside the projection body, single asks the query for exactly one matching item. The Bevy 0.18.1 Query documentation for single specifies the returned result. Handling its error explicitly lets the system enforce our uniqueness requirement instead of accepting whichever row an iteration happens to visit first. Follow the signature and body together. A perfectly correct call to percentage produces 50 if the query gives it the unselected sample. A perfectly correct projection produces nothing if the schedule never calls it. The two-row fixture and installed schedule bring both opportunities for failure within the test's reach. The deferred-command lesson showed why we also retain an observer: a row could exist when the schedule returned yet have been absent at the moment an earlier system looked. Here the display could finish at 37 after the observer already copied 99. Reading final state would miss that mistake, so the trace preserves the earlier moment for an assertion. Predict two plausible defects Use that distinction to predict two defects before running them. In a world beginning with stale display 99, omit the projection and run only the observer. Then start a fresh world at 99 and run the observer before the projection. For each schedule, predict the final display and the trace separately; follow the writes and copies in order rather than letting the eventual result overwrite your memory of what happened earlier. Hint 1: a passing helper does not execute itself The incomplete schedule never calls the projection. No system changes the display before the observer reads it. Hint 2: later writes cannot refresh an owned trace entry The reversed schedule eventually updates the current display, but the observer already copied its previous value into the trace. Prediction answer Omitting projection leaves both display and trace at 99. Reversing the systems leaves the final display at 37 but records 99 in the trace. Only the correctly ordered schedule both displays 37 and records 37. The supplied tests deliberately run those wrong schedules and check the predicted differences. Such a test passes when it exposes the counterexample correctly. The normal installed schedule has its own assertion requiring 37 in both places. Reading which schedule a test built is therefore part of understanding what its green result establishes. Complete the one projection body Now complete project_selected in a separate practice file prepared from the repository root. Its query and helper are supplied, so your body can focus on the two outcomes: project the single selected sample, or clear the old display when there is no unique sample. Keep the edit within that function. python3 learning/scripts/labs.py prepare evidence --dest work/evidence-practice python3 learning/scripts/labs.py check evidence --file work/evidence-practice/evidence.rs Initially, checks that reach the projection fail at its deliberate todo! . Helper tests and an omitted-system counterexample may already pass because neither needs that unfinished body. Use the whole checkpoint result to judge completion: all six canonical tests must pass and the program must run. Individual green rows tell you which paths already work, not whether the unfinished path can be ignored. Complete starter: evidence.rs use bevy_ecs::{prelude::*, schedule::ExecutorKind}; #[derive(Component)] struct Selected; #[derive(Component)] struct Sample { used: u32, capacity: u32 } #[derive(Resource)] struct DisplayValue(Option<u32>); #[derive(Resource, Default)] struct Trace(Vec<Option<u32>>); fn percentage(used: u32, capacity: u32) -> Option<u32> { if capacity == 0 { return None; } Some(((u64::from(used.min(capacity)) * 100) / u64::from(capacity)) as u32) } fn project_selected( samples: Query<&Sample, With<Selected>>, mut display: ResMut<DisplayValue>, ) { let _ = (samples, &mut display); todo!("project one selected row; clear the display when selection is not unique") } fn observe_display(display: Res<DisplayValue>, mut trace: ResMut<Trace>) { trace.0.push(display.0); } fn installed_schedule() -> Schedule { let mut schedule = Schedule::default(); schedule.set_executor_kind(ExecutorKind::SingleThreaded); schedule.add_systems((project_selected, observe_display).chain()); schedule } fn fixture() -> World { let mut world = World::new(); world.insert_resource(DisplayValue(Some(99))); world.init_resource::<Trace>(); world.spawn(Sample { used: 1, capacity: 2 }); world.spawn((Selected, Sample { used: 3, capacity: 8 })); world } fn main() { let mut world = fixture(); installed_schedule().run(&mut world); println!("display={:?} trace={:?}", world.resource::<DisplayValue>().0, world.resource::<Trace>().0); } #[cfg(test)] mod tests { use super::*; #[test] fn helper_defines_rounding_bounds_and_zero_capacity() { assert_eq!(percentage(3, 8), Some(37)); assert_eq!(percentage(9, 8), Some(100)); assert_eq!(percentage(0, 0), None); assert_eq!(percentage(u32::MAX, u32::MAX), Some(100)); } #[test] fn installed_projection_uses_the_selected_row_before_observation() { let mut world = fixture(); installed_schedule().run(&mut world); assert_eq!(world.resource::<DisplayValue>().0, Some(37)); assert_eq!(world.resource::<Trace>().0, vec![Some(37)]); } #[test] fn no_selected_row_clears_a_previous_display_value() { let mut world = fixture(); let selected: Vec<_> = world.query_filtered::<Entity, With<Selected>>() .iter(&world).collect(); for entity in selected { world.entity_mut(entity).remove::<Selected>(); } installed_schedule().run(&mut world); assert_eq!(world.resource::<DisplayValue>().0, None); assert_eq!(world.resource::<Trace>().0, vec![None]); } #[test] fn multiple_selected_rows_do_not_silently_pick_one() { let mut world = fixture(); world.spawn((Selected, Sample { used: 1, capacity: 2 })); installed_schedule().run(&mut world); assert_eq!(world.resource::<DisplayValue>().0, None); assert_eq!(world.resource::<Trace>().0, vec![None]); } #[test] fn a_green_helper_does_not_detect_an_omitted_system() { assert_eq!(percentage(3, 8), Some(37)); let mut world = fixture(); let mut incomplete = Schedule::default(); incomplete.set_executor_kind(ExecutorKind::SingleThreaded); incomplete.add_systems(observe_display); incomplete.run(&mut world); assert_eq!(world.resource::<DisplayValue>().0, Some(99)); assert_eq!(world.resource::<Trace>().0, vec![Some(99)]); assert_ne!(world.resource::<Trace>().0, vec![Some(37)]); } #[test] fn correct_final_display_can_hide_an_early_observer() { let mut world = fixture(); let mut reversed = Schedule::default(); reversed.set_executor_kind(ExecutorKind::SingleThreaded); reversed.add_systems((observe_display, project_selected).chain()); reversed.run(&mut world); assert_eq!(world.resource::<DisplayValue>().0, Some(37)); assert_eq!(world.resource::<Trace>().0, vec![Some(99)]); assert_ne!(world.resource::<Trace>().0, vec![Some(37)]); } } Complete worked answer: evidence.rs use bevy_ecs::{prelude::*, schedule::ExecutorKind}; #[derive(Component)] struct Selected; #[derive(Component)] struct Sample { used: u32, capacity: u32 } #[derive(Resource)] struct DisplayValue(Option<u32>); #[derive(Resource, Default)] struct Trace(Vec<Option<u32>>); fn percentage(used: u32, capacity: u32) -> Option<u32> { if capacity == 0 { return None; } Some(((u64::from(used.min(capacity)) * 100) / u64::from(capacity)) as u32) } fn project_selected( samples: Query<&Sample, With<Selected>>, mut display: ResMut<DisplayValue>, ) { display.0 = match samples.single() { Ok(sample) => percentage(sample.used, sample.capacity), Err(_) => None, }; } fn observe_display(display: Res<DisplayValue>, mut trace: ResMut<Trace>) { trace.0.push(display.0); } fn installed_schedule() -> Schedule { let mut schedule = Schedule::default(); schedule.set_executor_kind(ExecutorKind::SingleThreaded); schedule.add_systems((project_selected, observe_display).chain()); schedule } fn fixture() -> World { let mut world = World::new(); world.insert_resource(DisplayValue(Some(99))); world.init_resource::<Trace>(); world.spawn(Sample { used: 1, capacity: 2 }); world.spawn((Selected, Sample { used: 3, capacity: 8 })); world } fn main() { let mut world = fixture(); installed_schedule().run(&mut world); println!("display={:?} trace={:?}", world.resource::<DisplayValue>().0, world.resource::<Trace>().0); } #[cfg(test)] mod tests { use super::*; #[test] fn helper_defines_rounding_bounds_and_zero_capacity() { assert_eq!(percentage(3, 8), Some(37)); assert_eq!(percentage(9, 8), Some(100)); assert_eq!(percentage(0, 0), None); assert_eq!(percentage(u32::MAX, u32::MAX), Some(100)); } #[test] fn installed_projection_uses_the_selected_row_before_observation() { let mut world = fixture(); installed_schedule().run(&mut world); assert_eq!(world.resource::<DisplayValue>().0, Some(37)); assert_eq!(world.resource::<Trace>().0, vec![Some(37)]); } #[test] fn no_selected_row_clears_a_previous_display_value() { let mut world = fixture(); let selected: Vec<_> = world.query_filtered::<Entity, With<Selected>>() .iter(&world).collect(); for entity in selected { world.entity_mut(entity).remove::<Selected>(); } installed_schedule().run(&mut world); assert_eq!(world.resource::<DisplayValue>().0, None); assert_eq!(world.resource::<Trace>().0, vec![None]); } #[test] fn multiple_selected_rows_do_not_silently_pick_one() { let mut world = fixture(); world.spawn((Selected, Sample { used: 1, capacity: 2 })); installed_schedule().run(&mut world); assert_eq!(world.resource::<DisplayValue>().0, None); assert_eq!(world.resource::<Trace>().0, vec![None]); } #[test] fn a_green_helper_does_not_detect_an_omitted_system() { assert_eq!(percentage(3, 8), Some(37)); let mut world = fixture(); let mut incomplete = Schedule::default(); incomplete.set_executor_kind(ExecutorKind::SingleThreaded); incomplete.add_systems(observe_display); incomplete.run(&mut world); assert_eq!(world.resource::<DisplayValue>().0, Some(99)); assert_eq!(world.resource::<Trace>().0, vec![Some(99)]); assert_ne!(world.resource::<Trace>().0, vec![Some(37)]); } #[test] fn correct_final_display_can_hide_an_early_observer() { let mut world = fixture(); let mut reversed = Schedule::default(); reversed.set_executor_kind(ExecutorKind::SingleThreaded); reversed.add_systems((observe_display, project_selected).chain()); reversed.run(&mut world); assert_eq!(world.resource::<DisplayValue>().0, Some(37)); assert_eq!(world.resource::<Trace>().0, vec![Some(99)]); assert_ne!(world.resource::<Trace>().0, vec![Some(37)]); } } Check the printed reference with python3 learning/scripts/labs.py check evidence . The command with --file checks your body against the course's reference tests. For a direct native run, save a full block as src/main.rs in a fresh scratch package with this manifest: [package] name = "moss-evidence-lab" version = "0.1.0" edition = "2024" publish = false [workspace] [dependencies] bevy_ecs = { version = "=0.18.1", default-features = false, features = ["std"] } Run these commands from the scratch package, retaining its generated lockfile: cargo +1.93.1 generate-lockfile CARGO_TARGET_DIR=target cargo +1.93.1 test --locked CARGO_TARGET_DIR=target cargo +1.93.1 run --locked Expect six passed tests and the literal program output display=Some(37) trace=[Some(37)] . The pair now connects the selected sample to the installed projection and its downstream observer. It resolves the two different stale-value failures from the opening, within this miniature world. Know which kind of red you see When a check fails, first locate how far execution got. A missing toolchain prevents the intended compilation; a compiler diagnostic prevents the test assertion from running. An assertion failure means the program did run and its observation disagreed with the expected result. The starter's todo! is another runtime failure with a known cause: you reached an unfinished body. These cases call for different repairs, even though they can all appear as a failed command. A successful exit also needs interpretation. If a filter selects zero tests, none of the intended assertions ran. For a focused manual check, list the available test names before selecting the complete name with --exact . The following commands identify and run one precise integration check in this package: cargo +1.93.1 test --locked -- --list cargo +1.93.1 test --locked tests::installed_projection_uses_the_selected_row_before_observation -- --exact That focused command should report one passed test. The course runner similarly checks that the canonical named tests were discovered and passed, so an empty selection cannot count as completion. The Rust Book's test-running chapter explains the filtering rules and harness output when you need to interpret another selection. Write evidence that the broken program cannot satisfy So far, the course supplied the assertions and you repaired the implementation. Now keep the implementation fixed and choose the evidence yourself. The starting test checks percentage(1, 2) == Some(50) . It accepts the correct program, but it also accepts six deliberately defective versions, including one whose schedule never projects anything. That result gives us a concrete question for test design: what observation would make each wrong program disagree with the right one? The test-design command runs your actual test file, so it differs from the implementation checker that substitutes canonical tests. It first requires your tests to pass against the correct program. It then compiles each of six wrong programs and runs the same tests against them. A defect counts as detected only when its program compiles and a named test fails. A compiler error, ignored test, or empty selection cannot show that an assertion distinguished the behavior. python3 learning/scripts/evidence_practice.py prepare --dest work/evidence-test-design python3 learning/scripts/evidence_practice.py check --file work/evidence-test-design/evidence_tests.rs Prepare the file, then edit evidence_tests.rs by adding or changing ordinary #[test] functions. The runner places them in a test module beside the exact reference implementation above, where fixture , installed_schedule , DisplayValue , and Trace are already available. You can exercise those pieces directly without copying an implementation or main into the file. Preparation refuses an existing directory so a new attempt preserves your earlier tests. Complete initial test file: evidence_tests.rs #[test] fn an_exact_half_looks_reassuring() { assert_eq!(percentage(1, 2), Some(50)); } On the first run, the correct reference should pass and all six defects should survive . Every executed assertion can be green while the command exits unsuccessfully, because the test suite has not yet distinguished any of the wrong programs. This is useful feedback about the question your test asked. Unlike the starter's unfinished todo! , the test body ran; its one half-capacity example simply allowed all seven implementations to agree. Six stated defects your tests should reject Defect What a weak check misses Round a fractional percentage upward. An exact half has no rounding decision. Multiply inside u32 , wrapping before division. Small samples fit the intermediate calculation. Project the unselected row. A helper test has no selection or entity membership. Omit projection from the installed schedule. The helper remains correct when nothing calls it. Observe before projection. The final display can be correct after the observer already recorded stale data. Keep the old display when selection is absent or ambiguous. A fixture with exactly one selected row never reaches the error branch. Begin separating them by choosing a fractional input and writing its literal expected percentage. Then choose a large valid input that exercises the widened arithmetic. To investigate the installed behavior, run the real schedule in the supplied two-row fixture and inspect the observer's trace as well as current display. Finally change which rows carry the selection marker and decide what must replace stale 99 when there is no unique sample. Write each expectation before running it. Calling percentage to calculate the expected display would let the same arithmetic mistake supply both the actual result and its supposed check. Hint: why final state alone lets the ordering defect survive The reversed schedule records 99 and then updates the current display to 37. If your test checks only the final display, the wrong order passes. The trace is the evidence that the dependent observer saw the current value. Keep the stale starting value distinct from the expected result. Complete worked test file #[test] fn a_fraction_requires_flooring() { assert_eq!(percentage(3, 8), Some(37)); } #[test] fn a_large_full_sample_is_still_full() { assert_eq!(percentage(u32::MAX, u32::MAX), Some(100)); } #[test] fn the_installed_observer_sees_the_selected_projection() { let mut world = fixture(); installed_schedule().run(&mut world); assert_eq!(world.resource::<DisplayValue>().0, Some(37)); assert_eq!(world.resource::<Trace>().0, vec![Some(37)]); } #[test] fn unavailable_selection_clears_the_display_and_observation() { for selected_count in [0, 2] { let mut world = fixture(); if selected_count == 0 { let selected: Vec<_> = world .query_filtered::<Entity, With<Selected>>() .iter(&world) .collect(); assert_eq!(selected.len(), 1); for entity in selected { world.entity_mut(entity).remove::<Selected>(); } } else { world.spawn((Selected, Sample { used: 1, capacity: 2 })); } installed_schedule().run(&mut world); assert_eq!(world.resource::<DisplayValue>().0, None); assert_eq!(world.resource::<Trace>().0, vec![None]); } } The worked answer groups these distinctions into four tests. Your tests can use other names and groupings, provided they accept the correct behavior and produce an observable disagreement with every one of the six defects. To run the printed answer separately, use python3 learning/scripts/evidence_practice.py check --answer . Its output says WORKED ANSWER so you can distinguish that demonstration from evidence about your own saved file. Read the result as a mapping from each defect to the named test that caught it. When one survives, the feedback identifies a distinction your current tests have not established. If the tests reject the correct reference, fix their expectation or setup first; the runner stops there before counting defects. Adding --report work/evidence-test-design/result.json retains the selected file, source digest, and named outcomes for your field note. This records an actual local run separately from your reading-progress checkmarks. Catching all six gives us evidence against these six mistakes, not an exhaustive guarantee. Add a zero-capacity case and a used-above-capacity case as a transfer exercise, even though the current defects do not require them. Explain which additional wrong behaviors they would expose. This habit becomes especially useful for a meal involving two owners: checking only the creature's plausible reserve increase could miss a transfer that removed too much patch biomass. A browser claim needs browser evidence We have followed the value as far as a native observer. A browser adds another consumer, with its own opportunities to show stale text, wire a control incorrectly, or retain a previous run's display. The optional panel below lets you inspect that next boundary. Its projection and schedule execute a WebAssembly build of the exact Rust program checked by the local runner. Enable JavaScript and build the optional Rust preview to operate this panel. The reference outcome is current display 37 and observer 37. With the observer first, those values are 37 and 99. Once your projection body passes, use this command from the repository root to compile your practice file and rebuild the pages. The panel will then let you follow the same selected value through an actual browser display: python3 learning/scripts/preview.py evidence --file work/evidence-practice/evidence.rs python3 learning/scripts/build.py The command runs all six canonical tests and the native program before compiling that checked source with a small browser host. Reload the lesson and look for the Learner file build label, which identifies the source being demonstrated. A prebuilt panel labeled Printed reference is the answer's behavior; to reproduce it, omit --file . Distinguishing the two matters because a correct reference panel cannot verify an unfinished practice copy. Start with one selected row and inputs 3 / 8. With projection before observation, both readings should be 37. Reversing the order should leave the current display at 37 while the observer reports 99; omitting projection should leave both at 99. Restore the correct order, then choose no selected rows and expect both readings to become unavailable. These contrasts come from Rust resources read by the host, rather than a percentage recalculated in JavaScript. Record the build label together with the inputs, schedule choice, and displayed pair so the observation can be tied to the program you ran. After editing the implementation, rerun the preview command and rebuild: an already compiled program cannot pick up that source change on its own. A failed check or build does not publish a replacement, and the course builder omits a preview whose checked source changed. An already open page still represents its displayed build until reloaded. As in the native implementation checker, canonical tests replace test edits in the practice copy during this build. The same discipline applies when you return to current Moss. Pause, reset, and press Step three times at the maintenance-only checkpoint; the paired expectation is tick 3 and reserve 57. Record what that particular browser build actually shows. A still creature in a screenshot does not reveal whether its reserve was charged correctly, just as this native projection test cannot certify a separate Moss browser build. If the browser result disagrees, trace the value inward from the displayed text to the projected resource, installed schedule, and helper inputs. Find the first boundary where expected and observed values diverge. That keeps the repair tied to evidence: rewriting correct arithmetic before discovering that its system never ran could add another defect while leaving the original one in place. For that browser boundary, the course includes a precompiled Rust terrarium at the current maintenance checkpoint. Its displayed readings let you make an observation about that specific host, alongside the native practice you completed here. Carry a counterexample into the next review Look once more at the fixture and name the wrong program each feature can expose. Why did we include an unselected sample, begin with stale 99, and preserve the observer's trace instead of checking only the final display? This is the reasoning you can carry into the next test you design. Recall answer The unselected sample exposes incorrect query selection or “take the first row.” The stale initial value exposes omitted projection and failure to clear unavailable data. The trace exposes an observer that ran before the update even when final state is correct. The selected-query and schedule APIs were checked against Bevy ECS 0.18.1. The native lab now distinguishes helper arithmetic, projection, and observation for these cases; integration into real Moss and its browser still need their own evidence. The next bridge applies that separation to the canonical affordable-movement task, where a returned distance, a changed reserve, and a visible journey must agree.

title: Connect one affordable action to the world
summary: Return to the canonical learner-owned movement task and connect its one edit to a reviewed, visible consequence.
text: Fern has a destination and enough reserve to begin the journey. Before changing her position, though, the movement helper must decide whether the next cell is valid and whether she can pay for it. Preparing a proposal without yet changing the caller gives us room to reject a step that fails either check. This is the bridge to the existing assignment. Your single active edit remains move_one_cell in crates/moss-sim/src/lessons.rs , as selected by NOW.md . The canonical instructions and complete worked replacement live in docs/tutorial/today-v2.md . This chapter explains how the pieces connect; it does not create a second movement exercise or activate the prepared system. Bring one paid step to the review checkpoint This chapter connects the Rust and ECS tools you've practiced to the canonical one-cell movement assignment. We'll trace a proposed step through bounds and affordability checks, then follow how its prepared adapter resolves a target and fits into the intended schedule. Your current destination is a helper whose focused test passes and whose behavior you can explain for review. The later journey remains conditional on that reviewed activation. Open the one assignment To start moving Fern, open NOW.md in your working checkout and follow its linked guide. That is the canonical assignment, and it includes the short Rust explanation, exact test command, and complete answer needed for the edit. You can begin there without finishing the preceding thirteen Fieldnotes; this chapter connects the pieces when you want a fuller explanation of why they fit together. If you prefer to read alongside the browser, download the canonical movement guide as Markdown . The course build copies it directly from the repository, so the assignment and answer still have one source. Use the repository original when following its relative source links. Before changing the helper, run its focused test. At this checkpoint, it should reach the deliberate todo! in the function you will implement. Seeing that expected failure establishes that the runner can compile the program and reach your edit, giving you a useful starting point for the repair. scripts/with-toolchain.sh cargo test -p moss-sim --locked --test movement movement_charges_only_an_affordable_actual_step -- --exact Check the test name and selected-test count in that result. An empty selection has not reached the unfinished function, and a compilation diagnostic has not reached an assertion. The evidence lesson explains those distinctions so you can fix the stage that actually failed before reasoning about movement. A proposal is not yet a move Begin with a small case you can follow by hand: current cell (2, 2), target (4, 4), reserve 59, and a price of two energy units per cell. The selected rule moves along x before y and allows at most one cardinal step per call. Its candidate next position is therefore (3, 2), one cell away at a cost of two. We can work out that proposal before deciding to accept it. The function receives &mut Position , which gives it access to the caller's actual position. Writing through that reference changes the world immediately. Instead, copy the small Position value into a local next and calculate the proposed step there. The local value can change while the caller stays at (2, 2). If validation fails, discarding that copy is enough; if it succeeds, a later write through the reference commits the proposal. Now lower the starting reserve to one. The same proposed step costs two, so the accepted distance must be zero and both position and reserve must remain unchanged. If you moved the caller first, returning zero would only report a rejection after the move had already happened. Keeping the proposal separate gives rejection the behavior the return value promises. The same proposed cell under different starting conditions Before the call Accepted result What the case reveals (2, 2), reserve 59, target (4, 4), rate 2 (3, 2), reserve 57, distance 1 A paid x step. (2, 2), reserve 1, target (4, 4), rate 2 (2, 2), reserve 1, distance 0 Rejection without partial mutation. (2, 2), reserve 2, target (4, 4), rate 2 (3, 2), reserve 0, distance 1 Exact affordability is accepted. (2, 2), reserve 59, target (2, 2), rate 2 (2, 2), reserve 59, distance 0 Having a target does not imply travel. The earlier distinction between requested and actual payment matters here. Maintenance spends what the reserve can supply and saturates at zero. Movement accepts a step only when the whole price can be paid. A saturating subtraction would still produce a valid number for the one-unit animal, but it would let that animal travel without funding the step. The selected rule tells us which arithmetic operation is appropriate. Validate the coordinates before committing Affordability is only one reason to reject the proposal. Before committing a paid step, we also need to establish that the coordinates describe a valid move within this world. In a world of width 32, x may be zero through 31; a negative x or x equal to 32 is outside the world. Check both the current position and the target before changing either mutable value. A valid destination cannot make an invalid starting position a sound basis for movement, which is why the canonical answer validates before committing. We can also use the guarantees already established by construction. WorldConfig limits dimensions to 8 through 256, so converting those dimensions to signed coordinates is safe. The helper then uses checked arithmetic for distance and cost. Under this one-cell policy, the distance is zero or one; calculating it explicitly still makes the units and the assumptions behind payment visible. A call represents one opportunity to take a cardinal step. The rule does not include diagonals, obstacles, pathfinding, or several cells of travel at once. That small unit of work is deliberate: the ECS adapter calls the helper for eligible animals, and later ticks provide later opportunities. Adding a loop here would change what one call means and what its tests are meant to establish. Prediction: what should happen when only y differs? If the start is (4, 2) and the target is (4, 4), x already agrees. The next proposal is (4, 3). With exactly two reserve units and a rate of two, it commits that position and leaves zero. The else if in the canonical answer chooses one axis, so a call cannot move diagonally. The adapter resolves the target now The helper knows a destination position, but the ECS adapter has to find a currently eligible destination first. Fern carries Meadow's stable ID in her authored target. The prepared move_to_food system resolves that ID against current patches and requires positive biomass before calling the helper. If the patch is missing or empty, no movement call occurs and no travel is charged. The target ID can remain stored even if Meadow changes, just as the snapshot lookup lesson retained a report about an earlier world. That earlier report may be accurate for its observation time while no longer answering whether Fern may act now. The adapter performs the current lookup at the action boundary because neither a remembered target nor a displayed row supplies that fact. The query also decides which animals are eligible to attempt movement. It requires FoodTarget , mutable Position , mutable Energy , and the Creature marker. Flint has position and energy but no authored food target, so the system does not visit him. That difference comes from his component set; the system does not branch on his nickname or fox species. To read a patch position while mutating an animal position, the queries must describe disjoint access. The patch query excludes creatures, and the mutable query requires them, following the same reasoning as the preview lesson . The adapter copies Meadow's small position into the helper, then borrows Fern's position and energy for the possible change. The copy supplies the destination without creating another authoritative world. A green helper is one checkpoint After replacing the function body, rerun the exact focused test and read its assertions together. Returned distance, final position, and final reserve describe different consequences of one decision. They must agree: reporting a traveled cell without moving should fail, and the low-energy and invalid-coordinate cases must preserve both mutable values. This is the helper's contract before any system is installed. A passing helper is the point to request the review specified in NOW.md ; the canonical guide provides a short review request. That review checks the selected rule and deliberately connects the prepared adapter to the installed schedule. Until this transition is performed in your working checkout, the correct helper remains available code rather than active movement. The intended schedule runs maintenance, then movement, then tick completion. Consider an animal starting a tick with reserve two: maintenance spends one, leaving too little for a two-unit step. Movement must therefore reject it. Reversing the first two systems would allow a different outcome, even if both bodies were individually correct. Explicit ordering makes this chosen meaning part of the installed program. Two prepared installed-world tests are ignored at the current checkpoint. During reviewed activation, they become checks of target resolution, affordability after maintenance, the journey, and reset. Those tests reach relationships the helper cannot see, including whether its adapter was installed at all. The course's Rust terrarium currently shows the maintenance-only checkpoint, where Fern remains stationary despite the prepared movement code. Account for the expected journey Once activation has been reviewed and performed, use the route from (10, 10) to (16, 13) to predict a complete journey. The rule takes six x steps, followed by three y steps. The table is an expectation after reviewed activation , so compare it with the rebuilt browser at that stage rather than treating it as movement already present in the current preview. Expected installed behavior after movement activation Completed ticks Fern Other evidence 0 (10, 10), reserve 60 Flint 60; Meadow biomass 80. 1 (11, 10), reserve 57 One maintenance unit and two travel units paid. 9 (16, 13), reserve 33 Flint 51; Meadow still 80. 10 (16, 13), reserve 32 No new travel; Flint 50; Meadow still 80. Across the first nine ticks, Fern pays nine maintenance units and nine steps at two units each, leaving 60 − 9 − 18 = 33. On tick ten she is already at the target, so only maintenance is charged. Arriving on a patch does not yet consume its food: eating is a separate proposed rule. Unchanged biomass is therefore consistent with this completed movement journey. Debug the tenth tick: why might the reserve fall to 30 instead? A three-unit decrease would suggest that two travel units were charged despite zero actual distance, assuming maintenance remains one. Inspect the helper's returned distance and the location of payment before changing the UI. A retained target tells you the intended destination; it does not prove a cell was traveled. Bring a complete one-cell decision to review The helper's result now has a contract you can check: a rejected proposal leaves position and reserve alone; an accepted step changes both and reports the distance actually traveled. For now, implement the canonical helper, pass its focused test, and request the specified review. Those additional checks connect the helper's decision to the behavior a viewer sees. title: A finite meal has two sides
summary: Resolve two consumers against one finite patch and keep requested intake separate from actual gain.
text: Two consumers reach a patch containing five biomass units, and each requests three. Giving both of them three would create a sixth unit from nowhere. Make every meal account for its source We'll turn that shortage into a small transaction: validate the attempt, find the amount that fits both accounts, then change the consumer and patch together. You'll implement transfer while a supplied resolver makes the two consumers share the same dwindling supply. This gives mutable borrowing a concrete responsibility: each accepted gain must have a matching depletion. By the end, you should be able to explain the three-unit and two-unit meals, reject an impossible meal without partial changes, and use repeated attempts and reversed input order to check the rule. The same reasoning will apply when a later action consumes something another actor also wants. This isolated lab proposes a one-for-one conversion from biomass to reserve, with consumers already in contact and resolving by ascending stable ID. These are authored game rules rather than calibrated ecology. The exercise doesn't install eating in live Moss. Let the first meal change the second The movement bridge connected an accepted action to a visible consequence. A meal introduces a consequence shared by several actors: the supply one consumer removes is no longer available to another. Testing each meal against a fresh copy of the patch would make both seem correct while missing the problem between them. Our consumers have IDs 2 and 9. Each starts with zero reserve, capacity ten, and a request for three units. The patch starts with five. We'll deliberately store ID 9 first in the array but resolve the lower stable ID first. ID 2 should receive three, leaving two for ID 9. By the end, their combined reserve gain should equal the five units removed from the patch. The ID order is a policy we can reproduce, not a measure of fairness. If the same two consumers repeatedly compete under identical conditions, the lower ID keeps its priority. We could later investigate rotating or randomized priority, but first we need to know that every version of the policy accounts for the shared supply correctly. For that reason, the lab begins at contact. It doesn't decide when an animal becomes hungry, how it travels, or which species can eat a particular food. Those conditions will surround a meal in a larger world. Here we can concentrate on what an accepted transfer does to its two accounts. Find one amount that fits both accounts A request isn't necessarily the amount a consumer can receive. The patch may contain less than requested, or the consumer may have little room left in its reserve. Under our one-for-one conversion, the actual transfer is the smallest of three quantities: requested biomass, available biomass, and remaining reserve capacity. Consider a consumer at eight units out of ten. It requests four from a patch holding nine, but only two units fit. The accepted meal therefore removes two biomass and adds two reserve, leaving seven in the patch and ten in the consumer. Removing all four requested units would introduce a waste rule we haven't chosen. Crediting four while removing two would create reserve without a matching source. Meals bounded by supply and reserve capacity Inputs Accepted result Reserve 0/10; biomass 5; request 3 Take 3, gain 3, reserve 3, biomass 2. Reserve 0/10; biomass 2; request 3 Take 2, gain 2, reserve 2, biomass 0. Reserve 8/10; biomass 9; request 4 Take 2, gain 2, reserve 10, biomass 7. Reserve 10/10; biomass 9; request 4 Reject for no room; leave both accounts unchanged. We'll return a Meal containing biomass_taken and energy_gained . Their numbers are equal in this model, but their names describe different sides of the event. That makes the report understandable now and lets a later, explicitly chosen conversion policy explain any difference rather than hide it inside a generic “amount.” Check the transaction before changing either side A rejected meal must leave both accounts untouched. We'll keep that guarantee by completing the checks before either assignment. The first check in transfer validates that reserve doesn't exceed capacity. Only then can capacity minus reserve describe room without underflowing. The helper next checks contact, a nonzero request, nonempty supply, and available room. Each rejected condition returns a named error before assigning either account. This order also determines which error a caller receives when several conditions fail. An invalid reserve takes precedence over absent contact, for example. Most tests isolate one failed condition to make the boundary easy to see, but the implementation's ordering remains part of its contract. Once the checks succeed, we can calculate the accepted amount and both resulting balances. Bounding that amount by room guarantees that the next reserve fits within its valid capacity. The helper uses checked addition to make the expectation explicit. Bounding it by biomass likewise makes the patch subtraction safe. Only after calculating both results do we write them back. We haven't needed rollback code because rejected paths never started the transfer. The two mutable references give the function permission to change the accounts, but Rust doesn't infer the conservation rule from those references. That rule comes from calculating one accepted amount and applying it consistently to both sides. Keep the patch current between consumers A correct transfer still needs a caller that presents the current shared supply to each consumer. The supplied resolve function handles that competition around the helper. It builds a temporary list of array indices and sorts them by consumer ID. This preserves the input array's storage order while making the chosen action order explicit. Each outcome records the consumer's ID, so the result remains interpretable even when the input array is reversed. The loop then borrows one consumer at a time and passes the same mutable patch to transfer . After ID 2 eats, the patch contains two units. ID 9's call reads that updated balance, so its request for three is bounded to two. There is no earlier five-unit snapshot left in the calculation to spend again. Unique IDs are a caller obligation in this lab. Sorting duplicate IDs wouldn't establish a meaningful identity policy, and the resolver doesn't try to repair that malformed input. Keeping this assumption explicit lets us distinguish deterministic access order from validation of the roster itself. Immediate depletion matters even when an empty patch will eventually be removed. As the command lesson showed, a queued despawn can wait until a later boundary. Updating biomass now prevents another reward during that wait. A patch can remain in the world at zero and still be unavailable for a meal. Try the contest twice Predict the two accepted meals from five units, then reverse the input array and repeat the prediction. Finally, run the resolver again on the same depleted patch. Both consumers still have room in their reserves, but is that enough to accept another request? Hint 1: follow the selected order ID 2 acts before ID 9 in either array arrangement. Its three-unit meal changes the shared patch before ID 9 reaches the helper. Hint 2: carry the depleted patch into the repeat Room in reserve is only one requirement. After the first resolution, the shared patch has no biomass left for either consumer. Prediction answer The first resolution gives three units to ID 2 and two to ID 9, regardless of array order. The second rejects both attempts as empty-patch meals and leaves their reserves at three and two. Prepare a new practice file with these commands from the repository root. You'll implement transfer ; the resolver and fixtures are supplied so your helper is tested inside the shared contest. python3 learning/scripts/labs.py prepare meals --dest work/meals-practice python3 learning/scripts/labs.py check meals --file work/meals-practice/meals.rs The starter compiles and then reaches its intentional todo! . Replace the function body and repeat the check. Expect seven named tests to pass. If a rejected meal changes an account, follow the assignments back to the validation they should occur after. If reversing input changes the winners, inspect resolution order before changing the arithmetic.
