todo!("validate, bound the actual transfer, then update both accounts") } fn resolve(consumers: &mut [Consumer], patch: &mut Patch, requested_biomass: u32) -> Vec<(u32, Result<Meal, Rejection>)> { let mut order: Vec<usize> = (0..consumers.len()).collect(); order.sort_by_key(|&index| consumers[index].id); let mut outcomes = Vec::new(); for index in order { let consumer = &mut consumers[index]; let outcome = transfer(&mut consumer.energy, patch, requested_biomass, consumer.in_contact); outcomes.push((consumer.id, outcome)); } outcomes } fn pair() -> [Consumer; 2] { [Consumer { id: 9, energy: Energy { reserve_units: 0, capacity_units: 10 }, in_contact: true }, Consumer { id: 2, energy: Energy { reserve_units: 0, capacity_units: 10 }, in_contact: true }] } fn main() { let mut consumers = pair(); let mut patch = Patch { biomass_units: 5 }; for (id, outcome) in resolve(&mut consumers, &mut patch, 3) { println!("id={id} result={outcome:?}"); } println!("remaining biomass={}", patch.biomass_units); } #[cfg(test)] mod tests { use super::*; #[test] fn capacity_limits_both_depletion_and_gain() { let mut energy = Energy { reserve_units: 8, capacity_units: 10 }; let mut patch = Patch { biomass_units: 9 }; assert_eq!(transfer(&mut energy, &mut patch, 4, true), Ok(Meal { biomass_taken: 2, energy_gained: 2 })); assert_eq!((energy.reserve_units, patch.biomass_units), (10, 7)); } #[test] fn lack_of_contact_rejects_without_partial_mutation() { let mut energy = Energy { reserve_units: 2, capacity_units: 10 }; let mut patch = Patch { biomass_units: 5 }; let before = (energy, patch); assert_eq!(transfer(&mut energy, &mut patch, 3, false), Err(Rejection::NotInContact)); assert_eq!((energy, patch), before); } #[test] fn invalid_reserve_rejects_before_unsigned_subtraction() { let mut energy = Energy { reserve_units: 11, capacity_units: 10 }; let mut patch = Patch { biomass_units: 5 }; let before = (energy, patch); assert_eq!(transfer(&mut energy, &mut patch, 3, true), Err(Rejection::InvalidReserve)); assert_eq!((energy, patch), before); } #[test] fn zero_request_empty_patch_and_full_reserve_each_leave_state_unchanged() { for (reserve, biomass, request, expected) in [ (2, 5, 0, Rejection::ZeroRequest), (2, 0, 3, Rejection::EmptyPatch), (10, 5, 3, Rejection::NoRoom), ] { let mut energy = Energy { reserve_units: reserve, capacity_units: 10 }; let mut patch = Patch { biomass_units: biomass }; let before = (energy, patch); assert_eq!(transfer(&mut energy, &mut patch, request, true), Err(expected)); assert_eq!((energy, patch), before); } } #[test] fn stable_id_order_resolves_the_same_competition_after_input_reversal() { let mut a = pair(); let mut b = pair(); b.reverse(); let mut patch_a = Patch { biomass_units: 5 }; let mut patch_b = patch_a; let outcomes = resolve(&mut a, &mut patch_a, 3); assert_eq!(outcomes, vec![ (2, Ok(Meal { biomass_taken: 3, energy_gained: 3 })), (9, Ok(Meal { biomass_taken: 2, energy_gained: 2 })), ]); assert_eq!(resolve(&mut b, &mut patch_b, 3), outcomes); assert_eq!((patch_a.biomass_units, patch_b.biomass_units), (0, 0)); assert_eq!(a.iter().map(|c| c.energy.reserve_units).sum::<u32>(), 5); assert_eq!(a.iter().find(|c| c.id == 2).unwrap().energy.reserve_units, 3); assert_eq!(a.iter().find(|c| c.id == 9).unwrap().energy.reserve_units, 2); } #[test] fn depleted_patch_cannot_reward_a_second_resolution() { let mut consumers = pair(); let mut patch = Patch { biomass_units: 5 }; resolve(&mut consumers, &mut patch, 3); let before = consumers; assert_eq!(resolve(&mut consumers, &mut patch, 3), vec![(2, Err(Rejection::EmptyPatch)), (9, Err(Rejection::EmptyPatch))]); assert_eq!(consumers, before); assert_eq!(patch.biomass_units, 0); } #[test] fn bounding_before_addition_handles_the_numeric_limit() { let mut energy = Energy { reserve_units: u32::MAX - 2, capacity_units: u32::MAX }; let mut patch = Patch { biomass_units: u32::MAX }; assert_eq!(transfer(&mut energy, &mut patch, u32::MAX, true), Ok(Meal { biomass_taken: 2, energy_gained: 2 })); assert_eq!(energy.reserve_units, u32::MAX); assert_eq!(patch.biomass_units, u32::MAX - 2); } } Complete worked answer: meals.rs #[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)] struct Energy { reserve_units: u32, capacity_units: u32 } #[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)] struct Patch { biomass_units: u32 } #[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)] struct Meal { biomass_taken: u32, energy_gained: u32 } #[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)] enum Rejection { InvalidReserve, NotInContact, ZeroRequest, EmptyPatch, NoRoom } #[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)] struct Consumer { id: u32, energy: Energy, in_contact: bool } fn transfer( energy: &mut Energy, patch: &mut Patch, requested_biomass: u32, in_contact: bool, ) -> Result<Meal, Rejection> { if energy.reserve_units > energy.capacity_units { return Err(Rejection::InvalidReserve); } if !in_contact { return Err(Rejection::NotInContact); } if requested_biomass == 0 { return Err(Rejection::ZeroRequest); } if patch.biomass_units == 0 { return Err(Rejection::EmptyPatch); } let room = energy.capacity_units - energy.reserve_units; The lab uses the standard library, so you can also save the full block as meals.rs and use these commands from its directory: rustc +1.93.1 --edition=2024 --test meals.rs -o meals-tests ./meals-tests rustc +1.93.1 --edition=2024 meals.rs -o meals ./meals Expect seven passing tests and this program output: id=2 result=Ok(Meal { biomass_taken: 3, energy_gained: 3 }) id=9 result=Ok(Meal { biomass_taken: 2, energy_gained: 2 }) remaining biomass=0 Use the second attempt to test the first A successful first meal tells us that reserve can increase. The second attempt against the depleted patch asks a stronger question: did the first success actually consume its source? That repeat catches a helper that reports a transfer without applying depletion, as well as one that continues to reward an old availability reading. The competition test also checks more than the combined total. It reverses the inputs and asserts which consumer receives each amount. A resolver could conserve all five units yet allocate them under the wrong priority rule. Recipient identities and accounting totals test different promises. At the arithmetic boundary, one case begins two units below the largest possible capacity while both request and supply are enormous. Computing room first keeps the accepted addition at two. Adding the full request and capping later could overflow before reaching the cap, so the extreme input tests the order of the calculation. The rejection tests compare both accounts with their original values. That is how they detect a half-finished meal: reporting an error alone wouldn't prove that reserve and biomass were left alone. The ordinary capacity case complements them by checking the exact accepted depletion when a smaller meal does fit. A meal is complete when both accounts agree Our five-unit shortage now has a complete account: three went to ID 2, two to ID 9, and nothing remains to reward another visit. The tests establish that behavior for authored contact values and a one-for-one conversion. An ECS integration will additionally need to establish contact, schedule the interaction, and prevent ineligible actors from reaching it. Likewise, an interactive teaching model can help you explore request, supply, and capacity, while a browser view of the Rust world must report outcomes from that world. Watching a plausible animation wouldn't establish which helper ran or whether its accounts balanced. Keeping the source of a reading clear becomes more useful as several rules begin interacting. Recall why mutable access doesn't guarantee conservation The references permit mutation but don't choose its amount. Conservation follows from the explicit conversion rule, one bounded accepted transfer, and each consumer acting on the current shared supply. So far, the consumers arrive with contact already established. In choosing and revalidating a target , we'll leave time between noticing a patch and attempting a meal. That gives another consumer a chance to change the opportunity before the action arrives.

title: Choose, then revalidate a target
summary: Choose from a bounded snapshot, then check the live target again before committing a meal.
text: Fern chooses a nearby patch after seeing one unit of biomass there. Before she takes a bite, that unit is gone. Her observation can still be an accurate record of what she saw, even though the meal must now fail. Choose from an observation, then check the action We'll follow Fern's intention through three different values: an owned reading of a patch, the identity she selects, and the current patch she eventually tries to use. You'll implement select_target with a distance rule and a stable tie-breaker. The supplied observer and bite helper let us examine that choice before and after the world changes. The goal is to make a repeatable choice without treating it as permission to eat. You should finish able to explain why reversing observations leaves the chosen ID unchanged, why visibility doesn't establish contact, and why an emptied or missing target produces a rejection while the old reading remains intact. This isolated lab proposes a grid policy: choose the nearest observed nonempty patch within a Manhattan radius, break distance ties by stable ID, and require same-cell contact for a one-unit bite. These teaching rules don't activate choice, travel, or feeding in live Moss. Follow an intention from observation to action The finite-meal lesson made each consumer act on the patch's current balance. Now we'll put some time between learning about a patch and attempting to use it. That gap matters because another action can change the world while Fern retains her intention. We'll represent what she saw with an owned PatchReading : an ID, position, and biomass copied at observation time. The selector examines those readings and returns only the chosen ID. Later, the action helper uses that ID to find a current patch and checks whether a bite is still possible. Each stage has a different job. Observation limits what the actor knows. Selection expresses a preference among those known opportunities. Resolution checks whether the remembered interaction can happen now. If resolution simply searched the entire world for the best current patch, it could silently replace Fern's choice with information she never observed. Build the actor's local view To make the choice belong to Fern, first limit what information reaches it. The observation function can read authoritative patches to construct a local view, but the selector receives only the copied readings. This keeps its inputs smaller than the browser's global inspector. We may want to show every patch to a person investigating the simulation without giving every animal that same knowledge. For this lab, local means within a Manhattan distance from the actor. Add the absolute horizontal and vertical differences: from (0, 0), both (2, 0) and (1, 1) are two steps away, while (2, 1) is three. A radius of two includes the first pair and excludes the third. There are no walls or occlusion rules in this model. The arithmetic needs to support the coordinate type we chose. Subtracting two extreme signed coordinates can overflow before an absolute-value operation gets a chance to run. Our helper uses abs_diff separately on each axis, then converts the results to u64 before adding them. The standard integer reference describes the absolute-difference operation; the maximum-coordinate test checks that the combined distance remains correct. The selector repeats the radius filter even though the supplied observer already limits its output. That makes the selector's own contract hold when a caller supplies a broader set of readings. It doesn't establish when those readings were captured or whether their IDs belong to the current run. The fixture assumes unique identities within one run, leaving retained history and reset provenance to later work. Choose the nearest eligible reading Once we've excluded empty and out-of-range readings, we still need a repeatable answer when several candidates remain. We'll compare (distance, stable ID) pairs. Distance comes first; ID resolves only a distance tie. This means that a closer high-ID patch beats a farther low-ID patch, while reversing the input order can't change an equal-distance winner. Rust compares ordered tuples element by element, so min_by_key can express that policy directly. The iterator reference explains the operation. The consequential decision is the ordering of the fields in our key: reversing them would make identity more important than proximity. Choices from (0, 0) with radius four Observed candidates Selected result ID 9 at (1, 0), ID 2 at (0, 1), both nonempty ID 2: equal distances are resolved by stable ID. ID 1 at (4, 0), ID 9 at (2, 0), both nonempty ID 9: the closer patch wins. ID 0 at (1, 0) with zero biomass No target from this reading alone: the observed supply is empty. This policy is intentionally small enough to explain through those examples. It doesn't weigh danger, nutrition, crowding, or the energy needed to travel. Adding such criteria would require us to decide how they compare and which observations supply them. A deterministic choice gives us a result we can reproduce; it doesn't by itself show that the choice is good for the animal. It reaches capacity through a valid meal, then attempts another. Without that positive path, an implementation that rejected every action could look correct against a suite containing only failures. An intention still needs current permission Fern's old reading can still describe what she saw while her selected action correctly fails. In a larger ECS world, those values will have different owners and access paths. It doesn't keep the world unchanged until the action, turn visibility into contact, or create reserve capacity. Those conditions still need to hold when the selected interaction resolves. In authored populations and individual variation , we'll extend this care with evidence to comparing animals: a larger total or a different reserve needs an explanation grounded in the starting conditions.

title: Compare individuals fairly
summary: Give individuals different costs while holding the starting conditions fixed, then separate that comparison from a density change.
text: One run ends with 111 reserve units and another with 222. The second looks more successful until we count its animals: it has twice as many. Build populations whose differences you can explain To interpret those totals, we need to know what each animal started with and which cost it actually paid. You'll implement populate , validating an authored roster before spawning it and resolving each optional maintenance override into an individual component. Then we'll follow the same stable IDs through a pair of runs while changing the population size. The resulting reports should let you separate three questions: what a default supplies, what an individual stores, and what a larger aggregate means. You'll check that an invalid roster leaves the world unchanged and that doubling this maintenance-only population changes the total without improving either original animal's outcome. This isolated Bevy lab uses authored maintenance costs to study comparisons. Its profiles are teaching inputs rather than measurements of real species. It doesn't change Moss's fixture or the active assignment in NOW.md . Start with two individuals you can recognize Begin with two hares, IDs 10 and 20. Each starts with 60 reserve units and receives three maintenance executions. ID 10 costs two units per tick; ID 20 costs one. There is no feeding, movement, or interaction, so we can first ask a narrow question: what difference does the configured upkeep make under otherwise equal conditions? After three executions, ID 10 should have 54 units and ID 20 should have 57. Their three-unit difference follows from paying different rates three times. The upkeep system doesn't read the IDs, so identity doesn't cause the difference. IDs let us connect each outcome to its profile without assuming that ECS query order matches authoring order. As in target resolution , an identity gives us something stable to follow through changing collections. Now keep those two animals and add IDs 30 and 40 with the same pair of cost profiles. All four share the same declared area of 64 cells. Count per area rises from 2/64 to 4/64, but we have also doubled the starting reserve from 120 to 240. These facts belong beside the final totals if we want the comparison to mean anything. The original pair and a denser roster after three executions Run Shared conditions Outcome Two hares 64 cells; 60 reserve each; rates 2 and 1 ID 10 has 54; ID 20 has 57; total 111. Four hares 64 cells; 60 reserve each; rates 2, 1, 2, 1 The original individuals still have 54 and 57; total 222. The unchanged individual results are expected here. Area is experiment metadata; no system reads it to calculate space, contact, or competition. Doubling this roster changes the count and totals without giving the original animals another interaction. A finite feeding system could make added neighbors consequential, but maintenance alone can't demonstrate that effect. Choose when a cost becomes the animal's own To make the cost comparison repeatable, we need to decide when a default becomes an individual's stored value. Each authored Profile contains a species and an optional maintenance override. The species resource supplies defaults of Hare 2 and Fox 4. When we populate the world, we'll resolve the override once and store the result in the individual's Maintenance component. The running upkeep system then reads that component. This gives two hares a straightforward way to differ. ID 10 uses None , meaning “use the species default,” while ID 20 uses Some(1) . An explicit Some(0) is also valid in this experiment: it requests zero cost. Treating zero as though it meant absence would silently discard an authored value and replace it with the default. Resolving at spawn time has a consequence we should test. Changing the default afterward won't rewrite components that already exist. One test changes the Hare default to 99 and checks that the original pair still pays two and one. This differs from the earlier query lab, where maintenance read the shared rates resource on each execution. Either design can be useful; here we want each profile to remain a stable experimental input. The fallback comes from the standard Option API . Its method provides a value when the override is absent. The larger choice—when to apply that fallback and where to store the result—belongs to our model. Reading the resolved component makes it possible to explain an individual's cost without consulting a resource that may have changed later. Validate the whole roster before spawning it To compare individuals across runs, we need unambiguous IDs. This lab reserves zero as invalid and rejects duplicates, including an incoming ID that already belongs to an entity in the world. The identities are stable within this run; retained reports from several runs would also need a run identifier. There's a subtle failure case when importing several profiles at once. Suppose the world already contains ID 10, and a new batch offers valid ID 30 followed by duplicate ID 10. If we spawn while validating, the function could return an error after leaving ID 30 behind. The caller would have a rejected batch and a changed starting population. We'll avoid that partial result with two passes. First, populate collects existing IDs in a BTreeSet and validates every incoming profile against it. Inserting an ID reports whether it was new, so the same operation catches collisions with the world and repetitions inside the batch. Only after the complete pass succeeds does spawning begin. The resulting guarantee is specific: validation errors leave the population unchanged. We aren't adding rollback for allocation failure or arbitrary panics, and the supplied fixture ensures that the defaults resource exists. A focused guarantee is easier to use and test than a broad transaction promise the implementation can't fulfill. The function borrows the profile slice, but the world doesn't keep that borrow. The world keeps copied identity, species, and reserve values together with the resolved maintenance rate; it doesn't retain the profile slice or its optional override. Reporting makes another owned projection and sorts it by stable ID. Reversing spawn order may change ECS handles while leaving that report equal. Bevy 0.18.1's World API describes the immediate spawn operation used during this setup. Build the population boundary Your population constructor has two promises to keep: resolve valid profiles consistently and leave a rejected batch unapplied. Before editing, trace both the ordinary and rejected batches. For the ordinary pair, resolve each cost and calculate the two reserves after three executions. For the rejected extension, decide exactly when the duplicate ID should stop the function and whether any spawning should have occurred. Hint 1: finish validation first Collect existing SimId values, then reject incoming zero IDs or IDs that the set can't insert as new. Keep world.spawn out of this first pass. Hint 2: copy the resolved cost into each animal After validation, obtain the defaults. For each profile, use its override or matching species default and spawn the ID, species, reserve, and maintenance component together. Prediction answer The pair finishes at 54 and 57, while the doubled roster totals 222. The extension with ID 30 followed by existing ID 10 returns DuplicateId(10) and leaves only the original pair. A partially accepted extension would change the experiment before it began. Prepare a new practice file from the repository root. After the edit, expect eight passing tests. If a valid roster is reported as duplicate, inspect whether validation inserts the same ID twice. If an error leaves an extra animal, look for a spawn that happens before the full validation pass completes. #[derive(Component)] struct Maintenance(u32); #[derive(Resource, Clone, Copy)] struct Defaults { hare: u32, fox: u32, } impl Defaults { fn rate(self, species: Species) -> u32 { match species { Species::Hare => self.hare, Species::Fox => self.fox, } } } #[derive(Resource)] struct AreaCells(u32); #[derive(Clone, Copy)] struct Profile { id: u32, species: Species, initial_reserve_units: u32, maintenance_override: Option<u32>, } const PAIR: [Profile; 2] = [ Profile { id: 10, species: Species::Hare, initial_reserve_units: 60, maintenance_override: None, }, Profile { id: 20, species: Species::Hare, initial_reserve_units: 60, maintenance_override: Some(1), }, ]; world } fn fixture(profiles: &[Profile]) -> World { let mut world = empty_world(); populate(&mut world, profiles).expect("authored fixture IDs are valid"); world } fn upkeep(mut creatures: Query<(&Maintenance, &mut Reserve)>) { for (rate, mut reserve) in &mut creatures { reserve.0 = reserve.0.saturating_sub(rate.0); } } fn execute(world: &mut World, ticks: u32) { let mut schedule = Schedule::default(); schedule.set_executor_kind(ExecutorKind::SingleThreaded); schedule.add_systems(upkeep); for _ in 0..ticks { schedule.run(world); title: Let environmental input change supply
summary: Trace lit and dark ticks and show how the selected growth-and-meal order changes a patch at capacity.
text: An empty patch receives three new biomass units, and a grazer asks for a two-unit meal. At the end of the tick, the grazer might have two reserve units or none. We can produce both results using the same growth and meal functions: all we have to change is their order. Trace when new supply becomes available You'll implement renew , which adds only the biomass that fits and reports the actual addition. We'll give that helper a tick-based daylight cycle, then run it before and after a meal in two explicit Bevy schedules. Holding the grazer and patch fixed lets us attribute a missed meal to phase order. Follow both runs through the same four-tick day. By the end, you should be able to account for environmental additions, explain why the first meals differ, and show how equal final stores can conceal different paths. That is the distinction a helper test alone can't establish: correct operations still need a deliberate order when they share state. This isolated Bevy ECS 0.18.1 model uses a four-tick day and one-for-one food conversion as teaching rules. You'll implement bounded renewal and test it in two schedules. The reference doesn't install growth or feeding in live Moss or change NOW.md . Give one consumer a renewing supply The previous lesson made starting conditions explicit before comparing individuals. We'll use that discipline here by holding the consumer fixed. One grazer reaches one patch on every tick, so the difference we observe can't come from crowding, target choice, or another animal winning a contest. The patch begins empty, can hold four biomass units, and requests three new units on each lit tick. The grazer begins at zero reserve, can hold twenty, and requests a two-unit meal each tick. There is no travel, maintenance, or death. A meal still obeys the familiar supply and capacity bounds, converting each accepted biomass unit into one reserve unit. We store the single patch and grazer as resources to keep the scheduling question visible. This is a convenient shape for one pair, rather than a layout for a whole population. A many-actor world would use entities and queries, with stable identities and the contention handling from the meal lesson. Renewal introduces an accounting difference worth naming now. A meal moves existing units between stores; growth adds units from the environment. Daylight represents that external input here. There are no soil nutrients or decomposition in the model, so the addition doesn't establish a recycling loop. Locate daylight in executed time Growth needs a repeatable answer to whether this tick is lit, so we'll derive daylight from executed simulation time. Our default day lasts four executed ticks. Ticks one and two are lit, three and four are dark, and five begins the next lit phase. To calculate the position in that cycle, convert the one-based tick to a zero-based value with tick - 1 , then take the remainder modulo cycle_ticks . Positions below lit_ticks are lit. The constructor makes the remainder operation meaningful by rejecting a zero-length cycle. It also rejects a lit duration longer than the whole cycle. A day with no lit ticks is still valid, as is a day that is entirely lit. Zero darkness or zero light describes a scenario; zero cycle length would break the calculation. The schedule begins by incrementing its tick with checked_add . That gives growth the one-based tick it needs before evaluating daylight. Counter overflow stops the run before growth or eating instead of wrapping to an earlier day. The initial zero means no tick has executed, and is_lit rejects it as an executed-tick input. After a successful schedule run returns, the counter identifies the completed result we're inspecting. Neither growth nor daylight reads frame counts or elapsed milliseconds. Repeated inspection therefore can't bring another dawn. Faster playback can request more complete ticks, while pausing requests none. Keeping that pacing outside the rule lets us compare the same four-tick day regardless of how long we take to watch it. Add only the supply the patch can hold Before comparing schedules, we need renewal to give an honest answer at capacity. If a four-unit patch already contains three, a request for three more can add only one. The helper should both add one and return one, so the report records accepted supply rather than the larger request. Calculate remaining space before adding. Adding the whole request and clamping afterward can overflow first, especially near u32::MAX . Patch::new establishes that biomass doesn't exceed capacity, so capacity minus biomass gives valid room. Limiting the addition to that room preserves the same relationship after mutation. The patch fields are private, with the usual Rust module boundary: code in the defining module and its descendants can still access them. Such code must maintain the invariant too. The constructor and renewal helper give us a clear path through which to establish and preserve it. Darkness and a full patch both return an actual addition of zero, but they explain that number differently. Showing the daylight phase alongside current biomass and capacity lets a reader tell which condition applied. The supplied Flow resource records only the latest tick's addition and meal, and each system overwrites its field even when the outcome is zero. Otherwise, yesterday's successful growth could appear to continue through darkness. Let the meal use what exists at its turn With bounded renewal in place, we can isolate the scheduling choice without changing either action's arithmetic. Both schedules begin by selecting the next tick. One then runs growth followed by eating; the other runs eating followed by growth. We use .chain() to express those dependencies. Selecting a single-threaded executor would limit execution mode, but it wouldn't tell Bevy which biological order we intended. Start with the empty patch on lit tick one. Growth first adds three units, after which the grazer takes two. Eating first finds nothing, so that meal contributes zero even though growth adds three later in the same tick. Now start from a full patch instead: eating can make room that a later growth phase uses. The table shows both effects. Lit tick one with a growth request of three and meal request of two Starting patch Order Added / eaten Final biomass / reserve Empty: 0 of 4 Growth then meal 3 / 2 1 / 2 Empty: 0 of 4 Meal then growth 3 / 0 3 / 0 Full: 4 of 4 Growth then meal 0 / 2 2 / 2 Full: 4 of 4 Meal then growth 2 / 2 4 / 2 So ordering can change both access to food and the amount of external supply accepted. The same functions can be individually correct in either schedule. Choosing between their combined outcomes requires a model decision about when new material becomes available. Continue the empty-patch comparison through tick three, the first dark tick. Carry each patch forward from its own previous result. Does the schedule that missed its first meal catch up as soon as daylight ends? Hint 1: preserve each run's first result Growth before meal leaves one biomass after tick one. Meal before growth leaves three. Tick two begins with those different balances. Hint 2: distinguish stored food from new supply Darkness prevents a new addition, but it doesn't prevent a meal from using biomass already present. Find what each schedule retained after tick two. Prediction answer Growth before meal reaches biomass two and reserve four on tick two, then biomass zero and reserve six on tick three. Meal before growth reaches biomass four and reserve two, then biomass two and reserve four. The two runs first agree at the end of tick four, with biomass zero and reserve six. Their equal final state hides the earlier delay. Implement renewal and run both schedules Your edit is renew . It returns zero in darkness; during light, it adds what fits and returns the actual addition. The surrounding systems and two schedules are provided, so the same small arithmetic helper will be checked both directly and as part of a real Bevy execution. After you implement renewal, expect ten named tests and both four-tick traces to pass. A wrong addition near capacity points to the bound or the returned amount. A wrong first-tick reserve points to which phase made supply available before the meal. } Ok(Self { biomass_units, capacity_units, }) } } #[derive(Resource, Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)] struct Daylight { cycle_ticks: u64, lit_ticks: u64, } impl Daylight { fn new(cycle_ticks: u64, lit_ticks: u64) -> Result<Self, InvalidSetup> { if cycle_ticks == 0 || lit_ticks > cycle_ticks { return Err(InvalidSetup::InvalidDay); } Ok(Self { cycle_ticks, lit_ticks, }) } fn is_lit(self, tick: u64) -> bool { let zero_based = tick.checked_sub(1).expect("executed ticks begin at one"); zero_based % self.cycle_ticks < self.lit_ticks } } #[derive(Resource, Default)] struct Tick(u64); #[derive(Resource)] struct Rules { growth_units_per_lit_tick: u32, meal_units_per_tick: u32, } #[derive(Resource, Default)] struct Grazer { reserve_units: u32, } const RESERVE_CAPACITY_UNITS: u32 = 20; #[derive(Resource, Default)] struct Flow { added_units: u32, eaten_units: u32, } fn renew(patch: &mut Patch, lit: bool, requested_units: u32) -> u32 { let _ = (patch, lit, requested_units); todo!("add only the lit supply that fits; return the actual addition") } fn begin_tick(mut tick: ResMut<Tick>) { tick.0 = tick.0.checked_add(1).expect("tick counter exhausted"); } fn grow( tick: Res<Tick>, daylight: Res<Daylight>, rules: Res<Rules>, mut patch: ResMut<Patch>, mut flow: ResMut<Flow>, ) { flow.added_units = renew( &mut patch, daylight.is_lit(tick.0), rules.growth_units_per_lit_tick, ); } fn meal( rules: Res<Rules>, mut patch: ResMut<Patch>, mut grazer: ResMut<Grazer>, mut flow: ResMut<Flow>, ) { let space = RESERVE_CAPACITY_UNITS - grazer.reserve_units; let eaten = rules .meal_units_per_tick .min(patch.biomass_units) .min(space); patch.biomass_units -= eaten; grazer.reserve_units += eaten; flow.eaten_units = eaten; } #[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug)] enum Order { GrowthBeforeMeal, GrowthAfterMeal, } fn tick_schedule(order: Order) -> Schedule { let mut schedule = Schedule::default(); schedule.set_executor_kind(ExecutorKind::SingleThreaded); match order { Order::GrowthBeforeMeal => { schedule.add_systems((begin_tick, grow, meal).chain()); } Order::GrowthAfterMeal => { schedule.add_systems((begin_tick, meal, grow).chain()); Empty and full fixtures execute the actual schedules and assert their literal outcomes. Repeated inspection checks that reading the lab doesn't advance it. Reasoning for the one-lit-tick comparison Only tick one adds supply, so each run receives three units over the four ticks.
