The Bevy 0.18.1 schedule configuration source explains chained dependencies, and its executor documentation describes single-threaded execution. They tell us how to express an order. The empty patch and missed meal tell us why choosing that order matters. Equal endpoints can hide a missed meal Our opening grazer received no reserve because its turn came before the new supply. Renewal respected the patch's capacity in both schedules, but the order decided when the grazer could use the addition. By tick four, the equal final stores concealed that earlier delay. Reporting actual flows and intermediate states lets us explain both the accounting and the experience along the way. In terminal transitions and retained history , an earlier phase will change whether an animal may take its next action at all. We'll make that eligibility change explicit and preserve an account of it after the animal is removed.

title: Keep a disappearance explainable
summary: Record one terminal transition and distinguish a complete zero count from history that no longer covers the question.
text: Fern begins a tick with one reserve unit. Maintenance spends it, and our model now declares her dead. She must miss the later action, but removing her from the world shouldn't erase the explanation. Stop an action and keep an honest account of why You'll implement resolve_terminal so one alive-to-dead transition changes eligibility and produces one owned record. We'll follow that record after cleanup, then after a bounded journal has to forget it. This separates the state that governs what Fern may do from the evidence available to someone inspecting her history. The supplied tick and journal make both boundaries testable. You should finish able to prevent a terminal-tick action and a duplicate death, identify a removed individual by run and ID, and distinguish a known zero event count from an interval the retained history can no longer answer. This isolated lab proposes a terminal rule: an alive animal at zero reserve after maintenance becomes dead. It is a teaching policy rather than a scientific starvation model. Live Moss still keeps animals alive at zero, and the assignment in NOW.md remains unchanged. Change eligibility before the next action Growth and environmental input showed why a later phase must read the state produced by an earlier one. Here that state determines whether an animal can act at all. Our tick subtracts one reserve unit with a zero floor, resolves terminal transitions, and then allows only living animals to perform their action. That sequence gives us three responsibilities to keep distinct. Life state answers whether the animal is eligible now. A terminal event records the accepted transition. Cleanup removes the inactive object after it is no longer needed in the live collection. If eligibility depended only on removal, an animal awaiting cleanup could still take its turn. We'll first use ordinary structs and an ordered function so every step is easy to inspect. The next lesson puts the same concern into a Bevy schedule. The reason for checking eligibility again is the same in either form: an animal that was alive at the beginning of the tick can stop being alive before its action phase. Give a death one event The helper must distinguish a new death from an animal that remains dead, because only the transition earns a record. The resolve_terminal helper accepts exactly one situation: life is Alive and reserve is zero. It changes life to Dead , appends a terminal record, and returns true . Positive reserve or an already dead animal returns false without adding a record. The life check is what makes a repeated call harmless. Zero reserve may remain true for many later ticks, but the alive-to-dead transition has already happened. If we recorded an event whenever the number was zero, a single animal could appear to die repeatedly. Checking both the condition and the current life state gives the event its once-only meaning. It may be tempting to search history instead: if a death record exists, don't add another. That would make eligibility depend on how much history we retain. Once an old record was evicted, the same animal could qualify again. Current life state must own the decision, while history describes the decision that was made. Our record calls the cause Starved , naming the toy rule that accepted the transition. An animal authored at zero qualifies too. The word doesn't supply a physiological model or a grace period. If we later want a rescue meal, health loss, or a delay at zero, we'll need to change the rule and its timing explicitly. Keep a record that survives cleanup After removing Fern, a borrowed reference into her old vector element wouldn't be a usable historical record. We'll instead copy a Key containing run and individual ID into each event, alongside the tick, sequence number, and cause. The journal then owns the information needed to identify the transition without keeping the animal borrowed. The run number matters when a reset reuses individual IDs. Run seven's ID nine and run eight's ID nine identify different individuals. A nickname can't replace that context because names can repeat, change, or be absent. Within each run, this fixture assumes unique IDs. Each journal also belongs to one run. We can keep the old journal beside a new world's animals, but its collected ticks describe only its own run. A cross-run query returns unknown rather than borrowing the old coverage as evidence about new events. This extends the same ownership idea we used for saved inspector readings: retaining a value is useful when its provenance stays attached. Explain what a bounded journal can answer Keeping every event indefinitely would let a long-running browser session consume memory without a bound. Our journal retains at most a selected positive number of events. It appends at the back of a VecDeque and removes the oldest record from the front when full. The standard VecDeque reference describes those operations; our length check supplies the retention rule. Reserving allocation capacity alone wouldn't enforce it. Forgetting a row changes what the journal can prove, so it also tracks evicted-record count and a coverage interval. complete_from is the first completely retained tick; collected_through is the last completely collected one. Event sequence numbers keep increasing as old rows leave, preserving the distinction between the newest two records and the first two records ever produced. A tick becomes collected only after all its terminal producers have finished. We must finish an empty tick too, because “we collected no events” supports a zero count while “we haven't collected this tick” doesn't. The supplied methods enforce consecutive collection and reject appending to a tick that is already sealed. Eviction can also remove part of a tick. Suppose tick five produced several events and the oldest one is discarded while another tick-five event remains. We can still display the retained event, but we can no longer give a complete count for tick five. The conservative coverage boundary moves to tick six. Answers supported by the journal's coverage Requested interval Answer Entirely collected and completely retained Some(count) , including a valid zero. Overlaps a tick affected by eviction None : the complete count is unknown. Reaches an uncollected future tick or another run None : this journal doesn't establish the answer. Even Some(0) has a specific meaning: no matching terminal event occurred in that covered interval. It doesn't establish that the individual existed throughout it, remained alive, or had no event before it began. Those questions need population state or a different history interval. A zero result becomes useful when its question remains visible. Follow Fern through removal and eviction Start run seven with ID nine at reserve one and a journal limit of two events. Execute one tick, then remove dead animals from the vector. On each of the next two ticks, introduce another authored animal that reaches zero after maintenance. Predict Fern's action count, which events remain, and what the journal can say about her first tick afterward. Hint 1: check life before cleanup Maintenance reaches zero, terminal resolution changes life, and the action loop excludes dead animals. Removal happens only after those phases. Hint 2: follow coverage as well as rows The third record pushes the first out of a two-event journal. Once that happens, the remaining rows can't establish a complete count for tick one. Prediction answer Fern performs zero actions. Her event survives removal of the animal, then is evicted when the third event arrives. Two records remain and one has been evicted. Her count for tick one is unknown; her count across the completely covered ticks two and three is zero. Prepare a practice file from the repository root and implement resolve_terminal . The journal and tick phases are supplied. Your helper should recognize a state transition and record it, rather than search history to decide whether it is allowed. python3 learning/scripts/labs.py prepare history --dest work/history-practice python3 learning/scripts/labs.py check history --file work/history-practice/history.rs The initial check reaches an intentional todo! . After the edit, expect eight passing tests. One keeps a dead animal around after its original event has been evicted, checking that forgetting the event doesn't permit another death. If the action count reaches one on its terminal tick, inspect the action filter and phase order. Complete starter: history.rs use std::collections::VecDeque; #[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)] struct Key { run: u32, id: u32 } #[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)] enum Life { Alive, Dead } #[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)] enum Cause { Starved } #[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)] struct Terminal { sequence: u64, tick: u64, subject: Key, cause: Cause } #[derive(Debug)] struct Animal { key: Key, reserve_units: u32, life: Life, actions: u64 } struct Journal { run: u32, limit: usize, events: VecDeque<Terminal>, evicted: u64, complete_from: u64, collected_through: u64, next_sequence: u64, } impl Journal { fn new(run: u32, limit: usize) -> Self { assert!(limit > 0, "this journal requires positive retention"); Self { run, limit, events: VecDeque::new(), evicted: 0, complete_from: 1, collected_through: 0, next_sequence: 1 } } fn record(&mut self, tick: u64, subject: Key, cause: Cause) { assert_eq!(subject.run, self.run); assert_eq!(tick, self.collected_through.checked_add(1).unwrap()); let sequence = self.next_sequence; self.next_sequence = sequence.checked_add(1).expect("event sequence exhausted"); if self.events.len() == self.limit { let removed = self.events.pop_front().unwrap(); self.evicted = self.evicted.checked_add(1).expect("eviction count exhausted"); self.complete_from = self.complete_from.max( removed.tick.checked_add(1).expect("coverage tick exhausted")); } self.events.push_back(Terminal { sequence, tick, subject, cause }); } fn finish_tick(&mut self, tick: u64) { assert_eq!(tick, self.collected_through.checked_add(1).unwrap()); self.collected_through = tick; } fn terminal_count(&self, subject: Key, from: u64, through: u64) -> Option<usize> { if subject.run != self.run || from > through || from < self.complete_from || through > self.collected_through { return None; } Some(self.events.iter().filter(|event| event.subject == subject && event.tick >= from && event.tick <= through).count()) } } fn resolve_terminal(animal: &mut Animal, tick: u64, journal: &mut Journal) -> bool { let _ = (animal, tick, journal); todo!("change an eligible animal to dead and record that transition once") } fn step(animals: &mut [Animal], journal: &mut Journal) { let tick = journal.collected_through.checked_add(1).expect("tick exhausted"); for animal in animals.iter_mut().filter(|animal| animal.life == Life::Alive) { animal.reserve_units = animal.reserve_units.saturating_sub(1); } for animal in animals.iter_mut() { resolve_terminal(animal, tick, journal); } for animal in animals.iter_mut().filter(|animal| animal.life == Life::Alive) { animal.actions = animal.actions.checked_add(1).expect("action count exhausted"); } journal.finish_tick(tick); } fn animal(run: u32, id: u32, reserve_units: u32) -> Animal { Animal { key: Key { run, id }, reserve_units, life: Life::Alive, actions: 0 } } fn main() { let mut journal = Journal::new(7, 2); let mut animals = vec![animal(7, 9, 1)]; step(&mut animals, &mut journal); println!("life={:?} actions={} terminal={:?}", animals[0].life, animals[0].actions, journal.terminal_count(Key { run: 7, id: 9 }, 1, 1)); animals.retain(|animal| animal.life == Life::Alive); println!("live={} retained={}", animals.len(), journal.events.len()); step(&mut [animal(7, 10, 1)], &mut journal); step(&mut [animal(7, 11, 1)], &mut journal); println!("retained={} evicted={} complete={}..={}", journal.events.len(), journal.evicted, journal.complete_from, journal.collected_through); println!("old={:?} later={:?}", journal.terminal_count(Key { run: 7, id: 9 }, 1, 1), journal.terminal_count(Key { run: 7, id: 9 }, 2, 3)); } #[cfg(test)] mod tests { use super::*; #[test] fn terminal_transition_happens_once_before_later_action() { let mut journal = Journal::new(7, 4); let mut animals = [animal(7, 9, 1)]; step(&mut animals, &mut journal); step(&mut animals, &mut journal); assert_eq!((animals[0].life, animals[0].reserve_units, animals[0].actions), (Life::Dead, 0, 0)); assert_eq!(journal.events.iter().copied().collect::<Vec<_>>(), vec![ Terminal { sequence: 1, tick: 1, subject: Key { run: 7, id: 9 }, cause: Cause::Starved }]); } #[test] fn surviving_animal_acts_and_known_absence_is_zero() { let mut journal = Journal::new(7, 2); let mut animals = [animal(7, 9, 3)]; step(&mut animals, &mut journal); assert_eq!((animals[0].reserve_units, animals[0].actions), (2, 1)); assert_eq!(journal.terminal_count(animals[0].key, 1, 1), Some(0)); } #[test] fn repeated_resolution_in_one_tick_does_not_duplicate_the_event() { let mut journal = Journal::new(7, 2); let mut subject = animal(7, 9, 0); assert!(resolve_terminal(&mut subject, 1, &mut journal)); assert!(!resolve_terminal(&mut subject, 1, &mut journal)); assert_eq!(journal.events.len(), 1); } #[test] fn retained_identity_survives_removal_and_differs_across_runs() { let mut journal = Journal::new(7, 2); let mut animals = vec![animal(7, 9, 1)]; step(&mut animals, &mut journal); animals.retain(|animal| animal.life == Life::Alive); assert!(animals.is_empty()); assert_eq!(journal.events[0].subject, Key { run: 7, id: 9 }); let next_run = animal(8, 9, 4); assert_ne!(journal.events[0].subject, next_run.key); assert_eq!(journal.terminal_count(next_run.key, 1, 1), None); } #[test] fn eviction_preserves_order_and_exposes_lost_coverage() { let mut journal = Journal::new(7, 2); for id in [9, 10, 11] { step(&mut [animal(7, id, 1)], &mut journal); } assert_eq!(journal.events.iter().map(|e| (e.sequence, e.subject.id)).collect::<Vec<_>>(), vec![(2, 10), (3, 11)]); assert_eq!((journal.evicted, journal.complete_from, journal.collected_through), (1, 2, 3)); assert_eq!(journal.terminal_count(Key { run: 7, id: 9 }, 1, 3), None); assert_eq!(journal.terminal_count(Key { run: 7, id: 9 }, 2, 3), Some(0)); } #[test] fn eviction_within_one_tick_marks_the_entire_tick_incomplete() { let mut journal = Journal::new(7, 1); step(&mut [animal(7, 9, 1), animal(7, 10, 1)], &mut journal); assert_eq!(journal.events.len(), 1); assert_eq!(journal.events[0].subject.id, 10); assert_eq!(journal.complete_from, 2); assert_eq!(journal.terminal_count(Key { run: 7, id: 10 }, 1, 1), None); step(&mut [], &mut journal); assert_eq!(journal.terminal_count(Key { run: 7, id: 10 }, 2, 2), Some(0)); } #[test] fn uncollected_and_invalid_ranges_are_unknown() { let mut journal = Journal::new(7, 2); let key = Key { run: 7, id: 9 }; assert_eq!(journal.terminal_count(key, 1, 1), None); step(&mut [], &mut journal); assert_eq!(journal.terminal_count(key, 1, 1), Some(0)); assert_eq!(journal.terminal_count(key, 1, 2), None); assert_eq!(journal.terminal_count(key, 2, 1), None); } #[test] fn forgetting_a_record_does_not_revive_terminal_eligibility() { let mut journal = Journal::new(7, 1); let mut original = animal(7, 9, 0); assert!(resolve_terminal(&mut original, 1, &mut journal)); journal.finish_tick(1); step(&mut [animal(7, 10, 1)], &mut journal); assert_eq!(journal.events[0].subject.id, 10); assert!(!resolve_terminal(&mut original, 3, &mut journal)); assert_eq!((journal.events.len(), journal.evicted), (1, 1)); } } Read the transition beside its journal Now follow the helper through the parts that keep its explanation usable after the action has ended. The complete reference below contains the helper, bounded journal, and ordered tick in one file. Read the life check first, then follow a successful call into record . The checked counters stop on exhaustion instead of wrapping sequence or tick values into misleading history. Complete worked answer: history.rs use std::collections::VecDeque; #[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)] struct Key { run: u32, id: u32 } #[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)] enum Life { Alive, Dead } #[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)] enum Cause { Starved } #[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)] struct Terminal { sequence: u64, tick: u64, subject: Key, cause: Cause } #[derive(Debug)] struct Animal { key: Key, reserve_units: u32, life: Life, actions: u64 } struct Journal { run: u32, limit: usize, events: VecDeque<Terminal>, evicted: u64, complete_from: u64, collected_through: u64, next_sequence: u64, } impl Journal { fn new(run: u32, limit: usize) -> Self { assert!(limit > 0, "this journal requires positive retention"); Self { run, limit, events: VecDeque::new(), evicted: 0, complete_from: 1, collected_through: 0, next_sequence: 1 } } fn record(&mut self, tick: u64, subject: Key, cause: Cause) { assert_eq!(subject.run, self.run); assert_eq!(tick, self.collected_through.checked_add(1).unwrap()); let sequence = self.next_sequence; self.next_sequence = sequence.checked_add(1).expect("event sequence exhausted"); if self.events.len() == self.limit { let removed = self.events.pop_front().unwrap(); self.evicted = self.evicted.checked_add(1).expect("eviction count exhausted"); self.complete_from = self.complete_from.max( removed.tick.checked_add(1).expect("coverage tick exhausted")); } self.events.push_back(Terminal { sequence, tick, subject, cause }); } fn finish_tick(&mut self, tick: u64) { assert_eq!(tick, self.collected_through.checked_add(1).unwrap()); self.collected_through = tick; } fn terminal_count(&self, subject: Key, from: u64, through: u64) -> Option<usize> { if subject.run != self.run || from > through || from < self.complete_from || through > self.collected_through { return None; } Some(self.events.iter().filter(|event| event.subject == subject && event.tick >= from && event.tick <= through).count()) } } fn resolve_terminal(animal: &mut Animal, tick: u64, journal: &mut Journal) -> bool { if animal.life != Life::Alive || animal.reserve_units != 0 { return false; } animal.life = Life::Dead; journal.record(tick, animal.key, Cause::Starved); true } fn step(animals: &mut [Animal], journal: &mut Journal) { let tick = journal.collected_through.checked_add(1).expect("tick exhausted"); for animal in animals.iter_mut().filter(|animal| animal.life == Life::Alive) { animal.reserve_units = animal.reserve_units.saturating_sub(1); } for animal in animals.iter_mut() { resolve_terminal(animal, tick, journal); } for animal in animals.iter_mut().filter(|animal| animal.life == Life::Alive) { animal.actions = animal.actions.checked_add(1).expect("action count exhausted"); } journal.finish_tick(tick); } fn animal(run: u32, id: u32, reserve_units: u32) -> Animal { Animal { key: Key { run, id }, reserve_units, life: Life::Alive, actions: 0 } } fn main() { let mut journal = Journal::new(7, 2); let mut animals = vec![animal(7, 9, 1)]; step(&mut animals, &mut journal); println!("life={:?} actions={} terminal={:?}", animals[0].life, animals[0].actions, journal.terminal_count(Key { run: 7, id: 9 }, 1, 1)); animals.retain(|animal| animal.life == Life::Alive); println!("live={} retained={}", animals.len(), journal.events.len()); step(&mut [animal(7, 10, 1)], &mut journal); step(&mut [animal(7, 11, 1)], &mut journal); println!("retained={} evicted={} complete={}..={}", journal.events.len(), journal.evicted, journal.complete_from, journal.collected_through); println!("old={:?} later={:?}", journal.terminal_count(Key { run: 7, id: 9 }, 1, 1), journal.terminal_count(Key { run: 7, id: 9 }, 2, 3)); } #[cfg(test)] mod tests { use super::*; #[test] fn terminal_transition_happens_once_before_later_action() { let mut journal = Journal::new(7, 4); let mut animals = [animal(7, 9, 1)]; step(&mut animals, &mut journal); step(&mut animals, &mut journal); assert_eq!((animals[0].life, animals[0].reserve_units, animals[0].actions), (Life::Dead, 0, 0)); assert_eq!(journal.events.iter().copied().collect::<Vec<_>>(), vec![ Terminal { sequence: 1, tick: 1, subject: Key { run: 7, id: 9 }, cause: Cause::Starved }]); } #[test] fn surviving_animal_acts_and_known_absence_is_zero() { let mut journal = Journal::new(7, 2); let mut animals = [animal(7, 9, 3)]; step(&mut animals, &mut journal); assert_eq!((animals[0].reserve_units, animals[0].actions), (2, 1)); assert_eq!(journal.terminal_count(animals[0].key, 1, 1), Some(0)); } #[test] fn repeated_resolution_in_one_tick_does_not_duplicate_the_event() { let mut journal = Journal::new(7, 2); let mut subject = animal(7, 9, 0); assert!(resolve_terminal(&mut subject, 1, &mut journal)); assert!(!resolve_terminal(&mut subject, 1, &mut journal)); assert_eq!(journal.events.len(), 1); } #[test] fn retained_identity_survives_removal_and_differs_across_runs() { let mut journal = Journal::new(7, 2); let mut animals = vec![animal(7, 9, 1)]; step(&mut animals, &mut journal); animals.retain(|animal| animal.life == Life::Alive); assert!(animals.is_empty()); assert_eq!(journal.events[0].subject, Key { run: 7, id: 9 }); let next_run = animal(8, 9, 4); assert_ne!(journal.events[0].subject, next_run.key); assert_eq!(journal.terminal_count(next_run.key, 1, 1), None); } #[test] fn eviction_preserves_order_and_exposes_lost_coverage() { let mut journal = Journal::new(7, 2); for id in [9, 10, 11] { step(&mut [animal(7, id, 1)], &mut journal); } assert_eq!(journal.events.iter().map(|e| (e.sequence, e.subject.id)).collect::<Vec<_>>(), vec![(2, 10), (3, 11)]); assert_eq!((journal.evicted, journal.complete_from, journal.collected_through), (1, 2, 3)); assert_eq!(journal.terminal_count(Key { run: 7, id: 9 }, 1, 3), None); assert_eq!(journal.terminal_count(Key { run: 7, id: 9 }, 2, 3), Some(0)); } #[test] fn eviction_within_one_tick_marks_the_entire_tick_incomplete() { let mut journal = Journal::new(7, 1); step(&mut [animal(7, 9, 1), animal(7, 10, 1)], &mut journal); assert_eq!(journal.events.len(), 1); assert_eq!(journal.events[0].subject.id, 10); assert_eq!(journal.complete_from, 2); assert_eq!(journal.terminal_count(Key { run: 7, id: 10 }, 1, 1), None); step(&mut [], &mut journal); assert_eq!(journal.terminal_count(Key { run: 7, id: 10 }, 2, 2), Some(0)); } #[test] fn uncollected_and_invalid_ranges_are_unknown() { let mut journal = Journal::new(7, 2); let key = Key { run: 7, id: 9 }; assert_eq!(journal.terminal_count(key, 1, 1), None); step(&mut [], &mut journal); assert_eq!(journal.terminal_count(key, 1, 1), Some(0)); assert_eq!(journal.terminal_count(key, 1, 2), None); assert_eq!(journal.terminal_count(key, 2, 1), None); } #[test] fn forgetting_a_record_does_not_revive_terminal_eligibility() { let mut journal = Journal::new(7, 1); let mut original = animal(7, 9, 0); assert!(resolve_terminal(&mut original, 1, &mut journal)); journal.finish_tick(1); step(&mut [animal(7, 10, 1)], &mut journal); assert_eq!(journal.events[0].subject.id, 10); assert!(!resolve_terminal(&mut original, 3, &mut journal)); assert_eq!((journal.events.len(), journal.evicted), (1, 1)); } } Check this reference independently of your edited file with the following command: python3 learning/scripts/labs.py check history The expected program output is: life=Dead actions=0 terminal=Some(1) live=0 retained=1 retained=2 evicted=1 complete=2..=3 old=None later=Some(0) The first two lines show that an animal can stop participating while its explanation remains. The later lines show the journal's separate limit: retaining recent events doesn't make it a complete lifetime archive. Displaying the final None as zero would undo the distinction its query carefully preserved. Eligibility can end before its evidence does Fern's disappearance now has two different lifetimes. Her current life state changes before the action, and her owned record can remain after cleanup. Later, eviction can shorten our historical evidence without changing that terminal decision. Neither cleanup timing nor journal capacity needs to decide whether she may act again. Recall the three boundaries An owned key survives removal without borrowing the animal. The life check permits one alive-to-dead transition while zero reserve persists. Coverage treats a tick as incomplete if any of its events were evicted, even when other rows from that tick remain. The native tests exercise this ordered model, owned identities, eviction, and coverage queries. A live ECS integration would also need schedule checks, while a browser history panel would need an observation path showing identity, cause, and coverage after removal. The isolated result gives us the contract those integrations must preserve. In two hunters and one prey , the same immediate eligibility change will have another purpose: preventing a later hunter from receiving a second reward while the consumed entity is still waiting for cleanup.

title: Consume once, even before removal
summary: Let two hunters compete for one prey and make its immediate availability authoritative before deferred despawn.
text: Two hunters reach the same prey. The first succeeds and queues its removal, but the prey's entity is still present when the second hunter gets a turn. We need one capture to produce one reward, and we need the prey to miss its own later action. Make a capture take effect before cleanup You'll implement claim , combining the finite meal's accounting with the terminal transition's eligibility check. A supplied Bevy schedule will resolve both hunters, try the prey's action, and inspect the result while deferred removal is still pending. Leaving the entity present makes the immediate availability change visible. By the end, you should be able to show why only one hunter receives a reward, why a rejected claim leaves both participants unchanged, and why the consumed prey performs no later action. We'll then apply the queued cleanup and check what remains: one owned interaction record, independent of the entity's continued existence. This isolated Bevy ECS 0.18.1 lab proposes a whole-prey meal at same-cell contact, converting biomass to reserve one for one only when the entire gain fits. These teaching rules don't activate hunting, death, or movement in live Moss. Combine a transfer with a terminal transition Finite meals made two consumers share one current supply, while terminal history stopped a dead animal from acting before cleanup. A hunt brings both concerns into one accepted interaction. The hunter gains reserve, the prey loses biomass and eligibility, and an owned record explains the change. Our hunters have stable IDs 9 and 2. Each starts with zero reserve and capacity ten, and both target prey 40 at cell zero. The prey contains three biomass units. We spawn hunter 9 first but resolve by ascending stable ID, so hunter 2 gets the first opportunity. Its successful capture should leave nothing for hunter 9 to receive. This meal also differs deliberately from eating part of a patch. Our terminal policy consumes the whole prey, so all three units must fit. If a hunter has room for only one, we reject before claiming anything. Otherwise, accepting the kill and crediting one would imply a discarded remainder that the model never accounted for. The ID priority makes this small contest repeatable. It doesn't show fairness or real predator behavior: lower IDs keep winning otherwise identical contests. Once accounting and eligibility are established, another priority policy can be compared against them without confusing a change of winner with a double reward. Leave a rejected prey available A hunter that cannot accept the whole meal must leave the next hunter's opportunity intact. We'll establish every condition before claiming the prey, starting when the resolver locates the hunter's selected prey by stable ID. If that identity is missing, it doesn't redirect the action toward another animal. The claim helper then checks that the hunter is alive, the prey remains available with positive biomass, both occupy the same cell, and the hunter's reserve is valid. A valid reserve lets us calculate room as capacity minus reserve. The full biomass must fit in that room before any participant changes. This matters for the order of the contest: if hunter 2 starts at nine of ten units, rejecting its three-unit meal must leave prey 40 available for hunter 9. After acceptance, the helper computes the new reserve with checked addition. It then writes three connected changes: the prey becomes unavailable, its biomass becomes zero, and the hunter receives the full gain. The returned Some(gain) lets the caller record those actual units and queue structural cleanup. Rejected attempts return None . That intentionally combines the reasons in this focused lab; an inspector could use the named rejection style from the meal lesson if it needed to explain each one. Whatever return type we choose, the failed attempt must leave both participants unchanged so another eligible action can still resolve correctly. Make unavailability visible immediately Commands::despawn requests removal through a command buffer. While that command is pending, another query can still find the prey's components. The immediately written available field is therefore the state that prevents a second capture: hunter 9 reads the change made by hunter 2 before attempting its own claim. Queuing a Dead marker wouldn't automatically solve the timing problem. If its insertion were still pending, later systems couldn't use it to exclude the prey yet. A marker can serve another design well, but its visibility must match the moment at which the actor loses permission. Here the component field changes at the accepted transaction. The prey's action system illustrates the same distinction. Its query still finds entities with Prey , then checks availability before incrementing their action counts. The consumed prey remains present during this experiment but performs zero actions. Query membership answers whether the data exists; the eligibility field answers whether this rule may act on it. We need to check the schedule as well as the helper. Even a correct claim would permit a different tick outcome if prey action ran first. Conversely, the intended phase order couldn't prevent duplicate rewards if claim left availability unchanged. The next part of the fixture makes both promises observable. Keep the entity present long enough to inspect it The schedule chains hunt resolution, prey action, and observation of pending state. We also select the single-threaded executor, but the chain is what states our semantic order. The observation should find prey 40 still present, with zero biomass, unavailable, and an action count of zero. To expose that intermediate state, the lab turns off automatic intermediate deferred application and final deferred application. Bevy 0.18.1 supports automatic application along ordering dependencies and at the end of a schedule; allowing cleanup to happen there would hide the state we're investigating. These settings serve this experiment rather than prescribe how every schedule should be configured. After schedule.run , the program prints the pending observation and then calls schedule.apply_deferred on that same schedule. Its systems own the queued commands. Calling a different schedule wouldn't flush those command buffers and wouldn't complete this cleanup. Prey 40 through resolution and deferred cleanup Observation point State and outcome Before hunting Present, available, three biomass units. After hunter 2 succeeds Present, unavailable, zero biomass; removal queued. After hunter 9 and prey action Still unavailable; one reward, one terminal record, zero prey actions. After explicit deferred application No prey entity; the owned interaction record remains. Checking only the last row wouldn't establish why the second reward or prey action was prevented. Holding cleanup open lets the tests show that eligibility changed while the entity was still accessible. Record both participants in the same event Cleanup will remove the prey's components, so the accepted interaction needs an explanation that belongs to neither live participant. The capture records run seven, tick one, prey ID 40, hunter ID 2, and the three units gained. A future biography for either participant can refer to this interaction. Producing separate “matching” events for each biography would introduce another opportunity for their identities, times, or amounts to disagree. These are application IDs rather than retained ECS handles. Handles help the resolver access current entities; owned run and actor identities keep the record interpretable after despawn. The fixture assumes unique hunter and prey IDs within the run and assigns separate roles. It doesn't define role changes or cannibalism. The journal is a short vector because this fixture performs only a few controlled resolutions. A long-running world would need the previous lesson's bounded retention and visible coverage around these records too. Pursuit, injury, and escape also remain outside this one-contact transaction. Try another claim before cleanup Predict both hunter reserves, terminal-record count, and prey action count after the schedule runs but before commands are applied. Then run that schedule again with cleanup still pending. Finally, start a fresh fixture where hunter 2 has room for only one unit and decide who receives the three-unit prey. Hint 1: read the changed field The later hunter and repeated execution both encounter the prey's current unavailability. Its entity can remain present without becoming eligible for another reward. Hint 2: follow rejection before mutation The whole meal must fit. Hunter 2's insufficient-capacity attempt leaves the prey available for the next hunter. Prediction answer In the ordinary fixture, hunter 2 gains three, hunter 9 gains zero, one terminal event exists, and the prey performs zero actions. Repeating resolution before cleanup adds nothing. In the capacity fixture, hunter 2 stays at nine and hunter 9 gains the prey's three units instead. Prepare a practice file from the repository root and implement claim . The resolver, schedule, observation, and explicit cleanup are supplied so the helper's effects are checked at the relevant boundaries. python3 learning/scripts/labs.py prepare predation --dest work/predation-practice python3 learning/scripts/labs.py check predation --file work/predation-practice/predation.rs The first run reaches an intentional todo! . After your edit, expect eight passing tests. If the prey acts while awaiting cleanup, inspect both its eligibility check and the schedule order. If the wrong hunter wins, follow the stable-ID ordering before suspecting entity allocation. Complete starter: predation.rs use bevy_ecs::prelude::*; use bevy_ecs::schedule::{ExecutorKind, ScheduleBuildSettings}; #[derive(Component, Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq, PartialOrd, Ord)] struct Id(u32); #[derive(Component)] struct Hunter { target: Id, cell: i32, reserve_units: u32, capacity_units: u32, alive: bool } #[derive(Component)] struct Prey { cell: i32, biomass_units: u32, available: bool, actions: u32 } #[derive(Resource)] struct Moment { run: u32, tick: u64 } #[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)] struct Terminal { run: u32, tick: u64, prey: Id, hunter: Id, gained_units: u32 } #[derive(Resource, Default)] struct Journal(Vec<Terminal>); #[derive(Resource, Default)] struct Audit { pending: Vec<(Id, bool, u32, u32)>, acted: Vec<Id> } fn claim(prey: &mut Prey, hunter: &mut Hunter) -> Option<u32> { let _ = (prey, hunter); todo!("validate the whole-prey transfer, then immediately claim and credit it") } fn resolve_hunts( mut commands: Commands, moment: Res<Moment>, mut hunters: Query<(Entity, &Id, &mut Hunter)>, mut prey_query: Query<(Entity, &Id, &mut Prey)>, mut journal: ResMut<Journal>, ) { let mut order: Vec<(Id, Entity)> = hunters.iter().map(|(entity, id, _)| (*id, entity)).collect(); order.sort_by_key(|(id, _)| *id); for (_, entity) in order { let (_, hunter_id, mut hunter) = hunters.get_mut(entity).unwrap(); for (prey_entity, prey_id, mut prey) in &mut prey_query { if *prey_id != hunter.target { continue; } if let Some(gained_units) = claim(&mut prey, &mut hunter) { journal.0.push(Terminal { run: moment.run, tick: moment.tick, prey: *prey_id, hunter: *hunter_id, gained_units }); commands.entity(prey_entity).despawn(); } break; } } } fn prey_action(mut prey_query: Query<(&Id, &mut Prey)>, mut audit: ResMut<Audit>) { for (id, mut prey) in &mut prey_query { if !prey.available { continue; } prey.actions = prey.actions.checked_add(1).expect("action count exhausted"); audit.acted.push(*id); } } fn observe_pending(prey_query: Query<(&Id, &Prey)>, mut audit: ResMut<Audit>) { audit.pending = prey_query.iter().map(|(id, prey)| (*id, prey.available, prey.biomass_units, prey.actions)).collect(); audit.pending.sort_by_key(|row| row.0); } fn hunt_schedule() -> Schedule { let mut schedule = Schedule::default(); schedule.set_executor_kind(ExecutorKind::SingleThreaded); schedule.set_build_settings(ScheduleBuildSettings { auto_insert_apply_deferred: false, ..Default::default() }); schedule.set_apply_final_deferred(false); schedule.add_systems((resolve_hunts, prey_action, observe_pending).chain()); schedule } fn fixture(order: [u32; 2]) -> (World, Entity) { let mut world = World::new(); world.insert_resource(Moment { run: 7, tick: 1 }); world.init_resource::<Journal>(); world.init_resource::<Audit>(); for id in order { world.spawn((Id(id), Hunter { target: Id(40), cell: 0, reserve_units: 0, capacity_units: 10, alive: true })); } let prey = world.spawn((Id(40), Prey { cell: 0, biomass_units: 3, available: true, actions: 0 })).id(); (world, prey) } fn reserves(world: &mut World) -> Vec<(Id, u32)> { let mut rows: Vec<_> = world.query::<(&Id, &Hunter)>().iter(world) .map(|(id, hunter)| (*id, hunter.reserve_units)).collect(); rows.sort_by_key(|row| row.0); rows } fn main() { let (mut world, _) = fixture([9, 2]); let mut schedule = hunt_schedule(); schedule.run(&mut world); println!("reserves={:?}", reserves(&mut world)); println!("pending={:?}", world.resource::<Audit>().pending); println!("terminal records={}", world.resource::<Journal>().0.len()); schedule.apply_deferred(&mut world); println!("prey after cleanup={}", world.query::<&Prey>().iter(&world).count()); } #[cfg(test)] mod tests { use super::*; #[test] fn one_prey_rewards_one_hunter_before_structural_cleanup() { let (mut world, prey) = fixture([9, 2]); hunt_schedule().run(&mut world); assert_eq!(reserves(&mut world), vec![(Id(2), 3), (Id(9), 0)]); assert!(world.get::<Prey>(prey).is_some()); assert_eq!(world.resource::<Audit>().pending, vec![(Id(40), false, 0, 0)]); assert!(world.resource::<Audit>().acted.is_empty()); assert_eq!(world.resource::<Journal>().0, vec![Terminal { run: 7, tick: 1, prey: Id(40), hunter: Id(2), gained_units: 3 }]); } #[test] fn spawn_order_does_not_select_the_winner() { for order in [[9, 2], [2, 9]] { let (mut world, _) = fixture(order); hunt_schedule().run(&mut world); assert_eq!(reserves(&mut world), vec![(Id(2), 3), (Id(9), 0)]); assert_eq!(world.resource::<Journal>().0[0].hunter, Id(2)); } } #[test] fn repeated_resolution_while_cleanup_is_pending_does_not_reward_again() { let (mut world, prey) = fixture([9, 2]); let mut schedule = hunt_schedule(); schedule.run(&mut world); schedule.run(&mut world); assert!(world.get::<Prey>(prey).is_some()); assert_eq!(reserves(&mut world), vec![(Id(2), 3), (Id(9), 0)]); assert_eq!(world.resource::<Journal>().0.len(), 1); assert!(world.resource::<Audit>().acted.is_empty()); schedule.apply_deferred(&mut world); assert!(world.get::<Prey>(prey).is_none()); schedule.run(&mut world); assert_eq!(world.resource::<Journal>().0.len(), 1); } #[test] fn insufficient_capacity_rejects_without_consumption_and_later_hunter_can_win() { let (mut world, _) = fixture([9, 2]); for (id, mut hunter) in world.query::<(&Id, &mut Hunter)>().iter_mut(&mut world) { if *id == Id(2) { hunter.reserve_units = 9; } } hunt_schedule().run(&mut world); assert_eq!(reserves(&mut world), vec![(Id(2), 9), (Id(9), 3)]); assert_eq!(world.resource::<Journal>().0[0].hunter, Id(9)); } #[test] fn absent_contact_preserves_prey_and_allows_its_later_action() { let (mut world, prey) = fixture([9, 2]); world.get_mut::<Prey>(prey).unwrap().cell = 1; hunt_schedule().run(&mut world); assert_eq!(reserves(&mut world), vec![(Id(2), 0), (Id(9), 0)]); assert_eq!(world.resource::<Audit>().pending, vec![(Id(40), true, 3, 1)]); assert_eq!(world.resource::<Audit>().acted, vec![Id(40)]); assert!(world.resource::<Journal>().0.is_empty()); } #[test] fn dead_hunter_and_invalid_reserve_cannot_claim_prey() { let mut prey = Prey { cell: 0, biomass_units: 3, available: true, actions: 0 }; let mut hunter = Hunter { target: Id(40), cell: 0, reserve_units: 0, capacity_units: 10, alive: false }; assert_eq!(claim(&mut prey, &mut hunter), None); hunter.alive = true; hunter.reserve_units = 11; assert_eq!(claim(&mut prey, &mut hunter), None); assert_eq!((prey.available, prey.biomass_units, hunter.reserve_units), (true, 3, 11)); } #[test] fn exact_capacity_at_integer_limit_is_safe_and_zero_biomass_is_ineligible() { let mut prey = Prey { cell: 0, biomass_units: 3, available: true, actions: 0 }; let mut hunter = Hunter { target: Id(40), cell: 0, reserve_units: u32::MAX - 3, capacity_units: u32::MAX, alive: true }; assert_eq!(claim(&mut prey, &mut hunter), Some(3)); assert_eq!(hunter.reserve_units, u32::MAX); prey.available = true; hunter.reserve_units = 0; assert_eq!(claim(&mut prey, &mut hunter), None); assert_eq!(hunter.reserve_units, 0); } #[test] fn a_missing_target_grants_no_reward_or_terminal_record() { let (mut world, prey) = fixture([9, 2]); assert!(world.despawn(prey)); hunt_schedule().run(&mut world); assert_eq!(reserves(&mut world), vec![(Id(2), 0), (Id(9), 0)]); assert!(world.resource::<Journal>().0.is_empty()); assert!(world.resource::<Audit>().acted.is_empty()); } } Inspect the real schedule The complete reference below uses the course's pinned Bevy ECS dependency. Its mutable queries write different component types, Hunter and Prey , while both read identity. Follow a successful claim into the journal write and queued despawn, then continue through prey action to the pending observation. Complete worked answer: predation.rs use bevy_ecs::prelude::*; use bevy_ecs::schedule::{ExecutorKind, ScheduleBuildSettings}; #[derive(Component, Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq, PartialOrd, Ord)] struct Id(u32); #[derive(Component)] struct Hunter { target: Id, cell: i32, reserve_units: u32, capacity_units: u32, alive: bool } #[derive(Component)] struct Prey { cell: i32, biomass_units: u32, available: bool, actions: u32 } #[derive(Resource)] struct Moment { run: u32, tick: u64 } #[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)] struct Terminal { run: u32, tick: u64, prey: Id, hunter: Id, gained_units: u32 } #[derive(Resource, Default)] struct Journal(Vec<Terminal>); #[derive(Resource, Default)] struct Audit { pending: Vec<(Id, bool, u32, u32)>, acted: Vec<Id> } fn claim(prey: &mut Prey, hunter: &mut Hunter) -> Option<u32> { if !hunter.alive || !prey.available || prey.biomass_units == 0 || hunter.cell != prey.cell || hunter.reserve_units > hunter.capacity_units { return None; } let gain = prey.biomass_units; let room = hunter.capacity_units - hunter.reserve_units; if gain > room { return None; } let reserve = hunter.reserve_units.checked_add(gain).expect("gain fits validated room"); prey.available = false; prey.biomass_units = 0; hunter.reserve_units = reserve; Some(gain) } fn resolve_hunts( mut commands: Commands, moment: Res<Moment>, mut hunters: Query<(Entity, &Id, &mut Hunter)>, mut prey_query: Query<(Entity, &Id, &mut Prey)>, mut journal: ResMut<Journal>, ) { let mut order: Vec<(Id, Entity)> = hunters.iter().map(|(entity, id, _)| (*id, entity)).collect(); order.sort_by_key(|(id, _)| *id); for (_, entity) in order { let (_, hunter_id, mut hunter) = hunters.get_mut(entity).unwrap(); for (prey_entity, prey_id, mut prey) in &mut prey_query { if *prey_id != hunter.target { continue; } if let Some(gained_units) = claim(&mut prey, &mut hunter) { journal.0.push(Terminal { run: moment.run, tick: moment.tick, prey: *prey_id, hunter: *hunter_id, gained_units }); commands.entity(prey_entity).despawn(); } break; } } } fn prey_action(mut prey_query: Query<(&Id, &mut Prey)>, mut audit: ResMut<Audit>) { for (id, mut prey) in &mut prey_query { if !prey.available { continue; } prey.actions = prey.actions.checked_add(1).expect("action count exhausted"); audit.acted.push(*id); } } fn observe_pending(prey_query: Query<(&Id, &Prey)>, mut audit: ResMut<Audit>) { audit.pending = prey_query.iter().map(|(id, prey)| (*id, prey.available, prey.biomass_units, prey.actions)).collect(); audit.pending.sort_by_key(|row| row.0); } fn hunt_schedule() -> Schedule { let mut schedule = Schedule::default(); schedule.set_executor_kind(ExecutorKind::SingleThreaded); schedule.set_build_settings(ScheduleBuildSettings { auto_insert_apply_deferred: false, ..Default::default() }); schedule.set_apply_final_deferred(false); schedule.add_systems((resolve_hunts, prey_action, observe_pending).chain()); schedule } fn fixture(order: [u32; 2]) -> (World, Entity) { let mut world = World::new(); world.insert_resource(Moment { run: 7, tick: 1 }); world.init_resource::<Journal>(); world.init_resource::<Audit>(); for id in order { world.spawn((Id(id), Hunter { target: Id(40), cell: 0, reserve_units: 0, capacity_units: 10, alive: true })); } let prey = world.spawn((Id(40), Prey { cell: 0, biomass_units: 3, available: true, actions: 0 })).id(); (world, prey) } fn reserves(world: &mut World) -> Vec<(Id, u32)> { let mut rows: Vec<_> = world.query::<(&Id, &Hunter)>().iter(world) .map(|(id, hunter)| (*id, hunter.reserve_units)).collect(); rows.sort_by_key(|row| row.0); rows } fn main() { let (mut world, _) = fixture([9, 2]); let mut schedule = hunt_schedule(); schedule.run(&mut world); println!("reserves={:?}", reserves(&mut world)); println!("pending={:?}", world.resource::<Audit>().pending); println!("terminal records={}", world.resource::<Journal>().0.len()); schedule.apply_deferred(&mut world); println!("prey after cleanup={}", world.query::<&Prey>().iter(&world).count()); } #[cfg(test)] mod tests { use super::*; #[test] fn one_prey_rewards_one_hunter_before_structural_cleanup() { let (mut world, prey) = fixture([9, 2]); hunt_schedule().run(&mut world); assert_eq!(reserves(&mut world), vec![(Id(2), 3), (Id(9), 0)]); assert!(world.get::<Prey>(prey).is_some()); assert_eq!(world.resource::<Audit>().pending, vec![(Id(40), false, 0, 0)]); assert!(world.resource::<Audit>().acted.is_empty()); assert_eq!(world.resource::<Journal>().0, vec![Terminal { run: 7, tick: 1, prey: Id(40), hunter: Id(2), gained_units: 3 }]); } #[test] fn spawn_order_does_not_select_the_winner() { for order in [[9, 2], [2, 9]] { let (mut world, _) = fixture(order); hunt_schedule().run(&mut world); assert_eq!(reserves(&mut world), vec![(Id(2), 3), (Id(9), 0)]); assert_eq!(world.resource::<Journal>().0[0].hunter, Id(2)); } } #[test] fn repeated_resolution_while_cleanup_is_pending_does_not_reward_again() { let (mut world, prey) = fixture([9, 2]); let mut schedule = hunt_schedule(); schedule.run(&mut world); schedule.run(&mut world); assert!(world.get::<Prey>(prey).is_some()); assert_eq!(reserves(&mut world), vec![(Id(2), 3), (Id(9), 0)]); assert_eq!(world.resource::<Journal>().0.len(), 1); assert!(world.resource::<Audit>().acted.is_empty()); schedule.apply_deferred(&mut world); assert!(world.get::<Prey>(prey).is_none()); schedule.run(&mut world); assert_eq!(world.resource::<Journal>().0.len(), 1); } #[test] fn insufficient_capacity_rejects_without_consumption_and_later_hunter_can_win() { let (mut world, _) = fixture([9, 2]); for (id, mut hunter) in world.query::<(&Id, &mut Hunter)>().iter_mut(&mut world) { if *id == Id(2) { hunter.reserve_units = 9; } } hunt_schedule().run(&mut world); assert_eq!(reserves(&mut world), vec![(Id(2), 9), (Id(9), 3)]); assert_eq!(world.resource::<Journal>().0[0].hunter, Id(9)); } #[test] fn absent_contact_preserves_prey_and_allows_its_later_action() { let (mut world, prey) = fixture([9, 2]); world.get_mut::<Prey>(prey).unwrap().cell = 1; hunt_schedule().run(&mut world); assert_eq!(reserves(&mut world), vec![(Id(2), 0), (Id(9), 0)]); assert_eq!(world.resource::<Audit>().pending, vec![(Id(40), true, 3, 1)]); assert_eq!(world.resource::<Audit>().acted, vec![Id(40)]); assert!(world.resource::<Journal>().0.is_empty()); } #[test] fn dead_hunter_and_invalid_reserve_cannot_claim_prey() { let mut prey = Prey { cell: 0, biomass_units: 3, available: true, actions: 0 }; let mut hunter = Hunter { target: Id(40), cell: 0, reserve_units: 0, capacity_units: 10, alive: false }; assert_eq!(claim(&mut prey, &mut hunter), None); hunter.alive = true; hunter.reserve_units = 11; assert_eq!(claim(&mut prey, &mut hunter), None); assert_eq!((prey.available, prey.biomass_units, hunter.reserve_units), (true, 3, 11)); } #[test] fn exact_capacity_at_integer_limit_is_safe_and_zero_biomass_is_ineligible() { let mut prey = Prey { cell: 0, biomass_units: 3, available: true, actions: 0 }; let mut hunter = Hunter { target: Id(40), cell: 0, reserve_units: u32::MAX - 3, capacity_units: u32::MAX, alive: true }; assert_eq!(claim(&mut prey, &mut hunter), Some(3)); assert_eq!(hunter.reserve_units, u32::MAX); prey.available = true; hunter.reserve_units = 0; assert_eq!(claim(&mut prey, &mut hunter), None); assert_eq!(hunter.reserve_units, 0); } #[test] fn a_missing_target_grants_no_reward_or_terminal_record() { let (mut world, prey) = fixture([9, 2]); assert!(world.despawn(prey)); hunt_schedule().run(&mut world); assert_eq!(reserves(&mut world), vec![(Id(2), 0), (Id(9), 0)]); assert!(world.resource::<Journal>().0.is_empty()); assert!(world.resource::<Audit>().acted.is_empty()); } } Check the printed reference separately with this command: python3 learning/scripts/labs.py check predation The expected program output is: reserves=[(Id(2), 3), (Id(9), 0)] pending=[(Id(40), false, 0, 0)] terminal records=1 prey after cleanup=0 The pending tuple contains identity, availability, biomass, and action count, in that order. Its presence is useful evidence: the prey still existed when the action phase skipped it. Applying deferred commands removes the entity afterward while leaving the owned record intact. One claim settles the contest The opening contest now resolves without depending on immediate removal. Hunter 2's accepted claim changes the prey's eligibility and supply before either hunter 9 or the prey itself gets another opportunity. Cleanup can follow at its chosen boundary because it no longer carries responsibility for preventing another action. Recall why the checks precede the claim Deferred insertion and despawn may both remain unapplied while other work runs, so the immediate availability change supplies this lab's eligibility boundary. A hunter that cannot hold the full gain must reject before that change, preserving the prey for another eligible hunter. The eight native tests execute the miniature schedule, including reversed spawn order, repeated pending resolution, missing targets, and exact numerical limits. They establish the isolated interaction rather than a live Moss installation or browser result. The deferred settings match the installed 0.18.1 source; the versioned schedule reference provides further detail. In rest and commitment , we'll return to one individual's sequence of actions. A recoverable fatigue value and a remembered commitment will determine when it rests or works, while reserve continues to account for the energy those ticks consume.

title: Make rest a commitment you can inspect
summary: Keep fatigue separate from energy and compare a reactive choice with an activity that lasts for a stated number of ticks.
text: A grazer rests, works, rests, then works again. Each choice follows its fatigue rule, yet the sequence keeps switching around one threshold. Give rest a commitment you can trace We'll compare that reactive policy with one that remembers a minimum rest duration and waits for a lower fatigue threshold before waking. You'll implement decide as a pure activity transition; the supplied step will charge upkeep and apply the chosen action. Keeping those jobs separate lets repeated decisions remain decisions, rather than secretly consuming time. The two traces should help you explain when each creature rests, when it resumes foraging, and why recovery never creates reserve. You'll also check fast recovery, continued fatigue after the minimum, and cancellation of an old destination. The outcome is an inspectable activity policy, with its energy costs and timing still visible. This isolated standard-library lab proposes fatigue and activity rules for one creature. It installs nothing in live Moss and leaves NOW.md unchanged. After resolving one prey once , we'll focus on repeated decisions without food intake, travel, predation, or death. Recover fatigue without creating energy Our creature begins with twelve reserve units and six fatigue points. Every executed tick spends one reserve unit on maintenance, whichever activity is selected. A foraging tick adds two fatigue points, while a resting tick removes two. Fatigue stays between zero and ten; resting adds nothing to reserve. These integers describe different things. Reserve is an available energy store, so spending reduces it. Fatigue is an authored condition that increases during work and decreases during recovery. Putting a reserve increase inside the recovery function would give rest an energy source that this model never specified. We'll use “foraging” here to mean active searching rather than a successful meal. A creature can therefore forage without a selected target and still accumulate fatigue. A larger model would separately establish travel, action-time target validity, and actual food intake. This smaller example leaves intake out so that changing activity is the only effect we're comparing. Maintenance floors reserve at zero. If the creature continues resting there, its reserve remains zero; a bounded subtraction doesn't refill the account. The lab has no terminal transition, so its continued presence can't establish that rest would prevent death in an integrated ecosystem. Trace a decision with no memory First we'll reproduce the alternating behavior without adding any remembered activity. The reactive policy asks the same question before each action: is fatigue at least six? If so, it rests for the tick. Otherwise, it forages. Starting at six, the first rest reduces fatigue to four. The next decision sees four below the entry threshold and chooses work, returning fatigue to six. Nothing in that rule refers to what the creature did before. The third decision therefore sees the same fatigue as the first and repeats the rest, followed by another foraging tick. This alternating trace is consistent with its implementation. Whether we want it depends on the behavior we're trying to model. For example, switching might have a cost, or we might want recovery to finish before active work resumes. We'll explore the latter by adding both a minimum duration and a lower exit threshold. Those additions give the policy a reason to continue resting even after fatigue falls below the threshold that started it. Remember the work still owed to rest To keep resting after the entry condition stops being true, the policy needs another reason to continue. We'll represent both the remaining duration and the recovery needed to wake. The committed policy enters rest at fatigue six too. Once there, it requires at least two executed resting ticks and enough recovery to reach fatigue two or lower. Leaving rest requires both conditions. A creature that recovers quickly still owes its minimum duration, while a very fatigued creature can need more recovery after that duration ends. The lower exit threshold creates a gap between entering and leaving rest, often called hysteresis. The minimum adds a time requirement. Because our paired trace changes both features together, it can't isolate which one explains every difference. The focused tests will do that with fast recovery and unusually high starting fatigue. We'll store the commitment as Resting { ticks_left } . It counts resting actions still owed before the next decision. Entering with two, executing one rest, and storing one lets us follow the obligation through the tick. Calling the decision function again doesn't consume another action. With the default recovery of two, the committed creature rests on ticks one and two, then resumes foraging on tick three. Now that both policies are defined, compare their paths through the same four ticks: Two activity policies with one reserve unit of maintenance per tick Executed tick Reactive activity / fatigue Committed activity / fatigue Reserve in both runs 1 Rest / 4 Rest / 4 11 2 Forage / 6 Rest / 2 10 3 Rest / 4 Forage / 4 9 4 Forage / 6 Forage / 6 8 Both finish at reserve eight and fatigue six, although their intermediate activities differ. Reserve falls identically because maintenance occurs on every executed tick. The state remembered by the activity policy changes when fatigue recovers and when work resumes; it doesn't change that energy charge. The separation between deciding and executing is also important for an ECS host. A changed observation might cause a policy to be evaluated again, but reevaluation isn't elapsed time. Our pure decide function returns an activity value without mutating its caller. Only step charges maintenance, applies recovery or work, and reduces commitment. Make rest end the current destination We also need to decide what happens to a target while the creature rests. The activity enum puts a target only inside Foraging ; Resting contains its duration instead. Entering rest therefore discards the active destination. There is no separate movement target left beside a contradictory activity flag. Waking creates Foraging { target: None } . It doesn't restore the old patch ID or choose a new one. Recovery supplies evidence that the creature can leave rest, but it says nothing about whether an earlier destination remains appropriate. A remembered preference could be a separate value in a future design; it wouldn't automatically become permission to travel. A creature that stays in foraging mode also clears a target when the caller reports it invalid. Commitment can't make an invalid destination usable. Here the current-validity flag is supplied input; this helper doesn't establish that the patch exists, is reachable, or contains food when an action occurs. The enum makes resting without a target easy to express, while Option allows a forager that hasn't yet selected one. The Rust Book's enum chapter explains that language mechanism. Canceling rather than preserving the old destination is our model choice, made visible in the transition instead of hidden in a caller. Choose an activity before applying its effect Before editing, predict tick two in the default comparison. Then replace recovery two with recovery ten. After the first committed rest, fatigue will already be zero, but has the minimum duration been fulfilled? Finally, keep fatigue below the entry threshold and invalidate a forager's target. Decide what changes while its activity remains foraging. Hint 1: continue an existing commitment first Under the committed policy, a resting creature with ticks left keeps resting. Once the minimum ends, fatigue above the exit threshold requests one more resting tick. Otherwise, wake with no target. Hint 2: then consider entry and ordinary foraging Fatigue at or above the entry threshold starts rest with the chosen policy's duration. Below it, return foraging and retain an existing target only when the supplied validity flag permits it. Prediction answer Tick two is foraging under the reactive policy and resting under the committed policy. Fast recovery doesn't remove the second committed resting action. An invalid foraging target becomes None without requiring a switch to rest. Prepare a new practice file from the repository root and implement decide . The supplied step performs maintenance, decision, and the selected activity effect in that order. python3 learning/scripts/labs.py prepare rest --dest work/rest-practice python3 learning/scripts/labs.py check rest --file work/rest-practice/rest.rs The complete starter compiles and then reaches its intentional todo! . After the edit, expect eight passing tests. If reserve increases during rest, follow the effect function's writes. If the minimum disappears after one action, check whether the counter is being interpreted before or after execution. #[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)] enum Activity { Foraging { target: Option<SimId> }, Resting { ticks_left: u8 }, } impl Activity { fn target(self) -> Option<SimId> { match self { Self::Foraging { target } => target, Self::Resting { .. } => None, } } fn label(self) -> &'static str { match self { Self::Foraging { .. } => "forage", Self::Resting { .. } => "rest", } } } #[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug)] enum Policy { Reactive, Committed, } #[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)] struct Creature { reserve_units: u32, fatigue_points: u8, activity: Activity, } fn decide(current: Activity, fatigue: u8, target_valid: bool, policy: Policy) -> Activity { let _ = (current, fatigue, target_valid, policy); todo!("choose an activity while respecting commitment and target validity") } fn step(creature: &mut Creature, policy: Policy, target_valid: bool, recovery: u8) { creature.reserve_units = creature.reserve_units.saturating_sub(1); creature.activity = decide( creature.activity, creature.fatigue_points, target_valid, policy, ); match creature.activity { Activity::Resting { ticks_left } => { creature.fatigue_points = creature.fatigue_points.saturating_sub(recovery); creature.activity = Activity::Resting { ticks_left: ticks_left.saturating_sub(1), }; } Activity::Foraging { .. } => { creature.fatigue_points = creature.fatigue_points.saturating_add(2).min(MAX_FATIGUE); } } } fn fixture() -> Creature { Creature { reserve_units: 12, fatigue_points: 6, activity: Activity::Foraging { target: Some(SimId(7)), }, } } fn main() { for policy in [Policy::Reactive, Policy::Committed] { let mut creature = fixture(); println!("{policy:?}"); for tick in 1..=4 { step(&mut creature, policy, true, 2); println!( "tick={tick} {} reserve={} fatigue={} target={:?}", creature.activity.label(), creature.reserve_units, creature.fatigue_points, creature.activity.target() ); } } } #[cfg(test)] mod tests { use super::*; #[test] fn rest_recovers_fatigue_while_maintenance_still_spends_energy() { let mut creature = fixture(); step(&mut creature, Policy::Committed, true, 2); assert_eq!( creature, Creature { reserve_units: 11, fatigue_points: 4, activity: Activity::Resting { ticks_left: 1 } } ); } #[test] fn commitment_changes_the_same_reactive_trace() { let trace = |policy| { let mut creature = fixture(); (0..4) .map(|_| { step(&mut creature, policy, true, 2); (creature.activity.label(), creature.fatigue_points) }) .collect::<Vec<_>>() }; assert_eq!( trace(Policy::Reactive), [("rest", 4), ("forage", 6), ("rest", 4), ("forage", 6)] ); assert_eq!( trace(Policy::Committed), [("rest", 4), ("rest", 2), ("forage", 4), ("forage", 6)] ); } #[test] fn minimum_commitment_survives_early_recovery() { let mut creature = fixture(); assert_eq!(creature.reserve_units, 10); step(&mut creature, Policy::Committed, true, 10); assert_eq!(creature.activity, Activity::Foraging { target: None }); } #[test] fn completed_commitment_waits_for_the_recovery_threshold() { let mut creature = Creature { fatigue_points: 10, ..fixture() }; for _ in 0..100 { assert_eq!( decide(creature.activity, 0, false, Policy::Committed), creature.activity ); } assert_eq!(creature.reserve_units, 12); } } Complete worked answer: rest.rs const START_REST_AT: u8 = 6;
