the earlier --file command checks your implementation. The program should print this trace: Reactive tick=1 rest reserve=11 fatigue=4 target=None tick=2 forage reserve=10 fatigue=6 target=None tick=3 rest reserve=9 fatigue=4 target=None tick=4 forage reserve=8 fatigue=6 target=None Committed tick=1 rest reserve=11 fatigue=4 target=None tick=2 rest reserve=10 fatigue=2 target=None tick=3 forage reserve=9 fatigue=4 target=None tick=4 forage reserve=8 fatigue=6 target=None Explain the rest, then count the cost The trace explains the opening alternation without treating it as an arithmetic error. The reactive policy keeps responding to a single threshold, while the committed policy remembers an obligation and requires a lower fatigue level before leaving. Both are reproducible choices whose consequences we can inspect. The fast-recovery test makes the time requirement visible even after fatigue reaches zero. The high-fatigue case tests the other direction: finishing the minimum doesn't force waking before recovery is sufficient. Repeated calls to decide check that policy evaluation itself can't shorten rest or charge another unit of upkeep. The shared final reserve and fatigue don't make the two sequences equivalent. A meal available only on tick two could matter because one creature is searching then and the other is resting. That would require a new integrated scenario; this lab contains no meal and doesn't establish that two resting ticks is a good choice for Moss. The tests establish the transition and arithmetic in an ordinary Rust value. An ECS integration would additionally need to connect current target validity, activity effects, and the chosen phase order. An ecological comparison would need enough repeated opportunities to expose the costs and benefits of changing the policy. Recall why waking can leave the target empty Executed actions consume the rest duration; repeated decisions don't. Waking completes the recovery commitment, but it doesn't establish a current destination. Fatigue, energy, selected intent, and action eligibility each carry information the others can't supply. Keep those separate questions in view for the birth transaction . A successful transition there will need energy payments and explicit timing too, including a decision about when the new individual may first act.

title: Commit both parents before creating a child
summary: Validate and charge a pair atomically, then give a deferred newborn an explicit first action boundary.
text: Imagine that our birth system has already taken a payment from the first parent when it discovers that the second is still in cooldown. No child can be created, but one parent has lost reserve anyway. Plan a complete birth before paying for it You'll implement plan_birth using copied parent values, so a rejected proposal cannot partly change the world. We'll account for the two payments, child reserve, cooldown deadlines and new identity before returning one accepted result. The supplied ECS resolver will commit that result and queue the child. Then we'll follow the accepted birth through two further complications: several requests may share a parent, and a child may be visible before it is allowed to act. The expected outcome is a transaction you can explain from proposal through first turn, with tests that distinguish a rejected payment, a duplicate birth and a premature newborn action. This isolated Bevy exercise builds on rest and commitment , where recovery, reserve and permission to act had different meanings. Here we'll carry that distinction into deferred entity creation. The fixed costs and timing are authored teaching rules; the exercise leaves live Moss and NOW.md unchanged. Make one acceptance cover both parents Start with adults 1 and 2, each holding ten reserve units. Our rule charges three units to each parent and gives their child four, so an accepted birth leaves the parents at seven and seven. Of the six units they paid, four have moved into the child's reserve and two have been spent by the reproductive process. Following the units this way gives us a concrete accounting check before we involve the ECS world. Affording the payment is only part of being an eligible parent. Each animal must also be an adult, have reached its first eligible tick and be out of cooldown. Both participants must be present, and they must be distinct individuals: finding the same animal twice doesn't produce a pair. If either participant fails a condition, we'll reject the whole request while leaving both reserves alone. Cooldown determines when a successful parent may participate again. A birth on tick one assigns both parents a deadline of four, and the eligibility check accepts the parent once the current tick reaches that deadline. Ticks two and three are therefore too early; tick four is allowed. Expressing the rule in simulation ticks keeps its meaning stable when the browser draws more often or the reader pauses to inspect the world. Those future values need to be representable before we accept the birth. The planner will use checked arithmetic for the cooldown deadline, the child's first eligible tick and the next identity. A wrapped deadline could make a parent eligible again immediately, while a wrapped identity could give a new child an old animal's history. An overflow should therefore reject the request for the same reason an unaffordable payment does: we can't fulfill the complete outcome we promised. Plan with values; commit through borrows We can make that promise easier to keep by calculating the result away from the live components. plan_birth receives two copied Animal values and returns a Result . On success, the value contains both proposed parent states, the child and the next allocator value. On failure, it contains the reason for rejection. Because the function never receives references to the world's parents, it cannot accidentally take one parent's payment on the way to an error. The ECS resolver connects that calculation to the current world. It obtains mutable access to the two distinct parents, copies their states into the planner and, only if planning succeeds, writes the returned states back. All the expected ways to reject a birth therefore occur before those authoritative assignments. We're using a transaction in this local sense: one accepted result supplies all the changes. It doesn't promise durable storage or recovery if the process itself fails. This is also a useful application of the earlier borrowing lesson. We copy the small values needed to consider a proposal, while keeping mutation of the real parents in one clearly defined place. Bevy's 0.18.1 get_many_mut method helps us request both mutable accesses together; it rejects aliased or unavailable query items. The planner then answers the domain question that Bevy cannot answer for us: are these two animals allowed to produce a child now? The child needs a stable ID before its entity is spawned. As in the population lesson, the roster assumes those IDs are unique, so the resolver checks that the proposed child ID isn't already in the world. It advances the allocator immediately after each accepted birth. Otherwise, two accepted pairs could choose the same ID while both children were still waiting in the command queue, where a query wouldn't find them yet. Resolve an unordered pair once A complete plan protects one attempt, but the resolver must also control how often that attempt is made. A second problem appears when we gather possible pairs. A neighborhood scan may encounter adults 1 and 2 as both (1, 2) and (2, 1) , although they describe the same partnership. Sort the two IDs inside each pair and collect the resulting keys in a BTreeSet . Both encounters then produce one key, and the ordered set gives us a reproducible sequence for considering different pairs. Deduplicating requests doesn't settle competition between different partnerships. Consider (1, 2) followed by (1, 3) : the pairs are distinct, but parent 1 is shared. Once the first pair succeeds, its payment and cooldown change parent 1 immediately. The second request must read those current components and will find the parent ineligible. The set prevents repeated consideration of the same pair; current-state validation prevents a parent being reused by another pair. Ordering pairs this way favors lower IDs, because (1, 2) precedes (1, 3) . That's a deliberate simplification for a fixture whose result we want to explain exactly. A different pairing policy could use another recorded priority without changing the requirement that each attempt validate the current parents and commit one complete result. Each resolver pass consumes its requests once. A rejected request doesn't wait around to become a birth on a later tick, and LastBirths is cleared for the next pass so it describes only that tick's accepted births. Parentage has a longer life: the child stores its parents' IDs in a separate field. Founders use None because this fixture supplies no parentage for them, rather than asserting that they had no parents. Presence is not permission to act Now we can follow a successful proposal into the child's first opportunity to act. After accepting the plan and paying the parents, the resolver queues the child with Commands::spawn . That queues a structural change rather than inserting the entity immediately. Our schedule explicitly applies the commands before the action phase, so the newborn will be present when that phase queries the world. We now need to decide whether being present is enough to earn a turn. For this model, the child first acts on the following tick. A child born on tick one therefore receives first_eligible_tick = 2 , and the action system checks that field whenever it visits an animal. The newborn can appear in an inspection on its birth tick while still having an action count of zero. On tick two, the same entity becomes eligible and records its first action. Here an action only increments a counter, which lets us examine the timing without implementing movement or feeding again. Maturity remains a separate condition: the newborn has adult: false , so reaching its first action tick doesn't make it a potential parent. A later maturation rule would have to change that state explicitly. Begin tick → resolve pairs and queue children → apply commands → act if eligible Tick 1: child 100 exists; first eligible tick 2; action count 0 Tick 2: child 100 still exists; action count 1 A structural boundary makes the child visible; a separate domain check controls its first action. We could try to delay the first turn by relying on a convenient command-flush position, but that would make the rule fragile when the schedule changes. The explicit eligibility field continues to explain the intended timing even if an observation phase needs to see newborns earlier. The versioned Commands documentation describes how structural changes become visible; the first-eligible tick states what a visible child may do. Complete the transaction Before writing the planner, predict what happens when tick one receives the three requests (2, 1) , (1, 2) and (2, 1) . Then change parent 2's reserve to two and try the prediction again. Finally, restore affordable parents but choose timing that would overflow the cooldown deadline. For each variation, account for the parents as well as the child: a rejected birth should leave no partial payment behind. Hint 1: reject before constructing a successful plan Establish that the parents are distinct, eligible and able to pay, and that the child ID is nonzero and differs from both parent IDs. Then calculate the future deadlines and next allocator value with checked addition. Only after all these checks succeed should you construct a successful plan. Hint 2: return both resulting parents together Work on the copied parents: subtract each full payment and assign the same cooldown deadline to both. Construct one immature child with sorted parent IDs and first eligibility on the next tick, then return it together with both resulting parents and the new allocator value. The resolver will install that complete result. Prediction answer The three requests describe one unordered pair, so the ordinary fixture produces one child. Both parents finish at seven with cooldown deadlines of four. Reducing one parent's reserve below the payment rejects the birth without charging either parent, and a deadline overflow likewise produces an error before any plan is installed. Prepare the isolated file with the commands below, then replace plan_birth . The surrounding resolver already collects pairs, looks up current components, commits successful plans and queues children. That lets this edit concentrate on defining a complete accepted outcome, while the supplied schedule makes its effects testable. python3 learning/scripts/labs.py prepare births --dest work/births-practice python3 learning/scripts/labs.py check births --file work/births-practice/births.rs The starter's todo! is the intended first failure. Once you implement the planner, all eight named tests should pass. If a rejected pair changes a reserve, look for a world write outside the successful-plan branch. If a child acts on its birth tick, compare the stored first-eligible tick with the action system's check; being spawned successfully doesn't settle that separate permission. Complete starter file: births.rs use bevy_ecs::{ prelude::*, schedule::{ApplyDeferred, ExecutorKind}, }; use std::collections::{BTreeMap, BTreeSet}; const PARENT_COST: u32 = 3; const CHILD_RESERVE: u32 = 4; const COOLDOWN_TICKS: u64 = 3; #[derive(Component, Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)] struct Animal { id: u64, reserve: u32, adult: bool, cooldown_until: u64, first_eligible_tick: u64, parents: Option<[u64; 2]>, actions: u32, } fn adult(id: u64, reserve: u32) -> Animal { Animal { id, reserve, adult: true, cooldown_until: 0, first_eligible_tick: 1, parents: None, actions: 0, } } #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq)] enum Rejected { SameParent, Ineligible, Unaffordable, InvalidChildId, CounterOverflow, } #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq)] struct BirthPlan { a: Animal, b: Animal, child: Animal, next_id: u64, } fn plan_birth( mut a: Animal, mut b: Animal, tick: u64, child_id: u64, ) -> Result<BirthPlan, Rejected> { let _ = (a, b, tick, child_id); todo!("validate both parents and return one complete birth plan") } #[derive(Resource, Default)] struct Tick(u64); #[derive(Resource)] struct NextId(u64); #[derive(Resource, Default)] struct Requests(Vec<(u64, u64)>); #[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)] struct Birth { tick: u64, child: u64, parents: [u64; 2], } #[derive(Resource, Default)] struct LastBirths(Vec<Birth>); fn begin_tick(mut tick: ResMut<Tick>) { tick.0 = tick.0.checked_add(1).expect("tick counter overflow"); } fn resolve_births( mut commands: Commands, tick: Res<Tick>, mut next: ResMut<NextId>, mut requests: ResMut<Requests>, mut births: ResMut<LastBirths>, mut animals: Query<(Entity, &mut Animal)>, ) { births.0.clear(); let ids: BTreeMap<_, _> = animals .iter() .map(|(entity, animal)| (animal.id, entity)) .collect(); let pairs: BTreeSet<_> = std::mem::take(&mut requests.0) .into_iter() .map(|(a, b)| (a.min(b), a.max(b))) .collect(); for (a, b) in pairs { let (Some(&a_entity), Some(&b_entity)) = (ids.get(&a), ids.get(&b)) else { continue; }; if ids.contains_key(&next.0) { continue; } let Ok([(_, mut left), (_, mut right)]) = animals.get_many_mut([a_entity, b_entity]) else { continue; }; let Ok(plan) = plan_birth(*left, *right, tick.0, next.0) else { continue; }; *left = plan.a; *right = plan.b; next.0 = plan.next_id; commands.spawn(plan.child); births.0.push(Birth { tick: tick.0, child: plan.child.id, parents: plan.child.parents.expect("a planned child has parentage"), }); } } fn act(tick: Res<Tick>, mut animals: Query<&mut Animal>) { for mut animal in &mut animals { if tick.0 >= animal.first_eligible_tick { animal.actions = animal .actions .checked_add(1) .expect("action counter overflow"); } } } fn schedule() -> Schedule { let mut schedule = Schedule::default(); schedule.set_executor_kind(ExecutorKind::SingleThreaded); schedule.add_systems((begin_tick, resolve_births, ApplyDeferred, act).chain()); schedule } fn fixture(requests: Vec<(u64, u64)>) -> World { let mut world = World::new(); world.init_resource::<Tick>(); world.insert_resource(NextId(100)); world.insert_resource(Requests(requests)); world.init_resource::<LastBirths>(); world.spawn(adult(1, 10)); world.spawn(adult(2, 10)); world } fn readings(world: &mut World) -> Vec<Animal> { let mut rows: Vec<_> = world.query::<&Animal>().iter(world).copied().collect(); rows.sort_by_key(|animal| animal.id); rows } fn main() { let mut world = fixture(vec![(2, 1), (1, 2)]); let mut schedule = schedule(); for _ in 0..2 { schedule.run(&mut world); println!( "tick={} births={}", world.resource::<Tick>().0, world.resource::<LastBirths>().0.len() ); for animal in readings(&mut world) { println!( " #{} reserve={} cooldown={} eligible={} actions={} parents={:?}", animal.id, animal.reserve, animal.cooldown_until, animal.first_eligible_tick, animal.actions, animal.parents ); } } } #[cfg(test)] mod tests { use super::*; #[test] fn both_parents_pay_and_receive_the_same_deadline() { let exact = plan_birth(adult(1, PARENT_COST), adult(2, PARENT_COST), 1, 100).unwrap(); assert_eq!((exact.a.reserve, exact.b.reserve), (0, 0)); let plan = plan_birth(adult(2, 10), adult(1, 8), 1, 100).unwrap(); assert_eq!((plan.a.reserve, plan.b.reserve), (7, 5)); assert_eq!((plan.a.cooldown_until, plan.b.cooldown_until), (4, 4)); assert_eq!(plan.child.parents, Some([1, 2])); assert_eq!( ( plan.child.reserve, plan.child.first_eligible_tick, plan.next_id ), (4, 2, 101) ); } #[test] fn rejected_pair_cannot_partly_change_the_callers() { let a = adult(1, 10); let b = adult(2, 2); assert_eq!(plan_birth(a, b, 1, 100), Err(Rejected::Unaffordable)); assert_eq!( (a.reserve, b.reserve, a.cooldown_until, b.cooldown_until), (10, 2, 0, 0) ); let mut world = fixture(vec![(1, 2)]); world .query::<&mut Animal>() .iter_mut(&mut world) .find(|a| a.id == 2) .unwrap() .reserve = 2; schedule().run(&mut world); let rows = readings(&mut world); assert_eq!(rows.len(), 2); assert_eq!((rows[0].reserve, rows[1].reserve), (10, 2)); assert_eq!(world.resource::<NextId>().0, 100); assert!(world.resource::<LastBirths>().0.is_empty()); } #[test] fn cooldown_boundary_is_inclusive_and_immature_parents_are_rejected() { let later = Animal { first_eligible_tick: 5, ..adult(1, 10) }; assert_eq!( plan_birth(later, adult(2, 10), 4, 100), Err(Rejected::Ineligible) ); assert!(plan_birth(later, adult(2, 10), 5, 100).is_ok()); let first = plan_birth(adult(1, 10), adult(2, 10), 1, 100).unwrap(); assert_eq!( plan_birth(first.a, first.b, 3, 101), Err(Rejected::Ineligible) ); assert!(plan_birth(first.a, first.b, 4, 101).is_ok()); assert_eq!( plan_birth(first.a, first.child, 4, 101), Err(Rejected::Ineligible) ); } #[test] fn invalid_identity_and_counter_limits_reject_without_a_plan() { let a = adult(1, 10); let b = adult(2, 10); assert_eq!(plan_birth(a, a, 1, 100), Err(Rejected::SameParent)); for id in [0, 1, 2] { assert_eq!(plan_birth(a, b, 1, id), Err(Rejected::InvalidChildId)); } assert_eq!( plan_birth(a, b, u64::MAX - 1, 100), Err(Rejected::CounterOverflow) ); assert_eq!( plan_birth(a, b, 1, u64::MAX), Err(Rejected::CounterOverflow) ); } #[test] fn duplicate_unordered_requests_produce_one_child_and_one_charge() { let mut world = fixture(vec![(2, 1), (1, 2), (2, 1)]); schedule().run(&mut world); let rows = readings(&mut world); assert_eq!(rows.len(), 3); assert_eq!((rows[0].reserve, rows[1].reserve), (7, 7)); assert_eq!( world.resource::<LastBirths>().0, vec![Birth { tick: 1, child: 100, parents: [1, 2] }] ); assert_eq!(world.resource::<NextId>().0, 101); } #[test] fn flushed_newborn_is_present_but_cannot_act_until_the_next_tick() { let mut world = fixture(vec![(1, 2)]); let mut schedule = schedule(); schedule.run(&mut world); let child = readings(&mut world) .into_iter() .find(|a| a.id == 100) .unwrap(); assert_eq!((child.first_eligible_tick, child.actions), (2, 0)); schedule.run(&mut world); let child = readings(&mut world) .into_iter() .find(|a| a.id == 100) .unwrap(); assert_eq!(child.actions, 1); assert_eq!(child.parents, Some([1, 2])); } #[test] fn shared_parent_is_claimed_in_canonical_pair_order() { let mut world = fixture(vec![(3, 1), (2, 1)]); world.spawn(adult(3, 10)); schedule().run(&mut world); assert_eq!(world.resource::<LastBirths>().0[0].parents, [1, 2]); let rows = readings(&mut world); assert_eq!(rows.iter().find(|a| a.id == 3).unwrap().reserve, 10); assert_eq!(rows.len(), 4); } #[test] fn missing_parent_or_colliding_child_id_leaves_reserves_unchanged() { for (requests, next_id) in [(vec![(1, 99)], 100), (vec![(1, 2)], 2)] { let mut world = fixture(requests); world.resource_mut::<NextId>().0 = next_id; schedule().run(&mut world); let rows = readings(&mut world); assert_eq!(rows.len(), 2); assert_eq!((rows[0].reserve, rows[1].reserve), (10, 10)); assert!(world.resource::<LastBirths>().0.is_empty()); } } } Complete worked answer: births.rs use bevy_ecs::{ prelude::*, schedule::{ApplyDeferred, ExecutorKind}, }; use std::collections::{BTreeMap, BTreeSet}; const PARENT_COST: u32 = 3; const CHILD_RESERVE: u32 = 4; const COOLDOWN_TICKS: u64 = 3; #[derive(Component, Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)] struct Animal { id: u64, reserve: u32, adult: bool, cooldown_until: u64, first_eligible_tick: u64, parents: Option<[u64; 2]>, actions: u32, } fn adult(id: u64, reserve: u32) -> Animal { Animal { id, reserve, adult: true, cooldown_until: 0, first_eligible_tick: 1, parents: None, actions: 0, } } #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq)] enum Rejected { SameParent, Ineligible, Unaffordable, InvalidChildId, CounterOverflow, } #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq)] struct BirthPlan { a: Animal, b: Animal, child: Animal, next_id: u64, } fn plan_birth( mut a: Animal, mut b: Animal, tick: u64, child_id: u64, ) -> Result<BirthPlan, Rejected> { if a.id == b.id { return Err(Rejected::SameParent); } if !a.adult || !b.adult || a.first_eligible_tick > tick || b.first_eligible_tick > tick || a.cooldown_until > tick || b.cooldown_until > tick { return Err(Rejected::Ineligible); } if a.reserve < PARENT_COST || b.reserve < PARENT_COST { return Err(Rejected::Unaffordable); } if child_id == 0 || child_id == a.id || child_id == b.id { return Err(Rejected::InvalidChildId); } let cooldown_until = tick .checked_add(COOLDOWN_TICKS) .ok_or(Rejected::CounterOverflow)?; let first_eligible_tick = tick.checked_add(1).ok_or(Rejected::CounterOverflow)?; let next_id = child_id.checked_add(1).ok_or(Rejected::CounterOverflow)?; a.reserve -= PARENT_COST; b.reserve -= PARENT_COST; a.cooldown_until = cooldown_until; b.cooldown_until = cooldown_until; let child = Animal { id: child_id, reserve: CHILD_RESERVE, adult: false, cooldown_until: 0, first_eligible_tick, parents: Some([a.id.min(b.id), a.id.max(b.id)]), actions: 0, }; Ok(BirthPlan { a, b, child, next_id, }) } #[derive(Resource, Default)] struct Tick(u64); #[derive(Resource)] struct NextId(u64); #[derive(Resource, Default)] struct Requests(Vec<(u64, u64)>); #[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)] struct Birth { tick: u64, child: u64, parents: [u64; 2], } #[derive(Resource, Default)] struct LastBirths(Vec<Birth>); fn begin_tick(mut tick: ResMut<Tick>) { tick.0 = tick.0.checked_add(1).expect("tick counter overflow"); } fn resolve_births( mut commands: Commands, tick: Res<Tick>, mut next: ResMut<NextId>, mut requests: ResMut<Requests>, mut births: ResMut<LastBirths>, mut animals: Query<(Entity, &mut Animal)>, ) { births.0.clear(); let ids: BTreeMap<_, _> = animals .iter() .map(|(entity, animal)| (animal.id, entity)) .collect(); let pairs: BTreeSet<_> = std::mem::take(&mut requests.0) .into_iter() .map(|(a, b)| (a.min(b), a.max(b))) .collect(); for (a, b) in pairs { let (Some(&a_entity), Some(&b_entity)) = (ids.get(&a), ids.get(&b)) else { continue; }; if ids.contains_key(&next.0) { continue; } let Ok([(_, mut left), (_, mut right)]) = animals.get_many_mut([a_entity, b_entity]) else { continue; }; let Ok(plan) = plan_birth(*left, *right, tick.0, next.0) else { continue; }; *left = plan.a; *right = plan.b; next.0 = plan.next_id; commands.spawn(plan.child); births.0.push(Birth { tick: tick.0, child: plan.child.id, parents: plan.child.parents.expect("a planned child has parentage"), }); } } fn act(tick: Res<Tick>, mut animals: Query<&mut Animal>) { for mut animal in &mut animals { if tick.0 >= animal.first_eligible_tick { animal.actions = animal .actions .checked_add(1) .expect("action counter overflow"); } } } fn schedule() -> Schedule { let mut schedule = Schedule::default(); schedule.set_executor_kind(ExecutorKind::SingleThreaded); schedule.add_systems((begin_tick, resolve_births, ApplyDeferred, act).chain()); schedule } fn fixture(requests: Vec<(u64, u64)>) -> World { let mut world = World::new(); world.init_resource::<Tick>(); world.insert_resource(NextId(100)); world.insert_resource(Requests(requests)); world.init_resource::<LastBirths>(); world.spawn(adult(1, 10)); world.spawn(adult(2, 10)); world } fn readings(world: &mut World) -> Vec<Animal> { let mut rows: Vec<_> = world.query::<&Animal>().iter(world).copied().collect(); rows.sort_by_key(|animal| animal.id); rows } fn main() { let mut world = fixture(vec![(2, 1), (1, 2)]); let mut schedule = schedule(); for _ in 0..2 { schedule.run(&mut world); println!( "tick={} births={}", world.resource::<Tick>().0, world.resource::<LastBirths>().0.len() ); for animal in readings(&mut world) { println!( " #{} reserve={} cooldown={} eligible={} actions={} parents={:?}", animal.id, animal.reserve, animal.cooldown_until, animal.first_eligible_tick, animal.actions, animal.parents ); } } } #[cfg(test)] mod tests { use super::*; #[test] fn both_parents_pay_and_receive_the_same_deadline() { let exact = plan_birth(adult(1, PARENT_COST), adult(2, PARENT_COST), 1, 100).unwrap(); assert_eq!((exact.a.reserve, exact.b.reserve), (0, 0)); let plan = plan_birth(adult(2, 10), adult(1, 8), 1, 100).unwrap(); assert_eq!((plan.a.reserve, plan.b.reserve), (7, 5)); assert_eq!((plan.a.cooldown_until, plan.b.cooldown_until), (4, 4)); assert_eq!(plan.child.parents, Some([1, 2])); assert_eq!( ( plan.child.reserve, plan.child.first_eligible_tick, plan.next_id ), (4, 2, 101) ); } #[test] fn rejected_pair_cannot_partly_change_the_callers() { let a = adult(1, 10); let b = adult(2, 2); assert_eq!(plan_birth(a, b, 1, 100), Err(Rejected::Unaffordable)); assert_eq!( (a.reserve, b.reserve, a.cooldown_until, b.cooldown_until), (10, 2, 0, 0) ); let mut world = fixture(vec![(1, 2)]); world .query::<&mut Animal>() .iter_mut(&mut world) .find(|a| a.id == 2) .unwrap() .reserve = 2; schedule().run(&mut world); let rows = readings(&mut world); assert_eq!(rows.len(), 2); assert_eq!((rows[0].reserve, rows[1].reserve), (10, 2)); assert_eq!(world.resource::<NextId>().0, 100); assert!(world.resource::<LastBirths>().0.is_empty()); } #[test] fn cooldown_boundary_is_inclusive_and_immature_parents_are_rejected() { let later = Animal { first_eligible_tick: 5, ..adult(1, 10) }; assert_eq!( plan_birth(later, adult(2, 10), 4, 100), Err(Rejected::Ineligible) ); assert!(plan_birth(later, adult(2, 10), 5, 100).is_ok()); let first = plan_birth(adult(1, 10), adult(2, 10), 1, 100).unwrap(); assert_eq!( plan_birth(first.a, first.b, 3, 101), Err(Rejected::Ineligible) ); assert!(plan_birth(first.a, first.b, 4, 101).is_ok()); assert_eq!( plan_birth(first.a, first.child, 4, 101), Err(Rejected::Ineligible) ); } #[test] fn invalid_identity_and_counter_limits_reject_without_a_plan() { let a = adult(1, 10); let b = adult(2, 10); assert_eq!(plan_birth(a, a, 1, 100), Err(Rejected::SameParent)); for id in [0, 1, 2] { assert_eq!(plan_birth(a, b, 1, id), Err(Rejected::InvalidChildId)); } assert_eq!( plan_birth(a, b, u64::MAX - 1, 100), Err(Rejected::CounterOverflow) ); assert_eq!( plan_birth(a, b, 1, u64::MAX), Err(Rejected::CounterOverflow) ); } #[test] fn duplicate_unordered_requests_produce_one_child_and_one_charge() { let mut world = fixture(vec![(2, 1), (1, 2), (2, 1)]); An accepted result then coordinates immediate parent changes with deferred child creation, while the child's first turn remains separate from its maturity. Use those distinctions to explain what each phase contributes before reading the recall answer. The tests follow the proposal all the way into the installed schedule. They check both payments, the cooldown boundary, repeated requests, shared-parent competition and allocation or counter failures. The newborn test also finds the actual entity after commands are applied before asserting that it hasn't acted. That matters: an absent child with no actions would satisfy the number while missing the behavior we meant to prove. A correct transaction is a foundation for population behavior, not a reason to expect a sustainable population from this fixture. These adults have no upkeep, partner search or spatial eligibility, so repeated valid requests could keep producing children without the pressures found in the continuing meadow. The continuing population guide brings those rules together to investigate reproduction and food supply. Here we've established what each individual accepted birth must guarantee. Recall answer Parent payments and cooldown take effect immediately so another pair can't reuse those resources or permissions. The child entity appears when commands are applied, but its stable identity and first-eligible tick already belong to the accepted plan. Reaching that tick permits an action; reaching maturity permits reproduction. They answer different questions about the same child. In inherited traits and their origins , we'll examine one calculation inside a birth: how a child gets a bounded trait and what record lets us explain it later. The complete birth transaction remains the boundary around that additional choice.

title: Keep inheritance distinct from selection
summary: Copy and vary an offspring trait while preserving parents, units, identity, and enough provenance to replay the proposal.
text: Two parents have stride values of two and six cells per action. One child ends up with a stride of one; another has seven. To explain those children, we need to know more than their final numbers: which parent supplied the starting value, what change was proposed, and whether the trait's limits altered that proposal. Keep the explanation with the inherited trait You'll implement inherit , borrowing the parents and returning an owned record of the child's calculation. We'll establish a stable parent order, make two repeatable draws, and distinguish the proposed mutation from the change the bounds actually permit. The record will keep the identities, inputs and algorithm label needed to interpret its result later. By the end, you should be able to reproduce the specified children, explain a mutation that changes nothing at a boundary, and show why reversing the supplied parents doesn't change their roles in the calculation. This explains where variation came from; deciding whether a trait helps an animal will require a world in which that trait affects an outcome. This standard-library exercise isolates one authored inheritance rule: choose a bounded integer trait from one of two parents, then optionally change it by one. It is a toy game model rather than real genetics, and it leaves live Moss and the current assignment in NOW.md unchanged. Copying is one part of a birth In the previous lesson , we made an accepted birth pay both parents, allocate one child identity and set the child's first eligible tick. That transaction gives us somewhere to put a new individual. Here we'll examine one decision inside that larger process: given the child and two known parents, how should we calculate a trait and remember where it came from? We'll keep the parents fixed while exploring that calculation. They belong to run seven, with parent one carrying stride two and parent two carrying stride six. Stride means cells per completed action, with permitted values from one through eight. This file only generates the value; it doesn't run movement or charge energy for a stride. We'll be able to explain a child's seven without yet knowing whether seven helps that child in a world. The function can make this decision through a shared reference to the parent pair. It reads their identities and traits, then returns an owned origin record for the child. There's no reason for inheritance to change the parents' stored traits, so the signature doesn't lend it mutable access to those values. The result also owns the information it needs, allowing us to keep the explanation after the borrowed parent data is no longer available. The caller provides the child's already allocated identity. Our function can check that it is nonzero, differs from the parents and belongs to the same run, as well as rejecting duplicate parent identities. It can't see unrelated animals elsewhere in the world, though, so it cannot establish global uniqueness on its own. That responsibility stays with the birth allocator, which has the wider context. Follow the change from parent to child Start by separating the two operations that produced the child. Choosing parent one's stride copies an existing value of two. Proposing minus one then changes that inherited value to one. We call the second operation mutation, and we'll preserve both stages in the record so the final value doesn't hide the path that produced it. Those operations generate variation at creation time. Growth would change the same individual during its lifetime, while learning would change its behavior through experience; neither happens in this function. Selection asks another question again: which variants contribute to later populations under the world's rules? We aren't running survival trials or reproducing descendants here, so the resulting table can explain inheritance without establishing an evolutionary advantage. A mutation proposal can be minus one, zero or plus one. To apply it safely, we widen the inherited value to a signed integer, add the proposal, clamp the result to the trait's bounds, and convert the bounded result back to u8 . That order lets us reason about a negative change before returning to the unsigned representation used for a valid stride. At the lower bound, proposing minus one leaves a stride of one. That outcome looks identical to copying one with a zero proposal, but the two calculations tell different stories. Record both the proposed delta and the applied delta so we can distinguish them. Clamping is also part of the chosen variation policy: near a boundary, several proposals can lead to the same result, which changes the distribution of expressed values. Make the draw protocol explicit We also need an agreed way to choose a parent. If a generated index of zero means “the first array element,” simply reversing the caller's array could give the same seed a different meaning. The function therefore copies the pair and sorts it by stable key before making a choice. It leaves the caller's array untouched while giving our calculation a canonical order. For the choices themselves, this lab uses a small integer generator whose entire calculation is visible in the file. It starts from the supplied seed, multiplies its 64-bit state by a fixed constant, adds a fixed increment and returns the upper 32 bits. Multiplication and addition deliberately wrap; the integer documentation defines those operations independently of whether overflow checks are enabled in a build. Here wrapping belongs to the algorithm, rather than being an accident we hope the compiler will tolerate. The first output, reduced modulo two, chooses a parent from our sorted pair. The second, reduced modulo three, chooses the mutation proposal. We'll consume both outputs even when mutation is disabled, then use zero as the proposal in that copy-only mode. Making the draw sequence explicit keeps parent choice and the mutation setting from becoming unintentionally entangled. The generator is useful here because a reader can reproduce every step without depending on a random-number library. That small scope comes with limits: remainder mapping can introduce bias, and the example doesn't promise independently uniform mutations. Use it to understand a repeatable protocol, rather than taking it as a recommended generator for scientific sampling, security or a larger simulation. A seed is not a complete replay The calculation also needs to explain itself after the function returns. To decide what its owned record must retain, imagine coming back to one of its children much later. A final stride of three wouldn't tell you whether it was inherited unchanged or produced by a mutation. Our origin record therefore keeps the parent keys and values, the selected parent, the inherited value, the proposal, the applied change and the expressed result. It also keeps the child key, seed, mutation setting and algorithm label, giving the calculation enough context to explain itself. The label moss-traits-lcg64-v1 names the complete procedure: recurrence, output extraction, two-draw order, mapping and bounds. A seed only has meaning within such a procedure. Feeding the same integer to another library's generator, or changing our mapping while retaining the old label, wouldn't establish the same replay contract. The tests make that contract concrete at two levels. A literal generator-output test checks selected points in its sequence, while the inheritance tests check complete child records for meaningful inputs. Together they support repeatability for this specified function and its validated inputs. They don't promise identical outcomes after an arbitrary dependency change or a redesigned world schedule. In a larger simulation, generator ownership would become part of the design too. If every system shared one generator, an extra draw elsewhere could shift all later birth results. This exercise instead starts a local generator from each explicitly supplied seed, keeping that wider scheduling question outside the function. Whoever allocates birth-specific seeds must still decide how they are chosen; repeatedly supplying one seed won't create diverse siblings by itself. Specified examples with parents one/two carrying strides two/six Seed Source and proposal Expressed stride 3 Parent one, inherited two, proposal minus one. One cell per action. 5 Parent two, inherited six, proposal plus one. Seven cells per action. 6 Parent one, inherited two, proposal plus one. Three cells per action; copy-only mode gives two. Predict the provenance before editing Use the table to predict seed six with mutation enabled and then disabled. After that, reverse the parent array and decide which parts of the origin record should change. Finally, give both parents stride eight and consider a plus-one proposal. Follow the record through each case, rather than checking only the final stride. Hint 1: separate choice from mutation Sorting fixes what the first draw's parent index means. The mutation setting then determines whether to use the second draw's proposal; it doesn't change which parent supplied the inherited value. That lets the enabled and copy-only records be compared directly. Hint 2: record the requested and actual changes A plus-one proposal at stride eight reaches the upper bound. The expressed value stays eight, so the applied delta is zero even though the proposal is one. Keep both pieces of information in the result. Prediction answer Seed six chooses parent one and inherits two. With mutation enabled, the plus-one proposal produces three; copy-only mode leaves two. Reversing the input order produces the same records because the function sorts its copy first. At stride eight, a plus-one proposal instead keeps expressed eight and records an applied delta of zero. Prepare the practice file below and replace inherit . Its job is to validate the inputs, establish the canonical parent order, perform the two draws and assemble the complete origin record. The supplied generator and bounded-value helper let you focus on how those steps fit together. python3 learning/scripts/labs.py prepare inheritance --dest work/inheritance-practice python3 learning/scripts/labs.py check inheritance --file work/inheritance-practice/inheritance.rs The starter compiles and then reaches its unfinished todo! ; after your edit, all eight tests should pass. If reversing the parents changes the result, inspect the order before the first draw. If only a boundary case differs, compare the inherited, proposed and applied values before changing the generator. Those intermediate fields are useful diagnostics as well as a historical explanation. 2], parent_strides: [u8; 2], mutation_enabled: bool, source_parent: Key, inherited: u8, proposed_delta: i8, applied_delta: i8, expressed: u8, seed: u64, algorithm: &'static str, } #[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)] enum Rejected { Identity, ParentTrait } struct Rng { state: u64 } impl Rng { fn new(seed: u64) -> Self { Self { state: seed } } fn next_u32(&mut self) -> u32 { self.state = self.state.wrapping_mul(6_364_136_223_846_793_005) .wrapping_add(1_442_695_040_888_963_407); (self.state >> 32) as u32 } } fn bounded_stride(inherited: u8, delta: i8) -> u8 { (i16::from(inherited) + i16::from(delta)) .clamp(i16::from(MIN_STRIDE), i16::from(MAX_STRIDE)) as u8 } fn inherit(parents: &[Parent; 2], child: Key, seed: u64, mutate: bool) -> Result<Origin, Rejected> { let _ = (parents, child, seed, mutate); todo!("validate the parents, draw in a fixed order, and retain the child trait origin") } fn parents() -> [Parent; 2] { [Parent { key: Key { run: 7, id: 2 }, stride_cells_per_action: 6 }, Parent { key: Key { run: 7, id: 1 }, stride_cells_per_action: 2 }] } fn main() { let parents = parents(); for (index, seed) in [3, 5, 6].into_iter().enumerate() { let origin = inherit(&parents, Key { run: 7, id: 100 + index as u32 }, seed, true).unwrap(); println!("seed={} child={} source={} inherited={} proposed={} applied={} expressed={}", seed, origin.child.id, origin.source_parent.id, origin.inherited, origin.proposed_delta, origin.applied_delta, origin.expressed); } let copied = inherit(&parents, Key { run: 7, id: 103 }, 6, false).unwrap(); println!("copy-only={} algorithm={}", copied.expressed, copied.algorithm); } #[cfg(test)] mod tests { use super::*; #[test] fn child_origin_records_copy_mutation_and_independent_identity() { let origin = inherit(&parents(), Key { run: 7, id: 100 }, 6, true).unwrap(); assert_eq!(origin, Origin { child: Key { run: 7, id: 100 }, parents: [Key { run: 7, id: 1 }, Key { run: 7, id: 2 }], parent_strides: [2, 6], mutation_enabled: true, source_parent: Key { run: 7, id: 1 }, inherited: 2, proposed_delta: 1, applied_delta: 1, expressed: 3, seed: 6, algorithm: "moss-traits-lcg64-v1" }); } #[test] fn parents_are_unchanged_and_input_order_does_not_change_inheritance() { let original = parents(); let before = original; let a = inherit(&original, Key { run: 7, id: 100 }, 3, true).unwrap(); It borrows the parents for reading, works with small copied values and returns an owned record. If validation fails, no parent or child state has been partially changed. Before interpreting that chart, explain why equal values need not have the same origin, and what else you would need to call one value an improvement. Recall answers Many seeds are being mapped into a small set of bounded values, so different seeds can produce the same trait. The final stride alone omits the source parent and hides whether copying, mutation or clamping produced it. To call one stride an improvement, we'd also need an outcome and world rules connecting that trait to the outcome; this function supplies the variation without running that comparison. The native tests check the specified outputs, parent-order independence, immutable inputs, identity checks and bounded results. Connecting the record to actual ECS births or a browser lineage inspector would require another integration step. Keeping it available later also raises the retention question from terminal history : which earlier events can our stored evidence still explain? We now have an explanation for each child's value without having to call any child better adapted. In the continuing population guide , inherited upkeep affects an actual cost in a world with food, births and deaths; that gives a trait's consequences somewhere to unfold. In the next investigation , we'll compare matched scenarios and keep enough distribution and coverage information to question an appealing aggregate result.

title: Make a comparison explain its denominator
summary: Compare a declared intervention across matched cohorts, retaining losses and missing coverage in the report.
text: A chart reports one reserve unit per survivor. That could mean four animals are still alive with one unit each, or that only one animal remains from the original four. The average is doing its arithmetic correctly, but we need more context to interpret it. Make a comparison explain who it counts We'll compare two maintenance costs using matched starting cohorts, then inspect the individual outcomes behind their averages. You'll implement summarize to assemble an owned report with separate cohort and survivor means, distributions, run conditions and retained-history coverage. The supplied model lets us concentrate on what that report can legitimately say. The finished report should make a missing survivor group different from a measured zero and incomplete history different from no deaths. You'll use four paired runs to make a bounded claim about the chosen treatment, while retaining enough detail to question an appealing aggregate instead of accepting it at face value. This isolated experiment follows four authored animals for three ticks under a chosen maintenance rule. It uses the history lesson's proposed zero-reserve terminal policy, with no feeding, movement, births or live Moss integration. That small world lets us concentrate on comparison and reporting before applying the same questions to the continuing meadow. Ask a question the model can answer We'll ask how increasing maintenance from one to two units per tick changes survival over three ticks. The one-unit rule is our baseline, and the two-unit rule is the treatment we're comparing against it. For the comparison to say something about that change, each pair of runs must start with the same animals and reserves. Otherwise a difference in the outcome could have come from the starting group instead. Each starting cohort contains four stable IDs, with reserves between three and eight assigned by an explicit seeded generator. On an executed tick, the model applies any scheduled reserve grants, pays maintenance down to a floor of zero, marks zero-reserve animals dead and lets survivors increment an action counter. The main comparison schedules no grants, so its animals have only their initial reserve to spend. Dead animals remain in the roster with zero reserve and cannot become alive again. With no births or arrivals either, the same four individuals stay identifiable throughout the run. That makes “alive out of four” a useful fixed denominator. A changing population would need a report that also accounts for who entered and left, rather than carrying this denominator over unchanged. The birth transaction and predation resolver show some of the extra causes that appear in a richer world. Food intake, competing consumers, births and the order of actions can all affect who survives. We'll leave them out of this first reporting exercise, then take the same comparison habits back to the integrated guides, where those interactions are the point of the investigation. Match starting conditions within each pair For seed one, the generator supplies reserves of seven, four, four and four. Give that exact roster to both maintenance rules. If the treatment used a new sequence of draws, it might begin with more or less reserve, making its result ambiguous. Pairing the starting states removes that particular alternative explanation. The fixture uses the inheritance example's fixed-width recurrence, but maps four successive outputs to reserves with 3 + output % 6 . We name this procedure moss-cohort-lcg64-v1 . To reproduce a run, keep that label and mapping together with its seed, horizon, maintenance cost, initial policy and any pending interventions. The seed alone doesn't specify the experiment. The tests check matching before they check outcomes. At every chosen seed, they compare the canonical initial animal states used for the two costs. They then compare the completed runs with literal expected differences. These checks answer separate questions: did we start the pair fairly, and did the requested cost actually affect the executed model? A simulation that ignored the treatment could pass the first check while failing the second. A matching roster is necessary, but current reserve isn't the whole state. Suppose two runs show identical animals while only one has a reserve grant queued for the next tick. They can diverge without any further change to the maintenance rule. The canonical snapshot therefore includes pending grants, the completed tick, identity, reserve, life and action count. Tests expose both the queued-input difference and a clock difference between otherwise identical all-dead rosters. Camera position stays outside this model, while the experiment's specification must still be compared alongside its snapshot. Repeat the pair before generalizing One matched pair can explain its own difference; it can't show how that difference varies with a new starting cohort. Repeat the matched comparison for seeds one through four while keeping the treatment and horizon fixed. Record treatment survivors minus baseline survivors for each pair, giving minus three, minus two, minus two and minus two. Keeping those four differences lets us see how the result varies with the starting cohort, rather than replacing them immediately with a single average. Survivors after three ticks, from four initial animals per run Seed Maintenance 1 Maintenance 2 Paired difference 1 4 1 −3 2 3 1 −2 3 4 2 −2 4 4 2 −2 The table describes four specified cases. It doesn't establish a statistical guarantee about every possible ecosystem, and consecutive seeds from this small generator haven't been shown to provide independent scientific samples. What we can say is that, under the stated rules and horizon, the higher cost reduced survival in each of these four matched runs. The direction of that result also follows from the simple model: spending more can't add reserve, there is no feeding to compensate, and death stops later actions. Running several fixtures checks that we implemented the relationship consistently. It doesn't turn that relationship into a surprising ecological discovery. In the continuing meadow, where a behavioral change can affect both costs and access to food, interpreting the result will require more of the individual evidence. Keep the denominator and distribution For seed one's treatment, the final sorted reserves are zero, zero, zero and one. Our summarize function will report two means: the cohort mean divides the total reserve of one by all four original members, while the survivor mean divides one by the single remaining animal. Both are legitimate calculations, but only the first retains the original cohort as its denominator. Labeling the group is part of reporting the number. The mean type keeps an integer sum and count, postponing division rather than rounding to a floating-point result immediately. It also represents an empty group with None . If all four animals die, the cohort still has four members and a known mean of zero over four; the survivor group has no members and no mean. Substituting zero for that absence would make two different situations look like the same measurement. Even a correctly labeled mean can hide a distribution. Compare reserves of zero, zero, zero, eight with two, two, two, two: each cohort averages two, but their individual outcomes differ sharply. Filtering the first group to its positive member would report eight and hide three zeros altogether. We'll therefore keep the sorted reserve values and owned individual outcomes so an aggregate can be examined rather than merely accepted. Owning those outcomes also makes the report a stable record of the run. You can follow an unexpected average back to a named individual without keeping the world borrowed, and later changes to the original run won't rewrite the saved result. The report carries its own specification and collection boundary so its values can be understood in the context where they were observed. Coverage is part of the result Individual history introduces one more kind of missing information. The death journal uses the retained-coverage rule : when a journal with two slots receives a third record, it evicts the oldest. If even one record from a tick is lost, a query for the complete event count at that tick must report that it cannot answer, although other records from the tick may remain. Seed one's treatment makes this concrete because three animals become terminal on tick two. A two-slot journal retains two records and evicts one, leaving complete history only from tick three onward. Asking it for a complete count over the whole three-tick experiment therefore returns unknown. Keeping two visible records isn't enough to reconstruct the missing third event. The roster still tells us something useful: three members of this fixed cohort are dead. That present-day census doesn't recover all the lost event details, but incomplete history doesn't erase the census either. Keeping the two sources distinct lets the report say what is known about the ending population while remaining honest about which transitions it can explain. A test changes the retention limit from one slot to eight and checks that canonical biology stays the same. The journal should affect how much evidence we retain, rather than changing what the animals do. A later browser chart or exporter will need to preserve that distinction too; the native test establishes it for this model. Predict the report, then build it Before implementing the report, predict both means for seed one's treatment and decide whether its two-slot journal can count the full interval. Then raise maintenance to twenty, making all four animals die on the first tick. Consider what changes in each denominator: does the absence of survivors also remove the original cohort? Hint 1: choose a population before counting Build the two groups deliberately. The cohort includes the dead members retained in the fixed roster, while the survivor group includes only animals whose current life state is alive. Each mean needs its own sum and count. Hint 2: require complete collection and retention The journal can answer only if collection has reached the requested horizon and every tick in the requested interval remains complete. An unexecuted run hasn't collected evidence for its future ticks, even if its journal is currently empty. Prediction answer For seed one, the cohort mean is one over four and the survivor mean is one over one. The two-slot journal can't give a complete event count for the full interval. When all four die, the cohort remains a group of four with mean zero, while the empty survivor group has no mean. Prepare the practice file and replace summarize . The supplied code runs the tick model, constructs canonical snapshots and provides a checked mean helper. Your job is to assemble the owned report while preserving the distinctions between cohorts, survivors, retained events and complete coverage. python3 learning/scripts/labs.py prepare experiments --dest work/experiments-practice python3 learning/scripts/labs.py check experiments --file work/experiments-practice/experiments.rs The starter compiles and then reaches its intentional todo! ; after the edit, all nine tests should pass. If an average seems unexpectedly generous, inspect which individuals entered its denominator before changing the arithmetic. If incomplete history appears as zero deaths, follow the Option returned by the coverage query and check whether its absence was replaced with a number. Complete starter: experiments.rs use std::collections::VecDeque; const ALGORITHM: &str = "moss-cohort-lcg64-v1"; #[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)] struct Spec { seed: u64, maintenance_units: u32, ticks: u32, history_limit: usize } #[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)] struct Animal { id: u32, reserve: u32, alive: bool, actions: u32 } #[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq, PartialOrd, Ord)] struct Grant { tick: u32, id: u32, units: u32 } #[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)] struct Death { tick: u32, id: u32 } #[derive(Clone, Debug)] struct Run { spec: Spec, animals: Vec<Animal>, pending: Vec<Grant>, deaths: VecDeque<Death>, evicted: usize, complete_from: u32, collected_through: u32, } #[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)] struct Mean { sum: u64, count: usize } #[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)] struct Report { spec: Spec, algorithm: &'static str, outcomes: Vec<Animal>, pending: Vec<Grant>, initial: usize, survivors: usize, sorted_reserves: Vec<u32>, cohort_mean: Option<Mean>, survivor_mean: Option<Mean>, complete_death_count: Option<usize>, retained_deaths: Vec<Death>, complete_from: u32, collected_through: u32, evicted: usize, } fn mean(values: impl Iterator<Item = u32>) -> Option<Mean> { let (sum, count) = values.fold((0_u64, 0_usize), |(sum, count), value| (sum.checked_add(u64::from(value)).expect("sum exhausted"), count.checked_add(1).expect("count exhausted"))); (count > 0).then_some(Mean { sum, count }) } fn initial(spec: Spec) -> Run { assert!(spec.history_limit > 0); let mut state = spec.seed; let animals = (1..=4).map(|id| { state = state.wrapping_mul(6_364_136_223_846_793_005) .wrapping_add(1_442_695_040_888_963_407); Animal { id, reserve: 3 + ((state >> 32) as u32 % 6), alive: true, actions: 0 } }).collect(); Run { spec, animals, pending: vec![], deaths: VecDeque::new(), evicted: 0, complete_from: 1, collected_through: 0 } } fn advance(run: &mut Run) { let tick = run.collected_through.checked_add(1).expect("tick exhausted"); assert!(tick <= run.spec.ticks); for grant in run.pending.iter().filter(|grant| grant.tick == tick) { if let Some(animal) = run.animals.iter_mut().find(|animal| animal.id == grant.id && animal.alive) { animal.reserve = animal.reserve.checked_add(grant.units).expect("grant exceeds units"); } } run.pending.retain(|grant| grant.tick > tick); for animal in run.animals.iter_mut().filter(|animal| animal.alive) { animal.reserve = animal.reserve.saturating_sub(run.spec.maintenance_units); if animal.reserve == 0 { animal.alive = false; if run.deaths.len() == run.spec.history_limit { let removed = run.deaths.pop_front().unwrap(); run.complete_from = run.complete_from.max(removed.tick.checked_add(1).unwrap()); run.evicted = run.evicted.checked_add(1).unwrap(); } run.deaths.push_back(Death { tick, id: animal.id }); } else { animal.actions = animal.actions.checked_add(1).unwrap(); } } run.collected_through = tick; } fn execute(spec: Spec) -> Run { let mut run = initial(spec); for _ in 0..spec.ticks { advance(&mut run); } run } fn summarize(run: &Run) -> Report { let _ = run; todo!("build an owned report with separate denominators and honest journal coverage") } fn canonical(run: &Run) -> (u32, Vec<Animal>, Vec<Grant>) { let mut animals = run.animals.clone(); animals.sort_by_key(|animal| animal.id); let mut pending = run.pending.clone(); pending.sort(); (run.collected_through, animals, pending) } fn spec(seed: u64, maintenance_units: u32, history_limit: usize) -> Spec { Spec { seed, maintenance_units, ticks: 3, history_limit } } fn main() { println!("algorithm={ALGORITHM} ticks=3 seeds=1,2,3,4"); for seed in 1..=4 { let baseline = summarize(&execute(spec(seed, 1, 2))); let treatment = summarize(&execute(spec(seed, 2, 2))); println!("seed={seed} alive={}/{} -> {}/{} delta={}", baseline.survivors, baseline.initial, treatment.survivors, treatment.initial, treatment.survivors as i64 - baseline.survivors as i64); } let run = execute(spec(1, 2, 2)); let report = summarize(&run); println!("seed=1 treatment reserves={:?} cohort={:?} survivors={:?}", report.sorted_reserves, report.cohort_mean, report.survivor_mean); println!("journal death count={:?} retained={} evicted={} complete={}..={}", report.complete_death_count, report.retained_deaths.len(), report.evicted, report.complete_from, report.collected_through); println!("pending after horizon={}", canonical(&run).2.len()); } #[cfg(test)] mod tests { use super::*; #[test] fn reporting_keeps_dead_members_in_the_initial_cohort_denominator() { let run = execute(spec(1, 2, 8)); let report = summarize(&run); assert_eq!((report.initial, report.survivors), (4, 1)); assert_eq!(report.sorted_reserves, vec![0, 0, 0, 1]); assert_eq!(report.cohort_mean, Some(Mean { sum: 1, count: 4 })); assert_eq!(report.survivor_mean, Some(Mean { sum: 1, count: 1 })); assert_eq!(report.complete_death_count, Some(3)); } #[test] fn matched_cost_intervention_starts_from_identical_animals_for_every_seed() { for seed in 1..=4 { assert_eq!(canonical(&initial(spec(seed, 1, 8))), canonical(&initial(spec(seed, 2, 8)))); } let differences: Vec<_> = (1..=4).map(|seed| { let a = summarize(&execute(spec(seed, 1, 8))); let b = summarize(&execute(spec(seed, 2, 8))); b.survivors as i32 - a.survivors as i32 }).collect(); assert_eq!(differences, vec![-3, -2, -2, -2]); } #[test] fn report_owns_values_and_retained_records_after_the_run_changes() { let mut run = execute(spec(1, 2, 8)); let report = summarize(&run); run.animals.clear(); run.deaths.clear(); assert_eq!(report.initial, 4); assert_eq!(report.sorted_reserves, vec![0, 0, 0, 1]); assert_eq!(report.retained_deaths.len(), 3); } #[test] fn eviction_makes_complete_death_count_unknown_without_changing_biology() { let short = execute(spec(1, 2, 1)); let long = execute(spec(1, 2, 8)); assert_eq!(canonical(&short), canonical(&long)); let report = summarize(&short); assert_eq!(report.complete_death_count, None); assert_eq!((report.retained_deaths.len(), report.evicted), (1, 2)); assert_eq!(summarize(&long).complete_death_count, Some(3)); } #[test] fn fully_observed_zero_deaths_differs_from_no_collection() { let observed = summarize(&execute(spec(1, 0, 2))); assert_eq!(observed.complete_death_count, Some(0)); assert_eq!(observed.survivors, 4); assert_eq!(summarize(&initial(spec(1, 0, 2))).complete_death_count, None); } #[test] fn no_survivors_has_no_survivor_mean_and_does_not_erase_the_cohort() { let report = summarize(&execute(spec(1, 20, 8))); assert_eq!((report.initial, report.survivors), (4, 0)); assert_eq!(report.survivor_mean, None); assert_eq!(report.cohort_mean, Some(Mean { sum: 0, count: 4 })); assert_eq!(report.complete_death_count, Some(4)); } #[test] fn pending_interventions_are_part_of_state_and_change_future_outcomes() { let mut plain = initial(spec(1, 20, 8)); let mut granted = plain.clone(); granted.pending.push(Grant { tick: 1, id: 1, units: 30 }); assert_ne!(canonical(&plain), canonical(&granted)); advance(&mut plain); advance(&mut granted); assert_eq!(summarize(&plain).survivors, 0); assert_eq!(summarize(&granted).survivors, 1); assert!(granted.pending.is_empty()); } #[test] fn a_mean_cannot_replace_the_distribution() { let sparse = [0, 0, 0, 8]; let even = [2, 2, 2, 2]; assert_eq!(mean(sparse.into_iter()), mean(even.into_iter())); assert_ne!(sparse, even); } #[test] fn completed_tick_distinguishes_equal_rosters_with_different_future_eligibility() { let mut early = initial(spec(1, 20, 8)); advance(&mut early); let finished = execute(spec(1, 20, 8)); assert_eq!(early.spec, finished.spec); assert_eq!(early.animals, finished.animals); assert_eq!(early.pending, finished.pending); assert_eq!((early.collected_through, finished.collected_through), (1, 3)); assert_ne!(canonical(&early), canonical(&finished)); advance(&mut early); assert_eq!(early.collected_through, 2); } } The complete report and matched experiment The complete answer returns a report with the specification, algorithm label, individual outcomes, pending inputs, aggregates and retained coverage. Its sum helper checks overflow even though these four-animal fixtures sit comfortably within the limits. Together, those fields let a reader move from the summary back to the conditions and observations that produced it.
