advance(&mut early); let finished = execute(spec(1, 20, 8)); assert_eq!(early.spec, finished.spec); assert_eq!(early.animals, finished.animals); assert_eq!(early.pending, finished.pending); assert_eq!((early.collected_through, finished.collected_through), (1, 3)); assert_ne!(canonical(&early), canonical(&finished)); advance(&mut early); assert_eq!(early.collected_through, 2); } } Use the commands below to check the printed reference separately from your practice file. Your own implementation is still selected by the earlier --file command. python3 learning/scripts/labs.py check experiments The reference produces the following output. Compare its named groups and paired differences with your prediction, and notice where a report preserves an unavailable answer rather than supplying a convenient zero. algorithm=moss-cohort-lcg64-v1 ticks=3 seeds=1,2,3,4 seed=1 alive=4/4 -> 1/4 delta=-3 seed=2 alive=3/4 -> 1/4 delta=-2 seed=3 alive=4/4 -> 2/4 delta=-2 seed=4 alive=4/4 -> 2/4 delta=-2 seed=1 treatment reserves=[0, 0, 0, 1] cohort=Some(Mean { sum: 1, count: 4 }) survivors=Some(Mean { sum: 1, count: 1 }) journal death count=None retained=2 evicted=1 complete=3..=3 pending after horizon=0 Make a claim the evidence supports The opening average becomes interpretable when we name its denominator, retain the individual outcomes and state what history is missing. Across our four matched pairs, higher maintenance leaves fewer survivors under the specified rules and horizon. That is a supported comparison of these cases. Before calling a setup better for a game or an ecosystem, decide what that claim means and what evidence beyond these survival counts could support it. Recall answers The average alone doesn't reveal how many original members survived or how their reserves are distributed. One cohort can also hide sensitivity to starting conditions, while four chosen cohorts still don't settle every scenario. Enjoyment needs a player-facing question beyond survival, and these runs contain no reproduction or inherited change across generations from which to infer evolution. The tests establish the declared toy behavior and report contracts. Evaluating a scenario's balance, connecting it to a browser chart and judging the experience of watching it are further investigations with different evidence. A sound report helps with all of them because it exposes its denominator and gaps instead of quietly making those decisions for the reader. Take that report-reading habit into the continuing meadow's rest comparison or the hunting investigation . There, changing one rule affects access to food and later births as well as immediate costs. Choose a stated assumption to vary, predict which outcomes should differ, and retain the individual evidence that could prove your prediction wrong. The optional Rust survey begins with borrowed views and owned snapshots . We'll use a journal sentence to decide what an inspector may borrow temporarily and what a saved report needs to own.

title: Let a view borrow exactly what it needs
summary: Relate a journal view to its actual owner without tying it to a temporary search term.
text: The inspector wants to show a sentence from Fern's journal: “ate 1 unit.” An export wants to keep the same sentence after the journal has been cleared. The text is identical, but its destinations ask different things of our code. Let a borrowed view depend on the right owner You'll complete latest_with_kind , a search whose returned view borrows from the journal independently of the temporary search string. We'll compare that view with an owned snapshot, then use small compiler experiments to test what happens when text belongs to a local variable, a journal is cleared, or a borrow reaches its last use. The aim is to read a lifetime annotation as a relationship between a result and its actual source. By the end, you should be able to choose borrowing for a temporary inspection, copying for a retained export, and an appropriate correction when a reference would outlast the data it needs. This optional Rust supplement revisits ownership , owned reports and retained history . It uses a small journal fixture with Rust 1.93.1, edition 2024, and changes no ecological rule or active Moss assignment. The fixture gives us a manageable place to explore references before carrying the reasoning into a larger report API. One observation, two destinations Our journal contains four records in append order. Actor 7 has meals at ticks two and five, with an observation between them; actor 8 has a meal at tick six. To find actor 7's latest meal, we need to match both actor and kind, returning tick five. Taking the first meal would give an old result, while taking the newest record without checking its actor would describe somebody else. This gives the search a clear job before lifetimes enter the picture. Each Record owns its kind and note as strings, and the journal owns the vector containing those records. For a temporary inspector, a View can copy the small actor, tick and optional reserve fields while borrowing the note as &str . That avoids allocating the same sentence again, but it also connects the view to its source: every use of the borrowed text must occur while that text remains available. The export has a different need, so Snapshot gives its note an owned String . Calling snapshot() explicitly copies the text, paying for the independence we asked for. The export can then survive an amendment, eviction or the loss of the original journal altogether. It keeps the sentence as it was copied, rather than following later changes to the source. The choice therefore starts with the result's intended use. A brief inspection can borrow, while a retained report needs to cross an ownership boundary. Neither design is universally cheaper or better: borrowing couples use to the source, and copying creates storage the result must own. Lifetimes let the borrowed design state that coupling precisely. Name the relationship the caller needs Our search borrows two inputs: the journal and a kind string such as “meal.” Only one of them supplies text to the result. The kind is a search condition that we can forget once comparison finishes; the returned note comes from the journal. Look for that distinction in the signature below, which is also used in the complete file. fn latest_with_kind<'a>( journal: &'a Journal, actor: u64, kind: &str, ) -> Option<View<'a>> The name 'a connects the journal borrow to the reference stored inside the returned view. It describes a relationship that Rust must check, rather than choosing how many seconds or simulation ticks an allocation will live. The caller must keep the source valid for the uses of the view that the signature permits, and the function body must actually return references consistent with that promise. Giving kind the same named lifetime would unnecessarily tie the result to the search string as well. The example in main makes the difference visible: it creates an owned search string inside a short inner block, performs the search and uses the resulting view after that block ends. This works because the view borrows no part of the query. A dedicated test keeps that freedom in the API as the implementation changes. With only one borrowed input, Rust can often express the relationship without a name. The smaller helper writes fn last_note(journal: &Journal) -> Option<&str> , and lifetime elision connects its output to that sole input. A method's &self or &mut self receiver supplies the usual relationship for a returned reference. These are defined signature rules, explained in the Rust Reference ; the compiler isn't guessing which input you intended by reading the function body. The View<'a> type still needs a lifetime parameter because its fields retain a reference. Its implementation can use impl View<'_> , since snapshot doesn't need to name a relationship between that borrow and its owned output. Snapshot needs no lifetime parameter at all. This is another way the ownership decision shows up in the API: the borrowed type describes its connection to a source, while the owned result carries its own data. Complete the borrowed search Put the lifetime relationship to work by returning a view of the latest matching journal record. Prepare the practice file from the repository root and run its initial check. Only latest_with_kind is unfinished, so the starter should compile and then fail when the relevant tests reach its todo! . Keep the surrounding functions and tests while filling in that search body. python3 learning/scripts/labs.py prepare lifetimes --dest work/lifetimes-practice python3 learning/scripts/labs.py check lifetimes --file work/lifetimes-practice/lifetimes.rs Here “latest” means the last matching record in append order. The fixture appends chronologically, but the helper itself doesn't sort records or search for the greatest tick. Its None also has a precise meaning: no matching record is retained in the supplied journal. That answer doesn't tell us whether an event once happened and was evicted, or whether the actor is currently present in the world. Hint 1: search backward with both conditions Borrow the record collection with iter() , reverse the iterator and use find to require both the actor and kind. Searching from the end makes the first match the latest retained one without rearranging the journal or moving its strings. Hint 2: borrow the note and copy the small fields Map the optional matching record into a View . Borrow its note with &record.note , which Rust can coerce to &str , and copy the actor, tick and Option<u32> . In particular, copying the option preserves the difference between an absent measurement and a measured zero. Complete starter file: lifetimes.rs #[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)] struct Record { tick: u64, actor: u64, kind: String, note: String, reserve_units: Option<u32>, } #[derive(Debug, Default)] struct Journal { records: Vec<Record>, } #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq)] struct View<'a> { tick: u64, actor: u64, note: &'a str, reserve_units: Option<u32>, } #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq)] struct Snapshot { tick: u64, actor: u64, note: String, reserve_units: Option<u32>, } impl View<'_> { fn snapshot(&self) -> Snapshot { Snapshot { tick: self.tick, actor: self.actor, note: self.note.to_owned(), reserve_units: self.reserve_units, } } } fn latest_with_kind<'a>(journal: &'a Journal, actor: u64, kind: &str) -> Option<View<'a>> { let _ = (journal, actor, kind); todo!("borrow the last retained record matching actor and kind") } fn last_note(journal: &Journal) -> Option<&str> { journal.records.last().map(|record| record.note.as_str()) } fn fixture() -> Journal { Journal { records: vec![ Record { tick: 2, actor: 7, kind: "meal".into(), note: "ate 2 units".into(), reserve_units: Some(9), }, Record { tick: 4, actor: 7, kind: "observation".into(), note: "reserve uncollected".into(), reserve_units: None, }, Record { tick: 5, actor: 7, kind: "meal".into(), note: "ate 1 unit".into(), reserve_units: Some(10), }, Record { tick: 6, actor: 8, kind: "meal".into(), note: "ate 3 units".into(), reserve_units: Some(12), }, ], } } fn main() { let mut journal = fixture(); let view = { let search = String::from("meal"); latest_with_kind(&journal, 7, &search).unwrap() }; println!( "view: actor={} tick={} note={}", view.actor, view.tick, view.note ); let snapshot = view.snapshot(); journal.records.clear(); println!("retained rows: {}", journal.records.len()); println!( "export: actor={} tick={} note={} reserve={:?}", snapshot.actor, snapshot.tick, snapshot.note, snapshot.reserve_units ); assert_eq!(last_note(&journal), None); } #[cfg(test)] mod tests { use super::*; #[test] fn finds_latest_matching_actor_and_kind_in_append_order() { let journal = fixture(); let view = latest_with_kind(&journal, 7, "meal").unwrap(); assert_eq!((view.tick, view.actor, view.note), (5, 7, "ate 1 unit")); assert_eq!(view.reserve_units, Some(10)); } #[test] fn append_order_is_not_replaced_by_a_greatest_tick_search() { let mut journal = fixture(); journal.records.push(Record { tick: 1, actor: 7, kind: "meal".into(), note: "late archival copy".into(), reserve_units: None, }); let view = latest_with_kind(&journal, 7, "meal").unwrap(); assert_eq!((view.tick, view.note), (1, "late archival copy")); } #[test] fn empty_or_absent_match_is_none() { assert_eq!(latest_with_kind(&Journal::default(), 7, "meal"), None); let journal = fixture(); assert_eq!(latest_with_kind(&journal, 99, "meal"), None); assert_eq!(latest_with_kind(&journal, 7, "birth"), None); } #[test] fn view_borrows_the_original_note_allocation() { let journal = fixture(); let view = latest_with_kind(&journal, 7, "meal").unwrap(); assert!(std::ptr::eq(view.note, journal.records[2].note.as_str())); } #[test] fn query_need_not_live_as_long_as_the_returned_view() { let journal = fixture(); let view = { let query = String::from("meal"); latest_with_kind(&journal, 7, &query).unwrap() }; assert_eq!(view.note, "ate 1 unit"); } #[test] fn snapshot_survives_mutation_eviction_and_owner_drop() { let snapshot = { let mut journal = fixture(); let snapshot = latest_with_kind(&journal, 7, "meal").unwrap().snapshot(); journal.records[2].note.push_str("; amended"); journal.records.clear(); snapshot }; assert_eq!(snapshot.note, "ate 1 unit"); assert_eq!((snapshot.tick, snapshot.actor), (5, 7)); } #[test] fn uncollected_reserve_and_measured_zero_stay_distinct() { let mut journal = fixture(); let unknown = latest_with_kind(&journal, 7, "observation") .unwrap() .snapshot(); journal.records[1].reserve_units = Some(0); let zero = latest_with_kind(&journal, 7, "observation") .unwrap() .snapshot(); assert_eq!(unknown.reserve_units, None); assert_eq!(zero.reserve_units, Some(0)); assert_ne!(unknown, zero); } #[test] fn unicode_note_is_borrowed_whole_and_single_input_elision_works() { let mut journal = Journal::default(); journal.records.push(Record { tick: 1, actor: 7, kind: "observation".into(), note: "Fern — 水".into(), reserve_units: None, }); assert_eq!(last_note(&journal), Some("Fern — 水")); assert_eq!( latest_with_kind(&journal, 7, "observation").unwrap().note, "Fern — 水" ); } } Complete worked answer: lifetimes.rs #[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)] struct Record { tick: u64, actor: u64, kind: String, note: String, reserve_units: Option<u32>, } #[derive(Debug, Default)] struct Journal { records: Vec<Record>, } #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq)] struct View<'a> { tick: u64, actor: u64, note: &'a str, reserve_units: Option<u32>, } #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq)] struct Snapshot { tick: u64, actor: u64, note: String, reserve_units: Option<u32>, } impl View<'_> { fn snapshot(&self) -> Snapshot { Snapshot { tick: self.tick, actor: self.actor, note: self.note.to_owned(), reserve_units: self.reserve_units, } } } fn latest_with_kind<'a>(journal: &'a Journal, actor: u64, kind: &str) -> Option<View<'a>> { journal .records .iter() .rev() .find(|record| record.actor == actor && record.kind == kind) .map(|record| View { tick: record.tick, actor: record.actor, note: &record.note, reserve_units: record.reserve_units, }) } fn last_note(journal: &Journal) -> Option<&str> { journal.records.last().map(|record| record.note.as_str()) } fn fixture() -> Journal { Journal { records: vec![ Record { tick: 2, actor: 7, kind: "meal".into(), note: "ate 2 units".into(), reserve_units: Some(9), }, Record { tick: 4, actor: 7, kind: "observation".into(), note: "reserve uncollected".into(), reserve_units: None, }, Record { tick: 5, actor: 7, kind: "meal".into(), note: "ate 1 unit".into(), reserve_units: Some(10), }, Record { tick: 6, actor: 8, kind: "meal".into(), note: "ate 3 units".into(), reserve_units: Some(12), }, ], } } fn main() { let mut journal = fixture(); let view = { let search = String::from("meal"); latest_with_kind(&journal, 7, &search).unwrap() }; println!( "view: actor={} tick={} note={}", view.actor, view.tick, view.note ); let snapshot = view.snapshot(); journal.records.clear(); println!("retained rows: {}", journal.records.len()); println!( "export: actor={} tick={} note={} reserve={:?}", snapshot.actor, snapshot.tick, snapshot.note, snapshot.reserve_units ); assert_eq!(last_note(&journal), None); } #[cfg(test)] mod tests { use super::*; #[test] fn finds_latest_matching_actor_and_kind_in_append_order() { let journal = fixture(); let view = latest_with_kind(&journal, 7, "meal").unwrap(); assert_eq!((view.tick, view.actor, view.note), (5, 7, "ate 1 unit")); assert_eq!(view.reserve_units, Some(10)); } #[test] fn append_order_is_not_replaced_by_a_greatest_tick_search() { let mut journal = fixture(); } #[test] fn empty_or_absent_match_is_none() { assert_eq!(latest_with_kind(&Journal::default(), 7, "meal"), None); let journal = fixture(); assert_eq!(latest_with_kind(&journal, 99, "meal"), None); assert_eq!(latest_with_kind(&journal, 7, "birth"), None); } #[test] fn query_need_not_live_as_long_as_the_returned_view() { let journal = fixture(); let view = { let query = String::from("meal"); latest_with_kind(&journal, 7, &query).unwrap() }; assert_eq!(view.note, "ate 1 unit"); let unknown = latest_with_kind(&journal, 7, "observation") .unwrap() .snapshot(); journal.records[1].reserve_units = Some(0); let zero = latest_with_kind(&journal, 7, "observation") .unwrap() .snapshot(); assert_eq!(unknown.reserve_units, None); assert_eq!(zero.reserve_units, Some(0)); assert_ne!(unknown, zero); } #[test] fn unicode_note_is_borrowed_whole_and_single_input_elision_works() { let mut journal = Journal::default(); journal.records.push(Record { tick: 1, actor: 7, kind: "observation".into(), note: "Fern — 水".into(), reserve_units: None, }); assert_eq!(last_note(&journal), Some("Fern — 水")); assert_eq!( latest_with_kind(&journal, 7, "observation").unwrap().note, "Fern — 水" ); } } Run the learner-file command again to check your edit. The reference command, python3 learning/scripts/labs.py check lifetimes , independently runs the printed program and its eight tests. The program produces: view: actor=7 tick=5 note=ate 1 unit retained rows: 0 export: actor=7 tick=5 note=ate 1 unit reserve=Some(10) Several tests go beyond comparing text. A pointer comparison checks that the view refers to the original note rather than an equal replacement, while the snapshot test changes the source and drops its owner before reading the saved result. Equal strings would satisfy the visible message in both cases; these additional checks distinguish the ownership behavior the two destinations need. Make the compiler experiment small Now try a smaller function that can't keep its promise. It creates text locally and attempts to return a reference to that text. Save the complete probe as work/lifetimes-practice/dangling.rs , separately from the working lab, so its expected compilation failure is easy to inspect on its own. fn summary<'a>() -> &'a str { let text = String::from("actor=7 tick=5"); &text } fn main() { println!("{}", summary()); } rustc +1.93.1 --edition=2024 work/lifetimes-practice/dangling.rs -o work/lifetimes-practice/dangling Rust 1.93.1 rejects the probe with E0515 , reporting that the reference points to a local variable. The string belongs to summary and will be dropped when that function returns, so the caller would have no valid storage left to read. Writing a longer lifetime—or 'static —can't make the local owner survive. The annotation must describe a valid ownership relationship; it can't create one. Immediate correction: return the newly created value Replace the probe with this version, which returns the newly created string itself, and rerun the same compilation command. Running work/lifetimes-practice/dangling then prints actor=7 tick=5 . Ownership moves to the caller, which can keep the result. If the text already belonged to the caller, returning a borrow of that caller-owned text could have been a different valid design. fn summary() -> String { String::from("actor=7 tick=5") } fn main() { println!("{}", summary()); } The Rust Book's lifetime chapter develops this distinction between describing a reference's relationship and controlling storage duration. Our probe removes the journal, iterator and optional result so the compiler's objection has one clear cause: the returned reference outlives the local data it would refer to. End a view before changing its owner The local-string probe showed an owner disappearing at return. A journal can also invalidate borrowed text through mutation, so the order of uses now matters. Back in the working program, we read the view and make a snapshot before calling journal.records.clear() . Nothing uses the view afterward, so Rust can finish this ordinary borrow after its last use even though the enclosing block continues. Move a later println!("{}", view.note) below the clear and the situation changes: the program now asks to read text after an operation that may destroy it, producing E0502 . You can resolve that conflict by printing the view before clearing, or by printing snapshot.note afterward. The right correction depends on whether you need current borrowed text or a retained copy. Clearing the vector requires exclusive access, and the diagnostic is protecting the particular note that a later use of the view still needs. Adding lifetime names elsewhere won't change that sequence of events. This also explains why an inspector usually shouldn't own a journal and keep an ordinary reference into that same journal as another field. Construct a view when a caller borrows the journal, or keep a stable actor ID and resolve it when needed. When the result must survive a reset, use an owned snapshot. Those designs meet our needs without introducing the extra constraints of a self-referential owning structure. To check the boundary, consider three changes: dropping the temporary search string, clearing the journal, and replacing a measured zero with an absent measurement. Predict which affects the borrowed view's validity and which changes the meaning of the observation. They're easy to conflate if every problem is described loosely as missing data. Recall answer The query string can disappear because the view doesn't borrow it. Clearing the journal must wait until the view's last use, unless we first copy what needs to survive. Some(0) and None describe a measured zero and no measurement, respectively; that semantic distinction doesn't determine a reference's lifetime. Let the destination decide whether the text is borrowed The two destinations from the opening now have different, useful APIs. The inspector borrows its sentence from the journal, independently of the short-lived search string. The export owns a snapshot that survives clearing the journal. A lifetime annotation states the first relationship; copying creates the independence needed for the second. The native tests establish that small contract, leaving storage durability and wider retention policy to their own checks. Continue to ownership and formatting choices to decide how several readers can use the retained report and call different formatters. Or return to the population investigation to put owned results to work.

title: Choose the owner before the abstraction
summary: Compare concrete report formats with dynamic dispatch and distinguish shared ownership from permission to mutate.
text: The inspector wants “Inspector: actor=7 tick=5 reserve=10,” while a compact diagnostic panel wants “7@5:10.” Both should read the same retained report without changing it. We can support those two formats with an enum. Choose what owns the report and what calls the formatter We'll begin with those known styles, then let an independently written formatter join the same collection. You'll implement boxed_format and compare owned trait objects with borrowed and generic calls. A small compiler probe will show why the interface must offer a method that an object can dispatch. Once that calling decision is clear, we'll ask a separate question: what if several readers need to keep the report? The Rc , Arc and interior-mutability examples should help you distinguish shared ownership, cross-thread access and permission to mutate. The outcome is a reasoned choice for each requirement, without changing the authoritative ECS world's ownership. Optional Rust supplement. Continue from borrowed views and owned snapshots , with trait contracts available for recall. This standard-library lab uses Rust 1.93.1, edition 2024. Its formatters read an isolated report. They do not introduce a biological rule registry or wrap Moss's authoritative ECS world in shared mutable pointers. Start with the known choices Begin with the value being presented. Our Report owns its actor ID, tick, and optional reserve measurement, so it does not depend on a live entity or an allocation in the history journal. The formatter borrows that report long enough to produce a string. It must retain the meaning of the option: None prints “unknown,” while Some(0) prints zero. The compact line is diagnostic text for this exercise; a stored interchange format would need a versioned schema of its own. For two known choices, Style can describe everything we need. Its named variant owns a prefix, and its compact variant needs no extra data. A render method matches the variant and produces the appropriate line. Because both choices are values of the same enum type, a Vec<Style> already stores them together without a separate box for each element. Adding a variant also makes exhaustive matches ask what that new choice means. Now suppose a separately written formatter needs to join the same list. The test's IdOnly type knows how to print an identity but is not another Style variant. We want the collection's rendering loop to accept it through a shared interface. That extension is the reason to consider a trait object here. If the program continues to need only the two known styles, keeping the enum is a complete design. Separate the owner from the call The collection needs to own its formatters after the construction function returns, including a named formatter's prefix. Box<T> supplies an owning pointer, ordinarily to heap storage. Moving the box transfers that ownership to the recipient, and the recipient can borrow the stored value for a call. A zero-sized value such as our empty CompactFormat needs no allocation. The boxed module documentation describes that storage behavior; it is separate from choosing which render method to execute. The rest of the type, dyn ReportFormat , supplies the common calling interface. Behind each pointer is a particular formatter value, but the collection only needs to know that its render operation is available. Calling through the trait object selects the implementation using its dispatch information. The trait-object reference describes the data pointer and virtual method table involved. Combining this interface with Box lets one vector own formatter values of different concrete types. You can use the interface without transferring ownership. render_borrowed accepts &dyn ReportFormat , so it can temporarily borrow a local Style::Compact without putting it in a box. render_generic<F: ReportFormat> also borrows a formatter, but its caller selects a concrete type for F rather than using object dispatch. All three paths can render the same report. Decide first whether the call needs a borrowed value or a stored owner, then whether it needs a concrete type or a trait-object interface. There is a lifetime promise in the returned Box<dyn ReportFormat> too: this lab's return type defaults to a 'static object lifetime bound. A named formatter meets it by owning its prefix instead of borrowing a local string from construction. The box can still be dropped whenever its owner is finished with it; the bound says its contents cannot depend on a shorter-lived borrow. A formatter designed to borrow the caller's prefix would need an explicitly bounded object lifetime. Complete the owning adapter Put those ownership decisions into boxed_format , the one unfinished function. It receives an owned Style and must return the matching owned formatter adapter. Prepare the starter from the repository root; formatting methods, borrowed and generic call paths, the main program, and eight canonical tests are already supplied. python3 learning/scripts/labs.py prepare indirection --dest work/indirection-practice python3 learning/scripts/labs.py check indirection --file work/indirection-practice/indirection.rs The initial file compiles, then checks that use the adapter reach its TODO. For the named branch, follow the prefix as you match the enum: the function owns that string, so it can move it into NamedFormat and return the box. No clone is needed. Returning a reference to a temporary adapter would instead leave the caller borrowing a local value that has gone away, the lifetime mistake from the previous lesson. Hint 1: preserve the payload when matching Match Style::Named { prefix } and Style::Compact . In the named arm, the local prefix is the owned string moved from the selected variant. Hint 2: return a box from each arm Use Box::new(NamedFormat { prefix }) or Box::new(CompactFormat) . Both concrete types implement ReportFormat , so they can be coerced to the declared boxed trait-object return type. Complete starter file: indirection.rs #[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)] struct Report { actor: u64, tick: u64, reserve_units: Option<u32>, } trait ReportFormat { fn render(&self, report: &Report) -> String; } #[derive(Clone)] enum Style { Named { prefix: String }, Compact, } fn reserve_text(report: &Report) -> String { match report.reserve_units { Some(value) => value.to_string(), None => "unknown".into(), } } fn named_line(prefix: &str, report: &Report) -> String { format!( "{prefix}: actor={} tick={} reserve={}", report.actor, report.tick, reserve_text(report) ) } fn compact_line(report: &Report) -> String { format!("{}@{}:{}", report.actor, report.tick, reserve_text(report)) } impl ReportFormat for Style { fn render(&self, report: &Report) -> String { match self { Self::Named { prefix } => named_line(prefix, report), Self::Compact => compact_line(report), } } } struct NamedFormat { prefix: String, } struct CompactFormat; impl ReportFormat for NamedFormat { fn render(&self, report: &Report) -> String { named_line(&self.prefix, report) } } impl ReportFormat for CompactFormat { fn render(&self, report: &Report) -> String { compact_line(report) } } fn boxed_format(style: Style) -> Box<dyn ReportFormat> { let _ = style; The tests also exercise collection order, an empty formatter collection, Unicode prefixes, and the distinction between unknown and zero. Those are behavioral promises we checked for these implementations. The trait method's signature makes a formatter callable; it cannot by itself guarantee that every future implementation labels units correctly or avoids unrelated side effects. Know which methods can cross the object boundary We have a working collection of formatters; before adding methods to its interface, we need to know which calls it can continue to support. Look at what a call through the trait object has to know. Our render method takes a shared receiver, a concrete report argument, and returns an owned string, so the caller can make the same kind of call through every object. A method with its own generic type parameter asks for an additional choice of type at the call site. The object's dispatch information cannot provide a separate callable implementation for every type a future caller might select, so that generic method cannot be dispatched through this trait object. Save the following small experiment as work/indirection-practice/generic_object.rs to see where Rust rejects that change. trait Preview { fn decorate<T: std::fmt::Display>(&self, value: T) -> String; } fn main() { let _: Option<&dyn Preview> = None; } rustc +1.93.1 --edition=2024 work/indirection-practice/generic_object.rs -o work/indirection-practice/generic_object Immediate correction: give the dispatchable method a concrete argument Rust reports E0038 . Replace the entire probe with this version and rerun the compile command. Running work/indirection-practice/generic_object prints actor=7 . trait Preview { fn decorate(&self, value: &str) -> String; } struct Plain; impl Preview for Plain { fn decorate(&self, value: &str) -> String { value.to_owned() } } fn main() { let preview: &dyn Preview = &Plain; println!("{}", preview.decorate("actor=7")); } The correction gives the dispatchable method a concrete argument, matching the operation our callers need. Another design can keep a generic helper on the trait with where Self: Sized , excluding that method from object dispatch while leaving other methods available. You do not have to discard a whole trait because it contains such a helper. The complete dyn-compatibility rules describe the remaining constraints when you design a different interface. Share a snapshot only when needed We have decided how to store formatters and call their methods. A separate question arises if two panels must each keep the same report after the function that created them returns. The program's last line uses two Rc<Report> handles for that situation. Rc::clone adds another owner of the same allocation, so dropping the first handle leaves the second able to read the report. The separate Report::clone test instead creates a new report value whose reserve can change independently. Shared ownership is useful when those readers have independent lifetimes on one thread. If two inspector functions merely need the report during their calls, ordinary &Report borrows are enough. Rc uses non-atomic reference counting and is neither Send nor Sync , so its handles cannot be used to transfer this ownership across threads. The Rc documentation also explains the cycle limitations that matter when owned values point back to one another. For readers on different threads, Arc uses atomic reference counting. With the default allocator, Arc<T> can be Send and Sync when T satisfies both bounds. Our native test establishes those bounds for this report, shares it with a worker that formats it, joins the worker, and reads the report again. The atomic ownership count permits this sharing; it does not make an arbitrary payload safe. This is a native-thread example, so a browser worker would need its own setup and checks. Read the two bounds in terms of the access you need. Send permits transferring a value between threads; Sync permits sending shared references to that value between threads. A plain Box<dyn ReportFormat> does not retain either promise in its exposed type, even if a particular implementation happens to satisfy them. An API requiring both must say so with bounds such as dyn ReportFormat + Send + Sync and accept only implementations that meet them. Interior mutability still has rules So far the shared report has been read-only. To decide what a changing cache would require, separate keeping an allocation alive from accessing its contents. Keeping several owners alive does not grant any of them unrestricted permission to mutate it. If a local preview cache needs to change through a shared API, an interior-mutability type can supply a specific operation for that purpose. Cell supports copying or replacing small values, while RefCell lets code obtain borrows whose exclusivity is checked at runtime. Follow the cache test in two stages. While a read guard is alive, try_borrow_mut() returns an error because writing would conflict with that read. Dropping the guard ends the borrow, allowing the next attempt to update the preview. Calling ordinary borrow_mut() during the conflict would panic instead. The access rule has not disappeared; its check now happens at runtime, and the guard determines how long the access lasts. The RefCell methods describe both forms. That runtime borrowing mechanism is local to a thread. RefCell<T> is not Sync , although it can be Send when T is. Adding an atomic ownership count with Arc does not change the payload's sharing capability. If the real requirement is concurrent shared mutation, synchronization types such as Mutex or RwLock address it. The Arc thread-safety section connects these bounds to the inner value. You can check that distinction before any threads run. Save this optional probe as work/indirection-practice/arc_refcell.rs ; it asks the compiler whether the combined type has the required capability. Replace the requested type with Arc<String> and remove the unused RefCell import. The same command now compiles. This correction fits a read-only snapshot; it does not implement shared mutation. For our presentation problem, an owned snapshot and short formatter borrows already give each piece the access it needs. Moss's mutable simulation state can stay in its authoritative world, where system parameters state how it is accessed. Wrapping that world in Rc<RefCell<World>> would move conflicts to runtime and obscure the boundaries without helping either of our two formatting choices. Give each extra type a specific job The two lines from the opening still describe the same unchanged report. An enum keeps the known styles together; a trait object gives independently implemented formatters a common calling interface; a box lets the collection own them. Readers with independent lifetimes may need shared ownership, and mutation or cross-thread access adds further requirements. Keeping those decisions separate lets you choose the access the example actually needs. In accepting asynchronous results , an owned value will arrive after its request has been replaced. We'll use that delay to distinguish safe ownership transfer from the application's permission to accept the result.

title: Accept asynchronous results at a tick boundary
summary: Let native workers finish out of order while run and request identities keep stale work out of the authoritative tick.
text: You request one settings import, then replace it with another. The newer result arrives first, but the older worker is still running; meanwhile, a reset could make both answers belong to a previous world. Each worker may parse its input correctly and use memory safely while still delivering an answer the application must refuse. Let delayed work finish without accepting a stale result You'll implement receive , the boundary that checks a completion's run and request identity before staging its settings. We'll use controlled native workers to deliver results out of order, then follow an accepted result to the explicit tick that applies it. Replacement, cancellation and reset will each give us a way to withdraw permission before that commit. Alongside the receiver, a small real future will help distinguish creating async work from driving it. You should finish able to explain which guarantees belong to Rust's transfer rules, which belong to application identity, and why neither a completed worker nor a valid staged value changes the world between ticks. Isolated concurrency and async lab. Native worker threads parse owned strings into two toy settings. No network or file I/O is implemented, no biological rule runs, and no import is installed in live Moss. Controlled messages determine completion order without sleeps. Put three boundaries in the design Begin by separating the worker's job from the application's decision. The worker can say, “I finished parsing this request.” Only the application knows whether that request is still current. If it is, the application stages an accepted input for the next executed tick, where the authoritative settings change together. This gives us three moments to follow: completion produces data, acceptance grants permission to use it, and the tick commits it. Use two small settings so a partial update will be easy to see. The cost must be positive and no greater than capacity, while capacity may be at most one hundred. We begin with cost two and capacity ten, and each successful import replaces the pair as one value. These are illustrative configuration values for the lab. Their relationship gives validation something meaningful to protect without adding a balance rule to Moss. The worker owns the string it parses and sends back a Completion containing the request's run/request key and a Result . It never borrows the authoritative world. Consequently, finishing a parse cannot mutate the world on its own. The receiver can inspect the owned message and discard it if its key has become stale, even when its parsed settings are otherwise valid. Separate concurrency, threads, and futures Before implementing acceptance, clarify how delayed work gets to that boundary. Threads and futures can both appear in such a design, but they don't start or drive work in the same way. Our two imports can be in progress during overlapping periods, which is concurrency. Whether their parsing actually executes at the same instant is a separate question about parallelism. The lab uses native operating-system threads, but its correctness will depend on the messages we receive and accept, not on proving that the two processors were doing work simultaneously. A Rust future is another way to represent work whose result may come later. Calling an async function returns that future; it does not start a thread by itself. As the Future reference describes, polling either produces the ready result or reports that the work is pending. A runtime normally arranges later polling after the task is woken, allowing other work to proceed while a result is unavailable. We can inspect the language mechanism without introducing an I/O library. parse_ready has no suspension point or I/O, so its body can finish during its first poll. Constructing that future still does not execute the parse. One test uses an async block with a visible flag: the flag stays unchanged when the future is created and changes when the test polls it. This makes the distinction between creating work and driving it observable. The supplied poll_ready probe pins the future and polls it once using a no-op waker . It is deliberately limited to our immediately ready example and panics if the result is pending. There is no mechanism here to arrange another poll after a socket or timer becomes ready, so this probe is not an executor for asynchronous I/O. The native worker is what moves this parsing work away from the caller. Merely writing async around an expensive synchronous parse would not make the calculation yield: once polled, it would keep executing until it returned or reached a real suspension point. A larger import should choose its worker or runtime arrangement according to the I/O and CPU work involved. The acceptance rule we are about to write remains necessary whichever arrangement delivers the result. Read Send and Sync as access constraints Moving owned messages between native threads also asks Rust to check their transfer capabilities. Send permits transferring ownership of a value between threads, while Sync permits transferring a shared reference to it. The Rust Book's concurrency chapter explains these marker traits and how their automatic implementations depend on the constituent types. Our completion contains owned, transferable data, and a compile-time assertion checks that it implements both traits. The worker closure moves its input string and channel sender into the new thread, so neither depends on a borrow of the caller's world. We need no unsafe implementations to establish that ownership relationship. Those guarantees answer whether the data may cross a thread boundary safely. They cannot answer whether the user still wants request one after choosing request two. A correctly transferred old message could still overwrite the newer choice unless the receiver rejects it. Conversely, a future that is always driven on one thread may not need Send at all. Choose the transfer bounds for the execution platform and the identity checks for the application's meaning. Use two identities to reject two kinds of staleness Give each request a key containing both run identity and request number. Within one run, a new request supersedes the previous request and clears any result already staged for it. Reset starts a new run, where the numbering can begin again. Comparing only request one with request one would then confuse two different operations, so the run identity has to travel with the completion too. The receiver first asks whether there is a current request. It then checks that the completion belongs to the authoritative run, matches the current request's whole key, and has not already been processed. If any check fails, the message is ignored. Once the checks succeed, receive marks the request completed before examining success or failure, ensuring that a duplicate message cannot later replace the first accepted outcome. Now the contents of a current message can matter. Revalidate a successful settings value before storing it as AcceptedInput ; receiving a typed value does not excuse the boundary from protecting the settings relationship. A current error becomes interface error state and leaves the world's settings unchanged. A stale error never reaches that stage, so it cannot erase a newer staged success or tell the user that their replacement request failed. Cancellation follows the same idea by clearing the current request and any staged result. It does not have to terminate the operating-system thread to prevent a stale commit. The worker may still finish and send its owned message, but the receiver will find no current permission to accept it. Cooperative cancellation could avoid wasted work in a larger implementation; checking acceptance is still necessary when a completion races with cancellation. Keep the authoritative tick synchronous Even an accepted completion waits before changing the world. At the next tick, the application takes the staged input, checks its identity again, and assigns the settings pair before updating the completed-tick counter. The tick does not receive from a channel, block for a worker, or await a future. That keeps the state transition synchronous and lets an unfinished import remain separate from simulation advancement. This choice also explains what pausing means. A valid result can be ready and staged while the world is paused, but it will not apply between ticks. If the user replaces or cancels the request before stepping, the staged result is cleared instead. Another application could choose an immediate application boundary; ours gives the pending change a named moment whose behavior we can test. The same boundary matters for reproducible experiments . Wall-clock arrival time alone cannot tell a replay what the world accepted. A replay would need the accepted typed settings and the tick on which they were applied. This lab establishes that distinction without implementing an input journal or persistence. Control completion order with messages To test replacement reliably, make the newer completion arrive first on purpose. A standard channel carries the completions, and each worker waits on its own start gate. The driver releases the newer worker and receives its answer before releasing the older one. This gives the test an explicit sequence instead of asking a sleep duration to predict which thread will finish first. The driver can block while coordinating this native test because it operates outside the authoritative tick. It also joins both workers before returning, making their completion and cleanup part of the fixture. A browser event loop would need an appropriate nonblocking integration; the blocking driver exists to control this test's order, not to prescribe that interface. Two requests in run one Event Application result Request one asks for cost three, capacity thirty. It becomes current temporarily. Request two asks for cost four, capacity forty. It replaces request one. Request two completes first. The new settings are staged; the world still has two and ten. Request one completes later. Its result is ignored. One tick executes. The world commits four and forty, then reports tick one. Predict the acceptance before editing Follow three cases before editing the receiver. First, stage a valid result, then start a replacement request before the tick. Next, reset and create request one again before delivering the old run's request one. Finally, try a payload with cost three and a malformed capacity. In each case, separate what the worker produced from what the receiver may stage and what the tick may commit. Hint 1: replacement invalidates completed work too The latest-request rule applies to permission to commit, not merely work still in progress. Starting the new request clears the old staged input. Hint 2: compare the entire identity and validate the entire value A repeated request number belongs to a different run after reset. A malformed second field must reject the whole settings value rather than committing its valid first field. Prediction answer The replaced staged input never commits. The old run's request is ignored despite the reused number. The malformed payload produces a current error, and both authoritative settings retain their previous values. Your edit is only receive , where those acceptance decisions meet. Prepare a separate practice file; the request lifecycle, worker gates, and synchronous tick are already supplied. That leaves the body responsible for rejecting stale or duplicate messages and staging only a valid current outcome. python3 learning/scripts/labs.py prepare async --dest work/async-practice python3 learning/scripts/labs.py check async --file work/async-practice/async.rs The starter compiles and reaches its intentional todo! when reception runs. After the repair, nine tests should pass. If a late completion changes the settings, trace its complete key and check when staged input is cleared. A lock could serialize access, but it would not decide that an obsolete request has lost permission to commit. Complete starter: async.rs use std::future::Future; use std::sync::mpsc::{self, Sender}; use std::task::{Context, Poll, Waker}; use std::thread::{self, JoinHandle}; #[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)] struct Key { run: u64, request: u64 } #[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)] struct Settings { cost: u32, capacity: u32 } impl Settings { fn valid(self) -> bool { self.cost > 0 && self.cost <= self.capacity && self.capacity <= 100 } } #[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)] enum ImportError { Malformed, InvalidSettings } #[derive(Debug)] struct Completion { key: Key, result: Result<Settings, ImportError> } #[derive(Clone, Copy)] struct AcceptedInput { key: Key, settings: Settings } #[derive(Clone, Copy)] struct Request { key: Key, completed: bool } #[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)] struct World { run: u64, tick: u64, settings: Settings } #[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)] enum Reception { Staged, Failed, Ignored } struct App { world: World, next_request: u64, current: Option<Request>, staged: Option<AcceptedInput>, error: Option<ImportError>, } impl App { fn new() -> Self { Self { world: World { run: 1, tick: 0, settings: Settings { cost: 2, capacity: 10 } }, next_request: 0, current: None, staged: None, error: None } } fn request(&mut self) -> Key { self.next_request = self.next_request.checked_add(1).expect("request identity exhausted"); In reading a macro's generated work , we'll follow another less visible operation: a concise assertion whose expansion could accidentally evaluate the same expression twice.

title: Read the code a macro asks Rust to check
summary: Build a small diagnostic assertion, inspect what it expands into, and keep functions and concrete types as the default.
text: You have written the same pair of assertions several times: this reading belongs to actor 7, and its reserve is a measured zero rather than unavailable. A small macro can give that familiar check a labeled call. But suppose the reading comes from an expression that collects a report. Expanding the two comparisons carelessly could collect it twice. Account for the work inside a concise assertion You'll complete the expansion of assert_reading! , preserving one evaluation per input and borrowing the reading so its owner can keep using it. We'll inspect how the matcher supplies syntax, how generated locals preserve the evaluation contract, and how a compiler error reduces to an ordinary Rust operation. The expected result is an assertion whose behavior you can explain as precisely as its output. We'll also connect that reasoning to the Bevy derives you've already used: generated trait implementations grant capabilities, while explicit insertion and scheduling make the world do something. You can then decide when a macro earns its syntax and when an ordinary function or pair of assertions already does the job. Optional Rust supplement. This closes the selective survey with an isolated standard-library lab on Rust 1.93.1, edition 2024. It builds on trait capabilities and discriminating evidence . A separate Bevy 0.18.1 example explains derives. Neither example installs simulation behavior or creates a new rule framework. Keep the assertion smaller than the system The value under test is a Reading with an owned name, an actor ID, and an optional reserve. Our assertion checks the last two fields and leaves the name available to its owner. That tells us exactly what a passing call means: the identity and measurement match the expectation. Comparing whole readings, establishing that an actor is alive, or checking a complete lifetime would need additional evidence. We want a call that reads assert_reading!(reading, actor = 7, reserve = Some(0)) , keeping the expected identity beside the expected measurement. The labels actor and reserve are tokens chosen for this macro's syntax; Rust does not interpret them as named function arguments. Their order is fixed, with an optional trailing comma to make a multiline call comfortable. Before defining new syntax, keep in view what a function already offers. The supplied same_value<T: PartialEq> can perform the same comparison for many concrete types through an ordinary trait bound. Within one call, both arguments have the same T ; another call can choose a different type. Integers, strings, vectors, and optional values do not need a macro merely because they have different types. When a clear function signature expresses the operation, that is enough. The small benefit here is the labeled assertion form and the diagnostic labels it expands into. Each check is still an ordinary field comparison. The macro will not discover fields, infer their units, or decide a biological policy. If this calling form stops making tests easier to read, two explicit assert_eq! calls remain a complete way to state the requirement. Read the matcher and the expansion A macro_rules! definition describes the syntax it accepts with a matcher, then describes replacement syntax called the expansion. Our $reading:expr matcher accepts one Rust expression and binds that syntax to a metavariable. Using $reading in the expansion inserts the expression there. This differs from a function parameter: the macro is not handed a runtime value that has already been computed. Follow what would happen if the expansion inserted $reading once to read the actor and again to read the reserve. A call with a simple variable might seem fine, but a call with a report-producing expression would execute that expression twice. The two checks could then describe different collections of data. Our contract instead evaluates the reading expression, expected actor, and expected reserve once each, in that order, before either assertion. If one expression itself panics, later evaluation naturally cannot continue. We can preserve that contract by binding each input to a local and using those locals in the checks. The reading local holds a borrow, so asserting on an existing reading does not move its owned name. If the call supplies a temporary reading, the local borrow keeps it alive for the checks within the block. In the double braces, the outer pair delimits the macro's replacement and the inner pair becomes the block expression containing those locals. The matcher's $(,)? handles a smaller syntax choice: it accepts zero or one trailing comma. It does not ask the expansion to evaluate any input again. That is the only repetition pattern this assertion needs. The macros-by-example reference explains fragment matchers, repetition, and expansion when you need to extend such a calling form. Complete one expansion Prepare a separate practice file from the repository root, then replace the one TODO expansion in assert_reading . Keep its matcher and the rest of the file so the task stays focused on the generated checks. The starter already evaluates the inputs before stopping; its unrelated generic-function test may pass even while the assertion tests reach that unfinished expansion. python3 learning/scripts/labs.py prepare macros --dest work/macros-practice python3 learning/scripts/labs.py check macros --file work/macros-practice/macros.rs Hint 1: retain one evaluation per expression Bind let reading = &$reading; , then bind the expected actor as u64 and reserve as Option<u32> . Use these local values for the comparisons. Repeating the macro metavariable would repeat its supplied expression. Hint 2: assert the two different meanings Compare reading.actor with the expected actor and label the assertion “actor identity.” Then compare reading.reserve_units with the expected reserve and label it “reserve measurement.” Keep None distinct from measured zero. Complete starter file: macros.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq)] struct Reading { actor: u64, name: String, reserve_units: Option<u32>, } fn same_value<T: PartialEq>(actual: &T, expected: &T) -> bool { actual == expected } macro_rules! assert_reading { ($reading:expr, actor = $actor:expr, reserve = $reserve:expr $(,)?) => {{ let reading = &$reading; let actor: u64 = $actor; let reserve: Option<u32> = $reserve; let _ = (reading, actor, reserve); todo!("compare actor identity and the optional reserve measurement") }}; } fn fixture() -> Reading { Reading { actor: 7, name: "Fern".into(), reserve_units: Some(0), } } fn main() { let reading = fixture(); println!("zero equals unknown: {}", same_value(&Some(0_u32), &None)); } #[cfg(test)] mod tests { use super::*; use std::panic::catch_unwind; #[test] fn accepts_values_references_and_an_optional_trailing_comma() { let reading = fixture(); }); let panic = result.expect_err("wrong reserve must fail"); let message = panic.downcast_ref::<String>().unwrap(); assert!(message.contains("reserve measurement"), "{message}"); } #[test] fn wrong_identity_is_rejected_even_with_a_matching_reserve() { let result = catch_unwind(|| { assert_reading!(fixture(), actor = 8, reserve = Some(0)); }); let panic = result.expect_err("wrong actor must fail"); let message = panic.downcast_ref::<String>().unwrap(); assert!(message.contains("actor identity"), "{message}"); } #[test] fn unknown_can_be_the_expected_measurement() { let reading = Reading { reserve_units: None, ..fixture() }; assert_reading!(reading, actor = 7, reserve = None); assert!(same_value(&reading.reserve_units, &None)); } #[test] fn generic_function_handles_other_types_without_new_syntax() { assert!(same_value(&String::from("Fern"), &String::from("Fern"))); assert!(!same_value(&vec![2, 10], &vec![10, 2])); assert!(same_value(&None::<u32>, &None)); } } Complete worked answer: macros.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq)] struct Reading { actor: u64, name: String, reserve_units: Option<u32>, } fn same_value<T: PartialEq>(actual: &T, expected: &T) -> bool { actual == expected } macro_rules! assert_reading { ($reading:expr, actor = $actor:expr, reserve = $reserve:expr $(,)?) => {{ let reading = &$reading; let actor: u64 = $actor; let reserve: Option<u32> = $reserve; assert_eq!(reading.actor, actor, "actor identity"); assert_eq!(reading.reserve_units, reserve, "reserve measurement"); }}; } fn fixture() -> Reading { Reading { actor: 7, name: "Fern".into(), reserve_units: Some(0), } } fn main() { let reading = fixture(); let mut evaluations = 0; assert_reading!( { evaluations += 1; &reading }, actor = 7, reserve = Some(0) ); println!( "{}: actor={} reserve={:?}", reading.name, reading.actor, reading.reserve_units ); println!("source evaluations: {evaluations}"); println!("zero equals unknown: {}", same_value(&Some(0_u32), &None)); } #[cfg(test)] mod tests { use super::*; use std::panic::catch_unwind; #[test] fn accepts_values_references_and_an_optional_trailing_comma() { let reading = fixture(); assert_reading!(reading, actor = 7, reserve = Some(0)); assert_reading!(&reading, actor = 7, reserve = Some(0),); assert_reading!(fixture(), actor = 7, reserve = Some(0)); } #[test] fn borrowing_the_reading_does_not_move_its_owned_name() { let reading = fixture(); assert_reading!(reading, actor = 7, reserve = Some(0)); assert_eq!(reading.name, "Fern"); } #[test] fn each_input_runs_once_in_the_documented_order() { let mut calls: Vec<&str> = Vec::new(); assert_reading!( { calls.push("reading"); fixture() }, actor = { calls.push("actor"); 7 }, reserve = { calls.push("reserve"); Some(0) }, ); assert_eq!(calls, vec!["reading", "actor", "reserve"]); } #[test] fn generated_bindings_do_not_capture_callers_with_the_same_names() { let reading = fixture(); let actor = 7_u64; let reserve = Some(0_u32); assert_reading!(reading, actor = actor, reserve = reserve); assert_eq!((actor, reserve), (7, Some(0))); assert_eq!(reading.name, "Fern"); } #[test] fn measured_zero_does_not_match_unknown() { let result = catch_unwind(|| { assert_reading!(fixture(), actor = 7, reserve = None); }); let panic = result.expect_err("wrong reserve must fail"); let message = panic.downcast_ref::<String>().unwrap(); assert!(message.contains("reserve measurement"), "{message}"); } #[test] fn wrong_identity_is_rejected_even_with_a_matching_reserve() { let result = catch_unwind(|| { assert_reading!(fixture(), actor = 8, reserve = Some(0)); }); let panic = result.expect_err("wrong actor must fail"); let message = panic.downcast_ref::<String>().unwrap(); assert!(message.contains("actor identity"), "{message}"); } #[test] fn unknown_can_be_the_expected_measurement() { let reading = Reading { reserve_units: None, ..fixture() }; assert_reading!(reading, actor = 7, reserve = None); assert!(same_value(&reading.reserve_units, &None)); } #[test] fn generic_function_handles_other_types_without_new_syntax() { assert!(same_value(&String::from("Fern"), &String::from("Fern"))); assert!(!same_value(&vec![2, 10], &vec![10, 2])); assert!(same_value(&None::<u32>, &None)); } } Run python3 learning/scripts/labs.py check macros to check the printed reference, or use the learner-file command for your own expansion. The eight tests exercise values, references, temporaries, trailing commas, ownership, evaluation order, caller-local names, and the two different failure meanings. In the program output, the evaluation count gives our less visible promise a number you can inspect: Fern: actor=7 reserve=Some(0) source evaluations: 1 zero equals unknown: false To verify the failure meanings, two tests deliberately trigger assertion panics, catch them, and inspect their labels. With uncaptured output enabled, those expected panic messages may be printed even when the suite passes. Read the named outcomes and final result to distinguish a checked rejection from an uncaught failure. Hygiene does not evaluate your expression The expression-count tests cover how often generated work runs. Next, check whether the generated bindings can change which caller values that work refers to. Both the expansion and its caller may use the same local names. The hygiene test deliberately names caller variables reading , actor , and reserve , matching the bindings generated by the macro. The expressions supplied at the call still refer to their caller's variables, while the generated locals have their own context. Their matching spellings therefore do not accidentally redirect those references. This behavior is part of declarative macros' mixed-site hygiene. It does not mean every kind of name is resolved in a universally isolated scope. Paths to other items have their own lookup rules, and an exported macro may need $crate to reach a helper in its defining crate. Our private single-file assertion has no such exported helper, so its local-binding example is enough to investigate the problem here. Name resolution and evaluation count remain separate questions. Try replacing the shared reading local with (&$reading).actor in one check and (&$reading).reserve_units in the other. The generated names may still resolve correctly, but the report-producing expression is now present twice. The side-effect test catches the two evaluations that a simple variable argument could conceal. Reduce a generated error to ordinary Rust When the compiler points into an expansion, reduce the problem to the ordinary operation the macro generated. The following probe keeps the actor-type constraint from our assertion while removing the other fields. Save it separately as work/macros-practice/wrong_actor.rs ; it is an intentional failing experiment outside the passing lab. macro_rules! actor_id { ($value:expr) => {{ let actor: u64 = $value; actor }}; } fn main() { println!("{}", actor_id!("7")); } rustc +1.93.1 --edition=2024 work/macros-practice/wrong_actor.rs -o work/macros-practice/wrong_actor Rust 1.93.1 reports E0308 because the invocation supplies a &str where the generated binding requires u64 . Replace the call mentally with let actor: u64 = "7"; and the error becomes an ordinary type mismatch. Accepting an expression in a matcher does not promise that expression has the type the expansion needs. Normal type checking still applies to the generated Rust. Immediate correction Change only actor_id!("7") to actor_id!(7_u64) . Rerun the compile command, then run work/macros-practice/wrong_actor ; it prints 7 . If the input truly comes from text, parse it and handle the Result before calling. Removing the type constraint would conceal a different input contract. Recognize the derive you already use We can now read our own expansion, so let's connect that method to the generated implementations already present in the ECS examples. The assertion is a declarative macro, but its function-like call syntax does not identify that implementation mechanism on its own. A procedural macro can also use a function-like call. Procedural macros run compiler-invoked Rust code that consumes and produces token streams, and they can additionally appear as attributes or custom derives. Keeping invocation syntax separate from implementation helps when you trace a macro supplied by a library. You have already used procedural macros through Bevy's #[derive(Component)] and #[derive(Resource)] . They generate trait implementations that let your types participate in those ECS APIs. To connect that capability to behavior, recall the operations that follow: component values must be placed on entities, resources inserted into the world by type, and systems scheduled to act on them. Deriving the capability does not perform those operations. The optional main.rs below makes that separation visible with pinned Bevy 0.18.1. Its types already have the derives when an empty world is created, yet the world still contains no entities and no tick resource. Only the subsequent explicit insertion operations give it a marker containing seven and a tick resource containing zero. Complete Bevy derive observation use bevy_ecs::prelude::*; #[derive(Component)] struct Marker(u32); #[derive(Resource)] struct Tick(u64); fn main() { let mut world = World::new(); assert_eq!(world.entities().len(), 0); assert!(world.get_resource::<Tick>().is_none()); let entity = world.spawn(Marker(7)).id(); world.insert_resource(Tick(0)); assert_eq!(world.get::<Marker>(entity).unwrap().0, 7); assert_eq!(world.resource::<Tick>().0, 0); println!("marker=7 tick=0"); } To run the probe, create a fresh directory with these commands and save the displayed file as work/macros-derive/src/main.rs before running Cargo. The copied manifest and lockfile keep the course's pinned dependency selection. Offline mode uses the dependencies cached during setup. mkdir -p work/macros-derive/src cp learning/scripts/lab.Cargo.toml work/macros-derive/Cargo.toml cp learning/scripts/lab.Cargo.lock work/macros-derive/Cargo.lock cargo +1.93.1 run --offline --locked --manifest-path work/macros-derive/Cargo.toml Expect marker=7 tick=0 . As a diagnostic experiment, remove #[derive(Component)] and observe the trait-bound errors at component API calls. Restoring the derive supplies the missing capability, allowing those explicit operations again. The marker's value still does not make it a creature, and a zero tick resource still does not establish any executed simulation work. The versioned Component and Resource documentation defines the respective contracts. The procedural-macro reference is a useful next reading when generated implementations themselves become the subject of your work. Writing a derive, working with unsafe code, and using foreign-function interfaces are separate advanced studies rather than prerequisites for Moss. For the code we have here, finding the invocation and reducing its generated operation already gives us a practical debugging method. Concise syntax still has work to account for The opening assertion now borrows one evaluated reading, checks the expected identity and measurement, and leaves the name available. Its tests can reject repeated work as well as an incorrect value. Reading the expansion also gives compiler errors an ordinary operation to point to. The same approach explains why a derive can supply an ECS capability while leaving insertion and execution to explicit code. Bring that method back to the evidence lesson , or use the delayed-result lab when the hidden boundary is acceptance. For your next investigation in the evolving world, the return exercises ask you to apply these familiar ideas under a changed condition, with predictions and checks ready beside them.

title: A small world, understood.
summary: Course guide
text: Learn Rust by making a little life explain itself. Fern begins with 60 units of energy and a patch of grass in the distance. One executed tick changes her reserve; drawing another frame doesn't. Start by explaining that small difference, then use the same habit as the world grows: predict what should happen, write the Rust that makes it happen, and choose evidence that could show you were wrong. A field notebook for a little world Fern stands on an abstract gridded meadow. A line connects her reserve of 60 to an observation after one tick: 59. A distant patch of grass is a future destination. Fern · 60 Meadow one tick → 59 Observe before you explain. An illustration of the learning world. The current live simulation runs maintenance; the journey to Meadow remains your movement exercise. Fieldnotes is a new learning format alongside the existing Moss book. Each lesson develops a question through explanation, a small experiment, and a runnable Rust example. You can read straight through, listen while the current passage is highlighted, or save a note for another visit. Hints and complete answers are available whenever you want them. Keep one meadow as you learn. After the query, schedule, meal, and growth lessons, bring the pieces into a continuing project . Reconstruct whole ECS systems, write an investigation, and inspect your compiled source in the browser. Extend that saved project with funded births and descendants , give those animals local choices and paid journeys , then let fatigue interrupt a journey and hunters compete for prey . In the refuge capstone , choose how shelter belongs in that world, implement the complete system, and test your own prediction about its placement. Your earlier work stays in the same project; native tests and experiments let you investigate the final extension. Your live assignment remains yours. NOW.md in the Moss checkout is still the source of truth for active project work. The course labs and continuing meadow are separate from that live world, so working through them doesn't replace or complete the movement task. Begin with something you can inspect Fieldnote 01 · 25 min A tick is a promise Follow one reserve through a tick, then separate the world's state from the way it is drawn. Open fieldnote ↗ Fieldnote 02 · 35 min Who owns the next change? Predict which value changes when you move, copy, or borrow it. Make the compiler part of the experiment. Open fieldnote ↗ Fieldnote 03 · 35 min Ask the world a typed question Use a query signature to say which entities matter and which data the system may change. Open fieldnote ↗ Fieldnote 04 · 30 min Give the number a unit Separate a requested cost, an actual payment, and the reserve left. Let types and boundary tests keep the distinction visible. Open fieldnote ↗ Fieldnote 05 · 30 min Missing is a different state Describe an absent choice, an unresolved identity, and a present zero without turning them into the same result. Open fieldnote ↗ Fieldnote 06 · 35 min A rejected request has a reason Carry a form input through parsing and domain validation. Return a useful error instead of a misleading default. Open fieldnote ↗ Fieldnote 07 · 30 min Put the boundary in the code Give callers an honest public interface while keeping construction rules close to the values they protect. Open fieldnote ↗ Fieldnote 08 · 35 min Collect a report, release the world Turn borrowed observations into owned report rows, with explicit ordering and honest missing data. Open fieldnote ↗ Fieldnote 09 · 35 min A trait is a promise you can use Give identities meaningful comparison and reporting capabilities, then let a generic function state the capability it needs. Open fieldnote ↗ Fieldnote 10 · 35 min Prove that the borrows cannot meet Make read and write sets explicit, then use a dual-role entity to test the boundary. Open fieldnote ↗ Fieldnote 11 · 35 min Give the observations an order Bracket one real mutation with two observations. Explain how identical final values can hide different execution histories. Open fieldnote ↗ Fieldnote 12 · 40 min Change structure at a known boundary Follow a queued row across an explicit application point, then retain an observation after its entity is gone. Open fieldnote ↗ Fieldnote 13 · 40 min Make a test disagree with a plausible mistake Separate a correct helper from correct selection, schedule wiring, and the value an observer actually saw. Open fieldnote ↗ Fieldnote 14 · 35 min Connect one affordable action to the world Return to the canonical learner-owned movement task and connect its one edit to a reviewed, visible consequence. Open fieldnote ↗ Fieldnote 15 · 40 min A finite meal has two sides Resolve two consumers against one finite patch and keep requested intake separate from actual gain. Open fieldnote ↗ Fieldnote 16 · 40 min Choose, then revalidate a target Choose from a bounded snapshot, then check the live target again before committing a meal. Open fieldnote ↗ Fieldnote 17 · 40 min Compare individuals fairly Give individuals different costs while holding the starting conditions fixed, then separate that comparison from a density change. Open fieldnote ↗ Fieldnote 18 · 45 min Let environmental input change supply Trace lit and dark ticks and show how the selected growth-and-meal order changes a patch at capacity. Open fieldnote ↗ Fieldnote 19 · 45 min Keep a disappearance explainable Record one terminal transition and distinguish a complete zero count from history that no longer covers the question. Open fieldnote ↗ Fieldnote 20 · 45 min Consume once, even before removal Let two hunters compete for one prey and make its immediate availability authoritative before deferred despawn. Open fieldnote ↗ Fieldnote 21 · 40 min Make rest a commitment you can inspect Keep fatigue separate from energy and compare a reactive choice with an activity that lasts for a stated number of ticks. Open fieldnote ↗ Fieldnote 22 · 45 min Commit both parents before creating a child Validate and charge a pair atomically, then give a deferred newborn an explicit first action boundary. Open fieldnote ↗ Fieldnote 23 · 45 min Keep inheritance distinct from selection Copy and vary an offspring trait while preserving parents, units, identity, and enough provenance to replay the proposal. Open fieldnote ↗ Fieldnote 24 · 45 min Make a comparison explain its denominator Compare a declared intervention across matched cohorts, retaining losses and missing coverage in the report. Open fieldnote ↗ Fieldnote 25 · 40 min Let a view borrow exactly what it needs Relate a journal view to its actual owner without tying it to a temporary search term. Open fieldnote ↗ Fieldnote 26 · 45 min Choose the owner before the abstraction Compare concrete report formats with dynamic dispatch and distinguish shared ownership from permission to mutate. Open fieldnote ↗ Fieldnote 27 · 45 min Accept asynchronous results at a tick boundary Let native workers finish out of order while run and request identities keep stale work out of the authoritative tick. Open fieldnote ↗ Fieldnote 28 · 40 min Read the code a macro asks Rust to check Build a small diagnostic assertion, inspect what it expands into, and keep functions and concrete types as the default. Open fieldnote ↗ A language learned through consequences The opening lessons ask who owns a value and who may change it. Optional data, explicit errors, collections, and system order become useful as the world poses further questions: what if the target is gone, or two animals want the last unit of food? We'll slow down for the Rust reasoning behind those decisions while keeping familiar programming syntax brief. The 28 fieldnotes lead from that first tick through ecological experiments and selected advanced Rust. Lifetimes help explain borrowed observations; concurrency raises the question of when an arriving result may change the world. The learning path shows those connections and where to join the continuing project. On a later visit, return with a different question to practice choosing evidence in a changed fixture. Connect the rule, the schedule, and the view A helper test can show that a meal calculation handles its stated cases. An ECS integration test can show that the intended animals actually receive that meal in the installed schedule. A browser observation can then show what the compiled application exposes through its controls. We'll use all three, keeping clear which part of the explanation each supports. Open the local workbench when you're ready to run Rust. Reading needs only this static website: there is no account, and optional notes and progress stay in your browser. You can move between the explanation and your editor without giving up the diagrams, narration, or saved place that make a longer investigation easier to follow.

title: A path through a living world
summary: Course guide
text: First explain one change. Then follow what it makes possible. This route is for an experienced programmer developing practical Rust and ECS fluency. We'll spend time on ownership, borrowing, data modelling, and scheduling, introducing familiar syntax as it becomes useful. A value copied for an inspector becomes a way to reason about a meal proposal; an ordering edge becomes the difference between a rescue and a death. Those returns give the language ideas more than one setting in which to make sense. Choose your route. All 28 numbered lessons are available, with short isolated labs and complete answers.
