The cumulative guides connect those ideas in one saved course project. You can read ahead or return to an earlier question without unlocking anything. Live Moss work remains governed by NOW.md . Practical Rust and ECS fluency This first part builds the habits needed to change a Rust world with confidence. You’ll begin with values and borrowed access, shape the interfaces around them, and then connect whole systems through an explicit schedule. The practical outcome is being able to explain who may change a value, when the change becomes visible, and what a test would need to observe. Begin with A tick is a promise , where an observable state change gives mutation a purpose. Who owns the next change? follows the difference between copying a value, borrowing access, and moving ownership. Ask the world a typed question carries those permissions into components, resources, and queries, so a system's requested access also explains which entities it can visit. Once you can find and change a value, its representation matters. Give the number a unit makes arithmetic assumptions explicit; Missing is a different state handles absence; and A rejected request has a reason explains invalid input through Result . Modules , collections , and traits then help those choices work together through useful interfaces. Return to ECS access with disjoint query borrows , then ask when systems run in explicit schedule order . Deferred commands make visibility a separate question from ordering, and discriminating integration checks ask you to write tests that distinguish plausible mistakes. The bridge to the canonical movement task connects this reasoning with your live assignment. Along the way, the Rust terrarium lets you inspect the installed maintenance schedule through an actual compiled browser host. Ecosystem depth Here the language mechanisms acquire ecological consequences. Start with one transfer of food, then combine supply, competing claims and retained history in the continuing meadow. Later guides extend the same saved project until you can investigate how births, journeys, rest and capture interact, and design a shelter rule of your own. A meal is a useful next step because it changes two owners at once. Finite meals accounts for that transfer and resolves competition; target choice asks whether an earlier observation still permits an action now. Authored populations and individual costs supplies controlled comparisons before reproduction starts changing who belongs to the population. Growth and environmental input adds food to the ledger, while lifecycle and history connects terminal outcomes with bounded records. Predation , rest , and reproduction each isolate a different eligibility or timing problem. Inheritance preserves where a child's value came from, and repeated experiments asks what comparisons can justify. These short labs make individual rules inspectable before you combine their consequences. Use the continuing meadow after the core, meal, and growth work to connect upkeep, food, competition, and history in one saved Cargo project. The population extension adds paid births, maturation, and inherited upkeep. Then local observations and paid travel make reaching food part of survival, committed rest interrupts those journeys, and competing hunters makes one capture change the opportunities left in the tick. Each guide asks for whole-system decisions, keeps your earlier tests, and provides a complete worked checkpoint beside your implementation. The refuge capstone then asks you to take more responsibility for the design. Choose how to represent shelter, write the complete membership system, and connect it to observation and capture at the right moments. A grazer entering shelter after a hunter has seen it makes the timing problem concrete. Once your implementation handles that encounter, design a matched placement experiment and decide what its results support. Staged hints and complete module answers are available, but your hypothesis and investigation begin with your own choices. This course meadow is an authored game model you can investigate, separate from the live Moss simulation. Its implemented interactions don't select biological policies for your live project or establish scientific calibration. The compiled browser views accompany the route through hunting; the refuge extension uses native tests, owned reports, and a command-line experiment. Each gives you evidence about the part of the world it actually runs. A selective Rust survey These supplements widen the view after the practical core. Each starts from a problem the course has already made familiar, then follows it into a less frequently needed part of Rust. Choose a supplement when its question helps your current work; completing all four is not a prerequisite for the continuing meadow. Return to the wider language when the problem makes the detail useful. Lifetimes explains borrowed observations crossing an API boundary. Smart pointers and trait objects considers ownership and dispatch choices. Concurrency and async follows independent work through to an accepted input, while macros examines a small diagnostic helper and the code a derive asks Rust to check. Return with a different question The mixed return route changes six familiar fixtures so you have to choose which idea and evidence apply. Try its first three after the ECS core and its second three after the first fieldwork. Progressive hints and full reasoning remain available, with five tests you can keep in the continuing project. Concepts recur when the world makes their consequence visible. Idea First encounter Return later Ownership and borrowing Save an inspector reading Resolve a meal, retain history, borrow observations Absence and invariants A missing component or target An invalidated destination, unavailable history Explicit order Maintenance before completion Claims before rewards, newborn eligibility Testing and evidence A literal reserve trace A competing-actor regression, a scarcity experiment Leave a note about the point that surprised you, then return to that question after a gap. It often gives you a more useful starting place than a chapter number. Recall answers are immediately available; you don't need to pass a quiz before reopening the explanation.

title: Open the workbench
summary: Course guide
text: Read in the browser, then bring the compiler to the question. You can follow the explanations, diagrams, and teaching models without setting up Rust first. When you're ready to edit a lab, the local workbench compiles and tests your saved file. That gives you Rust's actual diagnostics while keeping the lesson beside your editor. The small browser teaching models provide a quicker way to test a prediction; their labels distinguish them from compiled Rust. A workbench you can trust By the end of this guide, you should have the course beside your editor and know whether a command is checking the printed answer or your own file. We’ll open the reading edition, verify the pinned toolchain, and run a small reference before preparing an unfinished exercise. That order separates a setup problem from a mistake in the code you are learning to write. The browser-build commands come afterward, for the lessons that need a compiled view. Open this edition From the root of the Moss checkout containing learning , build and serve the course. You need Python 3.11 or newer, with no additional Python packages: python3 learning/scripts/build.py python3 learning/scripts/serve.py Open Moss Fieldnotes on port 8091 and leave the terminal running while you read. Control-C stops the server, which binds only to your computer. Rebuild and reload after changing lesson sources. Keeping the same port also keeps the browser origin consistent, so your locally saved notes remain available. Check the tools selected by Moss The repository pins Rust 1.93.1 and Bevy ECS 0.18.1, the combination used for the course examples. From the same repository root, confirm that the toolchain is available: scripts/with-toolchain.sh rustc +1.93.1 --version scripts/with-toolchain.sh cargo +1.93.1 --version If rustup reports that it is missing, install it and repeat those checks: rustup toolchain install 1.93.1 --profile minimal --component rustfmt --component clippy The first two labs use only the standard library. The query lab also needs the locked Bevy ECS dependencies in Cargo's cache, which a normal Moss build prepares. On a new machine, use docs/development/README.md for the complete project setup. If a command can't find a cached crate, resolve that setup problem before interpreting it as a result of your exercise. Check the answer's starting point Run the opening references once to see the workbench's test output and sample trace: python3 learning/scripts/labs.py check observe python3 learning/scripts/labs.py check ownership python3 learning/scripts/labs.py check queries Each command extracts the exact marked example from its lesson, compiles it separately, requires its named tests to run, and then executes the sample program. The output identifies this as PRINTED REFERENCE . Its passing result establishes that the published example works for those cases on your machine; the next step is to select an edit of your own. Make an edit that belongs to you The ownership lesson starts with an unfinished inspector function. Prepare a fresh copy, open it in your editor, then check the file you've selected: python3 learning/scripts/labs.py prepare ownership --dest work/ownership-practice python3 learning/scripts/labs.py check ownership --file work/ownership-practice/ownership.rs The first check fails at the intended todo! . Replace the body of capture , save, and repeat the second command. Both checks identify the source as LEARNER FILE and name your path; after the edit, the required tests should pass. That label distinguishes feedback on your file from a run of the printed answer. Preparation refuses an existing destination; return to the same file for another attempt. Which tests are used for a short lab? When checking your copy, the runner uses the reference's trailing test module as the required course checks. Changing a copied assertion therefore cannot make an incorrect solution pass those checks. Keep additional exploratory tests in a separate scratch file. Later, the continuing project has a different workflow that retains and runs learner-authored integration tests alongside its required suites. See checked Rust run in the browser The maintenance terrarium runs the actual simulation crate, while the evidence lesson can run your completed projection exercise in a browser host. Both use local compilation. To reproduce their included references, install the pinned WebAssembly target and build the hosts: rustup target add --toolchain 1.93.1 wasm32-unknown-unknown python3 learning/scripts/runtime.py check python3 learning/scripts/runtime.py build python3 learning/scripts/preview.py evidence python3 learning/scripts/build.py For your own completed evidence exercise, add --file work/evidence-practice/evidence.rs to its preview command, then rebuild the course and reload. The panel identifies the source kind and compiled build. Rust source stays in the local workbench rather than being sent to a compiler service. The continuing route begins in one saved meadow project and keeps that directory through population , movement and local observation , rest , and hunting . Those guides supply their stage-specific check and preview commands, along with complete source answers. Follow their instructions as you extend the project; don't prepare a replacement copy each time you begin a new guide. Keep that same directory for the independent refuge capstone . Its stage check runs your growing collection of tests, and its native example compares shelter placements through printed reports. There is no additional refuge browser mode. If you want to reopen an earlier browser view after changing the source, rebuild it with that guide's preview command; a current build still displays only the rules and reports that its mode supports. What does the runner execute? These are local Rust programs running with your normal process permissions. The workbench runs original course examples or a file you explicitly select; it is not a sandbox for untrusted code. It doesn't accept source from the browser or start a local execution API. Build artifacts stay under learning/work , separate from the live simulation sources and active assignment. Open the live terrarium when a lesson calls for it The main Moss application has its own server. From the repository root, run: scripts/with-toolchain.sh trunk serve --locked --release It opens at port 8080 , separately from Fieldnotes; keep one simulation preview on that port. At the current live checkpoint, maintenance runs while the unfinished movement rule remains unscheduled. Full workspace tests still encounter that intentional exercise, so use the focused command named by a lesson when you're inspecting an existing rule. Know which file your test is checking When you return to active Moss development, open NOW.md . Your course work can help explain the decision in front of you while the live assignment remains the place to make that project change. For the course, a working reference establishes the toolchain and a check labelled LEARNER FILE identifies your selected edit. An initial failure at todo! is the intended starting point for that exercise. Begin with one observable tick , then use the ownership lesson to complete the inspector you prepared here.

title: Read, listen, investigate
summary: Course guide
text: Keep the lesson useful however you prefer to read. The explanation, diagrams, code, hints, and worked answers are ordinary page content. Links handle navigation and native disclosures open answers, so the reading route remains available when the optional tools are quiet. You can select text for a highlighter or another reading tool, enlarge it, or print a lesson with its answers included. Make the page fit the way you study This guide helps you choose a reading rhythm and keep the evidence you collect along the way. We’ll look at listening and focus controls, then notes and their backups, before explaining the different kinds of world shown in the course. You should leave knowing how to return to a useful passage and how to tell whether a result came from a teaching model, a Rust example, or the live simulation. Read and listen together Where generated narration is available, use the audio player or sticky Play audio control to listen with the current passage highlighted. You can seek within the recording, or turn off Follow highlighted passage while you inspect something elsewhere on the page. The player identifies how its recording was generated. These audio files are made from the course prose and saved with the reading edition, so playback works offline. They read prose and tables, but skip code and answer disclosures, so pause to work through those when the lesson reaches them. The page supplies the same prose in text. Listen offers another route through your browser's speech service, with passage highlighting, pause, resume, and stop. Open a worked answer before starting if you want its prose included. Available voices and pronunciation depend on your browser and operating system; some voices may use a network service, although the Fieldnotes reading page itself doesn't send text to a hosted narration service. You can also use an external immersive reader if it better suits how you listen, select, and annotate. Use Focus to hide the side columns while keeping the reading controls available, and adjust text size to suit the page. The size is saved with your reading record. Models advance only when you request it, giving you time to compare their state with the explanation before taking the next step. Accessibility checks and their limits The controls use ordinary buttons, links, fields, and disclosures. Development checks covered the skip link, keyboard use of hints, focus mode, generated narration, and narrow reading layouts. A full screen-reader and assistive-technology compatibility audit has not been completed. Keep a trace of your own thinking A useful field note can begin with a prediction and end with the observation that changed it. To keep a passage beside that note, select the text and choose Keep selected text . This saves a quotation without changing the original lesson. You can mark a lesson not started, reading, practicing, or reviewed as a reminder of where to return; opening an answer or trying a model never marks Rust tests as passed. Notes and progress belong to this browser origin. Export a reading record to back them up or move them to another device. Import merges notes and distinct saved passages with your existing writing. If local storage is unavailable, export before leaving so the current record doesn't depend on that storage. When a file picker is inconvenient, expand Use copy and paste , copy the record, and import its JSON on the other device. Pasted text and files follow the same validation and merge rules; invalid input leaves your existing record unchanged. Know which world you're observing The JavaScript teaching panels make one idea easy to try: a tick versus a camera change, where a write lands, or which entities match a query. Their labels explain the represented rule and its omissions. For compiler and schedule behavior, the lessons instead provide original Rust examples and exact local commands, so you can bring the question to the tool that can actually answer it. The evidence lesson's Rust panel runs a precompiled version of its Bevy exercise. You can compile your own edited file after its required tests pass, and the build label distinguishes it from the printed reference. The Rust terrarium uses a different source: the actual moss-sim crate, running the installed schedule in an independent world whose controls request ticks and read components. The continuing course project has its own compiled views. Beginning with fieldwork , you keep one saved implementation through descendants , paid travel , rest , and predation . Those views let you inspect the interacting course rules without installing them in live Moss. The curriculum page places this route alongside all 28 numbered lessons and the bridge to the existing movement guide. The refuge capstone extends that saved project through your own data, system, and experiment design. Its native tests and reports show whether protection works and how different placements affect the meadow. The existing browser modes continue to show their earlier scenarios without refuge configuration; rebuilding them from your new source doesn't add a refuge display. Keeping that boundary visible helps you choose the right evidence for a claim about your extension. Native tests, schedule integration, and browser observations answer related but distinct questions. The edition records them separately so a passing calculation isn't mistaken for proof of the displayed result, and an appealing animation isn't mistaken for evidence that the intended Rust ran. Learn from good sources, keep one coherent lesson The original Moss book supplies the world, its questions, and its ownership boundaries; Fieldnotes develops a new reading and practice format around them. Official Rust and Bevy documentation supports language and API claims, with links beside the relevant explanations. The design source registry records versions, retrieval dates, permitted use, and why each source belongs in the course. External talks and articles are most useful when you have a question to carry into them. The reading and viewing shelf pairs optional publisher-hosted talks and ecology context with original text routes back to a Moss experiment. Publisher-hosted media can be embedded when available, while the needed explanation stays in the lesson. Full copyrighted chapters and transcripts aren't copied into the course. Keep a place to return to Reading tools are useful when they help you follow an explanation and remember why a result mattered. Keep one question in a field note, export the record when you need to move it, and use the source label to identify the world behind an observation. The learning path will help you choose the next investigation; the workbench guide is there when you are ready to bring it to the compiler.

title: Good company for the next question
summary: Course guide
text: Bring another explanation to the question you're working on. Find a second explanation with a purpose Use this shelf when you can name the question another explanation might help answer. The companions below cover borrowed views, iterators, timing, energy and inheritance; each includes a reason to visit and a route back to a Moss example. Choose one, carry a concrete uncertainty into it, and return with a prediction or code decision you can check. There is no required viewing sequence. How long may an observation borrow its source? Jon Gjengset’s Crust of Rust: Lifetime Annotations develops a string-splitting example through the compiler's requirements. It is useful beside the lifetime supplement because you can follow how an interface acquires its constraints. If your immediate uncertainty is the difference between str and String , the shorter chapter on that comparison is another entry point. Watch on Jon Gjengset’s channel, starting at 17:10 Recorded April 22, 2020. The creator’s chapter markers place the missing-lifetime error at 17:10, the two-lifetime example at 57:49, and the string comparison at 1:03:19. As you watch, identify which input owns the text and which output borrows it. Then ask whether two borrowed inputs really need to remain valid for the same duration. Following those owners gives the annotations something concrete to describe, and makes a compiler error a clue about the relationship the interface is asking its caller to satisfy. Text route: a lifetime relates access to an owner A borrowed observation cannot outlive the data it refers to. An annotation describes a relationship among references; it doesn't keep a dropped value alive. If a report must remain useful after the world changes or disappears, it needs to own the information it will retain. A view used only during one inspection can instead express that shorter borrowed relationship. Consider capture in the ownership lesson . Its returned name is a String , so saving the observation doesn't retain a reference to the caller's nickname. Replacing that field with &str would change the report's contract with its source. Work out which use you want before trying to satisfy the compiler with an annotation such as 'static . What does an iterator actually yield? In Crust of Rust: Iterators , Jon Gjengset examines iterator contracts by implementing flattening. The opening fits beside collections and trait bounds, while the later implementation offers a deeper exercise once ordinary map , filter , and collect feel familiar. Watch the item type change at each boundary: saying that code “iterates over creatures” leaves open whether it receives values, references, or already-owned report rows. Watch on Jon Gjengset’s channel, starting at 1:45 Recorded May 27, 2020. The creator’s chapter markers introduce Iterator at 1:45, IntoIterator at 4:25, and associated types at 6:24. Text route: follow the item type through the pipeline An iterator supplies items through its Item associated type. A borrowed slice iterator yields references, but mapping a reserve reference to its numeric value can produce a copied number. Collecting those numbers into a vector then gives the report its own values without keeping the component borrows alive. The query lesson's audit follows that progression: a query yields borrowed components, a mapping constructs report rows, and the resulting vector can be sorted after collection. Name the sort key: that audit uses the display name. This orders its presentation; it does not establish stable identity or decide who should win a contested resource. Why can pictures and world updates use different rhythms? Glenn Fiedler’s Fix Your Timestep! develops fixed-step simulation and considers what happens when catch-up work exceeds the available time. Read it once a Moss tick already has a clear meaning, then use the physics example to think about the host's responsibility for requesting steps. Moss's discrete, integer biology has different rules from physics integration, but both need a relationship between elapsed time and executed work. Bring that relationship back to the redraw experiment. The host may decide when to request work, while each executed tick still has its defined consequences. Drawing another frame or changing the camera mustn't introduce extra biology. Moss's choice to avoid hidden-tab catch-up is an additional host policy; the article helps you reason about such a choice without choosing it for you. Keep a precise reference nearby Use the Rust Book to repair a specific conceptual gap, or Rustlings when you'd like more focused practice with compiler feedback. Both can support the question you're already working on; neither is a prerequisite track you need to finish before editing Moss. For a particular ECS method or access rule, start with Bevy ECS 0.18.1’s API reference . The official Bevy learning hub adds examples and migration guides. Check the version of an example before applying it, since current material may target a newer release than the pinned course programs. What does the energy ledger leave out? OpenStax’s Biology 2e: Energy Flow through Ecosystems , by Mary Ann Clark, Matthew Douglas, and Jung Choi, offers wider context after the growth lesson. Read with your Moss accounting table beside it and identify what each entry represents: input from outside the world, transfer between stores, or expenditure. Then consider which real mechanisms the simple table doesn't represent. Moss's integer reserve and biomass units are authored abstractions. A lossless meal and fixed growth increment make an invariant easy to inspect, but that convenience doesn't calibrate an organism. Before proposing another rule, write down one omitted mechanism and the measurement you would need to describe it. This gives a potential extension a question to answer beyond making the diagram look more lifelike. What would make an inheritance experiment evidence of selection? The same authors’ Population Evolution provides context for interpreting changing trait frequencies. After the inheritance example, carry this question into the reading: what evidence would distinguish a value being copied or mutated at birth from a trait becoming more common through differential survival or reproduction? A child differing from its parents establishes what the configured inheritance procedure did. Explaining a population change also requires identities, denominators, conditions, and observation coverage across the runs you compare. Use those records to challenge an appealing trajectory rather than treating the trajectory as its own explanation. The course's toy traits offer a way to inspect those distinctions without supplying a genetic model of a species. A shelf beyond the current need The Rustonomicon becomes useful when you need to reason about an actual unsafe boundary, including FFI. Ordinary Moss systems don't require that detour. The browser hosts use a small scalar export boundary, while lesson exercises keep domain logic in safe Rust; if you inspect an unsafe operation, begin with the invariant its caller must uphold before treating its syntax as something to reuse. Bring the explanation back to your world A companion has done its job when it changes what you can explain or test in Moss. Write down that connection before moving to another resource: perhaps a shorter borrow, a clearer iterator item type, or a better control for an ecological comparison. Then return to the lesson you came from, or choose a changed fixture in the mixed practice route and see whether the idea still helps. The video titles, dates, and chapter markers were checked against the creator’s published descriptions on September 23, 2026; the clips have not been reviewed minute by minute. The text routes are original explanations rather than copied transcripts. YouTube players load only when you choose to load them, and the original links remain available.

title: The Rust world, in the page
summary: Course guide
text: Step the Rust world, then inspect what changed. Here you can run the existing moss-sim crate through a small WebAssembly host. Fern, Flint, Meadow, their stores, and the tick counter belong to one Bevy ECS world. JavaScript requests a step or reset and draws the returned readings; the maintenance calculation still runs in Rust. Start by comparing a change to that world with a change to its presentation. Connect a click to a Rust tick We’ll use three steps and a redraw to trace the boundary between the simulation and its display. The expected result is deliberately small: Fern’s reserve falls from 60 to 57, while changing the picture leaves it at 57. Following that result from the controls to the schedule will help you decide which claims need a helper test, an integration test, or an actual browser observation. One world, two ways to inspect it Predict Fern's reserve after three Steps. Then resize the labels and redraw the view. Read the table to decide whether either presentation change spent any energy. Fern Flint Meadow Step Rust world Execute 10 Rust ticks Redraw only Reset Rust world Label size: 100% Loading the optional Rust runtime… Readings from the same Rust world Individual Cell (x, y) Reserve units Biomass units Fern · Hare · ID 1 Awaiting runtime Awaiting runtime Awaiting runtime Flint · Fox · ID 2 Awaiting runtime Awaiting runtime Awaiting runtime Meadow · Grass · ID 3 Awaiting runtime Awaiting runtime Awaiting runtime Precompiled Rust runtime, built locally from the repository. This page is an independent run; it does not control the other Moss browser tab or compile your edits in the browser. Reloading starts a fresh instance. Time advances only when you request ticks. Follow three ticks through the boundary In a fresh run, Fern and Flint each have 60 reserve units. The installed maintenance rule spends one per animal on every executed tick, so three single Steps should produce tick 3 with both reserves at 57. Meadow keeps biomass 80, and Fern stays at cell (10, 10). The current live checkpoint has not scheduled the unfinished movement exercise, so losing reserve doesn't yet make Fern approach the grass. Now use Redraw only several times and change the label size. Redrawing reads the components and rebuilds the display without calling Rust's tick function; label size changes the styling. The next reading should still show tick 3 and reserve 57. Watching those values stay fixed checks this host's request boundary, which is the distinction you predicted before clicking. It doesn't by itself check every camera and timing path in the main application. The table gives absence a visible meaning too. Meadow has biomass but no reserve component, so its reserve cell says “Not present.” A depleted animal instead has a reserve whose value is zero. The named shapes and the table let you identify individuals without relying on color, and the table retains the meaningful readings if the diagram isn't useful to you. Why do both animals remain at zero? The installed maintenance system uses saturating subtraction without implementing death, eating, or movement. From a fresh run, seven batches of ten ticks reach tick 70 with both animals still present at zero and Meadow still at 80. That result describes the current lifecycle boundary. The ecology lessons and continuing course meadow explore explicit terminal rules separately from this live schedule. Build the same runtime locally The static lessons remain readable without a Rust build. To include this executable view, follow the pinned toolchain and dependency setup in the local workbench , then run the commands below from the repository root. The WebAssembly target needs installing only if it is missing: rustup target add wasm32-unknown-unknown --toolchain 1.93.1 python3 learning/scripts/runtime.py check python3 learning/scripts/runtime.py build python3 learning/scripts/build.py python3 learning/scripts/serve.py If the course server is already running, keep it and reload after the build. The runtime has its own Cargo lockfile and output under learning/work , but depends directly on crates/moss-sim . Its native checks therefore exercise the installed schedule you'll observe here, without adding another rule to that schedule. How the page identifies a current build The builder fingerprints the simulation, host sources, and relevant manifests. If those inputs change, rebuilding the pages omits the stale binary and asks for another runtime build. An older binary therefore isn't presented as the result of your new sources. After an intentional simulation change, review the expected trace in this page too: the build can establish source freshness without establishing that the explanation still describes the new behavior. Give each check a question it can answer The three-step trace connects a small arithmetic rule with an installed system and a visible control. Each layer gives you evidence for a different part of that connection: Evidence for the maintenance example Check Question it answers What to inspect Lesson 01's small Rust reference Does the isolated subtraction obey its stated boundary cases? The exact reference tests and printed trace. The runtime host's native tests Does the installed Moss schedule change real components and complete ticks? Both animals, the unchanged patch and position, reset identity, and repeated reads. This browser view Can this WebAssembly build accept a click and present the resulting readings? Three Steps, redraw, label size, depletion and reset. Keep the tick separate from the picture A passing helper test explains its subtraction cases, but can't establish which schedule ran in the browser. An animation alone doesn't identify the source of its numbers. Following the dependency to the actual simulation and checking the native schedule alongside this view makes the result easier to explain when one layer differs from your expectation. Return to A tick is a promise to connect the observation with its smaller Rust example. In the scheduling lesson , the next complication is timing within the tick: a correct final value can coexist with an earlier observation that saw the wrong state.

title: One meadow, several consequences
summary: Course guide
text: At tick twelve, the limited meadow holds eight units of grass and no living grazers. In the more generous meadow, one grazer survives beside five units of grass. The first picture might look like a feeding bug: how could the animals starve when food was available? Build a meadow you can investigate one tick at a time You'll reconstruct two complete ECS systems in a saved Cargo project, then follow how their results reach feeding and starvation. A deliberate borrowing error will clarify the access each system needs, and a changed schedule will expose why order matters. From there, you'll write your own supply-timing investigation and inspect the compiled world in the browser. The goal is to explain those two endings through individual reserves, actual flows and retained events, with systems and tests you can keep extending. Your first continuing course project. You'll reconstruct and investigate a small, complete meadow in a saved Cargo project, then extend that same project in later guides. Its authored rules are separate from live Moss and the movement assignment in NOW.md . For now, each grazer has a fixed feeding contact; movement and the other ecological rules will come later. Keep one project through the investigation Earlier labs let you examine a meal or an ordering edge in isolation. Here those pieces have to cooperate: upkeep can leave a grazer empty, daylight can replenish its patch, and a meal can rescue it before starvation is resolved. Bring your reasoning from borrowing in systems and explicit ordering ; the arithmetic comes from the finite meal and daylight lessons. We can now ask whether those individually reasonable rules produce the tick we intended. From the Moss repository root, create a practice project and check its starting state: python3 learning/scripts/fieldwork.py prepare --dest work/fieldwork python3 learning/scripts/fieldwork.py check --project work/fieldwork Open work/fieldwork/Cargo.toml in your editor. This directory will hold your systems, questions, and tests throughout the cumulative route. It begins as a complete working implementation so you can observe the whole meadow before reconstructing parts of it. The initial check should pass nineteen required acceptance tests; that gives your next edit a useful comparison point. Setup and what the project check preserves Use the local setup with Rust 1.93.1 and cached Bevy ECS 0.18.1 dependencies. Preparation copies the library, lockfile, examples, and tests, and refuses an existing destination. When you return, reopen this directory rather than preparing it again. The checker runs the required course assertions separately in a temporary copy and also runs your saved tests; it does not replace those tests. A missing compiler or dependency cache needs a setup repair before compilation can tell you anything about the code. Run the comparison once before changing a system. It uses the same saved modules that you'll edit, and later compile for the browser: cargo +1.93.1 run --offline --locked --manifest-path work/fieldwork/Cargo.toml --example compare You don't need to explain every output yet. Keep the two endings in mind while we find the state, trace one tick, and then change the implementation deliberately. By the time we return to the browser, you'll have evidence for why those endings occur. Find the state and its owners Before reconstructing a system, locate the state it owns and the path that makes it run. Start at src/lib.rs , where the public interface exposes CourseWorld , Scenario , and owned reports. Follow CourseWorld::new into src/simulation.rs and find the installed schedule. That connection matters: a helper can calculate the right amount without ever being called during a tick. The schedule is where the world actually acquires the behavior described by those helpers. Files in your continuing practice project File Question it owns src/model.rs Which authored inputs are valid, and what data belongs to each entity? src/lifecycle.rs Who pays upkeep, and when does zero become terminal? src/supply.rs How much external input fits this lit tick? src/feeding.rs Who has contact, and what remains after earlier claims? src/history.rs Which outcomes remain knowable after event eviction? src/simulation.rs What runs when, and how do reset and observation work? As you follow the modules, distinguish the stored state from a reading of it. The world owns each grazer's reserve and each patch's biomass; snapshot(&self) copies those values into readings sorted by stable ID. Changing a reading therefore changes only your copy. The internal roster helps find entities by their handles, but it doesn't maintain another set of reserves. This gives tests and the browser a common way to observe the simulation while leaving changes to the systems that own those responsibilities. Follow one ordered tick Both comparison scenarios start IDs 1 and 2 with three reserve units each. ID 1 needs two upkeep units per tick, while ID 2 needs one; both may take a meal of up to two units from patch 100. The patch starts empty and can hold eight. Before tracing the entire run, consider the first tick: upkeep will leave the animals with one and two units, so their next opportunity depends on whether growth occurs before they try to eat. The diagram follows that opportunity through six phases. First advance the tick and clear its ledger. Then charge upkeep, accept growth on a lit tick, and resolve competing meals. Only after those meals do we mark any remaining zero-reserve grazers dead and seal the history interval. Reading a snapshot doesn't advance through these phases; it shows the result of the last completed step. Six phases of one course-world tick Advance the tick, pay upkeep, grow lit patches, resolve meals, resolve starvation, then complete history. Meals occur before starvation, so a zero-reserve grazer still has a chance to eat. 1 · Advance tick Clear the latest flow ledger 2 · Pay upkeep Living reserves may reach zero 3 · Grow patches Lit input, bounded by capacity 4 · Resolve meals Stable IDs; immediate depletion 5 · Resolve starvation Still at zero becomes dead 6 · Complete history The tick is available to inspect The schedule supplies meaning to zero: upkeep can reach it before a meal rescues the grazer. Terminal resolution waits until after that opportunity. The four-tick day lights ticks one and two, then darkens ticks three and four. Limited supply requests two new units on each lit tick; generous supply requests six. Growth accepts only what fits in the patch. When the grazers eat, lower IDs claim first and each transfer immediately reduces the biomass available to the next grazer. This makes the result reproducible, although it gives no guarantee of fairness to the animal that goes second. We can account for this tick because each operation has a different effect on stores. Upkeep removes units, growth adds units, and meals move units from one store to another. Consequently, ending stores plus actual upkeep paid must equal starting stores plus actual growth accepted. The word actual matters: an animal with one unit cannot pay a requested cost of three, and this model carries no unpaid debt. The ledger must describe what happened, because copying the requests would make that equality fail even when the state changes were correct. Reconstruct a whole typed system Upkeep is a useful first system to reconstruct because its arithmetic is small enough to hold in mind while choosing the ECS access. Read maintain in your copy of src/lifecycle.rs , then set its implementation aside and replace the complete function. Keep the imports and starve . Your function needs to choose its parameters, visit the intended entities, change their reserves, and leave an accurate ledger and event record. Begin with what that responsibility requires. The system reads the clock and each stable identity, mutates each grazer, and writes the shared ledger and journal. It doesn't need a patch: the opportunity to eat belongs to a later phase. Writing a query that requests a Grazer expresses that membership directly, rather than making the function search arbitrary entities for something it can charge. There is one less obvious requirement. Although upkeep payments don't compete with each other, their events enter the journal in traversal order. If reversing spawn order changes that sequence, it can also change which events a bounded history retains. Collecting and sorting owned IDs gives the system a declared order before it starts to mutate components. The acceptance suite checks that order as part of the complete snapshot. If you're listening, pause here to reconstruct the function. Generated narration skips code and answer disclosures, so open them when you need the next hint. Resume after you've run the check and compared its result with your prediction. Hint 1: write the access declaration first Use Res<Clock> , a mutable query fetching (Entity, &Identity, &mut Grazer) , and mutable ledger/history resources. Entity gives you a lookup handle, while Identity supplies the application ID whose order must remain stable. Hint 2: separate ordering from mutation Collect owned pairs of stable ID and entity handle, sort them, then fetch each mutable grazer. Skip dead rows and charge the smaller of available reserve and configured cost. Use that same actual amount for the reserve change and ledger, recording an event only when the payment is positive. Complete replacement: maintain in src/lifecycle.rs pub(crate) fn maintain( clock: Res<Clock>, mut grazers: Query<(Entity, &Identity, &mut Grazer)>, mut ledger: ResMut<TickLedger>, mut history: ResMut<History>, ) { let mut order: Vec<_> = grazers .iter() .map(|(entity, id, _)| (id.0, entity)) .collect(); order.sort_by_key(|(id, _)| *id); for (id, entity) in order { let (_, _, mut grazer) = grazers.get_mut(entity).expect("listed grazer still exists"); if grazer.life != Life::Alive { continue; } let paid = grazer.reserve_units.min(grazer.maintenance_units_per_tick); grazer.reserve_units -= paid; ledger.maintenance_units = ledger .maintenance_units .checked_add(u64::from(paid)) .expect("maintenance ledger exhausted"); if paid > 0 { history.record( &clock, EventKind::Maintenance { grazer: id, units: paid, }, ); } } } Run the project check and pay attention to its rescue case. That animal starts with one unit, requests upkeep of three, and later receives a meal of two. It must finish alive at two. The case checks two decisions at once: the upkeep ledger must record only one paid unit, and reaching zero during upkeep must leave the later meal available. A system that kills the animal immediately would take that opportunity away. Let a compiler error reveal a held borrow The working function separates collecting IDs from mutating grazers. To see why that separation matters in Rust, temporarily replace the entire maintain function with the version below. It tries to keep query items for the later loop instead of copying just the IDs and handles. Predict which access those retained items keep alive, then run the direct Cargo check so the diagnostic points into your own saved file. pub(crate) fn maintain(mut grazers: Query<(Entity, &Identity, &mut Grazer)>) { let borrowed: Vec<_> = grazers.iter().collect(); for (entity, _identity, _old) in borrowed { let (_, _, mut grazer) = grazers.get_mut(entity).unwrap(); grazer.reserve_units = grazer.reserve_units.saturating_sub(1); } } cargo +1.93.1 check --offline --locked --manifest-path work/fieldwork/Cargo.toml The expected error says that grazers cannot be borrowed mutably while an immutable borrow is still in use. Owning the vector doesn't make its contents independent of the world: the collected items still contain references into the query. The second loop uses those references while asking get_mut for exclusive access to the same component data, so the compiler cannot grant both accesses. Restore the complete function above and compare what crosses the boundary between its two loops. IDs and entity handles are owned lookup values; keeping them doesn't retain a component borrow. Each later lookup can therefore borrow a grazer briefly, perform its work, and release that access before the next iteration. The repair follows from deciding what the second phase actually needs to remember. Bevy's 0.18.1 Query documentation describes these fetched component references and entity handles. Connect a second system and challenge the schedule Now reconstruct grow in src/supply.rs , again keeping the module imports but replacing the whole function. The structure should feel familiar, while the access and accounting change: this query mutates patches, the daylight resource determines whether work happens, and the ledger records input from outside the world. Calculate remaining capacity before adding anything, so even a large growth request cannot overflow the biomass value on its way to being capped. Growth hint Return unless the current executed tick is lit. Sort owned patch IDs and handles, then accept the smaller of the growth request and remaining capacity. Increase biomass and the ledger by that accepted amount, preserving the same distinction between a configured request and an actual flow that you used for upkeep. Complete replacement: grow in src/supply.rs pub(crate) fn grow( clock: Res<Clock>, daylight: Res<Daylight>, mut patches: Query<(Entity, &Identity, &mut Patch)>, mut ledger: ResMut<TickLedger>, mut history: ResMut<History>, ) { if daylight.is_lit(clock.tick) != Some(true) { return; } let mut order: Vec<_> = patches .iter() .map(|(entity, id, _)| (id.0, entity)) .collect(); order.sort_by_key(|(id, _)| *id); for (id, entity) in order { let (_, _, mut patch) = patches.get_mut(entity).expect("listed patch still exists"); let added = patch .growth_units_per_lit_tick .min(patch.capacity_units - patch.biomass_units); patch.biomass_units += added; ledger.added_units = ledger .added_units .checked_add(u64::from(added)) .expect("growth ledger exhausted"); if added > 0 { history.record( &clock, EventKind::Growth { patch: id, units: added, }, ); } } } Once both systems pass, we can challenge a different claim: whether their results are used in the right order. In tick_schedule inside src/simulation.rs , temporarily move lifecycle::starve before feeding::feed , leaving the rest in place. The functions still compile, but the rescue acceptance test should now report a dead animal at zero where an alive animal at two was required. Correct subtraction and transfer helpers can't protect an opportunity that the schedule has already removed. Repair the tuple to the following sequence and retain its .chain() call: ( begin_tick, lifecycle::maintain, supply::grow, feeding::feed, lifecycle::starve, complete_tick, ).chain() Rerun the project check. The single-threaded executor ensures that systems execute serially; the chain declares which order the simulation requires. Those are separate choices, and the rescue case gives this particular ordering edge an observable purpose. Write a test for a question the suite leaves open So far, the comparison has changed how much food the meadow can receive. Your own investigation will change when it can receive food. Keep the generous scenario's population, capacities, and contacts, but compare six requested units on two lit ticks with three on all four. Both request twelve units per cycle before capacity limits. Would that be enough to preserve the same animals, or can the dark interval still matter? Write your prediction before creating work/fieldwork/tests/investigation.rs . Have the test construct both scenarios, advance twelve complete ticks, accumulate actual accepted growth, and compare survivors and individual reserves. Use the public API, which makes the test ask the same kinds of questions that a browser host can ask without accessing private components. The Rust Book's test organization chapter explains how integration tests exercise that public surface. Investigation hint Start the second case from a generous scenario, change its daylight to Daylight::new(4, 4) , and reduce its patch growth request to three. Sum each snapshot's ledger.added_units , because equal requests do not guarantee equal accepted growth when the patch can fill. Complete investigation.rs and the prediction it tests use moss_course_ecosystem::{CourseWorld, Daylight, Life, Scenario}; #[test] fn equal_potential_supply_can_have_different_timing_and_survivors() { let mut steady_setup = Scenario::generous_supply(); steady_setup.daylight = Daylight::new(4, 4).unwrap(); steady_setup.patches[0].growth_units_per_lit_tick = 3; let mut pulsed = CourseWorld::new(Scenario::generous_supply()).unwrap(); let mut steady = CourseWorld::new(steady_setup).unwrap(); let (mut pulsed_added, mut steady_added) = (0_u64, 0_u64); for _ in 0..12 { pulsed.step(); steady.step(); pulsed_added += pulsed.snapshot().ledger.added_units; steady_added += steady.snapshot().ledger.added_units; } let pulsed = pulsed.snapshot(); let steady = steady.snapshot(); assert_eq!(pulsed.grazers.iter().filter(|g| g.life == Life::Alive).count(), 1); assert_eq!(steady.grazers.iter().filter(|g| g.life == Life::Alive).count(), 2); assert_eq!((pulsed_added, steady_added), (34, 36)); assert_eq!(steady.grazers.iter().map(|g| g.reserve_units).collect::<Vec<_>>(), vec![3, 3]); assert_eq!(steady.patches[0].biomass_units, 0); } With steady input, every tick restores ID 1 from one to three and ID 2 from two to three. With pulsed input, the food runs out before the second dark tick, and the higher-cost animal dies on tick eight. Its absence then changes later consumption: at tick ten, only four of the six requested growth units fit in the patch, bringing total accepted input to thirty-four. Timing was the configuration we changed; unequal accepted supply is a consequence of how that timing interacts with capacity and consumption. The two runs therefore do not have equal actual intake. Run the project check and find your test's name in its output. Then temporarily assert that both grazers survive the pulsed run, observe the failure, and restore the expectation you can explain. This deliberate wrong prediction checks that Cargo discovers your file and that the assertion can distinguish the outcomes. Keep the test beside your systems when you return to the project. If you're following the audio, pause to read the complete investigation answer before continuing. Its explanation of tick ten is essential to interpreting the result: requesting the same supply and receiving the same supply are different experimental conditions, even when you choose other assertions for your own test. Observe your compiled world Once the reconstructed systems and your investigation pass, compile the saved project for the browser. Run these commands from the repository root, then reload this page: python3 learning/scripts/fieldwork_preview.py --project work/fieldwork python3 learning/scripts/build.py Opening the page and identifying the build Serve the course with python3 learning/scripts/serve.py if it isn't already open. The preview's source label distinguishes the course reference from your compiled project. Check it before interpreting a result, and check and rebuild again after changing sources: an earlier successful binary describes the earlier code. Choose limited supply, reset, and advance twelve ticks; then repeat with generous supply. These points from the original reference's native trace give you intermediate states to compare, so a different ending can be traced back to the tick where your build first diverged: Reference expectations for fixed contacts and the original two scenarios Tick Limited: reserves 1 / 2; biomass Generous: reserves 1 / 2; biomass 1 3 / 2; 0 3 / 4; 2 4 0 / 0; 0 1 / 5; 0 8 0 / 0; 4 0 / 7; 0 12 0 / 0; 8 0 / 8; 5 Limited supply loses ID 2 on tick three and ID 1 on tick four. Generous supply keeps both alive longer, but loses ID 1 on tick eight. Check those transitions in your browser build as well as the final stores. The table establishes the native reference expectation; your browser observation checks that the compiled host exposes the same behavior. The custom steady-supply investigation remains a native test unless that scenario is also added to a host. The inspector can show every patch, but each grazer still eats only from its authored contact. History adds when those actions happened: retained events name a run, tick, and stable ID. When a journal has evicted older events, use its coverage bounds before interpreting an absent starvation record. A complete interval starts strictly after complete_after_tick and includes collected_through_tick ; outside it, absence may mean unknown. Reset starts a new run and clears its history, while an owned report you saved beforehand continues to describe the old run. Explain the meadow through the opportunities it gave each animal We can now explain the opening picture. Food left at tick twelve couldn't rescue grazers that had already died in the dark interval. That explanation needed individual reserves, the order of a tick, and the timing of growth together. Your reconstructed systems and saved investigation connect those observations to the code that produced them. Keep this project for funded births and the next generation , where a child will enter the same upkeep and feeding loop. After that, local decisions and paid journeys will make reaching food another part of the explanation. Each extension keeps the earlier accounting available to test.

title: Return with a different question
summary: Course guide
text: Suppose an observation is empty. You know several ways that could happen: the entity might lack a required component, its commands might still be pending, or the history might not cover the time you're asking about. Recognizing the result isn't enough to choose between those explanations. These six returns change the fixtures from earlier lessons and ask you to decide what evidence would settle the question. Optional mixed practice. Try cases one through three after the ECS core, then four through six after the first cumulative fieldwork . Each is available whenever you want it; there are no grades or unlocks. The examples use isolated course worlds and leave live Moss and NOW.md unchanged. If you're listening, pause at the prediction before opening its hint or full answer; generated narration skips those disclosures and their code. The first three cases build small reporting worlds, while four and five use your actual fieldwork library. Case six uses the existing target lab, so it doesn't introduce another implementation of the same selection rule. Choose the evidence before the fix The aim of these returns is to diagnose a changed situation with ideas you already know. Each case starts with an observation or prediction, offers a hint when you need one, and develops a complete explanation you can check. Work through one case at a time: identify what is uncertain, choose an observation that separates the possible causes, and then compare it with the answer. Five of the worked checks can join your continuing project, so the reasoning remains available when that world changes. 1. Which rows changed, and which reading stayed old? Start with a reporting world containing the three rows below. Each execution of its decrement system requests Query<(&Identity, &mut Reserve), With<Active>> and removes one unit from every matching row. Before running the schedule, an observer saves an owned vector of identity and reserve pairs. Its reporting query does not require Active , so the writer and observer may include different rows. Initial reporting fixture Row Identity Reserve Active marker A 11 7 Present B 12 7 Absent C Absent 7 Present Run the decrement schedule twice, asking for extra reports between the runs. Predict each current reserve, the vector saved before execution, and a fresh vector afterward. In your explanation, account for why a row can be unchanged yet still appear in the report, and why another row can be absent from the report altogether. Finally, decide what owning the vector gives the caller: ownership of the components, or ownership of the values copied from them? Hint: separate the two membership rules The writer needs identity, reserve, and the active marker. The observer needs identity and reserve. Work out those two memberships before doing the subtraction, and remember that neither query supplies a component the entity lacks. Full reasoning and expected result Only A matches the writer, so the current reserves are five, seven, and seven. B still appears in the report because the observer doesn't require the marker; C appears in neither report because it lacks identity. The original vector stays [(11, 7), (12, 7)] , while the fresh vector is [(11, 5), (12, 7)] . The saved vector owns copied numbers, so subsequent component changes cannot update it, and reading extra reports does not execute the decrement schedule. If membership was uncertain, return to predicting query membership . If you expected the saved values to change, revisit a saved reading's ownership and the owned report . The final numbers are evidence for both ideas, but each difficulty needs a different explanation. 2. The observer saw 91. What would you inspect next? In this fixture, a selected sample contains two units out of seven, while an unselected sample contains four out of five. A projection system floors the selected percentage and writes it into a display resource. The display starts at 91, and another system copies its value into a trace. After one schedule run, that trace contains 91—the old value you hoped the projection would replace. Two installation mistakes could explain this result: the projection wasn't installed, or it ran after the observer. Choose one additional reading that would distinguish those explanations in this fixture. Predict both the final display and trace for each mistake, then for a repaired schedule. There's also a helper-only percentage test available; explain whether passing it would settle which system actually ran. Hint: look for a write that happened too late The earlier observation can be identical in both cases even if the final world differs. Ask whether either mistaken schedule still executes the projection after recording the trace. Full reasoning and expected result Read the final display. Without the projection installed, it remains 91 and the trace is [91] . With the order reversed, the projection eventually writes 28, but the earlier trace remains [91] . Correct order produces display 28 and trace [28] . The unselected sample would produce 80, giving the fixture another distinguishable outcome if the wrong membership were used. This reasoning assumes the supplied projection works when called; it doesn't imply that all stale displays have only two causes. The worked test executes all three schedules so it can distinguish their behavior, while a percentage helper test alone cannot establish installation or order. Return to required ordering edges or writing discriminating evidence according to which part of that diagnosis you want to revisit. 3. A handle, a visible component, and a retained observation Now the thing waiting to become visible is an entity rather than a calculated percentage. An empty world queues RowId(41) and immediately saves its entity handle. Observer A runs next, followed by an explicit ApplyDeferred , then observer B. Both observers save copied IDs. For this experiment, automatic intermediate application is disabled, while final application at the end of the schedule remains enabled. Predict A's vector, B's vector, and whether the saved handle resolves to RowId when the schedule returns. Then remove only the explicit intermediate application point and predict all three again. If the final world contains the row in both runs, decide whether that final state could tell you what A saw earlier. Keep the application settings beside your prediction; changing them would change the experiment. Hint: keep the experimental settings with the prediction With automatic insertion disabled, declaring an order does not supply an intermediate application point. In the altered schedule, final application still happens, but only after both observers have finished. Full reasoning and expected result With the intermediate point present, A saves [] , B saves [41] , and the handle resolves to 41 after the schedule. Without that point, both saved vectors are empty, although the final handle still resolves to 41. Applying the command later changes what a future query can fetch; it doesn't rewrite observations the earlier systems already copied. The reserved handle was therefore not proof of component visibility. These results depend on the stated experimental settings, rather than a general claim that chains never flush commands. Revisit explicit application points and identity versus an entity handle if the difference between reservation and observation was hard to place. 4. Can the accounting balance while the animal dies too early? Return to the actual fieldwork library with a smaller fixture. One grazer begins with two reserve units and capacity six. It requests five upkeep units, then a meal of three from its authored contact. The patch begins with one biomass unit, has capacity four, and requests growth of four on tick one, which is lit. The installed order is upkeep, growth, meals, then starvation—the same rescue opportunity you established in fieldwork. Predict the actual upkeep payment, accepted growth, meal transfer, ending stores, and life state. Then move starvation before meals in your imagined trace and work out the ending again. Would the total-store conservation equation necessarily expose that ordering mistake? Pause to write both outcomes, including the individual stores, before using the hint. Hint: a requested amount is not automatically an actual flow The reserve floor limits the payment, and the patch's remaining capacity limits growth. A meal transfers units between stores. Starvation changes which actions are still available; it doesn't create or remove patch biomass. Full reasoning and expected result Upkeep pays two and leaves the grazer at zero. Growth accepts three, filling the patch to four, then the meal transfers three. The grazer finishes alive at three and the patch holds one. The ledger records added three, upkeep two, eaten three, and no starvation. Ending stores of four plus payment of two equal starting stores of three plus accepted growth of three. A starvation-first schedule can instead leave a dead grazer at zero beside four units in the patch. The same conservation equation still balances because total stores are still four. Individual reserve and life assertions are what establish that the intended rescue opportunity occurred. The worked test calls CourseWorld::step , exercising your installed systems rather than recreating their arithmetic. Revisit accepted growth , actual transfer , or the connected tick to recover the part of the trace you need. 5. Zero deaths over which interval? An owned course report has an empty event vector, but also says its complete coverage starts strictly after tick four and extends through tick seven. Its current grazer is dead at zero reserve. Predict what starvations_between returns for four through seven, five through seven, and seven through eight. The intervals differ by only a boundary, so identify what each includes before interpreting the empty vector. The executable fixture reaches this state with no patches, four initial reserve units, upkeep of one per tick, and history capacity zero. It executes seven ticks. Trace when the animal dies and what happens to records produced then. How can a journal that retains no events still establish zero new deaths for a later interval? Hint: retained contents and collected coverage answer different questions Events were lost through tick four. Ticks five, six, and seven were executed without another terminal transition, while tick eight has not yet been collected. The report can use those facts even when it can't supply the earlier event records. Full reasoning and expected result The answers are None , Some(0) , and None . Four upkeep records and one starvation were evicted, making five lost events. The last loss happened in tick four; later empty ticks advanced the collected boundary without producing another death. Thus coverage excludes the death tick but includes the completed interval from five through seven. Dead state describes a present condition, not the missing interval's event count. The test's known starting state lets us explain how this particular history arose, but an empty report alone cannot recover it. Return to unknown versus zero and coverage boundaries if those answers were difficult to distinguish. Replacing an absent answer with zero would hide exactly the uncertainty this report preserves. 6. The chosen patch is already empty For this case, return to the isolated target lab ; the shared-meadow checkpoint itself uses fixed contacts. At observation time, an actor at zero, zero sees ID 17 at one, zero and ID 12 at zero, one. Both patches have two biomass units and lie within radius two. The selection policy compares Manhattan distance first, then stable ID when distances tie. Predict which patch it chooses. Before acting, the actor reaches that patch, but another completed meal empties it. The saved reading still says two units, and ID 17 remains visible with food. Decide what this action's resolver may do, then change the fixture again: what if the chosen patch has disappeared entirely? In each case, distinguish evidence that the earlier choice was reasonable from permission to take a meal now. Hint: distinguish choosing again from validating this action The tie rule chooses one identity. The resolver revalidates that identity against current state; a failure does not silently invoke another selection policy or establish contact with a different patch. Full reasoning and expected result ID 12 wins the equal-distance tie. Its currently empty state rejects the bite without reserve gain, even though the saved observation remains two. Removing ID 12 instead produces a missing-target rejection. Neither outcome authorizes a fallback meal at ID 17, and food remaining at the selected patch would still require current contact before transfer. Those answers follow the target lab's declared rules; the lab does not by itself prove that movement or another consumer actually ran. Its existing tests supply the executable evidence for selection and revalidation, so the file below doesn't duplicate the selector. Return to the tie rule , action-time revalidation , and rejection without partial mutation to connect a failed choice with the state it must leave unchanged. Keep five checks beside your investigation When you're ready to execute the worked cases, save the complete file below as work/fieldwork/tests/returns.rs in the persistent project prepared by fieldwork . Leave investigation.rs in place, and merge deliberately if you already have a returns.rs . These questions belong beside your own work so they can keep testing the same library as you extend it. Where the worked file runs You can download the complete worked test file , also kept in the repository at learning/practice/returns.rs . It depends on the project's Bevy ECS 0.18.1 and course library, so it runs as an integration test there rather than as a standalone rustc file. Run these commands from the Moss repository root: cargo +1.93.1 test --offline --locked --manifest-path work/fieldwork/Cargo.toml --test returns python3 learning/scripts/fieldwork.py check --project work/fieldwork The first should report five passing named tests. The second also runs the course acceptance suite and your other saved targets. Read a failure according to what it establishes: a missing compiler or dependency cache needs a setup repair, while an assertion failure gives you an observed result to investigate. Passing these native checks doesn't yet describe what a browser displays or how well you can explain the cause. Inside the file, membership , projection , and deferred build separate small ECS worlds; the other two tests call the public course API. The reporting helper needs mutable world access to prepare its query, but that access doesn't execute the decrement schedule. Before opening the full file, choose one assertion and name a plausible defect it would catch. That connects the code you're about to read with the evidence you wanted from the case. Leave with a question you can test again The same final number can come from different queries, schedules, or histories. These cases give you a way to separate those explanations: inspect membership, the moment of observation, and the interval your evidence covers before choosing a correction. If you're listening, pause to inspect the file and run its checks. Then leave yourself a specific return point, such as “Revisit command visibility because I inferred an earlier observation from the final world.” You can use that question on your next visit without repeating every case, and change the fixture again when the original answer has become too familiar. When you return to your continuing meadow , keep one of these checks beside your own investigation. The next extension should preserve the earlier question as well as add a new behavior. Complete worked file: tests/returns.rs //! Worked checks for “Return with a different question.” //! Save this whole file as work/fieldwork/tests/returns.rs, preserving any //! investigation.rs already there. This is an integration test, not a rustc lab. //! From the Moss repository root: //! cargo +1.93.1 test --offline --locked --manifest-path work/fieldwork/Cargo.toml --test returns //! python3 learning/scripts/fieldwork.py check --project work/fieldwork //! //! Cases 1–3 use separate, nonbiological Bevy worlds. Cases 4–5 execute the //! actual persistent course library. Case 6 returns to the existing target lab. mod membership { use bevy_ecs::{prelude::*, schedule::ExecutorKind}; #[derive(Component)] struct Identity(u32); #[derive(Component)] struct Reserve(u32); #[derive(Component)] struct Active; fn decrement(mut rows: Query<(&Identity, &mut Reserve), With<Active>>) { for (_, mut reserve) in &mut rows { reserve.0 = reserve.0.checked_sub(1).expect("fixture has enough units"); } } fn report(world: &mut World) -> Vec<(u32, u32)> { let mut query = world.query::<(&Identity, &Reserve)>(); let mut rows: Vec<_> = query .iter(world) .map(|(id, reserve)| (id.0, reserve.0)) .collect(); rows.sort_by_key(|(id, _)| *id); rows } #[test] fn case_1_required_components_and_owned_readings_answer_different_questions() { let mut world = World::new(); let a = world.spawn((Identity(11), Reserve(7), Active)).id(); let b = world.spawn((Identity(12), Reserve(7))).id(); let unnamed = world.spawn((Reserve(7), Active)).id(); let saved = report(&mut world); let mut schedule = Schedule::default(); schedule.set_executor_kind(ExecutorKind::SingleThreaded); schedule.add_systems(decrement); for _ in 0..2 { let _ = report(&mut world); // Reading does not run the schedule. schedule.run(&mut world); let _ = report(&mut world); } assert_eq!(world.get::<Reserve>(a).unwrap().0, 5); assert_eq!(world.get::<Reserve>(b).unwrap().0, 7); assert_eq!(world.get::<Reserve>(unnamed).unwrap().0, 7); assert_eq!(saved, vec![(11, 7), (12, 7)]); assert_eq!(report(&mut world), vec![(11, 5), (12, 7)]); } } mod projection { use bevy_ecs::{prelude::*, schedule::ExecutorKind}; #[derive(Component)] struct Chosen; #[derive(Component)] struct Sample { used: u32, capacity: u32, } #[derive(Resource)] struct Display(Option<u32>); #[derive(Resource, Default)] struct Trace(Vec<Option<u32>>); fn project(rows: Query<&Sample, With<Chosen>>, mut display: ResMut<Display>) { display.0 = rows.single().ok().and_then(|sample| { (sample.capacity != 0).then(|| { (u64::from(sample.used.min(sample.capacity)) * 100 / u64::from(sample.capacity)) as u32 }) }); } fn observe(display: Res<Display>, mut trace: ResMut<Trace>) { trace.0.push(display.0); } enum Order { Missing, Reversed, Correct, } fn run(order: Order) -> (Option<u32>, Vec<Option<u32>>) { let mut world = World::new(); world.spawn(( Sample { used: 2, capacity: 7, }, Chosen, )); world.spawn(Sample { used: 4, capacity: 5, }); world.insert_resource(Display(Some(91))); world.init_resource::<Trace>(); let mut schedule = Schedule::default(); schedule.set_executor_kind(ExecutorKind::SingleThreaded); match order { Order::Missing => { schedule.add_systems(observe); } Order::Reversed => { schedule.add_systems((observe, project).chain()); } Order::Correct => { schedule.add_systems((project, observe).chain()); } } schedule.run(&mut world); ( world.resource::<Display>().0, world.resource::<Trace>().0.clone(), ) } #[test] fn case_2_final_display_separates_missing_installation_from_wrong_order() { assert_eq!(run(Order::Missing), (Some(91), vec![Some(91)])); assert_eq!(run(Order::Reversed), (Some(28), vec![Some(91)])); assert_eq!(run(Order::Correct), (Some(28), vec![Some(28)])); } } mod deferred { use bevy_ecs::{ prelude::*, schedule::{ExecutorKind, ScheduleBuildSettings}, }; #[derive(Component)] struct RowId(u32); #[derive(Resource, Default)] struct Reserved(Vec<Entity>); #[derive(Resource, Default)] struct Seen { before: Vec<u32>, after: Vec<u32>, } fn enqueue(mut commands: Commands, mut reserved: ResMut<Reserved>) { reserved.0.push(commands.spawn(RowId(41)).id()); } fn before(rows: Query<&RowId>, mut seen: ResMut<Seen>) { seen.before = rows.iter().map(|row| row.0).collect(); seen.before.sort(); } fn after(rows: Query<&RowId>, mut seen: ResMut<Seen>) { seen.after = rows.iter().map(|row| row.0).collect(); seen.after.sort(); } fn run(intermediate_application: bool) -> (Vec<u32>, Vec<u32>, u32) { let mut world = World::new(); world.init_resource::<Reserved>(); world.init_resource::<Seen>(); let mut schedule = Schedule::default(); schedule.set_executor_kind(ExecutorKind::SingleThreaded); schedule.set_build_settings(ScheduleBuildSettings { auto_insert_apply_deferred: false, ..Default::default() }); schedule.set_apply_final_deferred(true); if intermediate_application { schedule.add_systems((enqueue, before, ApplyDeferred, after).chain()); } else { schedule.add_systems((enqueue, before, after).chain()); } schedule.run(&mut world); let saved = world.resource::<Seen>(); let handle = world.resource::<Reserved>().0[0]; ( saved.before.clone(), saved.after.clone(), world.get::<RowId>(handle).unwrap().0, ) } #[test] fn case_3_final_existence_does_not_rewrite_an_earlier_observation() { assert_eq!(run(true), (vec![], vec![41], 41)); assert_eq!(run(false), (vec![], vec![], 41)); } } use moss_course_ecosystem::{ CourseWorld, Daylight, GrazerSeed, Life, PatchSeed, Scenario, SimId, TickLedger, }; #[test] fn case_4_actual_course_tick_caps_growth_and_rescues_after_actual_upkeep() { let mut world = CourseWorld::new(Scenario { daylight: Daylight::new(4, 2).unwrap(), grazers: vec![GrazerSeed { id: SimId(8), reserve_units: 2, capacity_units: 6, maintenance_units_per_tick: 5, meal_units_per_tick: 3, feeding_site: Some(SimId(80)), }], patches: vec![PatchSeed { id: SimId(80), biomass_units: 1, capacity_units: 4, growth_units_per_lit_tick: 4, }], history_limit: 32, }) .unwrap(); let before = world.snapshot(); assert_eq!(before.tick, 0); world.step(); let after = world.snapshot(); assert_eq!(after.tick, 1); assert_eq!( (after.grazers[0].reserve_units, after.grazers[0].life), (3, Life::Alive) ); assert_eq!(after.patches[0].biomass_units, 1); assert_eq!( after.ledger, TickLedger { added_units: 3, maintenance_units: 2, eaten_units: 3, starvations: 0, } ); let before_stores = u64::from(before.grazers[0].reserve_units) + u64::from(before.patches[0].biomass_units); let after_stores = u64::from(after.grazers[0].reserve_units) + u64::from(after.patches[0].biomass_units); assert_eq!( after_stores + after.ledger.maintenance_units, before_stores + after.ledger.added_units ); assert_eq!(after.history.starvations_between(1, 1), Some(0)); } #[test] fn case_5_evicted_death_and_collected_empty_ticks_have_different_evidence() { let mut world = CourseWorld::new(Scenario { daylight: Daylight::new(4, 0).unwrap(), grazers: vec![GrazerSeed { id: SimId(9), reserve_units: 4, capacity_units: 4, maintenance_units_per_tick: 1, meal_units_per_tick: 0, feeding_site: None, }], patches: vec![], history_limit: 0, }) .unwrap(); for _ in 0..7 { world.step(); } let state = world.snapshot(); assert_eq!(state.grazers[0].life, Life::Dead); assert_eq!(state.grazers[0].reserve_units, 0); assert!(state.history.events.is_empty()); assert_eq!(state.history.evicted_events, 5); assert_eq!( ( state.history.complete_after_tick, state.history.collected_through_tick ), (4, 7) ); assert_eq!(state.history.starvations_between(4, 7), None); assert_eq!(state.history.starvations_between(5, 7), Some(0)); assert_eq!(state.history.starvations_between(7, 8), None); }

title: Let the next generation enter the same world
summary: Course guide
