text: Your meadow can now explain how an animal survives, but every life still began in the starting configuration. Let's allow two grazers to fund a child from their own reserves. The interesting part comes after the birth: that child must pay upkeep, compete for the same food, and eventually become a possible parent. Make the next generation participate in the same world You'll extend the saved meadow by choosing population data, writing a complete maturation system, and connecting a funded birth transaction to the existing schedule. We'll follow one child through visibility, first action and adulthood before comparing longer runs. Your tests and reports should establish that reserve comes from its parents, inherited upkeep affects a real payment, and a final census can hide substantial turnover. The earlier systems and investigations remain part of the project and its checks. Continue the saved course project. This guide extends the shared meadow with an authored two-parent rule and deterministic inheritance. Contacts remain fixed patch IDs. These course rules are separate from live Moss and NOW.md ; spatial choice, travel, rest, and predation enter the continuing project later. Extend the project you already understand Reopen work/fieldwork/Cargo.toml with your reconstructed systems and investigations still in place. The new population will depend on the upkeep, feeding, and ordering contracts you established there, so first run the existing check. Keeping tests/investigation.rs and any tests/returns.rs gives those earlier questions a chance to catch a regression as the project grows. python3 learning/scripts/fieldwork.py check --project work/fieldwork This extension crosses several files because a child needs configuration, stored state, scheduled behavior, and a way to be observed. We'll work through those responsibilities together, beginning with a short trace that shows what the resulting world should do. When you reach a construction prompt, choose your representation or system access before opening the corresponding module answer. Complete module answers and how to use them beside your project The complete change map shows the differences from the shared-meadow checkpoint. Use it to review deliberate edits; it cannot promise to apply cleanly over your own changes. The separate complete population checkpoint and its README provide a working comparison that you can unpack elsewhere. Continue developing in your existing directory. The extension's responsibilities and complete module answers Module Responsibility to construct or connect population/config.rs Bounded trait, founder records, policy inputs, and validation. population.rs Stage and origin components, full maturation system, owned population report, and cleanup. reproduction.rs Plan a complete two-parent outcome, then commit and queue its child. population/history.rs Bounded birth/maturation events and visible coverage. model.rs , lifecycle.rs , feeding.rs First-action eligibility and its checks in existing upkeep and feeding. simulation.rs , lib.rs Opt-in construction/reset, installation, ordered phases, and deliberate public exports. The construction has three broad passes: model and validate the inputs; connect stages and eligibility to existing systems; then plan and commit births. Each pass may require several files before it compiles, so complete the related edits before treating a compile error as a behavioral result. Save a runnable checkpoint after each complete pass. If you're listening, pause at each construction prompt to work in the code. Generated narration skips code blocks and answer disclosures; the module map remains available whenever you need the surrounding types or a complete implementation. Follow the child through four completed ticks Consider two founders starting with five reserve units each. Both have upkeep one, capacity eight, and a meal request of two. Patch 100 starts empty, holds up to twenty units, and receives six every tick. For this first trace, each parent transfers two reserve units to its child and pays one additional unit as a birth cost. The child receives four; neither parent gets those transferred units back. After upkeep and meals in tick one, each founder has six units. A three-unit debit leaves each at three and creates child 101 at four. Now predict the child's next two ticks. It is already visible in the completed report, but should it have paid upkeep before it existed? And should being able to eat make it eligible to reproduce? The native reference trace keeps those questions separate: Observed native reference trace; patch biomass is two at each listed tick Completed tick Sorted ID:reserve Population consequence 1 1:3, 2:3, 101:4 Child 101 is visible, juvenile, and first eligible at tick two. 2 1:4, 2:4, 101:5 Child pays upkeep and eats; parents remain on cooldown. 3 1:5, 2:5, 101:6 Child becomes adult. There is no available eligible partner. 4 1:3, 2:3, 101:7, 102:4 Parents one/two can pair again; child 102 begins its own deadlines. The policy behind this trace uses maturation delay two, parental cooldown three, living cap eight, and mutation cycle [0] . Child 101 first acts on tick two and matures on tick three. Its parents are still cooling down when it becomes adult, so there is no eligible partner; on tick four, sorted matching pairs the parents again and leaves 101 unpaired. Adulthood makes a birth possible, but does not guarantee that a suitable pair exists. Check the first tick's stores as well as its census. The founders begin with ten, pay two upkeep units, accept six growth units, and dissipate two birth-cost units. Twelve remain across the parents, child, and patch. A newborn whose reserve appeared from nowhere would break this account even if its stage and timing looked right. Model a population without changing old callers The trace suggests three different things an individual must remember: whether it is juvenile or adult, when it may first act, and how it acquired its inherited upkeep rate. Choose representations for those questions before looking at the answer. Keep life state distinct from developmental stage, because a juvenile can die and a living adult can still be ineligible to parent. Also write down the invalid configurations your constructor should reject; those decisions define what the later systems may safely assume. The worked design uses Stage , tick deadlines, and an optional BirthOrigin . Founders enter as adults without a birth origin in this run. A child retains its parent IDs, donor, copied value, proposed mutation, applied mutation, and resulting trait. The bounded type UpkeepTrait::new accepts values one through three, and that value becomes the individual's upkeep rate. Its actual payment still depends on how much reserve is available, just as it did in your earlier system. These additions needn't change the meaning of an existing scenario. Preserve the public shapes Scenario , GrazerSeed , Snapshot , GrazerReading , TickLedger , and EventKind , then add CourseWorld::new_population(scenario, config) and population_snapshot() . Construction returns a validation Result ; observation returns None when population mode is disabled. That distinction lets a caller tell an unavailable capability from an enabled population containing no animals. Modelling hint: put agreement checks at construction PopulationConfig::new provides defaults, but the world constructor must validate the complete config against its scenario. Founder trait records must cover exactly the scenario's grazer IDs, once each, and trait-derived upkeep must match the existing seed rate. Reject a duplicate, missing or unexpected ID, or a mismatched rate rather than silently changing the caller's scenario. Complete validation contract Require positive maturation delay, cooldown, contribution, and living cap. The founders must fit under the cap, two contributions must fit in the child's capacity, and a parent's debit plus the one-unit reserve floor must be representable. Birth cost may be zero. Require a nonempty mutation cycle containing only minus one, zero, or plus one. The first child ID must be above every authored grazer and patch ID; reject a configuration with no initial identity space left. The complete configuration module supplies the branches and error variants. Test rejection at the world boundary before proceeding. Start a valid population, execute a tick, save both reports, then attempt a reset using mutation cycle [2] . Predict what should happen to the run ID, current animals, and policy used by a later ordinary reset. Merely testing that two is an invalid delta would miss a reset that reports an error after partially changing the world. Complete learner test: tests/population_investigation.rs Add this file beside your earlier tests once the population entry points compile. It checks that rejection preserves both current reports and the valid policy used by the next ordinary reset. The population-stage command later in the guide discovers this saved test. use moss_course_ecosystem::{ CourseWorld, FounderTrait, PopulationConfig, PopulationError, Scenario, SimId, UpkeepTrait, }; #[test] fn rejected_mutation_cycle_preserves_world_and_future_reset() { let scenario = Scenario::generous_supply(); let config = PopulationConfig::new(vec![ FounderTrait { id: SimId(1), upkeep: UpkeepTrait::new(2).unwrap() }, FounderTrait { id: SimId(2), upkeep: UpkeepTrait::new(1).unwrap() }, ]); let mut world = CourseWorld::new_population(scenario.clone(), config.clone()).unwrap(); world.step(); let before = world.snapshot(); let population_before = world.population_snapshot().unwrap(); let mut invalid = config.clone(); invalid.mutation_cycle = vec![2]; assert_eq!( world.reset_with_population(scenario, invalid), Err(PopulationError::InvalidMutationCycle), ); assert_eq!(world.snapshot(), before); assert_eq!(world.population_snapshot().unwrap(), population_before); world.reset(); assert_eq!(world.snapshot().run, before.run + 1); assert_eq!(world.snapshot().tick, 0); assert_eq!(world.population_snapshot().unwrap().config, config); } Write the complete stage system With those states represented, implement mature from its responsibility: find living juveniles whose deadline has arrived and turn them into adults. The system must read the clock, identity, and life state, mutate the stage, and write a population event. Choose the complete query signature and traversal yourself before consulting the answer. As with upkeep, stable ID order keeps reversed spawn order from rearranging the journal and changing which records it retains. The component stores matures_at_tick: Option<u64> . A founder has no scheduled maturation, while a child has a deadline; only a living juvenile at or beyond that deadline transitions. Changing its stage to adult makes the transition happen once, even though the deadline remains in the past on later ticks. Maturation records an event but adds no reserve, so a newly adult grazer still depends on the same stores it had as a juvenile. Stage hint: retain handles, not component references Collect owned ID/handle pairs, sort them, then perform each mutable lookup. A vector containing borrowed query items would keep the earlier component access alive when you ask for mutable access. The fieldwork borrow experiment applies here too, although the state you're changing is different. Complete maturation answer and why it is ordered The full population module includes the system and its imports. Its query fetches (Entity, &Identity, &Grazer, &mut Individual) ; the system checks life, juvenile stage, and deadline together, checks the journal’s eviction-counter arithmetic, changes the stage, and records Matured . Stable traversal controls the event sequence without making maturity itself an energy source. The child must also become a customer of your existing upkeep and feeding systems. Add first-action eligibility to the private grazer representation and check it in both systems. First-arc founders remain eligible from tick one; a child first acts at its birth tick plus one. Its initial reproductive deadline equals its own maturity deadline, independently of the cooldown just assigned to its parents. Place visibility, action, and maturity on the tick We now have three boundaries to place: the entity becomes visible, the individual may act, and the juvenile becomes adult. Follow the diagram through one step. After time advances and ledgers clear, eligible juveniles mature; upkeep, growth, meals, and starvation then run. Births commit and their queued entities are applied, dead population entities are removed and cleanup is applied, and finally the histories are completed. A report taken afterward can therefore contain a newborn whose first permitted action is still in the future. A newborn enters after its birth tick's ordinary actions In order: advance tick and clear ledgers; mature juveniles; upkeep, growth, meals, starvation; commit births and apply deferred spawns; cleanup dead entities and apply deferred removals; complete reports. Newborns are visible at completion but first act next tick. Maturity has its own later deadline. 1 · Advance tick Clear both ledgers 2 · Mature juveniles Living, juvenile, deadline reached 3 · Run the existing loop Upkeep → growth → meals → starvation 4 · Resolve births Commit → queue → apply children 5 · Clean up dead rows Update roster → despawn → apply 6 · Complete evidence Both histories and population totals Born at t · first action t + 1 · maturity t + 2 The displayed two-tick maturation delay is the initial policy. Structural visibility, first action, and adulthood are separate boundaries. Install this population chain separately from the unchanged first-arc chain. Explicit ApplyDeferred steps make the observation points after birth and cleanup visible in the schedule. A reserved handle alone doesn't establish that a query can fetch the child yet, and Bevy may also insert command application along dependencies. If your test needs to observe a pending queue, control those settings as you did in the command lesson . To test eligibility rather than merely trust the ordinary order, design a probe that runs upkeep and feeding again after the birth flush, still within the birth tick. The child should produce neither event. Its final reserve alone is insufficient evidence: an illegal payment of two followed by an illegal meal of two would cancel numerically. This probe gives the guards something the usual birth-last schedule would otherwise hide. Make one birth a complete transaction The new systems can describe a child's life, but we still need to decide when a pair may create one. Each parent must be alive, adult, past cooldown, and able to pay while retaining one reserve unit. Both must share a contact ID that resolves to an actual patch. An empty patch can establish that contact; a missing ID or another grazer cannot. The worked policy sorts sites, sorts eligible parents within each site, and forms disjoint adjacent pairs, making the matching reproducible without promising fair access to a partner. Before writing the committing system, construct an owned ParentView and a proposed BirthPlan . Work through reserves five and four under the initial policy: two units from each parent enter the child, and one more from each is dissipated. Then change the second reserve to three. Decide everything the accepted plan must contain, and everything the rejected attempt must leave alone, before opening the implementation. Transaction hint: test the floor before debiting either parent A three-unit debit must leave at least one. Calculate both parent remainders and cooldowns, the child's state and origin, identity advancement, counters, and journal operation before installing any part of the outcome. Otherwise a failure discovered late could leave one parent charged for a birth that never happened. Full payment reasoning and implementation map Five/four becomes two/one, with child reserve four and dissipated cost two. Five/three rejects because the second parent would finish at zero. Rejection consumes no parent reserve, child ID, birth event, or accepted-birth ordinal. In the complete reproduction module , plan_birth returns the proposed outcome; resolve_births re-reads candidates, obtains short mutable borrows for distinct parents, commits the plan, reserves a slot, and queues the child. A queued child makes capacity accounting another part of the same transaction. Write a test with two funded pairs but only one available population slot: exactly one pair may pay, even before a query can see the first pair's child. Then try the accepted pair again in reverse order; its updated cooldown must prevent a second debit. For a rejected proposal, flush commands before checking that no child appeared, so an accidentally queued entity cannot escape the test. The accepted child inherits the shared feeding site and receives an ID above every authored grazer and patch; IDs aren't recycled within a run. Checked preflight also covers deadlines, ordinals, and accounting, because an overflow discovered after payment would leave the same kind of partial outcome as an unfunded parent. The atomic boundary is this birth: rejection leaves earlier upkeep and earlier accepted births in the tick intact. Make the inherited value affect an executed rule A child in this model needs an upkeep rate as well as reserve. The first accepted birth copies the lower-ID parent's trait, the next copies the higher-ID parent's, and subsequent births alternate. Apply the next delta from the configured repeating cycle and clamp the result to one through three. Because only accepted births advance that ordinal and the child allocator, rejected attempts don't change the trait or identity a later successful birth receives. Wire the resulting value into the child's actual maintenance_units_per_tick , then test its consequence. If the parents have traits one and three and the first delta is plus one, the child's trait should be two. On its first eligible tick without food, four reserve units should become two. An origin record could display the correct trait while the old default still controls upkeep; this test distinguishes that attractive but ineffective label from inherited behavior. Inheritance answer: preserve the difference between proposed and applied At trait one, a proposed minus one applies zero after clamping. Retain both values, the donor, and the resulting trait in the origin. The selected algorithm is upkeep-copy-cycle-v1 ; its next ordinal affects future births, so equal current reserves don't make two runs equivalent when their accepted birth counts differ. This is a deterministic authored policy, not a random generator or a genetic model. Lower upkeep has no compensating disadvantage here, so a changing trait distribution cannot by itself establish adaptation or inevitable improvement. To interpret that distribution, look at who was born, who died, and which deltas the authored cycle supplied. A useful tradeoff would need an additional benefit and cost that the simulation actually executes. Count lives without retaining every corpse Births make a world of permanently retained lifetime objects grow without bound. Population mode therefore records a terminal outcome, removes the dead entity, and updates the roster before observation. The earlier mode keeps its original dead rows. In the population report, current readings describe living individuals, while founders plus lifetime births minus lifetime starvations gives the same census even after the bodies have been removed. The resource account needs one addition too. A child's starting reserve was transferred within the world, whereas birth cost was dissipated. Across a completed tick, ending stores plus actual upkeep plus dissipated birth cost must equal starting stores plus accepted growth. Keep this assertion alongside the individual timing and parentage checks; moving the right total to the wrong child could satisfy the equation while violating the birth rule. The living cap limits how much population the implementation and game policy allow. It doesn't measure the meadow's carrying capacity. Count an otherwise eligible formed pair only when that cap specifically blocks its birth; several blocked pairs in one tick produce several pair counts but one blocked-tick count. A full population with no eligible pair produces neither. Those counters help distinguish a flat census caused by the cap from one caused by food or missing partners. Birth and maturation also need their own bounded journal, preserving the original event enum for growth, maintenance, meals, and starvation. The two journals fill at different rates and report separate complete intervals. Suppose base coverage is after tick four through ten, while population coverage is after seven through nine. A claim requiring both kinds of event is supported only for ticks eight and nine, where those intervals overlap. Coverage answer: an origin is not an entire biography A living child's fixed-size origin can still name its parents after their removal or the eviction of its birth event. It cannot reconstruct their missing events. Lifetime counters preserve census, while an interval query outside complete coverage returns unknown. Bounded journals and fixed-size origins retain useful evidence without recursively copying whole ancestry trees. Check the extension, then observe your saved build When construction and wiring are complete, use the population stage. It requires both the unchanged first-arc acceptance suite and the population suite, then runs your saved tests. Retaining the earlier investigations is part of the extension: their questions should remain answerable even as a new kind of individual enters the world. python3 learning/scripts/fieldwork.py check --project work/fieldwork --stage population python3 learning/scripts/fieldwork_preview.py --project work/fieldwork --population python3 learning/scripts/build.py Serve or reload the course as described in setup , and identify the learner or reference source in the preview. Follow the four-tick trace, locate child 101, and compare its origin, first eligible tick, maturity, and upkeep rate with actual payments in the resource events and ledger. It has an upkeep rate on its birth tick without making a payment then. Checking that distinction, together with patch state and the census, connects the native rules to what your compiled browser host displays. Resetting a mode without losing its meaning reset() repeats the selected mode and configuration with a new run identity. reset_with(scenario) explicitly selects first-arc mode, while reset_with_population selects population mode. Invalid inputs preserve both the old world and its reset configuration, as your rejection test checks. An owned report saved before a successful reset still describes the earlier run. Compare turnover, not only the ending Your supply investigation now has another possible outcome: a meadow can maintain a similar head count while replacing many of its inhabitants. The complete populations example compares steady supply of six units per tick with twelve on the first two ticks of each four-tick cycle. Both request twenty-four per cycle. Within each founder-trait pair it holds other policies and starting values fixed, uses mutation [0] , and runs forty ticks: cargo +1.93.1 run --offline --locked --manifest-path work/fieldwork/Cargo.toml --example populations Observed native reference totals after forty ticks Founder upkeep traits Supply Living Births Starvations 1, 1 Steady 6 15 11 1, 1 Pulsed 5 15 12 1, 2 Steady 5 14 11 1, 2 Pulsed 5 17 14 2, 2 Steady 3 1 0 2, 2 Pulsed 3 1 0 1, 3 Steady 5 14 11 1, 3 Pulsed 5 17 14 Look at the one/two founders. Both runs end with five living grazers, but pulsed supply produces three more births and three more deaths. The endpoint hides that turnover. All eight reference runs accepted 240 growth units, although equal requests needn't produce equal accepted input in another capacity fixture. The one/one pulsed run also records one capacity-blocked pair in one tick, giving you a specific place where the cap changed an opportunity. Now check how far the evidence reaches. Both journals hold 128 events, but these runs retain all forty ticks of birth history while their base journals have lost older events. Even the two/two run's starvations_between(1, 40) returns unknown, although its lifetime starvation counter is a known zero. The example prints both bounds so the retained event record isn't mistaken for a complete history. These deterministic cohorts are useful comparisons of declared conditions, not repeated random samples or evidence of evolution. A birth now starts a life the existing rules must support The child has become more than a new row in the census. Its parents fund its reserve, its first-action deadline separates visibility from participation, and its inherited upkeep affects what it pays once that turn arrives. Descendants compete for the same finite food, and those that reach adulthood can enter the pairing rules themselves. Births and deaths can therefore explain turnover that a final head count conceals. Keep a new question in your own test file. For example, predict whether increasing child capacity changes survival while the living cap and supply timing stay fixed, then choose an individual trace that could contradict your mechanism. Continue with a patch in sight is not a meal , where positions and paid travel make reaching that shared food a new part of the explanation.

title: A patch in sight is not a meal
summary: Course guide
text: Two grazers spot a patch with two units of food and head towards it. They both arrive, but only the first gets a meal. When you inspect the second grazer, its local observation still says the patch holds two units. That looks like a contradiction until you ask when the observation was made. The grazer saw real food before either animal moved; another grazer ate it before its turn to feed. Follow a local sighting through a paid journey You'll give the saved population world positions, write its complete observation system, and connect local choice to affordable movement and current contact. We'll then make the opening contest an integration test, checking the copied view separately from the patch that feeding actually depletes. By the end, the native reports and browser map should let you explain where a grazer looked, what it chose, what travel cost, and why arrival still didn't guarantee a meal. Newborns will enter that same spatial world with their first-action delay intact. Third cumulative course arc, checkpoint A. This guide extends your saved population project . Its daylight, finite meals, birth, maturity, inherited upkeep, and starvation continue under the same authored course rules. The new work stays separate from the live movement exercise in NOW.md ; fatigue, rest, and hunting follow in later checkpoints. Continue the world whose costs you can explain In the population project, a feeding-site ID was enough to connect a grazer to a patch. Once animals can move, that connection needs an explanation: the grazer has to discover the patch and reach it. We can add those steps while keeping the existing rules for paying upkeep, transferring food, and funding a child. Start in your existing work/fieldwork directory and run the population check so you have a known starting point. Keep your earlier investigation and return tests alongside the new work; they'll help catch changes that accidentally alter the older modes. python3 learning/scripts/fieldwork.py check --project work/fieldwork --stage population Reference files and where to keep your work You can read the population-to-mobile change map beside your implementation to see how the reference fits together. Because your project may contain different edits, treat that patch as a comparison rather than an automatic migration. The separate mobile checkpoint and its README contain the complete answer. If you unpack them, use another directory so your own project and tests remain the place where you're building. We'll follow a grazer from a local sighting to an attempted meal. First it needs a position and a way to describe what it sees. Then it can choose a destination and pay for the part of the journey it can complete. Finally, feeding and birth must use the resulting positions. Those three passes touch several modules, so the new mode becomes fully runnable at the mobile-stage check near the end. While you're connecting it, missing types or systems may prevent compilation; the older constructors should continue to run at each coherent saved stage. The table below gives you a place to look when you want to compare a complete module. Responsibilities and complete module answers File Question to answer in your implementation mobile/config.rs Which cells, rates, and authored mappings are valid? mobile/perception.rs What can this grazer observe, and which local opportunity does it retain or choose? mobile/movement.rs Which route prefix can be completed and paid for now? mobile.rs , mobile/history.rs How are spatial actors installed, contacts derived, and observations retained? mobile/scenarios.rs Which complete inputs define the short journey and continuing meadow? feeding.rs , reproduction.rs How do existing actions revalidate space and place a fully participating child? simulation.rs , lib.rs Which mode is installed, which phases run, and which public types are exported? Choose what a cell means before drawing it For the smallest journey, put a grazer at cell zero and its food at cell two. We need to know where the grazer is now, how far it can see, and how far it can afford to move. We'll also need to remember where it saw the food, because the observation and the eventual meal happen at different points in the tick. Sketch those values before choosing their types. Some will be components that systems update, some will describe the starting world, and some will be copied into a report so you can inspect what happened. The simulation uses Cell { x, y } rather than screen coordinates, so a browser can draw the same world at any size. Each coordinate is an unsigned integer starting at zero, and GridBounds gives the positive width and height it must stay below. For these grid journeys, distance is the horizontal separation plus the vertical separation, usually called Manhattan distance. Be careful when calculating it: subtracting a larger unsigned coordinate from a smaller one doesn't produce their separation. Take each absolute difference, widen it, and then add, so cells near the integer limit still have a valid distance. Representation hint A private Position component can wrap the cell shared by grazers and patches. A grazer also needs Motion , which names its sensing radius, maximum cells per tick, and travel units per cell. The reference keeps that motion together with copied local readings, a selected target, and tick markers in MobileActor . A patch has a place in the world without carrying all of a traveller's state. Complete configuration answer The configuration module supplies GrazerPlacement , PatchPlacement , SpatialConfig , and MobileScenario::new(scenario, population, space) . Each authored entity needs exactly one placement within the bounds. Grazers may share a cell, while distinct patch cells make a contact identify one patch location. Require a positive travel cost so affordability has a meaningful divisor, but allow zero speed for a stationary grazer and zero sensing radius for a same-cell view. Apply the motion checks to the newborn template too, since future children will use it. There is one old input that would undermine this design. A seed with a feeding-site ID already has permission to use that patch under the fixed-contact rules, even if you now place the grazer across the map. Mobile seeds therefore start with feeding_site: None , and validation rejects a conflicting seed by ID. Calling CourseWorld::new_mobile selects this spatial contract. The first-arc and fixed-contact population constructors keep their original meaning, so giving an animal a position doesn't silently change what an older lesson does. Keep reset failures atomic Validate the complete mobile specification before installing any part of it. If reset_with_mobile finds an out-of-bounds placement, both the current world and the configuration used by a later reset() must remain unchanged. A successful reset starts the selected mode under a new run ID with targets and observations cleared. The existing reset_with and reset_with_population operations still select first-arc and fixed-contact population mode respectively. Write the whole observation system A position lets us answer where an animal is, but it doesn't say what the animal knows. The browser's inspector can show every patch; giving that table to the choice system would let a grazer pursue food outside its sensing range. Instead, we'll give each grazer a small record of what it could see from its own cell. Implement that record-building phase as observe in src/mobile/perception.rs , with a complete system signature and body. The phase runs after upkeep and patch growth, while every grazer is still at its position from the previous tick. For each living grazer whose first action is due, read its position and sensing radius, then copy the patches within that Manhattan distance into its local readings. Include an empty patch if it's visible: seeing that a patch is empty is still useful information, even though the next phase won't choose it as food. Sorting those copies by stable patch ID keeps the resulting report reproducible when entity installation order changes. The copy is the important Rust step here. Each PatchObservation owns a patch ID, a cell, and a biomass value; it holds no reference into the patch query. When observe finishes, its query access can end, and later systems are free to move animals or change patch biomass. The choice system will still have a readable account of the earlier moment. That account can become stale, which is exactly what we need to represent in the two-grazer example. Trying to keep a borrow of the live patch instead would blur the difference between what was seen and what exists now. For this small world, the observation system can scan every patch and copy only the local ones. The selector receives that filtered vector, with no global inspector table or unrestricted world reference. A spatial index could make the scan cheaper later; it would still need to preserve this boundary between finding nearby entities and deciding what an animal is allowed to know. Once the grazer moves, a single coordinate in the report is no longer enough to explain its view. In the first tick of our short journey, it looks from cell zero, travels to cell one, and still intends to reach the patch at cell two. MobileGrazerReading.observed_cell preserves the first of those positions, its current cell gives the second, and PatchTarget.observed_cell will hold the third. Keep the observation tick as well. An absent observation means the grazer hasn't collected one; an observation with an empty vector means it looked and saw no patch. You now have enough information to write the system: it reads the clock and the two kinds of entity, then replaces each eligible grazer's copied view. If you're listening, pause to try the signature and body before opening the hints. Narration skips code and disclosures, so resume after you've compared your accesses with the complete module. Observation hint 1: list reads and writes The clock supplies the tick. Patches supply their identities, positions and biomass; grazers supply their positions and life/first-action state. The only component you need to mutate is MobileActor , where you replace the local readings and record the observation's origin and tick. Nothing in this phase spends reserve or moves an entity. Observation hint 2: a query shape // System parameters for observe; the full function also needs its body. clock: Res<Clock>, patches: Query<(&Identity, &Position, &Patch)>, mut grazers: Query<(&Position, &Grazer, &mut MobileActor)>, Copy patch ID, cell, and current biomass into each PatchObservation . The vector owns these values, so the later choice phase does not retain references into an earlier query iteration. Complete observation and choice answer The complete perception module includes both systems with their imports, eligibility checks, stable ordering, target-change accounting, and journal writes. Begin your comparison with the system signature: it needs to update the actor's stored view, but it can do that while borrowing the actor's position through a shared reference. It's tempting to request mutable access to everything associated with the grazer, but that would ask Bevy for more access than observation needs. Consider changing only the grazer's position fetch to &mut Position while the patch query still uses &Position . The two queries then claim incompatible access if they can match the same entity. Although we think of grazers and patches as different kinds of inhabitant, requiring Grazer in one query and Patch in the other doesn't prove an entity cannot have both components. An isolated native probe of that exact change compiled, then failed when Bevy initialized the schedule with error[B0001] . After your integrated checkpoint runs, try the change and notice where the failure occurs. Rust accepts the system's parameter types; Bevy's initialization check rejects their combined access to the world. Restore the shared position reference once you've seen the diagnostic, because observation has no reason to write a position. Why this error appears when the schedule starts The Bevy ECS 0.18.1 query documentation explains the access check, and the official B0001 explanation shows how conflicting system parameters cause it. Compare this with the compiler's held-borrow error in the first fieldwork guide : both concern incompatible access, but Bevy must also check the access declared by separate system parameters when it prepares the schedule. Choose an opportunity without reserving it With a local view in place, choosing food becomes a smaller problem: which of these observations should the grazer follow? Write your rule in words before translating it into query code. In this checkpoint, the grazer continues towards its previous target while that patch appears in the current tick's view with positive biomass. If the target no longer qualifies, it chooses the nearest visible nonempty patch, using stable ID to break an equal-distance tie. When no candidate remains, it clears the target and stays put. The model doesn't give it a global fallback or a random search step. The chosen PatchTarget needs an ID, an observed cell, and an observed tick. The ID lets a later action look up the same patch, while the cell gives movement its destination. The tick tells us whether this choice came from the view just collected. Without that last check, a remembered target could keep guiding the grazer after it had left sensing range. A grazer can refresh its observation of the same patch on successive ticks without recording a change of target ID. Choice reasoning: when a nearer patch appears Suppose the grazer is already heading towards a visible, nonempty patch when a nearer one grows fresh food. Under this continuation policy, it keeps its existing target; “nearest” governs the moment it needs a new choice. If the old patch empties or disappears from the current view, it compares the remaining candidates by distance and ID. Keeping retention and replacement explicit prevents query iteration order from accidentally deciding the policy. At this point the grazer has committed only to a destination. Choosing a patch hasn't locked any biomass or added any food to its reserve, so another grazer can make the same choice. This is the distinction behind action-time revalidation : an intention gives an action something to attempt, and the action must still discover whether it can succeed. Before we can attempt the meal, though, we need to get there. Pay for the route that actually happens Our grazer at cell zero knows about food at cell two, but knowing the destination doesn't pay for the journey. Movement follows the target's observed cell, taking horizontal steps before vertical ones. It may reject an ID that no longer identifies a patch, but it must keep using the destination the grazer actually observed. Patches are stationary here, so the distinction won't change this route; it will matter when an opportunity can move between observation and action. Suppose a grazer could travel three cells this tick, has five reserve units left after upkeep, and pays two units per cell. It can complete two cells for four units, leaving one in reserve. A possible meal at the destination can't fund the third step, because that meal hasn't happened yet. Integer division of reserve by the positive per-cell cost gives the number of whole steps it can afford. Affordability is only one limit. The grazer must also stop when it reaches its destination or uses its maximum cells for the tick, so the accepted distance is the smallest of those three bounds. Calculate that distance, the resulting cell, and the actual cost before mutating the entity. If there is no target, its speed is zero, it has already arrived, or it can't afford the first cell, the accepted journey costs nothing. Implement those bounds in src/mobile/movement.rs , then record the cells actually travelled and the units actually paid. The complete movement module shows both the arithmetic and the ECS adapter. Compare how it calculates a result before committing that result to position, reserve, and accounting. Travel answer: stop at arrival rather than spending the full allowance If the destination is one cell away, an allowance of four still permits only one useful step. Once you've bounded the total distance, take as much of it as needed along x and use the remainder along y; neither coordinate should pass its destination. Check the ledger and history arithmetic before committing the resulting position and reserve, so an accounting failure can't leave a partially recorded journey. The movement system also needs to recognize an opportunity it has already processed. last_travel_tick records that evaluation even when the accepted distance was zero, so a second invocation can't take another turn in the same tick. When you're investigating actual movement, use the Travelled events instead: those record journeys with a nonzero distance. We can now predict a complete journey. MobileScenario::short_journey() puts one grazer at (0,0) with reserve five and capacity eight. It pays one unit of upkeep each tick, can see three cells, and can travel one cell for one unit. Its meal request is two. Patch 100 at (2,0) holds three units and doesn't grow. Work out the first three ticks, including upkeep before travel, then compare your prediction with this observed native trace. Observed native short journey: y remains zero Tick Cell x / reserve Biomass Travel cells / cost Meal 1 1 / 3 3 1 / 1 0 2 2 / 3 1 1 / 1 2 3 2 / 3 0 0 / 0 1 The unchanged reserve can be misleading here. On tick two the grazer begins with three units, spends one on upkeep and one on travel, then eats two to finish at three again. On tick three it is already at the patch, so it pays only upkeep and eats the one remaining food unit. Both ticks end at reserve three, but they describe different journeys and meals. Position and actual flows explain what the ending balance alone can't tell you. Arrive, then check the meal against the current world Reaching the destination gives feeding a new fact to check: the grazer and its selected patch now occupy the same cell. Derive contact from those current positions and the selected patch ID. A patch can appear in the inspector or lie within sensing range while still being several cells away, so neither observation establishes contact. The meal phase then checks the contact again alongside current biomass, reserve room, and demand before using the existing immediate transfer between the two stores. This brings us back to the two grazers at the beginning. They can both observe two food units and both pay to reach the patch, because neither action reserves a meal. Feeding resolves grazer one first by stable ID, immediately transferring those units out of the patch. When grazer two's turn arrives, its copied view still contains two, but the current patch contains zero. It gets no meal. Follow the diagram from top to bottom and notice that nothing edits the old observation to make it agree with the later world; those two records describe different moments. The unsuccessful grazer gets another observation and choice on the next executed tick. It doesn't respond to the failed meal by choosing again inside the feeding system, which would give it an extra decision after seeing the first grazer's outcome. An accurate observation can become a stale meal claim Before movement both grazers observe patch 100 holding two units. They arrive together. Stable ID one consumes both units. ID two receives nothing, although its copied observation still contains two. New observation and choice occur next tick. 1 · Observe Both read patch 100: two units 2 · Travel Both pay to reach the same cell 3 · Resolve ID one Two units transfer; patch becomes zero 4 · Resolve ID two Old reading: two · actual meal: zero A selected target is not a reserved resource. The native investigation below confirms this sequence. The copied observation and current patch legitimately disagree after another actor's meal. Write a test that makes the stale claim real Let's turn that sequence into an investigation in tests/mobile_investigation.rs , alongside your existing tests. Give both grazers a starting cell of (0,0) , reserve four, upkeep one, speed one, travel cost one, sensing radius one, and meal request two. Put patch 100 at (1,0) with two units. Then add patch 101 at (2,0) with five units, and give neither patch any growth. That second patch matters: you can see it in the global inspector, but the grazers can't see it from their starting cell. It lets the test distinguish a legitimate later choice from a hidden same-tick fallback. Predict the first two ticks before opening the complete test. On tick one, each grazer pays upkeep and travel, reaching patch 100 with two reserve units. ID one eats its two units and finishes at four; ID two remains at two. Patch 101 must still hold five, because neither grazer observed it when making that tick's choice. On tick two, both grazer positions have changed, so their next observations can include patch 101. They can now choose it, travel there, and take two units each. The patch falls from five units to one, while the grazers again finish at reserves four and two. This time the repeated ending balances conceal a change of destination. Your assertions need to identify where the meals came from as well as how much each grazer ate. Investigation hint 1: inspect observation and state separately After tick one, both copied local readings should still show patch 100 with biomass two, even though the authoritative patch has reached zero. Neither reading should include patch 101. Asserting all three facts establishes that the grazers chose from their earlier local views, rather than secretly consulting the inspector's current global information. Investigation hint 2: challenge same-tick fallback A total for eaten units won't tell you which patch supplied them. Assert target ID, cell, reserve, and both patch stores so a meal from the wrong patch can't hide behind the right total. Then assert the legitimate choice of patch 101 on tick two: the rule forbids using unseen food during the first action, rather than forbidding that patch forever. Complete learner test: tests/mobile_investigation.rs This is a full integration-test file for your continuing project. It uses the public world and its installed schedule; it does not implement a second choice or feeding algorithm. The mobile-stage command below runs this file with your earlier tests. use moss_course_ecosystem::{ Cell, CourseWorld, Daylight, FounderTrait, GrazerPlacement, GrazerSeed, GridBounds, MobileScenario, Motion, PatchPlacement, PatchSeed, PopulationConfig, Scenario, SimId, SpatialConfig, UpkeepTrait, }; #[test] fn stale_local_claim_cannot_take_a_second_meal_or_skip_to_unseen_food() { let motion = Motion { sensing_radius: 1, max_cells_per_tick: 1, travel_units_per_cell: 1, }; let scenario = Scenario { daylight: Daylight::new(1, 0).unwrap(), grazers: [1, 2].into_iter().map(|id| GrazerSeed { id: SimId(id), reserve_units: 4, capacity_units: 8, maintenance_units_per_tick: 1, meal_units_per_tick: 2, feeding_site: None, }).collect(), patches: [(100, 2), (101, 5)].into_iter().map(|(id, units)| PatchSeed { id: SimId(id), biomass_units: units, capacity_units: 8, growth_units_per_lit_tick: 0, }).collect(), history_limit: 128, }; let mut population = PopulationConfig::new([1, 2].into_iter().map(|id| FounderTrait { id: SimId(id), upkeep: UpkeepTrait::new(1).unwrap(), }).collect()); population.max_living = 2; let space = SpatialConfig { bounds: GridBounds { width_cells: 3, height_cells: 1 }, grazers: [1, 2].into_iter().map(|id| GrazerPlacement { id: SimId(id), cell: Cell { x: 0, y: 0 }, motion, }).collect(), patches: vec![ PatchPlacement { id: SimId(100), cell: Cell { x: 1, y: 0 } }, PatchPlacement { id: SimId(101), cell: Cell { x: 2, y: 0 } }, ], newborn_motion: motion, }; let mut world = CourseWorld::new_mobile(MobileScenario::new(scenario, population, space)).unwrap(); world.step(); let first = world.mobile_snapshot().unwrap(); assert_eq!(first.tick, 1); assert_eq!(first.base.grazers.iter().map(|g| g.reserve_units).collect::<Vec<_>>(), vec![4, 2]); assert_eq!(first.base.patches.iter().map(|p| p.biomass_units).collect::<Vec<_>>(), vec![0, 5]); assert_eq!((first.ledger.travel_cells, first.ledger.travel_units), (2, 2)); assert_eq!(first.base.ledger.eaten_units, 2); for grazer in &first.grazers { assert_eq!(grazer.cell, Cell { x: 1, y: 0 }); let target = grazer.target.unwrap(); assert_eq!((target.patch, target.observed_tick), (SimId(100), 1)); assert_eq!(grazer.visible_patches.len(), 1); assert_eq!(grazer.visible_patches[0].patch, SimId(100)); assert_eq!(grazer.visible_patches[0].biomass_units, 2); } world.step(); let second = world.mobile_snapshot().unwrap(); assert_eq!(second.tick, 2); assert_eq!(second.base.grazers.iter().map(|g| g.reserve_units).collect::<Vec<_>>(), vec![4, 2]); assert_eq!(second.base.patches.iter().map(|p| p.biomass_units).collect::<Vec<_>>(), vec![0, 1]); assert_eq!(second.base.ledger.eaten_units, 4); assert_eq!(second.population.totals.births, 0); for grazer in &second.grazers { assert_eq!(grazer.cell, Cell { x: 2, y: 0 }); let target = grazer.target.unwrap(); assert_eq!((target.patch, target.observed_tick), (SimId(101), 2)); } } Run this exact case while investigating it, then use the complete stage check before the browser build: cargo +1.93.1 test --offline --locked --manifest-path work/fieldwork/Cargo.toml --test mobile_investigation stale_local_claim_cannot_take_a_second_meal_or_skip_to_unseen_food -- --exact Pause narration while you run and inspect the test. A failure should help you choose where to look. If patch 101 loses food on tick one, the action may be bypassing contact or choosing a fallback inside feeding. If both grazers receive the first patch's two units, check whether the transfer depletes current biomass immediately; using each copied observation as the available amount would spend the same food twice. If the first tick passes but the grazers stay at the empty patch on tick two, follow what happens to their old targets when the fresh observation reports zero biomass. What has been checked in the reference This exact worked test passed against the frozen native checkpoint in an isolated Cargo copy. Run it against your saved implementation too, and check that the named case actually executed. A compilation failure or a filter that runs zero tests can't tell you whether the two-tick behavior is correct. Give the newborn a place in the same world Founders aren't the only grazers that will inhabit this world. As soon as the existing population rule produces a child, observation and movement will expect that child to have a position too. Extend the birth transaction to require both parents at an actual shared patch cell after their actions. The patch can be empty and still provide that meeting place. Once the transaction has found it, check the child's placement and the history's eviction-counter arithmetic alongside the payment, ID, deadlines, and origin that birth already prepares. A full journal can evict its oldest event; it does not by itself make a birth invalid. Queue the child's position together with its other components, using the configured newborn motion. It keeps its inherited upkeep and becomes eligible to act at birth tick plus one, but starts without a target, local readings, or a prior travel tick. Copying a parent's target would claim the child had already made an observation. Adding its position in a later phase would create a different problem: other systems could see a newborn before it had the components their mobile queries require. Installing the complete bundle gives the child a place immediately while still preserving its first-action delay. Newborn answer and test boundary The full reproduction module shows the additional preflight and the complete queued bundle. After the birth flush, you should be able to find the placed child in public mobile readings. A deliberately late invocation of observation, travel, or meals in the same tick must still leave that child inactive. Check events and flows as well as its ending reserve, because an illegal expense and an illegal gain could cancel in the balance. Install the phases and account for the journey The systems now describe a journey, but their order determines which version of the world each one sees. Start the tick and clear its ledgers, then mature eligible children, pay upkeep, and grow patches. Observe all actors before any of them chooses or travels. After travel, derive contact and resolve meals, then starvation and births. Apply the queued children, clean up dead rows, apply those removals, and only then mark the histories complete. Follow that order in the complete schedule , explaining what each phase needs from the one before it. In particular, keep observation out of the movement loop. If you observe one grazer, move it, and then observe the next, the two grazers no longer make their decisions from the same moment. Separating those phases is what makes the copied readings a coherent account of the world before travel. Travel also changes the explanation for missing energy. The units paid for movement leave the measured stores, just as upkeep and birth costs do. To check a tick, add ending grazer reserves and patch biomass to actual upkeep, actual travel payment, and dissipated birth cost; that should equal starting stores plus accepted growth. Meals and birth contributions move units between stores, so they don't add another loss. Use MobileSnapshot for this accounting: it includes the base and population reports along with the travel costs that the older snapshot cannot show. To explain how a particular journey led to a meal, you need more than a correct total. Target changes, accepted travel, and newborn placements go into a third bounded journal. Their events have to cover the same interval as the resource events you're comparing, and a birth may bring the population journal into the explanation too. Use the intersection of those coverage intervals. The current target tells you what a grazer intends now; it can't recover the route from an event that has been evicted. Lifetime travel totals remain useful even when that detailed explanation is no longer available. Observe the saved mobile build Now connect the tested journey to the map you'll inspect. Check the saved project, compile its current sources, then rebuild the course page with that artifact. The short journey gives you a known sequence against which to compare the displayed positions and observations. python3 learning/scripts/fieldwork.py check --project work/fieldwork --stage mobile python3 learning/scripts/fieldwork_preview.py --project work/fieldwork --mobile python3 learning/scripts/build.py The first command runs the earlier compatibility suites, the new mobile acceptance cases, and your saved tests. Once they pass, the second command compiles those checked sources to WASM, and the final command makes that build available to the page below. You'll then be looking at the spatial behavior of your saved Rust project. The map and its tables give you another way to inspect the result, including whether the presentation agrees with the native evidence. Check the source label before starting so you know whether the page loaded your learner project or the reference. In the short journey, take one tick and compare the grazer's current map position with the origin of its local view. Then follow it to the patch and compare observed biomass with the patch's current biomass after feeding. Changing the selected grazer or redrawing the report should leave the completed tick unchanged. After a source edit, run the check and build commands again before looking for its effect here. Once you can explain the short journey, switch to the continuing meadow to see travel interact with birth and turnover. Both presets use mutation cycle [0] , keeping inheritance unchanged while space becomes consequential. You can also add the complete native example as examples/mobile.rs in your project and run it below. Its declared 120-tick meadow finished with four living grazers after 32 births and 32 starvations, having spent 173 travel units. Four inhabitants at the end could look like a quiet population until you inspect all the arrivals and departures that produced it. cargo +1.93.1 run --offline --locked --manifest-path work/fieldwork/Cargo.toml --example mobile The histories put a limit on how far back you can explain that run. At tick 120, resource history covers ticks 100–120, mobile history 70–120, and population history 1–120. An explanation that needs all three can therefore cover only 100–120, even though the lifetime travel counter still knows about all 173 units. If you change a rule, compare the full starting configuration, the same horizon, and the accounting output as well as the final population. This authored run doesn't establish population stability, and current positions can't reconstruct its evicted journeys. An accurate observation can lead to an empty meal The second grazer's empty meal now makes sense without treating its observation as an error. It saw food, chose the patch, and paid to reach it, but another grazer consumed the food before its meal was resolved. Keeping those moments separate let you represent the animal's limited knowledge and still make an accurate transfer against the current world. In the resting checkpoint , a commitment will interrupt this same journey while upkeep continues. We'll use the records of what was observed, intended and actually done to distinguish a recovered grazer from one that is ready to travel again.

title: A pause still has a cost
summary: Course guide
text: Our grazer can see food two cells ahead, and it still has enough reserve to reach it. Instead, it stops. For the next two ticks its fatigue falls, but so does its reserve: resting has interrupted the journey without removing the cost of staying alive. Make a pause change the journey without creating energy You'll choose an activity representation, write the complete ECS system that performs rest, and connect its guards to observation, travel, meals and births in your saved project. A fast-recovery test will separate being recovered from having fulfilled a commitment; a matched meadow comparison will then ask what an extra rest action changes over a longer run. The expected outcome is a pause you can explain through activity, fatigue, reserve and fresh observations, with native tests and a browser view exposing the same interrupted journey. Continue your saved course project from the mobile guide , normally work/fieldwork . This chapter adds an authored rest policy to that isolated world; it doesn't activate rest in live Moss or change NOW.md . The traces below were checked against the complete resting checkpoint. Give the journey a reason to pause So far, a grazer with food in sight can keep walking as long as it can pay for the next step. We already have the machinery for that journey: a local observation, a chosen patch, paid movement, and a meal after arrival. Rest will fit around those decisions by introducing a second question before the grazer acts: is it still foraging, or has it committed to a pause? You'll make that distinction in your existing project, keeping the observation system, population rules and investigations you've already written. The new work asks you to choose a representation for activity, write a complete ECS system that performs a rest action, and design a test that catches an early wake. We'll first follow a small journey so those implementation decisions have a concrete behavior to explain. If you'd like a gentler introduction to the idea of fatigue, the isolated rest lesson is a useful preparation. Use the worked checkpoint alongside your project The review-only change map shows where this extension touches the mobile checkpoint. Because your own files may have diverged, use it to find the relevant changes rather than applying it as an automatic upgrade. The complete resting checkpoint provides full files to compare with your work. Keep your saved directory and its tests; those earlier investigations still have something to say about the expanded world. A rest restores capacity for effort, but doesn't feed the grazer Reserve already has a clear job in our world: it pays upkeep, movement and birth contributions. We'll keep that meaning and give fatigue a separate one. Every cell the grazer actually travels adds two fatigue points, while a rest action removes up to two. These rules allow a tired grazer to recover even as its reserve falls, which is the tradeoff we want to investigate. Charging actual travel matters here. A grazer that can't afford a step hasn't done the work of moving, so an attempted journey shouldn't add fatigue. Neither should observing a patch, choosing it, or eating a stationary meal. The isolated rest lesson charged each abstract foraging tick; now that we have real movement to measure, we can attach effort to that specific outcome instead. For the first policy, fatigue has a maximum of ten points. A grazer enters rest when a decision finds it at six or more, and it can leave only when fatigue is two or less and it has completed at least two rest actions. The two conditions happen to finish together in the ordinary journey. Later we'll change recovery so we can see why both are needed. Keep these quantities recognizable in your code. Reserve units pay for an action, fatigue points describe its effort, and the rest commitment counts executed actions. They're related by our rules, but they aren't interchangeable merely because each can be represented by an integer. Follow one grazer from departure to arrival MobileScenario::resting_journey() places a grazer at cell zero and a food patch at cell five. The grazer can see the patch, walks one cell per tick, and starts with twenty reserve units. Each tick costs one unit of upkeep, and each travelled cell costs another. On arrival it can request a two-unit meal, up to its reserve capacity of twenty-four. The patch starts with twenty units and doesn't grow; there are no competitors or potential partners to complicate this first journey. With the policy above, the first three steps bring the grazer to cell three with six fatigue points. The next decision therefore starts a rest, even though food is still visible and movement is affordable. Before reading the table, carry that story through ticks four, five and six: consider the remaining commitment as well as fatigue, and remember that upkeep continues throughout the pause. Observed native default journey: end-of-tick values; y remains zero Tick Cell x Reserve Fatigue Activity / actions owed Meal units 1 1 18 2 Foraging 0 2 2 16 4 Foraging 0 3 3 14 6 Foraging 0 4 3 13 4 Resting / 1 0 5 3 12 2 Resting / 0 0 6 4 10 4 Foraging 0 7 5 10 6 Foraging 2 The rest actions on ticks four and five reduce fatigue from six to two, while reserve drops from fourteen to twelve. On tick six, a new decision sees that both exit conditions are satisfied and lets the grazer resume its journey. It finally reaches food on tick seven, when a two-unit meal replaces exactly that tick's upkeep and travel payments. Reserve stays at ten even though several things happened. Reading the flows alongside the ending value makes those events visible. Remember what the grazer has committed to We need the state of a resting grazer to explain what it can do next. Fatigue alone can't do that: an animal might have recovered enough while still owing an action, or finished its minimum pause while remaining too tired to leave. Sketch a representation that can express both situations before opening the answer. The reference uses Activity::Foraging and Activity::Resting { remaining_ticks } . This is a useful job for an enum because the countdown belongs only to the resting state. With two separate booleans such as resting and ready , we'd have to explain which combinations are meaningful and keep them synchronized. The enum gives the countdown a home in the state that needs it. If that pattern is unfamiliar, the Rust Book's enum chapter develops it, and its match chapter shows how to access a variant's data. In this API, remaining_ticks means executed rest actions still owed. Merely calling a decision system, waiting in the browser, or reading a report doesn't reduce it. Zero is also a valid resting state: the minimum commitment is complete, but the next decision still needs to check whether fatigue is low enough. That distinction suggests two systems. The decision system enters rest with a full commitment, stays with the current activity when its exit conditions aren't met, or wakes the grazer when they are. The action system then performs the chosen rest by reducing fatigue and spending one owed action. Keeping these jobs separate prevents a decision from accidentally doing the work it was only meant to authorize. A rest commitment advances through executed actions A decision enters resting with two actions owed. An action reduces fatigue and leaves one action owed. The next action leaves zero owed. A later decision wakes only when fatigue also meets the exit threshold. Reading a report advances none of these stages. Decision: enter rest Two actions owed Execute one rest action Recover · one action owed Execute the next rest action Recover · zero actions owed Later decision: check both conditions Zero owed AND fatigue low enough A report read executes no action. With unusually fast recovery, fatigue can reach zero in the first action while one action remains owed. The investigation below makes that distinction observable. The diagram follows a fast recovery, where fatigue reaches zero after the first rest action. The grazer still owes another action, so it remains resting through the next tick and wakes only at a later decision. That later decision also gives it a fresh look at the world. Entering rest clears the current target through the choice phase; an old observation may remain in the inspector as history, but it cannot authorize movement or feeding. When the grazer wakes, observation runs before choice, even if it ends up choosing the same patch again. Add the optional policy without breaking earlier callers Expose RestPolicy through MobileScenario::with_rest(policy) , leaving earlier scenario literals and mobile reports usable. With no policy, travel behaves as before and CourseWorld::rest_snapshot() returns None . With a policy, the tick-zero report contains initialized state and zero executed actions. This distinction lets callers tell disabled rest from enabled rest that hasn't happened yet. Keep these public names and report shapes for the course checks while choosing your private organization. Configuration hint Require exit_at_points < enter_at_points <= maximum_fatigue_points , positive effort no larger than the maximum, positive recovery, and a positive minimum commitment. A history limit of zero is valid: it intentionally retains no events. Recovery can exceed current fatigue; charge only the actual decrease. Complete policy and representation answer The rest module defines policy, actor state, counters, and owned readings. The mobile configuration module validates the optional policy before installation or reset. Invalid policy must leave the existing world and its stored reset configuration intact; a zero commitment is an error, not an invitation to repair user input silently. Write the system that performs a rest Now implement execute in src/mobile/rest/systems.rs , including its parameters and iteration. Start by asking what information the job needs. It must read the executed clock, stable identity and grazer eligibility so it knows who may act. It must change the mobile actor's rest state and update the rest accounting resource. Position and reserve aren't part of that mutation: recovery changes neither, so the system doesn't need mutable access to them. Use the ordering pattern you've already met in the action systems: collect entity handles together with stable IDs, sort the pairs, then visit the actors through the query. Recoveries don't compete for a shared food store, but their event order still matters once a bounded journal begins discarding old entries. A stable processing order keeps that evidence reproducible. Before applying recovery, check whether this actor can perform a rest action now. Dead grazers, foragers, children before their first eligible tick and actors that already rested this tick must all be skipped. For an eligible resting actor, the actual recovery is the smaller of its current fatigue and the policy's recovery amount. Subtract that amount, then reduce a positive commitment without allowing it to underflow. Notice what happens when fatigue is already zero. Recovery contributes zero points, but the actor may still be completing an owed action. It must therefore spend that commitment and record a Rested event. If you skip the whole action when recovery is zero, a fast-recovering grazer can remain committed forever. Prepare the counter additions before changing the actor, including the eviction counter if recording this action displaces an old event. This keeps state and evidence together without making a full journal prevent recovery. If you're listening, this is a useful place to pause and write the system. Narration follows the reasoning, while the code and hidden answers remain available to read. Compare your access choices with the signature hint before consulting the complete module. System hint 1: a typed signature // Parameters for execute; write the complete function body. clock: Res<Clock>, mut actors: Query<(Entity, &Identity, &Grazer, &mut MobileActor)>, state: Option<ResMut<RestState>>, Option<ResMut<RestState>> permits the shared mobile schedule to run when rest is disabled. Return immediately when the resource is absent. An enabled world installs matching actor state; the internal expectation checks that installation invariant. System hint 2: guard both kinds of repetition last_rest_tick prevents duplicate recovery and countdown spending. last_transition_tick belongs to the decision system and prevents repeated activity transitions. A wake decision must also reject an actor that already rested this tick, so a second late decision cannot grant travel after recovery. Complete activity systems and accounting answer The complete systems module contains both decide and execute . The supporting module checks counter additions, including history eviction arithmetic, before commitment. Compare your guard placement as carefully as the arithmetic: a correct subtraction in an ineligible phase still implements the wrong behavior. Put rest where it can affect the next action The new decision must run early enough to stop an otherwise valid journey. Install it before observation, then keep observation, choice, travel, rest execution, contact and meals in that order. Upkeep and growth have already happened; starvation and birth resolution follow the actions. The complete schedule shows how this fits around the existing deferred boundaries. Even a single-threaded schedule needs these dependencies, because a different order would describe a different rule. Upkeep remains a cost for every eligible living grazer, including one that is resting beside food. Rest blocks travel, feeding and reproduction, and this policy has no hunger override. A grazer can therefore starve while its fatigue is recovering. That's an uncomfortable consequence of the chosen behavior, but it gives us a reason to investigate the policy rather than quietly crediting reserve during recovery. Movement also needs to respect the available fatigue capacity. At fatigue nine, with a maximum of ten and a cost of two points per cell, there isn't room for even one whole step. Accepting the step and clipping its fatigue charge afterward would make position, energy payment and effort disagree about what happened. Extend the movement plan to limit accepted cells before committing any of those changes; the complete movement module shows how the two accounting resources are prepared together. Crossing the rest threshold during travel doesn't undo that travel or start a second decision. The current foraging action may still finish with a meal at valid contact, and the next tick's decision will see the new fatigue. The same separation works in the other direction: completing recovery doesn't grant an extra foraging action later in the same tick. Each tick follows the activity chosen for it. Prediction answer: could a stationary grazer rest forever? If a forager never travels, its fatigue remains zero under this effort rule. It does not enter rest just because ticks pass. Once an actor is resting, it may execute extra recovery actions after its minimum reaches zero if fatigue remains above the exit threshold. These are different reasons for staying in the current activity. Make the test distinguish recovery from permission to leave Our ordinary journey demonstrates a pause, but it can't tell us whether the minimum commitment works. Recovering from six points to two already takes two actions, so an implementation that ignores the countdown could produce the same trace. To expose that shortcut, change only recovery to six. The first rest action now removes all fatigue, leaving the commitment as the only reason to stay for another tick. Create tests/rest_investigation.rs beside your existing tests and write this case before opening the answer. Step the real CourseWorld and compare the base, mobile and rest reports at ticks three through six. You're looking for a specific distinction: tick five must complete the second rest action even though it recovers zero points, and tick six must begin a fresh observation before movement resumes. Include a repeated report read along the way to check that inspecting the countdown doesn't spend it. The worked file also keeps a matched two-versus-three-action comparison. That second test checks whether an extra committed action delays the same journey; we'll return to its consequences when comparing the full meadow below. Investigation hint 1: a counterexample to early waking After tick four, expect zero fatigue and one action owed. Tick five must remain at cell three, spend one upkeep unit, recover zero points, and complete the second action. A test checking only fatigue would accept an early wake. Investigation hint 2: a counterexample to stale continuation The target should be absent during rest. At tick six, expect a new observation from cell three stamped tick six, a newly selected patch, and paid travel to cell four. The old tick-three observation cannot authorize that step. Complete investigation file: tests/rest_investigation.rs Place this complete file beside your existing integration tests. It requires your continuing project's moss_course_ecosystem crate. Run the exact Cargo command following the answer; the resting-stage check also runs this file with your retained tests. use moss_course_ecosystem::{Activity, Cell, CourseWorld, MobileScenario, RestPolicy}; fn policy(minimum_rest_ticks: u32, recovery_points_per_tick: u32) -> RestPolicy { RestPolicy { maximum_fatigue_points: 10, effort_points_per_cell: 2, enter_at_points: 6, exit_at_points: 2, minimum_rest_ticks, recovery_points_per_tick, history_limit: 128, } } #[test] fn fast_recovery_does_not_cancel_the_second_committed_action() { let scenario = MobileScenario::resting_journey().with_rest(policy(2, 6)); let mut world = CourseWorld::new_mobile(scenario).unwrap(); for _ in 0..3 { world.step(); } let third = world.rest_snapshot().unwrap(); assert_eq!(third.grazers[0].fatigue_points, 6); assert_eq!(third.grazers[0].activity, Activity::Foraging); assert!(world.mobile_snapshot().unwrap().grazers[0].target.is_some()); world.step(); let fourth = world.rest_snapshot().unwrap(); let fourth_mobile = world.mobile_snapshot().unwrap(); assert_eq!((fourth.tick, fourth.grazers[0].fatigue_points), (4, 0)); assert_eq!(fourth.grazers[0].activity, Activity::Resting { remaining_ticks: 1 }); assert_eq!((fourth.ledger.rest_actions, fourth.ledger.recovered_points), (1, 6)); assert_eq!(fourth_mobile.grazers[0].cell, Cell { x: 3, y: 0 }); assert!(fourth_mobile.grazers[0].target.is_none()); assert_eq!(fourth_mobile.base.grazers[0].reserve_units, 13); assert_eq!((fourth_mobile.ledger.travel_cells, fourth_mobile.base.ledger.eaten_units), (0, 0)); assert_eq!(fourth_mobile.base.ledger.maintenance_units, 1); assert_eq!(world.rest_snapshot().unwrap(), fourth); assert_eq!(world.mobile_snapshot().unwrap(), fourth_mobile); world.step(); let fifth = world.rest_snapshot().unwrap(); let fifth_mobile = world.mobile_snapshot().unwrap(); assert_eq!(fifth.grazers[0].activity, Activity::Resting { remaining_ticks: 0 }); assert_eq!((fifth.grazers[0].fatigue_points, fifth.ledger.recovered_points), (0, 0)); assert_eq!((fifth_mobile.ledger.travel_cells, fifth_mobile.base.ledger.eaten_units), (0, 0)); world.step(); let sixth = world.rest_snapshot().unwrap(); let sixth_mobile = world.mobile_snapshot().unwrap();
