assert_eq!(sixth_mobile.grazers[0].cell, Cell { x: 4, y: 0 }); assert_eq!(sixth_mobile.base.grazers[0].reserve_units, 10); } #[test] fn two_and_three_actions_change_arrival_and_later_opportunities() { let mut two = CourseWorld::new_mobile( MobileScenario::resting_journey().with_rest(policy(2, 2)), ).unwrap(); let mut three = CourseWorld::new_mobile( MobileScenario::resting_journey().with_rest(policy(3, 2)), ).unwrap(); for _ in 0..6 { two.step(); three.step(); } let two_mobile = two.mobile_snapshot().unwrap(); let three_mobile = three.mobile_snapshot().unwrap(); assert_eq!((two_mobile.tick, three_mobile.tick), (6, 6)); assert_eq!((two_mobile.grazers[0].cell.x, two_mobile.base.grazers[0].reserve_units), (4, 10)); assert_eq!((three_mobile.grazers[0].cell.x, three_mobile.base.grazers[0].reserve_units), (3, 11)); assert_eq!(two.rest_snapshot().unwrap().grazers[0].activity, Activity::Foraging); assert_eq!(three.rest_snapshot().unwrap().grazers[0].activity, Activity::Resting { remaining_ticks: 0 }); assert_eq!(three_mobile.base.ledger.eaten_units, 2); assert_eq!(two.rest_snapshot().unwrap().grazers[0].activity, Activity::Resting { remaining_ticks: 1 }); assert_eq!(three.rest_snapshot().unwrap().grazers[0].activity, Activity::Foraging); two.step(); three.step(); assert_eq!(two.snapshot().grazers[0].reserve_units, 8); assert_eq!(three.snapshot().grazers[0].reserve_units, 10); } cargo +1.93.1 test --offline --locked --manifest-path work/fieldwork/Cargo.toml --test rest_investigation Run both investigations and use the first differing observation to locate the problem. Travel on tick five suggests that waking ignores the commitment; a countdown that gets stuck at zero fatigue suggests that the action was skipped when there was nothing left to recover. If reserve rises while resting, recovery has probably become entangled with energy accounting. The answer's separate assertions let you distinguish those failures instead of treating the final position as the only evidence. Carry the rule into births and retained observations A newborn needs a sensible rest state even though it can't act yet. Install it with zero fatigue, Foraging , no rest markers, and the same empty target and observation used in the mobile checkpoint. Its first eligible tick remains the tick after birth. The normal rest phases occur before births, but explicit eligibility checks also protect this rule if you later add a phase or rearrange a schedule. The parents need an additional check too. Reproduction is available only while foraging, so current activity belongs alongside maturity, reserve, cooldown, contact and location in the birth validation. Check it before either parent pays for the child. The birth integration and mobile installation and contact show how these guards extend the earlier transaction without changing its meaning. To inspect these interactions, the rest report owns readings and keeps a separate bounded journal of entry, waking, travel effort and rest actions. Join a rest reading to its mobile reading by stable ID, within the same run and tick. Be careful when comparing a lifetime total with the current roster: fatigue belonging to an animal that has died no longer appears in its living row. The current fatigue sum therefore can't explain every point of effort accumulated during the run. History has a similar limit. A call to rest_actions_between(first, last) returns None when the journal can't cover that interval; a known interval with no actions returns zero. An explanation that connects rest, travel, food and births needs a period covered by all four journals. The history module makes that boundary explicit, while lifetime counters continue to retain totals after individual events have been evicted. Does a longer rest help this meadow? Return recovery to two and compare minimum commitments of two and three actions. This choice of comparison is deliberate. A one-action minimum and a two-action minimum would both take two actions to reduce fatigue from six to two, so the shorter commitment wouldn't actually change behavior. To learn about a constraint, we need a case in which that constraint can affect what the grazer does. In the short journey, the difference appears at tick six. The two-action grazer can move to cell four, while the three-action grazer must finish resting at cell three. The latter has spent less on travel so far, but it will also arrive at food later. Those consequences pull in different directions, so a larger reserve at one intermediate tick wouldn't by itself tell us which policy supports the longer run. Choose a horizon and make a note of what you expect to change: arrival time, meals, travel payments, rest actions, births or the living census. Keep starting reserves, placement, sensing, supply and birth rules identical between the two policies, then record both outcomes, including extinction. For the full meadow, retain the configuration and journal coverage with each result, as in the matched-experiment lesson . Repeating the same deterministic run checks reproducibility; changing a matched scenario asks a new question about the policy. Comparison reasoning An extra rest action can remove more fatigue, delay a meal, and change later contact or birth opportunities. Those effects can oppose one another. The same final reserve can conceal different activity and therefore different next-tick possibilities. State the measured horizon and rule set rather than calling one policy better for the ecosystem. The complete native example runs the recovery variations from our short journey and then follows the meadow for 120 ticks under each minimum. Its starting conditions are declared in the scenario fixtures . Save it as examples/resting.rs in your project and run: cargo +1.93.1 run --offline --locked --manifest-path work/fieldwork/Cargo.toml --example resting Observed native meadow at tick 120; only minimum rest actions differ Minimum Living Births / starvations Travel cells / rest actions Actual growth / upkeep / birth cost 2 0 7 / 11 36 / 21 98 / 108 / 14 3 1 10 / 13 71 / 53 308 / 258 / 20 In this authored meadow, the two-action population is extinct by tick forty, while the three-action population still has grazer one at tick 120. The longer pause has changed a whole chain of opportunities, so treat this as a result to explain under these inputs, rather than a generally superior rest policy. Even admitted growth differs: full patches reject excess growth, whereas feeding makes room for more. Equal configured supply doesn't guarantee equal energy entering the world. Bring your saved implementation into the browser Once your investigation passes, run the resting-stage check and compile the saved project for the browser. The stage check keeps your tests and adds the earlier course contracts alongside the new rest cases, so a correct pause must still coexist with correct travel, meals and births. python3 learning/scripts/fieldwork.py check --project work/fieldwork --stage resting python3 learning/scripts/fieldwork_preview.py --project work/fieldwork --resting python3 learning/scripts/build.py Start with the interrupted journey and inspect activity, fatigue, reserve and position at the same completed tick. Then select fast recovery and start a new run. You should be able to point to the moment when fatigue is zero but another rest action is still owed. Selecting a different animal or pausing to read leaves the simulation tick unchanged; an animal rests only when the Rust simulation executes that action. The source label identifies the compiled project being observed. Your native tests establish behavior in its Rust schedule, while this view lets you check how the compiled reports appear and how the controls operate. The checkpoint notes describe the policies and verification in more detail. Recovery and permission to leave have separate evidence We can now account for the grazer that stopped short of food. Its earlier steps accumulated enough fatigue to trigger a commitment, and the next two actions fulfilled that commitment while upkeep continued. Only a later decision reopened the journey. Keep the fast-recovery test as you change the policy: it captures the moment when being recovered and being free to leave become two different things. In the hunting checkpoint , a grazer's journey can end permanently. We'll make one capture change its eligibility immediately, then follow the consequences for another hunter, a later meal and a possible birth in this same world.

title: One capture changes the rest of the tick
summary: Course guide
text: Two hunters arrive beside the same grazer. Each has seen a possible meal, but there is only one animal to consume. A successful capture has to feed one hunter, disappoint the other, and prevent the grazer from taking its next action. Carry one capture through the rest of the tick You'll design the full capture transaction and its ECS adapter in the continuing project, bringing two mutable bodies together only after the proposed outcome has passed its checks. We'll use a small contention scene to test both acceptance and the lost actions afterward, then compare rest policies with and without hunters in the meadow. By the end, you should be able to follow a capture from earlier local observation through immediate eligibility changes, later meals and births, and the budget shared by both kinds of animal. Continuing course project: the complete tests and native traces below have been verified against the frozen hunting checkpoint. Its biological policy is an authored model, not a calibrated account of predation, and it does not activate hunting in live Moss. Give the hunter a consequence in the existing world In the previous guide , fatigue interrupted a grazer's journey and delayed its next meal. The grazer remained in the world, so it could recover and try again. Capture introduces a different interruption: this individual will never return to its destination. Its reserve will support another animal, but it will no longer deplete a patch or contribute to a birth. Those missing actions change the opportunities available to the survivors, which is why hunting belongs in the same world as movement, meals, and births. Continue your saved work/fieldwork project and retain its earlier tests. Your main task is to design the whole capture transaction and the ECS system that applies it. We'll first work through a small encounter where every unit is easy to account for, then decide how to represent its participants and obtain the two mutable borrows. Once that encounter is tested, the longer meadow run will show how the same rule changes population outcomes. Working files and complete answers The review-only change map shows the extension from resting, and the complete hunting checkpoint provides all worked files. Open them beside your own project when you want to compare an implementation. The diff is a map for deliberate edits, not a promise that it will apply over your changes; replacing your saved directory would also discard the investigations you have accumulated. Follow one capture before implementing it For the small encounter, put grazers one and two beside a patch containing ten biomass units, with hunters 100 and 101 on that same cell. Each grazer starts with five reserve units and each hunter with four. Everybody pays one upkeep unit before hunting, so the capture phase begins with four in each grazer and three in each hunter. Both hunters choose grazer one; stable-ID order gives hunter 100 the first attempt. We will use these same participants when we write the integration test. Our capture rule transfers the prey's current reserve. Hunter 100 must first afford its one-unit attack cost, leaving two units, and then have room for all four prey units. Its capacity is eight, so the accepted result is six in the hunter and zero in grazer one. The combined stores have fallen by exactly the attack cost. Moving the four units from one animal to the other didn't create energy or spend it; the attack did. Now change only hunter 100's capacity to five. After the proposed payment it would hold two, but adding all four prey units would take it to six. We could invent a rule for partially consuming an animal, but that would introduce a new question about what remains alive or where the excess goes. For this checkpoint, the whole attempt is rejected. Hunter 100 therefore keeps its three units, grazer one keeps four, and hunter 101 can still make its own attempt. The word proposed matters here. If the function subtracts the attack cost before discovering the capacity failure, rejection has already changed the hunter. Work out affordability, the complete gain, and the final values before writing either body. The same reasoning applies to fatigue: when rest is enabled, the accepted attack effort must fit the hunter's remaining fatigue capacity. A rejected capture spends neither attack reserve nor effort, although any travel completed earlier in the tick has already been paid for. Write this acceptance contract in your own words before opening the hints. Include what must be true about the participants as well as their budgets: a living, active hunter must target a distinct living grazer, both must be eligible this tick, the target must come from the current tick’s observation, and their current cells must match. The amount transferred comes from that current grazer, because the reserve recorded in an earlier observation may have changed during travel. Planning hint: separate proposed values from committed values First check that the hunter can pay. Then calculate its reserve after payment, check that the entire prey reserve fits, and calculate the accepted final reserve. Check fatigue capacity and every counter addition before applying those values, including the eviction counter if recording the event will displace an old entry. A full bounded journal evicts its oldest event; fullness alone must not reject a capture. You can keep these results in a small plan or local variables; the important boundary is that rejection occurs before mutation. Planning hint: a future meal cannot fund this attack A hunter holding zero cannot pay a one-unit attack cost even when its prey holds twenty. Adding the prey's reserve before testing affordability would let the hunter borrow from an outcome that hasn't been accepted. Check the starting reserve first, just as paid travel could not borrow against the patch at its destination. Using reserve as the edible amount keeps this first model small: there is no second animal biomass store to maintain. It also has a deliberate consequence. A grazer at zero reserve supplies no modeled food, so hunters ignore it even though a later patch meal might still rescue it. This is a rule of the game we're constructing, not a claim about an animal's physical mass. Give both participants one authoritative body The calculation uses the same kinds of values on both sides: reserve, capacity, life, and action eligibility. Those values currently live inside the private grazer component alongside its meal request and patch contact. A hunter needs the first group but has no use for the second. This is a concrete reason to split the component now; before hunters existed, the extra separation would have had much less work to do. A private Body component can own the shared state while a smaller grazer component retains feeding settings. A hunter gets that same kind of body plus its attack settings, all attached to one entity. Upkeep can then operate on bodies, whereas patch feeding still requires the grazer role. There is only one reserve for each animal: the capture, maintenance, and feeding systems all borrow that value instead of synchronizing copies in separate animal tables. Before editing, follow the old reserve field through the code and decide which queries need body access and which also need a role. Reproduction needs two adult grazers with eligible bodies; having enough reserve alone doesn't make a hunter a parent. The old public seeds and readings can stay as they are, with their reserve fields projecting the body and their meal fields projecting the grazer component. Keeping those adapters stable lets your earlier tests continue to describe the same behavior while the private representation changes. Representation hint: make the terminal cause unambiguous The reference body has a terminal enum with alive, starved, and captured states; capture carries the hunter's stable ID. This gives later systems one place to check eligibility and prevents a combination such as “captured and starved.” The public grazer reading can still project its existing alive/dead value while the interaction history retains the more specific cause. Complete body and projection answer Compare the component definitions with the world and public projections . Then follow the same body through upkeep and starvation , patch feeding , and birth payment . These files show the whole refactor, including the queries that preserve role-specific behavior. With the representation chosen, hunters can enter through authored configuration, just as grazers did. MobileScenario::with_hunters(HuntConfig::new(seeds)) supplies their identities, budgets, upkeep, positions, motion, attack payment, and attack effort. Validate the complete specification before replacing a world, especially IDs shared across animals and patches. The child allocator must also see hunter IDs so a later birth cannot reuse one. Configuration, reset, and disabled-mode answer The configuration module rejects duplicate IDs, invalid bounds or budgets, and invalid attack settings before installation. A failed reset preserves both the current world and the specification used by a later ordinary reset. hunt_snapshot() returns None when hunting is disabled; an enabled report with no living hunters still retains its configuration and lifetime evidence. An empty living table therefore does not imply disabled rules. Carry an observation as far as it can legitimately go Our same-cell encounter makes contact easy to see, but the meadow's animals move. A hunter may observe a grazer at one cell and arrive there after the grazer has left. To preserve that distinction, collect local prey readings before any animal travels, then let the selector work with those owned readings. It receives the identity, cell, and reserve that were visible at that moment; it doesn't keep a reference that silently turns into current global information. The selection policy follows your patch selector: continue toward the current prey while it remains eligible in the new local view, otherwise choose the nearest eligible grazer with stable ID breaking a distance tie. Positive reserve and current life are part of observation eligibility. The resulting target records an observed cell and tick, which gives travel a specific destination without promising that a capture will succeed there. At the capture phase, first require the target’s observed tick to match the current tick. An old retained target cannot regain permission merely because the animals happen to meet again. Current positions then answer a narrower question: are these two animals actually together? If the prey moved away, that answer is no. Looking up its new cell may be convenient for the programmer, but using it as a replacement destination would give the hunter information it never observed. It must wait for a later observation and choice, just as a grazer whose selected patch was emptied couldn't consume from another patch inside the same meal attempt. Prediction: what should a failed pursuit cost? The completed route still costs its accepted travel reserve and effort. The failed capture costs no attack reserve and adds no capture effort, because those belong to an accepted action that never occurred. The next executed observation phase can reveal where the prey went. Complete perception and movement answer Local prey observation and choice produce the owned view, and hunter movement follows its observed destination. Compare them with your existing target policy : the opportunity is now an animal, but the boundary between an intention and a permitted action remains useful. Rest supplies another reason a pursuit can end. A resting hunter cancels its target and cannot travel or attack, while a resting grazer remains possible prey. We're keeping the existing commitment and recovery rules rather than adding a hunger override. Hunters can die of starvation under those rules; in this checkpoint they are authored, nonreproducing individuals, and grazers have no fleeing behavior. Turn the plan into an ECS operation We now know what information the capture needs and which values it changes. The adapter has to bring the two bodies together without confusing stable identity with storage location. Build an ID-to-entity lookup from the current query, visit hunters in stable-ID order, and resolve each hunter's selected prey through that lookup. The entity handles are useful for these component accesses; the event you retain afterward should use the application IDs and run identity that remain meaningful after cleanup. There are two borrowing moments in each attempt. During planning, shared access is enough to inspect life, roles, cells, and budgets and calculate the proposed result. During commitment, both bodies need mutable access because the hunter receives reserve while the prey loses it. Copying the small calculated values into locals lets the planning borrows end before requesting those two writable query items. You aren't moving the bodies out of the world or constructing replacements; you are changing the same values that later systems will read. The reference uses one query containing bodies, positions, mobile actor state, and optional role components. Its get calls provide shared views while it plans; get_many_mut([hunter_entity, prey_entity]) then obtains the two distinct items together. The Bevy ECS 0.18.1 documentation explains that missing entities, duplicate entities, or mismatched components return an error. Passing that access check doesn't establish contact or affordability, so the biological checks still belong in your plan. Implement the whole adapter now, including its system parameters, ordering, rejection paths, and commit. If you're listening, this is a useful place to pause narration and work with the code; the disclosures below contain hints and complete files that audio skips. Start with the first hunter's accepted path, then trace what the second hunter will read after it. Adapter hint: what can be collected in advance? You can collect the stable order and entity lookup before resolving claims. Do not treat copied initial reserves or eligibility as authority for every claim, though: the first accepted capture changes those values. Each later attempt needs the current bodies. Likewise, two separate mutable queries need genuinely disjoint access filters; different role names alone do not prove an entity cannot contain both components. Adapter hint: a rejected first attempt is still an opportunity for the second hunter In the capacity-five variant, hunter 100 is first but cannot fit the whole transfer. Leave both bodies and attack accounting unchanged, then let hunter 101 inspect the same current prey. Stable ordering determines who tries first, not who must win. Complete transaction and adapter answer The capture module contains planning and commitment. Its supporting state and report module and bounded history show how arithmetic is checked before biological mutation, including the count of evicted history entries. The bounded journal may discard an old entry to retain a new one; it is arithmetic overflow, not a full journal, that must prevent a partially recorded transaction. Compare the whole path rather than only the final addition and subtraction. Let the capture change the rest of the tick A captured grazer is more than a food store. Earlier in the tick it may have travelled toward a patch, and later it would normally eat there or contribute to a birth. Removing it at the end of the tick is therefore too late to decide which of those actions are still allowed. The capture needs to change its body's eligibility at the same moment that reserve changes hands, so the second hunter and the later grazer systems all encounter the same result. That is the sequence shown below. Both hunters observe the prey, but only the first accepted claim transfers its reserve and marks it captured. The second hunter then encounters a terminal body, as do the later meal and birth systems. Cleanup eventually removes the entity, but permission to use it has already changed. An inspector could still find its components between commitment and cleanup without that presence making another action legitimate. One capture closes every later use of the prey Two hunters observe one prey. The first accepted transaction pays its attack cost, transfers the prey reserve, and immediately marks the prey captured. The second hunter receives no reward. Later feeding and birth resolution reject the captured prey before deferred cleanup removes it. Observe one available prey Two intentions · no reservation Commit one funded capture Cost paid · reserve transferred Prey immediately terminal Second hunter: claim rejected No second gain · no attack payment Captured prey: later actions rejected No patch meal · no funded birth Deferred structural cleanup The terminal state is part of the accepted transaction. Despawning later is cleanup, not the exclusivity mechanism. A queued despawn cannot supply this guarantee by itself because commands may not yet have been applied when the next claimant runs. Queuing a dead marker leaves the same timing problem if that marker is the only authority. Write the terminal state immediately, as in the isolated predation lesson , and make every later action respect it. Starvation must do so too: setting a captured body's reserve to zero must not give the same death a second cause. The schedule makes these consequences visible by placing hunting after travel and rest, but before grazer meals, starvation, and births. Completed travel remains part of the tick even if the traveller is subsequently captured; a later meal does not. Births still occur after hunting and give each child first eligibility on the following tick. The body refactor must preserve that timing while initializing the child's funded reserve and inherited upkeep separately from its empty target, fresh fatigue, and absent action markers. There is one more guard on the hunter itself: stamp a successful capture with its executed tick. Immediate prey death prevents other hunters from consuming that prey, while the hunter's stamp prevents a repeated invocation from awarding it another capture against a different prey in the same tick. A failed claim does not set that stamp because no action has been accepted. Build a test where the forbidden action could happen The small encounter gives us a way to check all of these effects through the public world. Add tests/hunt_investigation.rs to your continuing project and build the fixture described at the start. Grazer two is there for a reason: without hunters, the two grazers can both eat and then fund a birth. If we used only one grazer, a zero birth count after capture would tell us nothing about terminal eligibility, because a two-parent birth was impossible from the beginning. Run that no-hunter control first and require the birth to happen. Then run the same grazer and patch setup with the two hunters. Both choose grazer one, hunter 100 finishes with six reserve, and hunter 101 remains at three. Grazer two eats two units and finishes with six, leaving eight in the patch, while no birth occurs. The survivor's meal matters as much as the missing prey meal: disabling all feeding whenever a hunt occurs would otherwise produce a misleadingly quiet result. Write your assertions before opening the full file. Think about which plausible wrong implementation each one excludes. Two credited hunters reveal stale eligibility; a missing survivor meal reveals an overbroad exclusion; a birth after capture reveals that parental validation used state that was no longer current. The second test changes the first hunter's capacity to five, so a rejection must leave the prey available for hunter 101. Investigation hint: check the participants as well as the totals Require one capture record naming hunter 100 and prey one in the first case. Check both hunter reserves, the surviving grazer ID and reserve, the patch store, and the actual attack and transfer amounts. The total reserve could be right even if it was credited to the wrong actor. Check starvation separately so capture cannot be counted as a second terminal cause. Complete investigation file: tests/hunt_investigation.rs This full integration file belongs in your continuing project beside its earlier tests. It requires moss_course_ecosystem and exercises the public installed schedule. The second case gives the first hunter too little capacity and verifies that a rejected claim leaves the opportunity for its competitor. use moss_course_ecosystem::{ Cell, CourseWorld, Daylight, EventKind, FounderTrait, GrazerPlacement, GrazerSeed, GridBounds, HuntConfig, HuntEventKind, HunterSeed, MobileScenario, Motion, PatchPlacement, PatchSeed, PopulationConfig, RestPolicy, Scenario, SimId, SpatialConfig, UpkeepTrait, }; fn fixture(with_hunters: bool, first_hunter_capacity: u32) -> MobileScenario { let cell = Cell { x: 0, y: 0 }; let motion = Motion { sensing_radius: 0, max_cells_per_tick: 0, travel_units_per_cell: 1, }; let scenario = Scenario { daylight: Daylight::new(1, 0).unwrap(), grazers: [2, 1].into_iter().map(|id| GrazerSeed { id: SimId(id), reserve_units: 5, capacity_units: 8, maintenance_units_per_tick: 1, meal_units_per_tick: 2, feeding_site: None, }).collect(), patches: vec![PatchSeed { id: SimId(1000), biomass_units: 10, capacity_units: 10, growth_units_per_lit_tick: 0, }], history_limit: 128, }; let population = PopulationConfig { founders: [2, 1].into_iter().map(|id| FounderTrait { id: SimId(id), upkeep: UpkeepTrait::new(1).unwrap(), }).collect(), maturation_ticks: 2, cooldown_ticks: 3, contribution_units_per_parent: 2, birth_cost_units_per_parent: 1, child_capacity_units: 8, child_meal_units_per_tick: 2, max_living: 8, mutation_cycle: vec![0], history_limit: 128, }; let space = SpatialConfig { bounds: GridBounds { width_cells: 1, height_cells: 1 }, grazers: [2, 1].into_iter().map(|id| GrazerPlacement { id: SimId(id), cell, motion, }).collect(), patches: vec![PatchPlacement { id: SimId(1000), cell }], newborn_motion: motion, }; let rest = RestPolicy { maximum_fatigue_points: 10, effort_points_per_cell: 2, enter_at_points: 6, exit_at_points: 2, minimum_rest_ticks: 2, recovery_points_per_tick: 2, history_limit: 128, }; let initial = MobileScenario::new(scenario, population, space).with_rest(rest); if !with_hunters { return initial; } initial.with_hunters(HuntConfig::new([101, 100].into_iter().map(|id| HunterSeed { id: SimId(id), reserve_units: 4, capacity_units: if id == 100 { first_hunter_capacity } else { 8 }, maintenance_units_per_tick: 1, attack_units: 1, attack_effort_points: 2, cell, motion, }).collect())) } #[test] fn one_capture_cancels_the_preys_later_opportunities() { let mut control = CourseWorld::new_mobile(fixture(false, 8)).unwrap(); control.step(); let control_report = control.mobile_snapshot().unwrap(); assert_eq!(control_report.population.totals.births, 1); assert_eq!(control_report.base.grazers.len(), 3); assert_eq!(control_report.base.ledger.eaten_units, 4); assert_eq!(control_report.base.patches[0].biomass_units, 6); let mut world = CourseWorld::new_mobile(fixture(true, 8)).unwrap(); world.step(); let mobile = world.mobile_snapshot().unwrap(); let hunt = world.hunt_snapshot().unwrap(); assert_eq!((mobile.run, mobile.tick), (hunt.run, hunt.tick)); assert_eq!(hunt.tick, 1); assert_eq!((hunt.initial_hunters, hunt.living_hunters), (2, 2)); assert_eq!(hunt.hunters.iter().map(|h| (h.id, h.reserve_units)).collect::<Vec<_>>(), vec![(SimId(100), 6), (SimId(101), 3)]); Counting that transfer as another loss would make a correct capture appear to destroy energy. The same argument gives us the full tick equation below. Travel and birth add their own costs, and growth adds only the biomass actually accepted by the patches. Each quantity comes from an actual flow, because limited reserve can reduce upkeep payment, an affordable prefix can shorten travel, and a full patch can reject growth. Grazer upkeep belongs to the base ledger, while hunter upkeep and attack costs belong to the hunting report. A capture is a grazer exit but not a grazer starvation. The table keeps those responsibilities visible without requiring you to guess whether a familiar total now includes a new animal. Combine reports without counting a flow twice Report Relevant responsibility Base snapshot and ledger Grazer reserves, patch biomass, grazer upkeep, growth, meals, and grazer starvation. Population report Grazer stages, births, funding, birth dissipation, and lifetime grazer starvations. Mobile and rest reports Grazer positions, travel payment, fatigue, and rest outcomes. Living grazers plus lifetime grazer starvations plus captures must equal founders plus births. For hunters, living individuals plus hunter starvations equals the authored count because this policy has no hunter reproduction. Recording one capture as both a hunting success and a grazer exit is useful; adding those two descriptions together as separate deaths is not. Keep enough evidence to explain the count A count tells us how many captures occurred, but an individual story also needs the interaction records. Those records link hunter and prey through stable IDs and a run identity, while each bounded journal exposes the interval it can still describe completely. To connect travel, rest, feeding, birth, and capture, use the intersection of the relevant coverage intervals. A lifetime counter can remain known after early events have been evicted; it cannot reconstruct their order or participants. Return to the meadow with a question The same-cell test has isolated the transaction, so now we can let it interact with movement, supply, and rest. Use four runs of 120 executed ticks: minimum rest commitments two and three, each without hunters and with the declared pair. Adding hunters is a different intervention: each arrives with sixteen reserve units, so those runs begin with thirty-two additional stored units. They keep the first child-ID cursor the same when hunters are removed, so that comparison does not accidentally change an identity-dependent decision. The result gives us a specific interaction to investigate in the retained history, rather than a general claim that one rest policy is better. title: Give shelter a rule you can test
summary: Course guide
text: A hunter sees a grazer outside shelter. By the time the hunt resolves, the grazer has moved into a refuge in the hunter's own cell. The earlier observation was valid, and contact is real, but this capture should now fail. Build shelter, then challenge your explanation of its effect This capstone asks you to choose both a representation and a claim to investigate in your saved world. You'll write the whole membership system, connect its current answer to perception and capture, and design tests where contact or funding cannot conceal a broken protection rule. Then compare refuge placements with matched inputs in a native experiment. The outcome should be an implemented policy, evidence that distinguishes plausible mistakes, and a conclusion you can defend within the report's coverage limits—even if the meadow contradicts your prediction. Independent capstone, native extension. Continue the same saved project from the hunting guide , preserving your earlier systems and tests. Refuge is an authored game rule, separate from live Moss and NOW.md . The worked scenarios and exact investigation have been checked both in the reference and in a continuing saved project. Run your own tests and comparison to establish what your implementation does. Begin with a claim you could be wrong about So far, each continuing guide has given you a new interaction and a fairly specific question to pursue. This time you'll choose how to represent the feature and what you want to learn from it. Keep those jobs separate. First make a refuge obey an explicit contract in the existing world. Then decide whether a particular placement produces the outcome you predicted. A correct implementation may give an unwelcome experimental result, and that result can still teach you something. Before opening a module answer, write a short claim in your field note. For example: “Protecting the feeding patch will leave more grazers alive at tick 120 than protecting a cell away from food.” Explain the mechanism you expect, name an observation that would contradict it, and choose which individuals or events you would follow if the ending surprised you. You can choose another claim, but make it specific enough that the comparison can disagree with you. Keep the existing initial population, reserves, and comparison horizon the same across your treatments. A refuge introduces permission to avoid capture, not another energy store. If a protected run starts with more reserve, you would have changed two causes at once. You will also need more than the survivor count: protected grazers can still starve, compete for finite food, produce children, and encounter the living cap. A possible hypothesis and what would challenge it Protection at a feeding patch could preserve grazers that already reach food. It could also leave more consumers sharing that food, change births, or allow hunters to starve earlier. An equal or smaller final grazer census would contradict the predicts-more claim, but would not identify its cause. Retain capture and starvation totals, accepted food input, births, and at least one individual trace so those alternatives can be examined. Decide exactly what shelter promises For the worked extension, a refuge is a static authored cell. A grazer occupying that cell is protected: hunters omit it from their local prey observations and cannot capture it while it remains there. Hunters can enter the same cell, patches remain visible, and grazing can still occur. This is a change to observation and capture eligibility, rather than a wall or a new pathfinding problem. Protection is assessed at the current cell; crossing a refuge between assessment points does not protect a later capture at an unprotected destination. Protection leaves the other accounts alone. A sheltered animal still pays upkeep; resting still prevents meals and births under the rule you already implemented; travel still costs reserve. The feature supplies no recovery, food, or special destination preference. An animal reaches shelter only if its existing movement brings it there, which makes placement part of the experiment instead of quietly giving the grazer a new fleeing strategy. Now consider departure. A grazer can leave refuge after the hunters have observed the world. It is no longer protected, but that fact doesn't give a hunter an observation it never made. Keep the existing selected-target contract: another observation opportunity must discover the grazer before a hunt can name it. This creates the opposite test to the opening example. Arrival must withdraw permission from an old target; departure must not invent a new target. Keep these boundaries while choosing an implementation Refuges are optional. Disabled and enabled with no sites are different reported capabilities, although neither protects anyone. Sites have no occupancy cap, and this extension adds no random movement, fleeing, injury, refuge resource, or hunter reproduction. Keep the prior rest, funded birth, maturation, and inherited upkeep rules. These choices bound the feature you are transferring into the existing architecture. Choose the data before the system Sketch the public configuration and private per-grazer state before consulting the worked shapes. The configuration needs enough information to locate each static site and reject ambiguous placements. The private state needs to say whether a grazer's current cell belongs to a refuge. Decide which values are authored and which are derived, and what a caller would need in an owned report to understand the answer after the world changes. A useful distinction is between a site's identity and an animal's identity. A refuge may persist while many different grazers use it, so it shouldn't borrow a grazer's ID or enter the birth allocator. Likewise, membership should not duplicate the animal's reserve, activity, or terminal state. Those already belong to the shared body and activity components. Your new data should describe the new relationship, leaving those existing owners authoritative. Write the rejection cases beside the constructor. What should happen if two sites use one ID, if two IDs name the same cell, or if a site lies outside the grid? What does an empty list mean? Then apply the same questions to reset: a rejected new configuration must leave both the current world and the policy used by its next ordinary reset intact. Validation has to finish before replacement begins. Representation hint: a static site and a current membership answer different questions The worked design gives sites a small separate ID type and stores a cell for each. A grazer's private membership stores an optional site ID plus the tick when that cell was assessed. An owned public row includes the grazer ID and current cell as well, so the caller can interpret that assessment. The row is a current reading, not a history of visits. Worked public adapter contract The worked interface uses RefugeId , RefugeSeed { id, cell } , and RefugeConfig::new , added through MobileScenario::with_refuges . CourseWorld::refuge_snapshot() returns None when disabled and an owned report when enabled. Positive unique site IDs, unique cells, and in-bounds placements are validated together. Site and animal IDs have separate types and namespaces, so RefugeId(1) can coexist with SimId(1) without using the child allocator. Your private component names and layout can differ while this public adapter lets the common experiments and course checks ask the same questions. Write the whole membership system Write the complete ECS system now: its parameters, query membership, per-grazer lookup, state update, and assessment time. Start with the access it needs. Read site configuration, the clock, and the positions of grazer entities; change only their membership. Reserve and life already have authoritative owners, but locating a cell doesn't require borrowing those fields. Choose each access for the question this system answers rather than requesting every component associated with an animal. The important branch is the one that finds no refuge. Suppose the previous assessment put a grazer in site seven, then travel moves it elsewhere. Leaving its old value alone would turn a cached observation into permanent protection. Every refresh must write the answer for the current cell, including None outside shelter. Treating absence as an instruction to skip the update would preserve the very state that has become stale. Decide how the system finds a site. A linear scan can be enough for a small authored list; a cell-keyed lookup can express the uniqueness established by validation. Either way, the lookup must use current grid cells, not renderer coordinates or the cell from an earlier prey observation. If you keep derived membership, be able to name every boundary at which it can become stale. System hint: inspect the permissions before writing the loop Collect configuration access, clock access, and the grazer query on paper first. Read the configuration, clock, and positions through shared access, and request mutable access only for membership. The report projection can read identities separately; this spatial update does not need them. A private helper can answer which site contains a cell, but the exercise also requires the typed adapter that visits the intended entities and writes the result. Complete system answer The complete refuge module defines its private membership, validated site lookup, typed refresh system, and owned report together. Its query reads Position , mutates RefugeMembership , and uses With<Grazer> for membership. The optional refuge resource keeps the existing disabled mode available. Each visited component receives a complete new answer from the current cell and clock, including None outside a site. Initial installation and newborn setup use that same lookup. If you're listening, pause to write the full system and compare its access declaration with the module answer when you need help. Resume once you can explain why it clears departed membership. Use the same lookup contract when installing the initial population and placing a child. A newborn can be visible in a completed report before its first eligible action tick. Its position and membership should already describe where it is; protection must not be delayed merely because upkeep and hunting still exclude it on its birth tick. This is another reason not to infer membership from whether an animal happened to act. Refresh where the answer can change The opening encounter tells us where to place the system. First assess membership before hunter perception so a protected grazer is absent from the local prey list. Then let the existing movement systems execute. Assess membership again before capture, because the travel just performed may have moved a selected grazer into shelter or an unobserved one out of it. These two assessments answer the same spatial question at different moments. Read the diagram from top to bottom. The first assessment constrains what the hunter may observe. Travel changes positions. The second assessment constrains what the selected interaction may do now. Capture must use that current answer while keeping the target from the earlier observation. Neither assessment executes a meal or adds a cost. Refuge membership across observation and travel Assess current grazer membership, then observe locally and choose targets. Travel changes cells. Assess membership again before the selected capture. A target observed outside shelter can enter refuge and reject capture; an unseen grazer leaving shelter needs a later observation. Assess membership Observe and choose Travel Assess membership again Revalidate selected capture Observation supplies a target. Current protection can reject it. Membership is current only relative to a known assessment boundary. A stored target does not preserve an earlier permission. Connect both consumers of membership deliberately. Filtering the prey observation prevents a hidden grazer from becoming a target, but cannot handle the arrival case by itself. Checking only the capture prevents a protected kill, but would still let hunters select and pursue prey the observation policy says they cannot see. Those are separate promises, so give each an assertion that can fail independently. Ordering hint: test the two uses of membership A fixture starting in refuge can expose a missing perception filter; a fixture entering refuge during travel can expose missing current revalidation. Inspect the copied prey list and its observation tick as well as the final membership. These tests distinguish two uses of the state, rather than proving that removing either refresh call must change a normal run. With static sites, initial and newborn setup already assign membership, and the prior post-travel assessment can leave it current for the next observation. Deleting only the pre-observation refresh may therefore leave these public outcomes unchanged. That refresh explicitly reassesses the state at the declared boundary, while these two fixtures establish the filtering and capture contracts. Choose a test that exposes the mistake Once the feature is connected, switch from construction to investigation. Choose one claim from your field note and design a public integration test around it before opening the worked file. Use CourseWorld and owned reports, keeping private components behind their adapter. Write down the inputs that make the assertion discriminating: what other rejection might make a broken refuge appear to work? For the opening arrival case, an ordinary moving hunter can be a poor test. It travels toward the prey's observed old cell while the grazer moves somewhere new, so they may fail contact even if protection is broken. A stationary hunter already at the grazer's destination removes that alternative explanation. Now both are in the same cell when capture resolves, and refuge membership is the reason the treatment should differ. The worked fixture uses a two-by-one grid. Grazer 1 begins at cell zero with reserve six, capacity eight, upkeep one, and a two-unit meal request. It can sense and move one cell, paying one reserve unit for that move. Patch 1000 at cell one holds five units, with no growth. Hunter 100 waits at cell one with reserve four, capacity ten, upkeep one, and attack cost one. It can sense the grazer but has speed zero. There is one founder and no partner; rest is disabled for this short investigation. First predict the run without a refuge. After upkeep and travel, the grazer has four reserve units. The hunter has three after upkeep, enough to pay its attack before receiving the prey. Then put a refuge at cell one while keeping every other input the same. Follow not only the capture count but also the grazer's later meal, patch biomass, hunter reserve, and each account's actual cost. Worked arrival reasoning and observed native result The native reference confirms the predicted contrast. Without protection, the hunter pays one and receives four, ending at six. The captured grazer gets no meal, so patch biomass stays five. With protection, the hunter remains at three with no attack charge; the grazer eats two, finishes at six, and leaves three biomass. Both runs begin with fifteen stored units. Ending stores plus the appropriate upkeep, travel, and attack costs should account for those same fifteen units. For the companion test, move the refuge to cell zero. The grazer begins hidden, then leaves shelter and reaches the stationary hunter during tick one. It should still get its meal because the hunter has no selected prey for that action. A fresh tick-two observation can change that. Check the absence of a target on the departure tick as well as the later capture; merely checking current unprotected membership would miss the perception boundary. Worked departure reasoning and observed native result The native reference finishes tick one with the grazer at six and the hunter at three, without a capture. Tick-two upkeep leaves five and two. Fresh observation selects the grazer, allowing a funded one-unit attack and five-unit transfer that brings the hunter to six. The investigation asserts the observation and capture ticks alongside these balances, rather than inferring when perception occurred from the final reserve. If you're listening, pause here to construct your fixture and write the test before reading the complete answer. The answer can be a comparison against your reasoning rather than the first source of the question. Keep the file beside your earlier hunting and rest investigations instead of replacing them. Complete public investigation file: tests/refuge_investigation.rs Save this complete file beside your earlier investigations. It checks the worked arrival and departure mechanisms through the public course API; your own hypothesis may need another fixture. The exact decoded reference block passed both native tests. Run it against your saved implementation to compare those reference expectations with your own systems. // Save as work/fieldwork/tests/refuge_investigation.rs in your continuing project. // From the Moss repository root: // cargo +1.93.1 test --offline --locked --manifest-path work/fieldwork/Cargo.toml --test refuge_investigation use moss_course_ecosystem::{ Cell, CourseWorld, Daylight, FounderTrait, GrazerPlacement, GrazerSeed, GridBounds, HuntConfig, HunterSeed, MobileScenario, Motion, PatchPlacement, PatchSeed, PopulationConfig, RefugeConfig, RefugeId, RefugeSeed, Scenario, SimId, SpatialConfig, UpkeepTrait, }; fn fixture(refuge_cell: Option<Cell>) -> MobileScenario { let start = Cell { x: 0, y: 0 }; let destination = Cell { x: 1, y: 0 }; let motion = Motion { sensing_radius: 1, max_cells_per_tick: 1, travel_units_per_cell: 1, }; let scenario = Scenario { daylight: Daylight::new(1, 0).unwrap(), grazers: vec![GrazerSeed { id: SimId(1), reserve_units: 6, capacity_units: 8, maintenance_units_per_tick: 1, meal_units_per_tick: 2, feeding_site: None, }], patches: vec![PatchSeed { id: SimId(1000), biomass_units: 5, capacity_units: 5, growth_units_per_lit_tick: 0, }], history_limit: 128, }; let population = PopulationConfig { founders: vec![FounderTrait { id: SimId(1), upkeep: UpkeepTrait::new(1).unwrap(), }], maturation_ticks: 2, cooldown_ticks: 3, contribution_units_per_parent: 2, birth_cost_units_per_parent: 1, child_capacity_units: 8, child_meal_units_per_tick: 2, max_living: 8, mutation_cycle: vec![0], history_limit: 128, }; let space = SpatialConfig { bounds: GridBounds { width_cells: 2, height_cells: 1 }, grazers: vec![GrazerPlacement { id: SimId(1), cell: start, motion }], patches: vec![PatchPlacement { id: SimId(1000), cell: destination }], newborn_motion: motion, }; let initial = MobileScenario::new(scenario, population, space) .with_hunters(HuntConfig::new(vec![HunterSeed { id: SimId(100), reserve_units: 4, capacity_units: 10, maintenance_units_per_tick: 1, attack_units: 1, attack_effort_points: 2, cell: destination, motion: Motion { max_cells_per_tick: 0, ..motion }, }])); match refuge_cell { None => initial, Some(cell) => initial.with_refuges(RefugeConfig::new(vec![RefugeSeed { id: RefugeId(7), cell, }])), } } #[test] fn entering_refuge_rejects_a_previously_observed_same_cell_capture() { let plain = fixture(None); let protected = fixture(Some(Cell { x: 1, y: 0 })); assert_eq!(plain.scenario(), protected.scenario()); assert_eq!(plain.population(), protected.population()); assert_eq!(plain.space(), protected.space()); assert_eq!(plain.hunters(), protected.hunters()); let mut control = CourseWorld::new_mobile(plain).unwrap(); control.step(); let control_mobile = control.mobile_snapshot().unwrap(); let control_hunt = control.hunt_snapshot().unwrap(); assert!(control.refuge_snapshot().is_none()); assert!(control_mobile.base.grazers.is_empty()); assert_eq!(control_mobile.base.patches[0].biomass_units, 5); assert_eq!(control_hunt.hunters[0].reserve_units, 6); assert_eq!((control_hunt.ledger.captures, control_hunt.ledger.attack_units, control_hunt.ledger.transferred_units), (1, 1, 4)); assert_eq!(control_mobile.base.ledger.eaten_units, 0); let mut world = CourseWorld::new_mobile(protected).unwrap();
